name: Carrie Brown
summary: Carrie Brown, known on the Bowery as "Old Shakespeare," was found strangled and mutilated in Room 31 of the East River Hotel in Manhattan on April 24, 1891. Ameer Ben Ali was convicted of second-degree murder that July, but Governor Benjamin Odell commuted his sentence in 1902 after new evidence cast doubt on the case. The man seen entering the hotel with Brown was never identified.
lastSeen: Night of April 23, 1891, checking into the East River Hotel, New York City, with an unidentified man

sources.title: Smithsonian Magazine - A Sensational Murder Case That Ended in a Wrongful Conviction
New England Historical Society - The Sad Story of Salem's Carrie Brown
Murder by Gaslight - Carrie Brown: Jack the Ripper in America, Part 2
Murder by Gaslight - The Rescue of Ameer Ben Ali
Wikipedia - Murder of Carrie Brown

narrative: Carrie Brown was a longtime resident of the Bowery district of Manhattan who was nicknamed "Shakespeare" or "Old Shakespeare," reportedly because she liked to quote the playwright. According to the New England Historical Society, she was born Caroline Montgomery in the early 1830s, married a man named Charles Brown, and lived for a time in Salem, Massachusetts, where she had children before moving to New York in the 1860s. Sources disagree about her exact age: the New England Historical Society describes her as 56 at her death, while Smithsonian Magazine gives her age as 60.

On the night of April 23, 1891, Brown took a room at the East River Hotel, a lodging house on the Manhattan waterfront, in the company of a man. According to Murder by Gaslight, the pair were entered in the register as "C. Nicolo and wife." The next morning, April 24, a hotel employee found her body in Room 31. Accounts agree that she had been strangled and that her body had been mutilated with a knife. The man who had accompanied her was gone, and so was the key to the room.

The killing came less than three years after the Whitechapel murders in London, and newspapers speculated that "Jack the Ripper" had come to New York. No evidence was ever found to support that idea. Within about 32 hours, according to Smithsonian Magazine, police arrested Ameer Ben Ali, an Algerian man known locally as "Frenchy," who had been staying in a room across the hall. The prosecution relied largely on testimony that a trail of blood led from Room 31 to his room.

Ben Ali's trial opened in late June 1891, and on July 3, 1891, the jury found him guilty of second-degree murder. He was sentenced to life imprisonment and sent to Sing Sing; Smithsonian Magazine reports that he was transferred in 1893 to the state asylum for insane criminals at Matteawan. He maintained that he was innocent.

Doubts about the verdict grew over the following decade. Journalist Jacob Riis, who had been at the scene, stated in an affidavit that he had seen no blood in the hallway. A New Jersey businessman, George Damon, came forward to say that a hired man who left his employment shortly after the murder had left behind a bloody shirt and a key stamped with the number 31, as recounted by Murder by Gaslight from contemporary newspaper reports. In 1902, Governor Benjamin Odell Jr. commuted Ben Ali's sentence, and he returned to Algeria after about eleven years in custody.

No one else was ever charged. The identity of the man who checked into the hotel with Carrie Brown has never been established, and the case is regarded as unsolved. Brown was buried in Salem, Massachusetts, according to the New England Historical Society.

name: Andrew & Abby Borden
summary: Andrew Borden and his wife Abby were found hacked to death in their Fall River, Massachusetts home. Their daughter Lizzie was acquitted of the murders. The case became one of the most famous unsolved murders in American history and spawned decades of debate, books, and plays.
lastSeen: August 4, 1892, 92 Second St., Fall River, MA

sources.title: Lizzie Borden - Wikipedia
Lizzie Borden | Rhyme, Biography, Trial, & Facts | Britannica (archived copy)
How Lizzie Borden Got Away With Murder | Smithsonian Magazine

narrative: On the morning of August 4, 1892, Andrew Jackson Borden, a prosperous 69-year-old businessman, and his second wife, 64-year-old Abby Durfee Borden, were found hacked to death inside the family home at 92 Second Street in Fall River, Massachusetts. Abby was killed first, struck roughly 18 to 19 times in an upstairs guest room sometime between about 9:00 and 10:30 a.m. Andrew was slain about an hour later as he lay on a downstairs sofa, receiving 10 or 11 blows to the head and face from a hatchet-like weapon. Andrew's younger daughter, 32-year-old Lizzie Andrew Borden, who was in the house, alerted the family's maid, Bridget Sullivan, and neighbors were summoned.

The investigation was hampered by the era's limited forensic methods and by a crime scene that was not tightly secured. Police recovered several hatchets and axes from the basement, including a hatchet head with a broken handle that prosecutors would later suggest was the weapon, but no blood-soaked clothing or definitive murder implement was ever conclusively tied to the killings. Suspicion fell on Lizzie because of her presence in the home, her shifting accounts of her whereabouts, her reportedly composed demeanor, and testimony that she had tried to buy the poison prussic acid the day before the murders and later burned a dress. She was arrested on August 11, 1892, and a grand jury indicted her on December 2, 1892.

Lizzie Borden's trial opened on June 5, 1893, before a three-judge panel of the Massachusetts Superior Court in New Bedford and drew intense national press coverage. Represented by prominent attorneys, including former Massachusetts governor George Robinson, the defense benefited from a largely circumstantial prosecution case, the exclusion of her inquest testimony and the prussic-acid evidence, and prevailing assumptions that a well-bred Victorian woman was incapable of such violence. On June 20, 1893, the all-male jury deliberated for roughly an hour to ninety minutes and acquitted her on all counts.

Because Lizzie Borden was acquitted and no other person was ever charged or convicted, the murders remain officially unsolved. Numerous theories have been advanced over the decades, variously implicating Lizzie, the maid Bridget Sullivan, an unknown intruder, or other relatives, but these remain historical speculation rather than proven fact. Lizzie, who inherited a substantial share of her father's estate, stayed in Fall River, bought a larger house she named Maplecroft, and lived largely ostracized by local society until her death on June 1, 1927; her sister Emma died days later that same year.

The case became one of the most enduring in American true-crime folklore, immortalized by the inaccurate skipping-rope rhyme that credits Lizzie with giving her mother 'forty whacks' and her father 'forty-one' (the actual blows numbered far fewer, and Abby was her stepmother). The Second Street house now operates as the Lizzie Borden House museum and bed-and-breakfast, and the murders have inspired films, plays, operas, books, and television dramas. Modern scholars and writers continue to reassess the evidence, the trial's fairness, and the social attitudes of gender and class that shaped its outcome, but the identity of the killer has never been legally established.

name: Stanford White
summary: Architect Stanford White, 52, was shot dead on June 25, 1906, at the rooftop theater of Madison Square Garden by Harry K. Thaw, husband of Evelyn Nesbit. Thaw's first trial ended in a hung jury in 1907; at his second, in 1908, he was found not guilty by reason of insanity and committed to Matteawan State Hospital. He was declared sane and released in 1915.
lastSeen: June 25, 1906, Madison Square Garden rooftop theater, New York City

sources.title: Library of Congress - Murder of Stanford White and the First "Trial of the Century": Topics in Chronicling America
PBS American Experience - The Love Triangle
Mental Floss - 10 Facts About the Original 'Trial of the Century'
Wikipedia - Stanford White
Wikipedia - Harry Kendall Thaw

narrative: Stanford White was one of the best-known American architects of his era, a partner in the firm McKim, Mead and White. According to PBS's American Experience, his work included the second Madison Square Garden and the Washington Square Arch in New York. He was born in New York City on November 9, 1853.

On the evening of June 25, 1906, White was attending the opening of the musical Mam'zelle Champagne at the rooftop theater of Madison Square Garden, a building he had designed. During the performance, Harry Kendall Thaw, heir to a Pittsburgh railroad and coal fortune, approached White's table and shot him at close range. White, who was 52, died at the scene. Thaw was arrested immediately; the shooting took place in front of a full audience.

Thaw was married to Evelyn Nesbit, a former model and chorus performer. According to PBS, Nesbit had come to New York as a teenager and had been involved with White when she was 16, several years before she married Thaw in April 1905. Thaw's defense centered on his claim that he had acted because of what White had done to Nesbit, and her testimony about her relationship with the architect became the most widely reported part of the proceedings.

The Library of Congress's guide to newspaper coverage of the case records that Thaw's first trial began on January 23, 1907, and that the jury deadlocked in April 1907. A second trial began on January 9, 1908. On February 1, 1908, the jury found Thaw not guilty by reason of insanity, and he was committed to the Matteawan State Hospital for the Criminally Insane in New York. The case was widely described in the press as the "trial of the century."

Thaw was therefore never convicted of the killing. In August 1913 he escaped from Matteawan and crossed into Canada; he was eventually returned to New York. In 1915 a jury found him sane, and he was released from custody. He died in Florida in February 1947.

Because the identity of the person who fired the shots was never in dispute, the case is not an unsolved one. Its legal outcome, however, was a verdict of not guilty by reason of insanity followed by a period of confinement in a state hospital, rather than a criminal conviction.

name: Virginia Christian Case
summary: Ida Belote, 51, was killed in her Hampton, Virginia, home on March 18, 1912. Her 16-year-old laundress, Virginia Christian, was convicted of first-degree murder by an all-white, all-male jury in April 1912 and was electrocuted at the Virginia State Penitentiary on August 16, 1912, a day after turning 17. She was the first woman put to death in Virginia's electric chair.
lastSeen: March 18, 1912, Ida Belote's home, Hampton, VA

sources.title: Library of Virginia (The UncommonWealth) - Virginia Christian: The Last Woman Executed by Virginia?
Library of Virginia (The UncommonWealth) - Souls of the Departed: Ida V. Belote
City of Hampton - The Tragic Case of Virginia Christian (Hampton History Museum program)
Wikipedia - Virginia Christian

narrative: Ida Virginia Belote was a widow living in Hampton, Virginia. According to the Library of Virginia, she was born in North Carolina in March 1861, married James E. W. Belote in 1879, and had eight children; her husband died in June 1911. Virginia Christian, a Black teenager born in Hampton on August 15, 1895, worked for Belote as a laundress. Accounts of the case say Christian had left school at about 13 to help support her family after her mother became paralyzed.

On March 18, 1912, Belote was killed in her home. According to accounts of the trial, Belote had accused Christian of stealing a skirt and a locket, and a confrontation followed in which Belote was struck with a broom handle and a towel was forced into her throat, causing her to suffocate. The Library of Virginia notes that two of Belote's young daughters found their mother's body and later gave testimony at the coroner's inquisition. Christian was arrested the same day.

Christian was indicted within days and tried in Elizabeth City County on April 8 and 9, 1912. The jury was made up entirely of white men. Her attorneys, who included J. Thomas Newsome, argued that the killing had not been planned. The jury deliberated for 23 minutes before finding her guilty of first-degree murder, and she was sentenced to death. Virginia's highest court declined to review the case in June 1912.

Christian's family, her lawyers and others petitioned Governor William Hodges Mann to commute the sentence, citing her age. Records held by the Library of Virginia include letters from both the Christian and Belote families as well as from the prosecutor. The governor granted a short reprieve but refused to commute the sentence.

Christian was electrocuted at the Virginia State Penitentiary in Richmond on the morning of August 16, 1912, one day after her seventeenth birthday. According to the Library of Virginia, she remained the only woman executed by the Commonwealth after executions were centralized at the penitentiary in 1908 until Teresa Lewis was put to death in 2010. She is also described as the last female juvenile offender executed in the United States.

The case has continued to draw attention from historians because of the defendant's age, the composition of the jury and the speed of the proceedings. In 2025 the Hampton History Museum hosted a public program re-examining the case.

name: New Orleans Axeman Victims
summary: An unidentified attacker known as the Axeman struck homes in and around New Orleans between May 1918 and October 1919, killing six people and injuring several others, many of them Italian grocers and their families. A letter published in March 1919 claimed the killer would spare any home where jazz was playing. Two men convicted in one attack were freed after the witness recanted; no one else was ever held responsible.
lastSeen: N/A

sources.title: Smithsonian Magazine - The Axeman of New Orleans Preyed on Italian Immigrants
Country Roads Magazine - The Axeman of New Orleans
Legends of America - The Axeman of New Orleans
Wikipedia - Axeman of New Orleans

narrative: Between May 1918 and October 1919, a series of night-time attacks on sleeping residents of New Orleans and neighboring Gretna, Louisiana, was attributed to an unknown assailant whom the press called the Axeman. In most of the incidents, accounts say, the intruder entered by chiseling out a panel of a back door and used an axe or hatchet that often belonged to the household. Valuables were generally left untouched. Many of the victims were Italian immigrant grocers or their relatives.

The first attack in the series came on May 23, 1918, when grocer Joseph Maggio and his wife Catherine were killed in their home. On June 27, 1918, grocer Louis Besumer and Harriet Lowe were attacked; Lowe died that August after surgery. Before her death she accused Besumer, who was charged with murder and acquitted by a jury on May 1, 1919. Anna Schneider, who was pregnant, survived an attack on August 5, 1918, and Joseph Romano died of head injuries after an attack on August 10, 1918.

In March 1919, Charles and Rosie Cortimiglia were badly injured and their two-year-old daughter Mary was killed in Gretna. Rosie Cortimiglia accused two neighbors, Iorlando Jordano and his teenage son Frank. Both were convicted; Frank was sentenced to hang and his father to life imprisonment. Rosie Cortimiglia later withdrew her accusation, and according to Smithsonian Magazine the two men were released in December 1920.

Days after the Gretna attack, on March 13, 1919, a letter signed as coming from the Axeman appeared in the press. It said the writer would pass over New Orleans on the night of March 19 and would spare any place where a jazz band was playing. Accounts describe dance halls filling and bands playing in homes across the city that night; no attack was reported. The authorship of the letter has never been established.

Three further attacks followed in 1919. Steve Boca survived an attack on August 10, and 19-year-old Sarah Laumann survived one on September 3. On October 27, 1919, grocer Mike Pepitone was fatally attacked in his bedroom; his wife reported seeing a large man fleeing. That was the last attack attributed to the Axeman.

No one was ever identified as the attacker. Smithsonian Magazine notes that a similar run of attacks on Italian grocers took place in 1910 and 1911, and that comparable attacks occurred elsewhere in Louisiana in 1920 and 1921; whether one person was responsible for all of them is a matter of historical debate. The case remains unsolved.

name: Virginia Rappe
summary: Actress Virginia Rappe died in San Francisco on September 9, 1921, of peritonitis from a ruptured bladder, four days after falling ill at a Labor Day party in Roscoe "Fatty" Arbuckle's suite at the St. Francis Hotel. Arbuckle was tried three times for manslaughter; two juries deadlocked and the third acquitted him on April 12, 1922. What caused the rupture was never established.
lastSeen: September 5, 1921, Hotel St. Francis, San Francisco, CA

sources.title: Bar Association of San Francisco - The Many Trials of Fatty Arbuckle
Smithsonian Magazine - The Skinny on the Fatty Arbuckle Trial
BBC News - 'Fatty' Arbuckle and Hollywood's first scandal
EBSCO Research Starters - Film Star Fatty Arbuckle Is Acquitted of Manslaughter
Wikipedia - Virginia Rappe
Wikipedia - Roscoe Arbuckle

narrative: Virginia Rappe was a Chicago-born model and film actress who had appeared in a number of silent pictures. Her year of birth is disputed: Wikipedia, citing Cook County birth registers, gives July 7, 1891, which would make her 30 when she died, while other accounts, including one published by the Bar Association of San Francisco, give 1895.

On Labor Day, September 5, 1921, Rappe attended a party in a suite of rooms taken by comedian Roscoe "Fatty" Arbuckle at the St. Francis Hotel in San Francisco. During the afternoon she became seriously ill in one of the bedrooms. According to the BBC, Arbuckle consistently said he had found her collapsed in the bathroom and had helped her to a bed. Rappe remained at the hotel for a time and was later moved to a sanitarium, where she died on September 9, 1921. The cause of death was peritonitis resulting from a ruptured bladder.

Maude Delmont, who had accompanied Rappe to the party, told authorities that Arbuckle had assaulted her. Arbuckle was arrested and initially held on a murder charge, which was reduced to manslaughter. Smithsonian Magazine notes that Delmont was never called to testify, and that medical evidence presented at trial indicated Rappe had a chronic bladder condition. The BBC likewise reports that she suffered from chronic cystitis.

Arbuckle was tried three times in San Francisco. According to the Bar Association of San Francisco, the first trial ran from November 14 to December 4, 1921, and ended with the jury deadlocked, a majority favoring acquittal. The second trial, from January 11 to February 3, 1922, also ended in a hung jury, this time with a majority favoring conviction. The third trial began on March 13, 1922.

On April 12, 1922, the third jury acquitted Arbuckle after deliberating for only a few minutes. The jurors issued a written statement saying that a great injustice had been done to him and that no evidence connected him with any crime. Despite the acquittal, Will H. Hays barred Arbuckle from the screen days later; the ban was lifted in December 1922, but his career did not recover.
No one else was charged in connection with Rappe's death, and the question of what caused her bladder to rupture was never resolved. She is buried at Hollywood Forever Cemetery in Los Angeles.

name: William Desmond Taylor
summary: Film director William Desmond Taylor, 49, was shot in the back at his bungalow in the Alvarado Court Apartments in Los Angeles on the evening of February 1, 1922; his body was found the next morning. Actress Mabel Normand had visited him shortly before. Police and the press examined many possible suspects, but no one was ever arrested or tried, and the case remains unsolved.
lastSeen: February 1, 1922, his bungalow at the Alvarado Court Apartments, Los Angeles, CA

sources.title: USC Libraries Regional History Collection - William Desmond Taylor (archived)
EBSCO Research Starters - Director Taylor's Murder Ruins Mabel Normand's Acting Career
IrishCentral - William Desmond Taylor: Murder of a Hollywood director unsolved
Wikipedia - William Desmond Taylor

narrative: William Desmond Taylor was a prominent director of the silent era. According to the University of Southern California's regional history archive, he was born William Cunningham Deane-Tanner in Ireland on April 26, 1872, came to the United States in 1890, and ran an antiques business in New York before abruptly leaving his wife and daughter in 1908. He later took the name Taylor, entered films, directed more than forty pictures and served as president of the Motion Picture Directors Association.

On the evening of February 1, 1922, actress Mabel Normand visited Taylor at his bungalow in the Alvarado Court Apartments in the Westlake district of Los Angeles. By her account she left at about 7:45 p.m. with a book he had given her, and he walked her to her waiting car. The next morning, February 2, Taylor's employee Henry Peavey arrived for work and found him dead on the floor. He had been shot once in the back with a small-caliber handgun.

The USC archive records that neighbors reported hearing a shot during the night, and that inquest witnesses described seeing a dark-haired man leaving the bungalow. Accounts of the case agree that the scene was compromised before detectives took control of it: EBSCO's summary says neighbors and at least one studio representative removed or disturbed items in the house, and IrishCentral describes studio figures going through Taylor's belongings.

Investigators and newspapers considered a wide range of people. Among those discussed in press coverage and later books were Taylor's former valet Edward Sands, who had a record for forgery and embezzlement and could not be located after the killing; Normand; actress Mary Miles Minter, whose letters were found in the house; and Minter's mother, Charlotte Shelby. None of them was charged, and no evidence was ever produced that conclusively tied any individual to the shooting.

Another theory raised at the time, noted by the USC archive, was that Taylor had been targeted because he had sought help from federal authorities against drug dealers supplying Normand. Decades later, a claim emerged that former actress Margaret Gibson had confessed to the killing shortly before her death in 1964; this has not been verified.

The murder followed closely on the Arbuckle trials and contributed to pressure on the film industry to regulate itself, with Will Hays taking charge of the studios' new trade association in 1922. Taylor was buried at what is now Hollywood Forever Cemetery. No one was ever arrested or tried, and the case is still regarded as an unsolved homicide.

name: Bobby Franks
summary: Fourteen-year-old Bobby Franks was abducted and killed in Chicago on May 21, 1924, by Nathan Leopold and Richard Loeb, two wealthy students. Both confessed and pleaded guilty; after a sentencing hearing in which Clarence Darrow argued against execution, each received life plus 99 years on September 10, 1924. Loeb died after an attack in prison in 1936, and Leopold was paroled in 1958.
lastSeen: May 21, 1924, walking home from school in Kenwood, Chicago

sources.title: Smithsonian Magazine - Why Leopold and Loeb Committed Cold-Blooded Murder in the 'Crime of the Century'
History.com - Leopold and Loeb murder Bobby Franks
Chicago Sun-Times - This week in history: Robert "Bobby" Franks found murdered
Wikipedia - Leopold and Loeb

narrative: Robert "Bobby" Franks, born September 19, 1909, was the 14-year-old son of a wealthy Chicago family living in the Kenwood neighborhood. On the afternoon of May 21, 1924, he was walking home from school when he was offered a ride by Richard Loeb, 18, who knew him, and Nathan Leopold, 19. Both were from prominent Kenwood families and had attended the University of Chicago. According to History.com, Loeb was a distant relative of the boy.

Franks was killed inside the rented car shortly after he got in. That night Leopold and Loeb hid his body in a drainage culvert beneath railroad tracks near Wolf Lake, on the far south side of the city. They then contacted the Franks family by telephone and by letter, demanding $10,000 in ransom, to make the crime appear to be a kidnapping for money.

The plan failed the next day. On May 22, 1924, a passer-by found the body in the culvert before any ransom could be paid. The Chicago Sun-Times' contemporary coverage, republished by the paper, shows that police at first considered drowning before head wounds were noted. Near the body, investigators found a pair of eyeglasses. According to Smithsonian Magazine, the glasses had an unusual hinge sold by a single Chicago supplier, and only three such pairs had been sold, one of them to Leopold. The typewriter used for the ransom letter was also later recovered.

Questioned by prosecutors, both men confessed by May 31, 1924. Their accounts agreed on nearly everything except which of them had struck the blows. Their stated motive, as summarized by History.com, was the wish to carry out a so-called perfect crime.

The families hired Clarence Darrow. Rather than go before a jury, Darrow had both defendants plead guilty, so that the only question was the sentence, to be decided by Judge John R. Caverly of the Cook County court. After a hearing lasting about a month, in which Darrow made a lengthy argument against capital punishment, Caverly on September 10, 1924, sentenced each defendant to life imprisonment for the murder plus 99 years for the kidnapping.

Loeb died on January 28, 1936, after being slashed with a razor by a fellow inmate at Stateville Penitentiary; the inmate was tried and found not guilty. Leopold was paroled on March 13, 1958, after 33 years in prison, moved to Puerto Rico, and died there on August 29, 1971.

name: Judge Joseph Force Crater
summary: New York Supreme Court Justice Joseph Force Crater, 41, vanished on the evening of August 6, 1930, after dining with two companions at a restaurant on West 45th Street in Manhattan. A grand jury heard 95 witnesses without learning his fate. He was declared legally dead in 1939 and police closed the file in 1979; a 2005 letter alleging he was killed and buried at Coney Island was never confirmed.
lastSeen: August 6, 1930, outside Billy Haas's Chophouse, 332 West 45th Street, New York City

sources.title: History.com - Joseph Force Crater becomes the "missingest man in New York"
NBC News - Judge Crater, is that you?
ABC News - Long-Concealed Letter May Be Key to N.Y. Judge Mystery
The Seattle Times - Letter may solve 1930 mystery of missing judge
Wikipedia - Joseph Force Crater

narrative: Joseph Force Crater was born on January 5, 1889, in Easton, Pennsylvania, and built a legal career in New York City, where he was active in Democratic politics. On April 8, 1930, Governor Franklin D. Roosevelt appointed him a justice of the New York Supreme Court for New York County. He had been on the bench about four months when he disappeared.

According to History.com, Crater was vacationing in Maine with his wife, Stella, when he returned to New York on August 3, 1930, telling her he would be back within about a week. On the morning of August 6 he went through papers in his chambers, had portfolios of documents taken to his Fifth Avenue apartment, and arranged for roughly $5,000 to be withdrawn from his bank accounts.

That evening he arranged for a single ticket to a Broadway comedy and then went to Billy Haas's Chophouse at 332 West 45th Street, where he dined with William Klein, a lawyer, and Sally Lou Ritz, a showgirl. What happened when the three left is not settled. Klein and Ritz at first told investigators that Crater got into a taxi at about 9:30 p.m.; they later said that they had taken the cab and that Crater had walked off down the street. No confirmed sighting followed.

The disappearance was not made public for nearly a month. News of it broke on September 3, 1930, setting off a large police investigation and nationwide press coverage. A grand jury convened that October called 95 witnesses and compiled close to 1,000 pages of testimony but was unable to determine whether Crater was alive or dead. In January 1931 his wife found envelopes in their apartment containing checks, securities and a note from him, in a drawer that police had previously searched; the discovery produced no resolution.

At his wife's request, Crater was declared legally dead in 1939. The New York police formally closed the missing-person case in 1979. Over the decades many theories were put forward, including that he left voluntarily or that he was killed because of what he knew about political corruption, but none was proved.

In August 2005, police disclosed that a woman who had recently died had left a letter, to be opened after her death, asserting that Crater had been killed by several men, among them a police officer and his brother, a cab driver, and buried under the Coney Island boardwalk near the present site of the New York Aquarium. News reports at the time said detectives were reviewing the claim. According to Wikipedia's summary of later reporting, police found no records showing that remains had been recovered when the site was excavated in the 1950s. No remains have been identified as Crater's.

name: Starr Faithfull
summary: Starr Faithfull, 25, was found dead on the beach at Long Beach, New York, on June 8, 1931, three days after leaving her family's Manhattan apartment. An autopsy found she had drowned and had bruises and a sedative in her system. Investigators considered homicide, suicide and accident; a grand jury issued no indictments and a December 1931 inquest reached no conclusion.
lastSeen: June 5, 1931, leaving her family's apartment at 12 St. Luke's Place, New York City

sources.title: New England Historical Society - The Mysterious Death of Starr Faithfull Reveals the Sordid Secret of a Boston Mayor
Derry News - Column: Remembering the tragic life of Starr Faithfull (archived)
Wikipedia - Death of Starr Faithfull

narrative: Starr Faithfull was born Starr Wyman in Evanston, Illinois, in January 1906, and grew up largely in New Jersey and Massachusetts. After her mother remarried in 1925, she and her sister took the surname of their stepfather, Stanley Faithfull, and the family settled in Greenwich Village in Manhattan. According to the New England Historical Society, she made repeated ocean voyages in the late 1920s and was known for slipping aboard liners during sailing-day parties.

On the morning of June 5, 1931, Faithfull left the family apartment at 12 St. Luke's Place. At about 6:30 a.m. on June 8, a beachcomber found her body on the sand at Long Beach, on the south shore of Long Island. She was wearing a dress and stockings; the rest of her outer clothing and accessories were missing. An autopsy concluded that she had drowned; it also recorded numerous bruises and a substantial quantity of a barbiturate sedative in her system.

Nassau County District Attorney Elvin Edwards treated the death as a probable homicide and halted the planned cremation so that a grand jury could examine the case. A search of the family's apartment turned up Faithfull's diary, which she called her "Mem Book." Its entries referred to men by initials, among them "AJP," which the press connected to Andrew J. Peters, a former mayor of Boston and a relative of her mother by marriage.

Her stepfather told investigators that Peters had sexually abused Faithfull beginning when she was about 11, and he produced records of a 1927 settlement under which Peters had paid the family $20,000. Peters publicly denied any improper conduct. He was questioned during the investigation but was never charged with any offense, and no evidence was presented tying him to her death.

The homicide theory was weakened later in June 1931 when Dr. George Jameson-Carr, a ship's surgeon, turned over letters Faithfull had written to him in the days before she disappeared, in which she spoke of ending her life. Stanley Faithfull maintained that the letters were forged and that his stepdaughter had been murdered. The grand jury proceedings ended without indictments.

Investigators continued to look at the case until December 1931, when a brief inquest was held and the jury reached no finding on whether the death was a homicide, a suicide or an accident. The case has never been officially resolved. It inspired several books, including John O'Hara's 1935 novel BUtterfield 8.

timeline.event: Starr Faithfull is born in Evanston, Illinois.

name: Charles Lindbergh Jr.
summary: The infant son of aviator Charles Lindbergh was kidnapped from the family estate in Hopewell, New Jersey. A ransom was paid but the baby's body was found two months later. Bruno Richard Hauptmann was convicted and executed in 1936. Some historians have questioned whether Hauptmann acted alone or was innocent.
lastSeen: March 1, 1932, family estate in Hopewell, NJ

sources.title: Lindbergh kidnapping - Wikipedia
Lindbergh Kidnapping - Federal Bureau of Investigation
Lindbergh baby kidnapping - Britannica (archived copy)
Bruno Hauptmann executed, April 3, 1936 - HISTORY

narrative: On the night of March 1, 1932, 20-month-old Charles Augustus Lindbergh Jr. was taken from the second-floor nursery of the family's newly built home near Hopewell, New Jersey. The toddler was the son of aviator Charles A. Lindbergh, who in 1927 had become an international celebrity for the first solo nonstop transatlantic flight. Nurse Betty Gow discovered the child missing at about 10 p.m., and a ransom note demanding $50,000 was found on the nursery windowsill. Outside, investigators recovered a homemade wooden ladder, apparently used to reach the window, along with footprints in the mud. The case immediately drew national and international attention.

Over the following weeks the kidnappers sent a series of ransom notes bearing a distinctive symbol of interlocking circles, eventually raising the demand to $70,000. Dr. John F. Condon, a retired Bronx schoolteacher, volunteered as an intermediary and, using the pseudonym "Jafsie," communicated with a man he met in cemeteries. On April 2, 1932, Condon delivered $50,000 to a man at St. Raymond's Cemetery in the Bronx. Much of the ransom was paid in gold certificates whose serial numbers had been recorded, a decision that later proved central to the investigation because such bills were about to be withdrawn from circulation.

On May 12, 1932, the child's badly decomposed body was found by a passing truck driver in woods a few miles from the Lindbergh home. An autopsy attributed death to a blow to the head, and investigators concluded the child had likely died on or near the night of the abduction. Authorities circulated the recorded serial numbers of the ransom bills, and over the next two years the marked gold certificates surfaced periodically in the New York area. On September 18-19, 1934, a ransom bill was traced to Bruno Richard Hauptmann, a German-born carpenter living in the Bronx; more than $14,000 of the ransom money was found hidden in his garage.

Hauptmann's trial opened January 2, 1935, at the Hunterdon County Courthouse in Flemington, New Jersey, in a media spectacle often called the "Trial of the Century." The prosecution, led by Attorney General David T. Wilentz, presented the ransom money, handwriting analysis linking Hauptmann to the notes, Condon's address and phone number found written inside a closet in Hauptmann's home, and expert testimony that a board from his attic matched wood in the kidnap ladder. Hauptmann insisted he was innocent, claiming the money had been left with him by a business associate, Isidor Fisch, who had returned to Germany and died. On February 13, 1935, the jury convicted him of first-degree murder and he was sentenced to death. After appeals and clemency petitions failed, Hauptmann was executed in the electric chair at the New Jersey State Prison on April 3, 1936, maintaining his innocence to the end.

The kidnapping prompted Congress to pass the Federal Kidnapping Act of 1932, popularly known as the "Lindbergh Law," which made transporting a kidnapping victim across state lines a federal crime and expanded FBI jurisdiction. Hauptmann's conviction and execution remain matters of historical record. However, in the decades since, some authors, journalists, and researchers, among them Ludovic Kennedy and Lloyd Gardner, have argued that the investigation was flawed and that Hauptmann may not have acted alone or may have been wrongly convicted; his widow, Anna Hauptmann, pursued unsuccessful lawsuits against New Jersey in the 1980s. These challenges are contested and have not overturned the verdict; many historians and former FBI officials continue to regard the evidence against Hauptmann as persuasive. The case endures as one of the most studied and debated crimes in American history.

name: Paul Bern
summary: MGM producer Paul Bern, 42, was found dead of a gunshot wound at his Beverly Hills home on September 5, 1932, two months after marrying actress Jean Harlow. A note was found and a coroner's jury ruled the death a suicide. His former common-law wife, Dorothy Millette, was found drowned in the Sacramento River days later. Later writers have disputed the ruling, but it has never been changed.
lastSeen: September 5, 1932, his home in Beverly Hills, CA

sources.title: Wikipedia - Paul Bern
Time - "Shedunit" (review of Deadly Illusions), October 1, 1990 (archived)
All That's Interesting - Jean Harlow
History.com - Jean Harlow dies

narrative: Paul Bern was born Paul Levy on December 3, 1889, in Wandsbek, now part of Hamburg, Germany, and came to the United States with his family as a child. After working in the theater he moved to Hollywood in the early 1920s, where he wrote and directed films before becoming a producer at Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer and an assistant to production chief Irving Thalberg. He was among those behind Grand Hotel, which was released days after his death.

Bern helped advance the career of actress Jean Harlow, and the two married on July 2, 1932. On September 5, 1932, he was found dead from a gunshot wound to the head at their home on Easton Drive in Beverly Hills. He was 42. Harlow had spent the night at her mother's house. Police found a short handwritten note at the scene, addressed to "Dearest Dear," in which the writer spoke of making good a wrong and of humiliation. Authorities treated it as a suicide note.

A coroner's jury found that Bern had taken his own life; according to Time magazine, the verdict described the motive as undetermined. Harlow told investigators she knew nothing that could explain the death. Bern's funeral was held on September 9, 1932, at Inglewood Park Cemetery.

Attention soon turned to Dorothy Millette, with whom Bern had lived in New York years earlier and who was described as his common-law wife. She had spent a long period in a sanitarium, and Bern had supported her financially. Millette traveled to California in 1932, and her body was recovered from the Sacramento River shortly after Bern's death. Her death was determined to be a suicide; she had been a passenger on the river steamer Delta King.

Questions about the official finding have persisted. In 1960 the writer Ben Hecht asserted in a magazine article that Bern had been murdered, prompting Los Angeles County District Attorney William B. McKesson to review the records; he closed the matter and characterized the claim as an unconfirmed rumor. In 1990, former MGM story editor Samuel Marx published a book stating that studio executives had reached the house before police were called, and arguing that Millette had shot Bern. Time, reviewing the book, noted that a key part of that account rested on a secondhand story attributed to a deceased studio security chief.
These theories have not been tested in any legal proceeding, and no one was ever charged. The official ruling of suicide stands.

Bern marries actress Jean Harlow.

name: Cleveland Torso Murders
summary: At least 12 people were killed, decapitated and dismembered in and around Cleveland's Kingsbury Run between September 1935 and August 1938. Only two victims were positively identified and no one was ever convicted. In 2024 the Cuyahoga County Medical Examiner's Office and the DNA Doe Project began exhuming unidentified victims for genetic genealogy testing.
lastSeen: N/A

sources.title: Encyclopedia of Cleveland History (Case Western Reserve University) - Torso Murders
DNA Doe Project - Kingsbury Run John Doe #4
DNA Doe Project - Kingsbury Run John Doe #6
CBS News - Nearly a century after the Torso Killer terrorized Cleveland, DNA testing aims to identify victims
WOIO Cleveland 19 - First victims of Torso Killer to undergo DNA testing for identification revealed
Wikipedia - Cleveland Torso Murderer

narrative: The Cleveland Torso Murders were a series of killings attributed to an unidentified offender, sometimes called the Mad Butcher of Kingsbury Run. According to the Encyclopedia of Cleveland History at Case Western Reserve University, the remains of about 12 people, seven men and five women, were found between 1935 and 1938, all of them decapitated and dismembered. Some researchers have argued that the true number of victims was higher, but 12 is the figure generally treated as the official count.

The first two bodies were found on September 23, 1935, in Kingsbury Run, a ravine on the city's east side. One was identified through fingerprints as Edward Andrassy, 29. A third victim, Florence Polillo, was found on January 26, 1936. Further remains were discovered between June 1936 and August 1938, including a man found on June 5, 1936, who became known as the Tattooed Man because of the six tattoos on his body. Andrassy and Polillo were the only victims positively identified; a third was tentatively identified as Rose Wallace on the basis of dental records.

The investigation involved Cleveland Safety Director Eliot Ness, county coroner Samuel Gerber and police detective Peter Merylo, who worked on the case for years. According to CBS News, the Tattooed Man remained unnamed even though his fingerprints and tattoos were recorded and a plaster cast of his head was shown to large crowds at the 1936 Great Lakes Exposition.

No one was ever tried for the murders. Frank Dolezal was arrested in August 1939 and, according to the Encyclopedia of Cleveland History, confessed to killing Polillo; he died in the county jail before any trial, in what was officially recorded as a suicide by hanging. Published accounts state that he had withdrawn his confession. Dr. Francis Sweeney, a physician, was questioned by Ness and has been named as a suspect in later accounts, but he was never charged and died in 1964. Neither man was convicted of any of the killings.

In the summer of 2024, the Cuyahoga County Medical Examiner's Office began working with the nonprofit DNA Doe Project to exhume unidentified victims buried in a potter's field and to attempt identification through investigative genetic genealogy. Cleveland television station WOIO reported in August 2024 that the first two sets of remains exhumed were those of the Tattooed Man and a second unidentified man. The DNA Doe Project's case pages listed both cases as still undergoing testing when they were checked in September 2026, and no identification had been announced. The murders remain unsolved.

Remains of Florence Polillo are discovered.

name: Thelma Todd
summary: Film actress Thelma Todd, 29, was found dead of carbon monoxide poisoning in her car inside a Pacific Palisades garage on December 16, 1935. A coroner's jury found the death appeared accidental and a grand jury inquiry produced no charges. No one was ever charged, and theories of foul play have never been substantiated.
lastSeen: Early morning of December 15, 1935, dropped off by her chauffeur near her apartment above Thelma Todd's Sidewalk Café, Pacific Palisades, CA

sources.title: Wikipedia - Thelma Todd
Golden Globes - Forgotten Hollywood: The Unsolved Mystery of the Death of Thelma Todd
New England Historical Society - The Mysterious Death of Massachusetts Movie Star Thelma Todd
EBSCO Research Starters - Film Star Thelma Todd's Death Cannot Be Explained

narrative: Thelma Todd was a film actress born in Lawrence, Massachusetts, on July 29, 1906, who by 1935 was 29 and well known for her film work. She was also the public face of Thelma Todd's Sidewalk Café, a restaurant in Pacific Palisades, and lived in an apartment in the same building.

On the night of Saturday, December 14, 1935, Todd attended a party at the Trocadero restaurant in Hollywood. According to published accounts, her chauffeur drove her home in the early hours of Sunday, December 15, and she arrived at about 4 a.m. That is the last time she is reliably reported to have been seen alive.

On the morning of Monday, December 16, her maid found her body in the front seat of her 1934 Lincoln Phaeton, which was parked in a garage on the hillside above the restaurant. The garage was part of the property occupied by her business partner, the director Roland West, and his wife, Jewel Carmen. Todd was still wearing the evening clothes from Saturday night. The cause of death was carbon monoxide poisoning.

A coroner's inquest was held on December 18, 1935. According to Wikipedia's summary of the record, the jury found that the death appeared to be accidental but recommended further investigation. A Los Angeles County grand jury then heard testimony over several weeks. It returned no indictments; accounts differ on how to characterize the outcome, with some stating that the panel found no evidence of foul play and others that its members were divided. The explanation most often given for an accident is that Todd, unable to get into her apartment, went up to the garage and ran the car's engine to keep warm.

Because of her fame and the unusual circumstances, the death has been the subject of speculation for decades. Writers have proposed that she was killed or deliberately shut in the garage, and have pointed to various people in her life, including figures connected to organized crime. The Golden Globes' historical feature on the case and the New England Historical Society both describe these as theories rather than established facts. Some later accounts also describe injuries that they say were noted at autopsy, but these claims are disputed and were not the basis of any official finding.
No one was ever arrested or charged in connection with Thelma Todd's death, and the official conclusion of accidental death has never been changed.

Todd attends a Saturday night party at the Trocadero in Hollywood.

name: Amelia Earhart
summary: Pioneer aviator Amelia Earhart and navigator Fred Noonan vanished over the Pacific Ocean during her attempt to circumnavigate the globe. She was declared legally dead in 1939. Multiple theories exist including the crash-and-sink theory and the Gardner Island castaway theory. Her fate remains one of aviation's greatest mysteries.
lastSeen: July 2, 1937, somewhere over the central Pacific Ocean

sources.title: Amelia Earhart - Wikipedia
Speculation on the disappearance of Amelia Earhart and Fred Noonan - Wikipedia
Top 3 Theories for Amelia Earhart's Disappearance - National Geographic
Sonar image was not Amelia Earhart's plane, but deep-sea explorers say search continues - CBS News
Amelia Earhart's long-lost plane likely located in lagoon, expedition team claims - CBS News
Amelia Earhart's Disappearance: 3 Leading Theories - HISTORY
Amelia Earhart mystery: New clues spark expeditions that hinge on rival theories - CNN

narrative: Amelia Earhart, already the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic, set out in 1937 to become the first woman to circumnavigate the globe by air. Flying a twin-engine Lockheed Electra 10E with navigator Fred Noonan, she departed Oakland, California, on May 20, 1937, on an eastbound route. Over the following weeks the pair hopped across the Caribbean, South America, Africa, South Asia and Southeast Asia, and by June 29, 1937, they reached Lae, New Guinea, having covered roughly 22,000 of the planned 29,000 miles.

The most demanding stretch remained: a flight of about 2,500 miles from Lae to Howland Island, a flat sliver of coral in the central Pacific barely visible from the air. Success depended on Noonan's celestial navigation and on radio contact with the U.S. Coast Guard cutter Itasca, stationed off Howland to guide them in. Earhart and Noonan left Lae on July 2, 1937. As the flight neared its destination, Itasca received a series of voice transmissions in which Earhart reported she was 'running low on gas' and, in a final message, described flying along a 'line of position 157 337.' The aircraft was never seen again.

The disappearance triggered what was then the largest and most costly air and sea search in U.S. history, involving Navy and Coast Guard ships and aircraft, including the battleship USS Colorado and the carrier USS Lexington, sweeping roughly a quarter-million square miles of ocean. The search was called off around July 18-19, 1937, having found no trace of the plane or its crew. Earhart was declared legally dead in absentia on January 5, 1939.

No explanation has ever been confirmed, and several competing hypotheses remain in circulation. The 'crash-and-sink' theory, favored by the U.S. Navy at the time and by many researchers since, holds that the Electra exhausted its fuel and ditched in deep water near Howland, sinking with little trace. A rival 'castaway' hypothesis, advanced most prominently by The International Group for Historic Aircraft Recovery (TIGHAR) and its director Ric Gillespie, argues that Earhart and Noonan followed their line of position south to uninhabited Gardner Island (now Nikumaroro), landed on the reef flat and died as castaways. Proponents point to bones found on Nikumaroro in 1940; an examination by physician D.W. Hoodless in 1941 judged them to be a male's, while a 2018 reanalysis by anthropologist Richard Jantz argued the measurements were consistent with Earhart. A separate theory that the pair were captured by Japanese forces is dismissed by most historians as lacking credible evidence. Each account remains an unproven hypothesis.

Modern expeditions continue to test these ideas with sonar, forensic and archaeological methods. In January 2024 the firm Deep Sea Vision released a sonar image of a plane-shaped anomaly roughly 100 miles from Howland, but after revisiting the site the team announced in November 2024 that the object was a natural rock formation, not the Electra. Attention has also turned to the 'Taraia Object,' an anomaly in Nikumaroro's lagoon that researchers from the Archaeological Legacy Institute and Purdue University planned to examine on expeditions in 2025 and 2026. As of 2026, none of these efforts has produced confirmed wreckage, and the fate of Amelia Earhart and Fred Noonan officially remains unsolved.

name: Betty June Binnicker & Mary Emma Thames
summary: Betty June Binnicker, 11, and Mary Emma Thames, 8, were found killed in Alcolu, South Carolina, on March 23, 1944. George Stinney Jr., a 14-year-old Black boy, was convicted in a one-day trial and executed on June 16, 1944. In December 2014 a judge vacated his conviction, finding his constitutional rights had been violated. No one else has been charged.
lastSeen: March 22, 1944, riding their bicycles in Alcolu, SC

sources.title: Death Penalty Information Center - South Carolina Vacates the Conviction of 14-Year-Old Executed in 1944
Christian Science Monitor - Executed at age 14, George Stinney exonerated 70 years later
Facing South - Judge exonerates 14-year-old boy executed in 1944
Wikipedia - George Stinney

narrative: Betty June Binnicker, 11, and Mary Emma Thames, 8, lived in Alcolu, a segregated mill town in Clarendon County, South Carolina. According to published accounts, the two girls went out on their bicycles on March 22, 1944, looking for flowers, and did not come home. Their bodies were found the next day, March 23, in a ditch.

George Stinney Jr., a 14-year-old Black boy who lived in Alcolu, was taken into custody on March 23. Police said he had confessed, but according to the Death Penalty Information Center no written record of a confession has ever been produced. He was questioned without a parent or lawyer present.

Stinney was tried on April 24, 1944. The whole proceeding, including jury selection, took place in a single day. Accounts collected by the Death Penalty Information Center and the Christian Science Monitor describe a trial of about three hours before an all-white, all-male jury, which returned a guilty verdict after roughly ten minutes. His court-appointed lawyer called few or no witnesses, conducted little cross-examination and filed no appeal. Stinney was executed in the electric chair on June 16, 1944. He is widely described as the youngest person executed in the United States in the twentieth century.

Decades later, members of Stinney's family sought to have the case reopened. His sister gave a sworn statement that she had been with him at the relevant time. Circuit Judge Carmen Mullen issued an order on December 16, 2014, vacating the conviction. She found that Stinney had been denied due process and effective assistance of counsel, and that any confession was likely coerced given his age and the circumstances of his questioning.

The 2014 ruling is often reported as an exoneration. According to the Death Penalty Information Center's summary, the order set aside the conviction because of constitutional violations and did not make a finding about who committed the killings. Stinney's family has always maintained that he was innocent, and, as reported by Facing South, argued that a boy of his size could not physically have committed the killings.
With the conviction vacated and Stinney long dead, there is no standing conviction for the deaths of Betty June Binnicker and Mary Emma Thames. No other person has ever been charged.

The girls' bodies are found in a ditch; George Stinney Jr., 14, is taken into custody.

name: Recy Taylor
summary: Recy Taylor, a 24-year-old Black sharecropper, was abducted and raped by six white men while walking home from church in Abbeville, Alabama, on September 3, 1944. Two all-white grand juries declined to indict anyone. Rosa Parks investigated for the NAACP. The Alabama Legislature apologized in 2011; Taylor died in 2017 at 97.
lastSeen: N/A

sources.title: NBC News - Recy Taylor, Alabama woman raped by six white men, dies at 97
National Women's History Museum - Biography: Recy Taylor
GBH News - How Recy Taylor Spoke Out Against Her Rape, Decades Before #MeToo
Wikipedia - Recy Taylor

narrative: Recy Taylor was born on December 31, 1919, and in 1944 was a 24-year-old married mother working as a sharecropper in Henry County, Alabama. On the evening of September 3, 1944, she was walking home from a church service in Abbeville when a car carrying seven armed white men stopped beside her. According to the National Women's History Museum, she was forced into the car at gunpoint, driven to a wooded area and raped by six of the men. She was then left blindfolded at the side of a road and threatened with death if she spoke about what had happened.

Taylor reported the assault. The men in the car were identified to the authorities, and published accounts state that at least one of them admitted what had taken place. No arrests followed. NBC News reported that an attempt was also made to pay Taylor to stay silent.

The Montgomery branch of the NAACP sent Rosa Parks, then an investigator for the organization, to Abbeville to interview Taylor. Parks and other activists formed the Committee for Equal Justice for Mrs. Recy Taylor, which drew national attention to the case and pressed the governor of Alabama, Chauncey Sparks, to act.

An all-white, all-male Henry County grand jury heard the case on October 3 and 4, 1944, and declined to indict after about five minutes of deliberation. Following the public campaign, the state opened a further investigation, and a second grand jury considered the matter on February 14, 1945. It also refused to return indictments, even though, according to the National Women's History Museum, additional men had by then made admissions to investigators. No one was ever prosecuted, and none of the men was ever convicted of any offense in connection with the attack.

The case received renewed attention after historian Danielle McGuire published a book that documented it in detail. In 2011 the mayor of Abbeville and county officials apologized, and on April 21, 2011, the Alabama Legislature adopted a resolution apologizing to Taylor for the state's failure to prosecute, calling that failure morally abhorrent and repugnant.
A documentary film about her experience was released in December 2017. Recy Taylor died in a nursing home in Abbeville on December 28, 2017, three days before her 98th birthday.

A second grand jury also refuses to indict.

Recy Taylor dies in Abbeville at age 97.

name: Suzanne Degnan
summary: Six-year-old Suzanne Degnan was abducted from her bedroom in Chicago's Edgewater neighborhood on January 7, 1946, and killed. William Heirens, 17, pleaded guilty in September 1946 to her murder and two others and received three life sentences. He soon recanted and maintained his innocence until his death in custody in 2012, after more than 65 years in prison.
lastSeen: January 7, 1946, family home in Chicago, IL

sources.title: Chicago Sun-Times - Confessed 'Lipstick Killer' William Heirens dead at 83
CBS News - 'Lipstick Killer' William Heirens dies after over 65 years in prison
DNAinfo Chicago - 70 Years After 'Lipstick Murders,' Doubt Over Killer's Guilt Still Lingers
Wikipedia - William Heirens

narrative: Suzanne Degnan, 6, lived with her family in an apartment at 5943 North Kenmore Avenue in the Edgewater neighborhood on Chicago's North Side. On the morning of January 7, 1946, her family found that she was missing from her first-floor bedroom. A note demanding $20,000 in ransom and warning the family not to contact the police or the FBI had been left behind.

Police searched the area the same day and found parts of the child's body in sewers and drains near her home. According to a DNAinfo Chicago retrospective, investigators concluded that she had been dismembered in the laundry room of a nearby apartment building on North Winthrop Avenue, and the last of her remains were not recovered until more than a month later. Her funeral was held on January 11, 1946.

The killing was investigated alongside the 1945 murders of two Chicago women, Josephine Ross and Frances Brown. At the Brown scene, a message written in lipstick on a wall asked to be caught before the writer killed again, which led newspapers to call the offender the Lipstick Killer.

On June 26, 1946, William Heirens, a 17-year-old University of Chicago student, was arrested after an attempted burglary on the North Side. According to the Chicago Sun-Times, he was questioned for days without a lawyer and was given sodium pentothal; he later said that police had beaten him. Prosecutors relied on fingerprint and handwriting evidence that they said linked him to the ransom note. On September 4, 1946, Heirens pleaded guilty to the three murders, and on September 5 he was sentenced to three consecutive life terms.

Heirens withdrew his confession shortly afterward and said for the rest of his life that he had pleaded guilty only to avoid execution. His supporters argued that the fingerprint and handwriting evidence was unreliable and that the confession had been coerced. The courts and the state did not accept those arguments: a clemency petition was denied in 2002, and the Illinois Prisoner Review Board repeatedly refused parole, voting unanimously against release in 2007. Members of the Degnan family opposed his release at those hearings.

Heirens died on March 5, 2012, at the age of 83, after being taken from Dixon Correctional Center to a Chicago hospital. He had been in custody for more than 65 years, and his conviction was never overturned.

name: Texarkana Moonlight Murders
summary: Five people were killed and three wounded in four nighttime attacks in and around Texarkana, on the Texas-Arkansas border, between February 22 and May 3, 1946. The attacker, called the Phantom Killer, was never identified. The main suspect was never charged with the murders, and the case remains unsolved.
lastSeen: Various dates, Texarkana TX/AR area

sources.title: Encyclopedia of Arkansas - Texarkana Moonlight Murders
Wikipedia - Texarkana Moonlight Murders
The Lineup - Phantom Killer: The Unsolved Mystery of the Texarkana Murders
All That's Interesting - The Texarkana Moonlight Murders

narrative: The Texarkana Moonlight Murders were four attacks carried out over about ten weeks in the spring of 1946 in and around Texarkana, a city divided between Bowie County, Texas, and Miller County, Arkansas. According to the Encyclopedia of Arkansas, five people were killed and three were wounded. The attacks took place at night, on weekends, and the unidentified assailant became known in the press as the Phantom Killer.

The first attack came on February 22, 1946, when Jimmy Hollis, 25, and Mary Jeanne Larey, 19, were confronted by a masked man with a gun while parked on a secluded road on the Texas side. Hollis was beaten and suffered skull fractures, and Larey was assaulted. Both survived and gave descriptions of a man wearing a white cloth mask.

On March 24, 1946, Richard Griffin, 29, and Polly Ann Moore, 17, were found shot dead in a car on a lovers' lane in Bowie County. On April 14, Paul Martin, 16, and Betty Jo Booker, 15, were found shot to death in the area of Spring Lake Park; their bodies were discovered some distance apart. Both double murders were committed with a .32 caliber handgun.

The final attack took place on May 3, 1946, at a farmhouse in Miller County, Arkansas, about ten miles northeast of Texarkana. Virgil Starks, 37, was shot through a window and killed. His wife, Katie Starks, was shot twice in the face but managed to reach a neighbor's house and survived. A .22 caliber weapon was used, unlike the .32 caliber handgun of the earlier killings.

The investigation drew in local police, both county sheriffs, the Arkansas State Police and the Texas Rangers, led by Captain Manuel T. Gonzaullas. In July 1946, Arkansas state trooper Max Tackett arrested Youell Swinney, a man with a record for car theft and counterfeiting. According to published accounts, Swinney's wife told officers that he was responsible for the killings, but she later withdrew her statements and could not be compelled to testify against him. Swinney was never charged with any of the murders. He was convicted of car theft and imprisoned as a habitual offender, and was released in 1973 after a successful appeal. Some investigators said they believed he was responsible, but this was never tested in court.
No one has been charged with the attacks, and the case is regarded as an unsolved cold case. It was the basis for the 1976 film The Town That Dreaded Sundown.

name: Elizabeth Short (The Black Dahlia)
summary: The mutilated body of 22-year-old Elizabeth Short was found in a vacant lot in Los Angeles. Her body had been severed at the waist, drained of blood, and posed. The case became one of the most famous unsolved murders in American history, generating hundreds of confessions but no confirmed suspect.
lastSeen: January 9, 1947, at the Biltmore Hotel, Los Angeles

sources.title: Black Dahlia - Wikipedia
George Hodel - Wikipedia
Black Dahlia, 77 years later: Where does the case stand now? - Deseret News
Black Dahlia Murder: Retired LAPD detective reveals new evidence - The South Pasadenan

narrative: Elizabeth Short, a 22-year-old born in Boston on July 29, 1924, had moved to Southern California in the 1940s and was living transiently in the Los Angeles area when she was killed. On the morning of January 15, 1947, a woman walking with her child found Short's nude body in a vacant lot on South Norton Avenue in the Leimert Park neighborhood. The body had been severed at the waist, drained of blood, and mutilated, with lacerations extending the corners of the mouth. According to police and press accounts, the lack of blood at the scene indicated she had been killed elsewhere. Newspapers soon dubbed her the "Black Dahlia." The last confirmed sighting reported by investigators was around January 9, 1947, when a married salesman, Robert "Red" Manley, said he dropped her at the downtown Biltmore Hotel after a trip from San Diego.

The Los Angeles Police Department mounted a massive investigation. The FBI assisted by identifying Short from fingerprints transmitted from Los Angeles. Investigators pursued more than 150 suspects and fielded scores of confessions, most of which were deemed false. Police reported that whoever killed Short may have had some anatomical or medical knowledge, based on how the body had been cleanly bisected. In the weeks after the killing, someone claiming to be the killer contacted a newspaper editor, and on January 24, 1947, an envelope arrived at a newspaper containing Short's birth certificate, photographs, and an address book, items reportedly cleaned with gasoline. Subsequent notes were signed the "Black Dahlia Avenger," but the sender never turned himself in, and the material did not lead to an arrest.

Over the decades, many people have been named as suspects or persons of interest, though no one has ever been criminally charged. Among the most discussed is Dr. George Hodel, a Los Angeles physician who was placed under DA/LAPD electronic surveillance at his home between February 15 and March 27, 1950. Police did not charge him, and reporting notes that authorities could not establish that he and Short had ever met. Hodel died on May 17, 1999. His son, retired LAPD detective Steve Hodel, later published books, beginning with Black Dahlia Avenger in 2003, arguing that his father was the killer. Other named individuals, including Robert Manley, Leslie Dillon, and Mark Hansen, were investigated and cleared. In careful terms, none of these individuals was convicted, and their identification as suspects reflects investigative interest rather than proven guilt.

As of 2026 the Black Dahlia murder remains officially open and unsolved, and is among the oldest unsolved cases in Los Angeles County. The LAPD's Robbery-Homicide Division still retains the evidence, and detective Mitzi Roberts has described the case as active and ongoing while noting the absence of physical evidence tying any single theory, including Steve Hodel's, to the crime. Reporting has cited fingerprints on a purported killer's letter that did not match records, but there are no publicly reported DNA or genetic-genealogy breakthroughs in the case. The FBI has stated the case is likely to remain unsolved given the passage of time. Given the age of the crime, most or all plausible suspects are deceased.

George Hodel, a long-discussed suspect who was never charged, dies at age 91.
On the case's 77th anniversary, reporting confirms it remains open but unlikely to be solved, with no publicly reported forensic breakthrough.

name: Beverly Potts
summary: Ten-year-old Beverly Potts disappeared on the evening of August 24, 1951, after attending a Showagon performance at Halloran Park, a short walk from her home on Cleveland's west side. One of the largest searches in the city's history found no trace of her. No one has been charged, and she has never been found.
lastSeen: August 24, 1951, about 9:30 p.m., Halloran Park, Cleveland, OH

sources.title: Wikipedia - Disappearance of Beverly Potts
The Clermont Sun - Marc Hoover: The disappearance of Beverly Potts
Plain Press - Documentary to air on disappearance of Beverly Potts
Wikipedia - William Henry Redmond

narrative: Beverly Rose Potts was born on April 15, 1941, and lived with her parents and older sister on Linnet Avenue on the west side of Cleveland, Ohio. On the evening of Friday, August 24, 1951, she and a friend rode their bicycles to Halloran Park, less than a quarter of a mile from her home, to watch the Showagon, a traveling summer talent show.

According to published accounts, the friend had to be home before dark and left at about 8:45 p.m., while Beverly stayed to see the end of the performance. The show finished at around 9:30 p.m. The last reported sighting came from a 13-year-old boy who knew her and said he saw a girl he believed to be Beverly walking across the park at about that time. She did not arrive home, and her family reported her missing that night.

The search that followed was described at the time as the largest in the city's history. Dozens of officers were assigned to the case full time and large numbers of volunteers joined them. Searchers went through vacant lots, sewers and waterways, and the FBI circulated thousands of notices around the country. Police questioned known sex offenders in the area. Nothing belonging to Beverly was ever recovered.

Over the following decades a number of men came to police attention, but none was charged in connection with the disappearance. In November 1951 a man who had demanded money from the family was arrested; he admitted extortion, was cleared of any involvement in the disappearance and was imprisoned for blackmail. In 1955 a man arrested in Los Angeles claimed responsibility, but his account did not match the facts and he withdrew it. In 1980 two detectives disclosed that a tip received in 1974 had led them to a man who had lived near the park, but prosecutors concluded that there was not enough evidence to bring charges.

In 1988 Cleveland police tried to question William Henry Redmond, a former carnival worker then facing a charge in a 1951 child murder in Pennsylvania; he declined to discuss the Potts case, was never charged in it, and died in 1992 without having been convicted in the Pennsylvania case. Anonymous letters sent to a Cleveland newspaper beginning in 2000, in which the writer claimed responsibility, were investigated and came to be regarded as a probable hoax.

Beverly's mother died in 1956 and her father in 1970. Her sister, Anita, continued to look for answers until her own death in 2006. A local documentary about the case was broadcast in the Cleveland area in 2024. Beverly Potts has never been found and the case remains open.

name: Bobby Greenlease
summary: Six-year-old Bobby Greenlease was taken from his Kansas City school on September 28, 1953, by Bonnie Heady and killed the same day by Carl Austin Hall. His family paid a $600,000 ransom before his body was found. Hall and Heady pleaded guilty in federal court and were executed on December 18, 1953. More than half the ransom was never recovered.
lastSeen: September 28, 1953, Notre Dame de Sion School, Kansas City, MO

sources.title: Federal Death Penalty Project - Bonnie Brown Heady and Carl Austin Hall
Legends of America - Greenlease Kidnapping in Kansas City, Missouri
Wikipedia - Murder of Bobby Greenlease

narrative: Robert Cosgrove Greenlease Jr., known as Bobby, was born on February 3, 1947, and was the son of a wealthy Kansas City, Missouri, car dealer. In September 1953 he was a six-year-old pupil at Notre Dame de Sion school in the city.

On the morning of September 28, 1953, a woman came to the school and said that she was the boy's aunt and that his mother had suffered a heart attack. The school released him to her. The woman was Bonnie Emily Heady, who was acting with her companion, Carl Austin Hall. According to accounts of the case, the pair drove the child across the state line into Johnson County, Kansas, where Hall shot him later that day. They buried his body in the yard of Heady's house in St. Joseph, Missouri.

Over the following days the kidnappers sent ransom demands to the Greenlease family, giving the impression that the boy was alive. The family paid $600,000, which was the largest ransom paid in the United States up to that time. Hall and Heady then travelled to St. Louis.

In St. Louis, Hall's heavy spending attracted attention, and a cab driver reported him. Police arrested Hall on October 6, 1953, and Heady was taken into custody that night at an apartment on Arsenal Street. Both made admissions, and on October 7 investigators recovered the child's body from the grave in St. Joseph.

The two were prosecuted in federal court in Kansas City. They pleaded guilty to kidnapping, and a jury was convened to decide the penalty. On November 19, 1953, the jury recommended death after deliberating for about an hour, and both were sentenced accordingly. Hall and Heady were executed together in the gas chamber at the Missouri State Penitentiary in Jefferson City on December 18, 1953, 81 days after the abduction.

Only about $288,000 of the ransom was ever recovered, leaving roughly $312,000 unaccounted for. According to published accounts, two St. Louis police officers involved in Hall's arrest were later convicted of perjury in connection with the handling of the money. The missing portion of the ransom has never been found. The murder itself is considered solved.

name: Frank Olson
summary: Army biochemist Frank Olson, 43, died on November 28, 1953, after falling from a window of the Hotel Statler in New York, nine days after CIA colleagues gave him LSD without his knowledge. The death was treated as a suicide. A 1994 forensic re-examination raised the possibility of homicide, but prosecutors brought no charges and a 2012 family lawsuit was dismissed.
lastSeen: November 28, 1953, Hotel Statler, New York City

sources.title: vLex - Olson v. United States, 953 F.Supp.2d 223 (D.D.C. 2013)
Courthouse News Service - CIA Murder Claims Are Credible, but Too Late
WJLA - Frank Olson lawsuit against CIA dismissed
Wikipedia - Frank Olson

narrative: Frank Olson, born July 17, 1910, was a scientist who worked on biological weapons at Fort Detrick, Maryland, and with the Central Intelligence Agency. According to the facts recited in a later federal court opinion, a CIA employee put LSD into a bottle of Cointreau from which Olson drank. He had not been told. The dosing took place on November 19, 1953.

Days later Olson was in New York, staying at the Hotel Statler in Manhattan, where he shared a room with CIA employee Robert Lashbrook. At about 2 a.m. on November 28, 1953, Olson went through the window of the room and fell to the street. He died shortly afterward. The death was treated as a suicide.

The LSD experiment became public in 1975, when the Rockefeller Commission's report on CIA activities led to the disclosure that CIA personnel had been given drugs in covert tests, including Olson nine days before his death. The government acknowledged the drugging, and Congress passed a private law in 1976 under which the family received $750,000, or $187,500 for each of four family members, in full settlement of claims arising from the death.

Olson's sons continued to doubt the official account. In 1994 they had their father's body exhumed and examined by a team led by forensic scientist James Starrs. According to published accounts of the findings, the team reported an injury to the head that most of its members believed had been inflicted before the fall, and Starrs described the evidence as suggestive of homicide. The Manhattan District Attorney's office opened an inquiry in 1996 but concluded that there was not enough evidence to take the matter to a grand jury.

On November 28, 2012, Eric and Nils Olson sued the United States in federal court in Washington, alleging that CIA personnel had killed their father and concealed it. On July 17, 2013, U.S. District Judge James Boasberg dismissed the case, holding that the claims were filed too late and were barred by the 1976 settlement. According to Courthouse News Service, the judge observed that the public record supported many of the family's factual allegations, but he did not rule on how Olson died.
No one has ever been charged in connection with Frank Olson's death, and no court or official body has determined that it was a homicide.
