name: Janett Christman
summary: Thirteen-year-old Janett Christman was sexually assaulted and strangled on the night of March 18, 1950, while babysitting at a home in Columbia, Missouri. The couple she was working for found her body when they returned in the early hours of March 19. A man who was questioned was never charged, and the killing remains unsolved.
lastSeen: March 18, 1950, babysitting job in Columbia, MO

sources.title: The Lineup - The Babysitter: The Gruesome Murder of Janett Christman
Midwest Crime File - The Babysitter Murder: The Story of Janett Christman and Marylou Jenkins
Find a Grave - Janett Christman (1936-1950)
Wikipedia - The babysitter and the man upstairs

narrative: Janett Christman was born in Columbia, Missouri, on March 21, 1936. On Saturday, March 18, 1950, three days before her 14th birthday, she agreed to babysit the three-year-old son of Ed and Anne Romack at their home on the edge of Columbia while the couple spent the evening out.

According to accounts of the case, at about 10:30 p.m. the Columbia police received a telephone call from a girl who was screaming and who asked them to come quickly. The line went dead before she gave a name or an address, and the call could not be traced.

The Romacks returned home in the early hours of March 19. They found the porch light on and the front door unlocked, and Ed Romack discovered Janett's body on the living room floor. She had been beaten about the head, sexually assaulted and strangled with the cord of an electric iron. The child she had been looking after was unharmed. A side window had been broken from the outside, and a garden hoe was found nearby. Accounts of the investigation state that fingerprints and blood samples were collected and that dogs followed a scent for some distance from the house before losing it.

The investigation was shared between the Columbia Police Department and the Boone County Sheriff's Department, and later accounts describe friction between the two agencies over control of the case. A number of men were questioned in the first weeks.

Attention eventually turned to a 27-year-old local man who knew both the Romacks and the Christman family and for whom Janett had previously babysat. According to published accounts, he had been with the Romacks earlier that evening and left before the time of the murder. He was questioned at length, reportedly without a warrant or a lawyer, and is reported to have passed a polygraph examination. A grand jury considered the matter and found that there was not enough evidence to charge him. He was never charged with any offense in connection with the death and is reported to have died in 2006.

Writers on the case have noted its similarities to the 1946 killing of Marylou Jenkins, 20, in the same part of Columbia. Floyd Cochran was convicted of that murder and executed in 1947, and some authors have questioned that conviction. No connection between the two crimes has been established. Janett Christman's murder has also been cited as an influence on the urban legend of the babysitter and the man upstairs. No one has ever been charged with her killing.

name: Marilyn Sheppard
summary: Marilyn Sheppard was bludgeoned to death in her Bay Village, Ohio home. Her husband, Dr. Sam Sheppard, was convicted of murder in 1954 but his conviction was overturned. Retried in 1966, he was acquitted. His case inspired the TV show and film 'The Fugitive.' The actual killer was never conclusively identified.
lastSeen: July 4, 1954, family home in Bay Village, OH

sources.title: Sam Sheppard - Wikipedia
Sheppard v. Maxwell - Wikipedia
Sheppard Murder Case | Encyclopedia of Cleveland History, Case Western Reserve University
Sheppard v. Maxwell, 384 U.S. 333 (1966) | Justia U.S. Supreme Court Center (archived copy)
Sheppard v. Maxwell (1966) | The First Amendment Encyclopedia, MTSU

narrative: In the early morning hours of July 4, 1954, Marilyn Reese Sheppard, 31 and pregnant, was bludgeoned to death in the bedroom of her lakeside home in Bay Village, Ohio, a suburb of Cleveland. Her seven-year-old son slept in a nearby room and was unharmed. Her husband, Dr. Samuel H. Sheppard, an osteopathic physician, told investigators that he had fallen asleep on a downstairs couch, was awakened by his wife's cries, and struggled with a 'bushy-haired intruder' who knocked him unconscious both in the bedroom and later near the beach below the house. He was treated for injuries after the killing.

Suspicion quickly focused on Sheppard. Cleveland newspapers, led by the Cleveland Press and its editor Louis Seltzer, ran front-page editorials demanding his arrest and questioning why he had not been jailed. He was indicted and, after a nine-week trial conducted amid intense publicity, was convicted of second-degree murder on December 21, 1954, and sentenced to life in prison. His first defense attorney was William Corrigan.

After Corrigan's death, F. Lee Bailey took over the defense and pursued federal appeals. In Sheppard v. Maxwell, 384 U.S. 333, the U.S. Supreme Court on June 6, 1966, voted 8-1 to overturn the conviction, holding that the 'massive, pervasive and prejudicial' pretrial and trial publicity, together with the trial judge's failure to control a 'carnival atmosphere' in the courtroom, had denied Sheppard the fair trial guaranteed by the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The decision became a landmark on the tension between free press and fair trial, prompting courts to adopt tools such as change of venue, jury sequestration, and gag orders.

Ohio retried Sheppard in the fall of 1966. With Bailey as counsel and reporters restricted in the courtroom, the jury deliberated about 12 hours and returned a verdict of not guilty on November 16, 1966, acquitting him. Sheppard resumed medical practice briefly and later worked as a professional wrestler. He died on April 6, 1970, at age 46; the reported cause was liver failure (Wernicke encephalopathy has also been cited).

The case is widely credited as an inspiration for the 1963-1967 television series 'The Fugitive' and its 1993 film adaptation, though its creators did not formally acknowledge it. In the 1990s, Sheppard's son, Sam Reese Sheppard, sought to clear his father's name and, in a 2000 civil suit against the State of Ohio, argued that Sheppard had been wrongfully imprisoned. The defense pointed to Richard Eberling, a window washer who had worked at the Sheppard home, as a possible alternative suspect; Eberling was later convicted in an unrelated 1984 murder and died in prison in 1998. Eberling was never charged in Marilyn Sheppard's death and denied involvement; his status as a suspect remains an attributed theory, not an adjudicated fact.

On April 12, 2000, after a lengthy civil trial, a Cuyahoga County jury rejected the wrongful-imprisonment claim. An Ohio appeals court later ruled in 2002 that the estate lacked standing to bring the claim. No one has ever been convicted of the murder, and it remains officially unsolved. The competing narratives, an innocent man convicted amid a media circus versus a guilty husband freed on a technicality, have never been legally resolved.

name: Emmett Till
summary: Fourteen-year-old Emmett Till, a Black teenager from Chicago, was abducted and brutally murdered near Money, Mississippi, on August 28, 1955, after allegedly whistling at a white woman. Roy Bryant and J.W. Milam were tried for the murder and acquitted by an all-white jury in September 1955; protected by double jeopardy, they admitted the killing in a paid 1956 Look magazine interview. No one was ever convicted, and the case became a catalyst for the Civil Rights Movement.
lastSeen: August 24, 1955, Bryant's Grocery Store, Money, MS

narrative: Emmett Louis Till was a 14-year-old Black teenager from Chicago who was visiting relatives in the Mississippi Delta during the summer of 1955. On August 24, 1955, he entered Bryant's Grocery and Meat Market in the small town of Money, Mississippi, where he had an encounter with Carolyn Bryant, the 21-year-old white woman who ran the store with her husband. Accounts of what occurred have long been disputed, but Till was accused of whistling at, flirting with, or otherwise offending Bryant. Decades later, in interviews reported by historian Timothy Tyson, Bryant was said to have recanted the most serious parts of her testimony, though she denied recanting when questioned by the FBI.

In the early morning hours of August 28, 1955, Carolyn Bryant's husband, Roy Bryant, and his half-brother, J.W. Milam, abducted Till at gunpoint from his great-uncle Mose Wright's home in Leflore County. The two men beat Till severely, shot him, and dumped his body in the Tallahatchie River, weighted down with a cotton-gin fan. His mutilated body was recovered from the river on August 31, 1955, and was identifiable only by a ring he wore.

Till's mother, Mamie Till-Mobley, insisted on an open-casket funeral in Chicago so the public could see what had been done to her son. Tens of thousands of mourners viewed the body, and photographs published in Jet magazine and the Black press shocked the nation and much of the world. The funeral and images became a galvanizing moment for the emerging civil-rights movement, helping to spur activism in the months and years that followed.

Bryant and Milam were tried for murder in September 1955 in Sumner, Mississippi. The trial began on September 19, and on September 23, 1955, an all-white, all-male jury acquitted both men after deliberating for roughly an hour. The acquittal drew national and international condemnation. In January 1956, protected from further prosecution by the constitutional prohibition on double jeopardy, Bryant and Milam confessed to the killing in a paid interview with William Bradford Huie published in Look magazine. No one was ever convicted in connection with Emmett Till's murder.

The U.S. Department of Justice reopened the case in 2004 under its Cold Case Initiative; Till's body was exhumed and an autopsy conducted, but in February 2007 a Mississippi grand jury declined to indict Carolyn Bryant. The DOJ reopened the matter again in 2017 following reports that Bryant had recanted, and closed it in December 2021 without charges, citing insufficient evidence. In June 2022, researchers found an unserved 1955 arrest warrant for Carolyn Bryant Donham on a kidnapping charge, but a Leflore County grand jury again declined to indict her in August 2022. Donham died on April 25, 2023, at age 88. On July 25, 2023, President Biden established the Emmett Till and Mamie Till-Mobley National Monument, spanning sites in Illinois and Mississippi. The case remains officially closed and legally unresolved, with no living perpetrators ever held to account.

name: Barbara & Patricia Grimes
summary: Sisters Barbara, 15, and Patricia Grimes, 12, vanished on December 28, 1956, after going to see an Elvis Presley film at Chicago's Brighton Theater. Their bodies were found beside a rural road southwest of the city on January 22, 1957. A man who confessed later recanted and the charges were dropped. No one has been convicted, and the case remains open.
lastSeen: December 28, 1956, Brighton Theater, Chicago, IL

sources.title: NBC News - Chicago Grimes Sisters' Murders Hit 59 Years Without Answers
CBS Chicago - 2 Investigators: The Unsolved 1956 Murder Of The Grimes Sisters
Chicago Reader - Death and the Maidens

narrative: Barbara Grimes, 15, and her sister Patricia, 12, left their family's home on Chicago's Southwest Side on the evening of December 28, 1956, to see the Elvis Presley film Love Me Tender at the Brighton Theater. According to NBC News, an older sister and younger brother were to meet them at a bus stop afterwards, but the girls never arrived. Patricia was three days short of her thirteenth birthday, and many reports give her age as 13.

The search that followed has been described as one of the most labor-intensive missing-person efforts in Cook County history, involving hundreds of officers. NBC News reports that Presley himself issued a public appeal asking the girls to come home. Some early investigators believed the sisters had run away, a view their parents rejected.

On January 22, 1957, a construction worker driving past noticed two unclothed, frozen bodies behind a guard rail on German Church Road in an unincorporated area near Willow Springs, in what CBS Chicago describes as present-day Burr Ridge. They were identified as Barbara and Patricia. According to published summaries of the autopsy, examiners found no clearly fatal injuries and attributed the deaths to secondary shock from exposure to cold, estimating that the sisters had died within hours of their disappearance. Their death certificates list the deaths as murders.

Days after the discovery, police arrested Edward "Bennie" Bedwell, a 21-year-old drifter, after restaurant owners said they had seen him with two girls resembling the sisters. After prolonged questioning he signed a confession and was charged on January 27, 1957. He then recanted, saying the statement had been coerced, and its details conflicted with the autopsy findings on the time of death. The charges were dropped in March 1957. Other men were questioned over the following months and years, and none was prosecuted.

Retired West Chicago police officer Raymond Johnson, who began researching the case around 2009, has argued publicly that Charles Melquist, who was convicted of the 1958 murder of 15-year-old Bonnie Leigh Scott, may have been responsible. Melquist was never charged in the Grimes case and died in 2010; the theory has not been confirmed by authorities. CBS Chicago reported in 2018 that the Cook County Sheriff's Office was still working the case, with a cold case detective assigned. No one has been convicted in the deaths of Barbara and Patricia Grimes.

name: Daniel Barter
summary: Four-year-old Daniel "Danny" Barter vanished on June 18, 1959, from his family's campsite on Perdido Bay, Alabama. A search lasting more than a week, with hundreds of volunteers, divers and bloodhounds, found no trace of him. The FBI and the Baldwin County Sheriff's Office reopened the case in 2008, and investigators believe he may have been abducted.
lastSeen: June 18, 1959, family campsite on the shore of Perdido Bay, AL

sources.title: CNN - FBI reopens 1959 case of missing 4-year-old
The Charley Project - Daniel Barter (archived)

narrative: Daniel Barter, known as Danny, was four years old when he disappeared during a family camping trip to Perdido Bay on the Alabama Gulf Coast. According to the Charley Project, he was born on December 12, 1954, and lived with his family in Mobile, about an hour's drive from the campsite. CNN reported that he was the third youngest of Paul and Maxine Barter's seven children.

On the morning of June 18, 1959, Danny had just come back from a trip to a store with his father, CNN reported. The Charley Project states that he was last seen playing near the bank of the bay between 9:30 and 10:00 a.m., barefoot and wearing only gray boxer shorts, while his parents prepared fishing gear. His mother began looking for him ten to fifteen minutes after she had last seen him and could not find him.

The search was immediate and extensive. According to the CUE Center for Missing Persons, it involved several hundred volunteers and emergency personnel, U.S. Navy personnel, bloodhounds, helicopters, skin divers and mounted posses. Because the area is swampy and home to alligators, hunters killed and opened alligators to check for remains; none were found. The CUE Center's summary says the bloodhounds repeatedly followed the boy's scent to the same spot on a nearby road. No physical evidence of what happened to him was recovered.

Danny's mother told the Mobile Register in 1959 that her son was afraid of the water and that she had come to believe someone picked him up along the road. The Charley Project records that the family later described incidents before the disappearance in which unknown men appeared to be watching the children, including a man seen looking into the boys' bedroom window in Mobile. Investigators were not able to confirm an abduction at the time, and no ransom demand was ever received.

In 2008 the FBI and the Baldwin County Sheriff's Office reopened the case. An FBI spokeswoman told CNN in 2009 that a lead arose when someone was overheard discussing what had happened to the boy in a public place; no further details were released. The FBI published an age-progressed image, and relatives gathered at the campsite in June 2009 to mark fifty years. The Charley Project notes that many original investigative files have been lost or destroyed. Danny's father died in 1965 and his mother in 1995. No arrest has been made and Danny has never been located; the Charley Project classifies the case as a non-family abduction.

name: Henry Lee Lucas Victims
summary: Henry Lee Lucas confessed to hundreds of murders but most were unverifiable. He was confirmed in several cases including the murder of his mother and with accomplice Ottis Toole. A Texas task force eventually cleared him of all but a few confessed murders. He died in prison in 2001.
lastSeen: N/A

sources.title: Henry Lee Lucas - Wikipedia
The Story of Henry Lee Lucas, the Notorious Subject of Netflix's 'The Confession Killer' - TIME
Henry Lee Lucas Claimed He Killed 600 People - Oxygen
The Twilight of the Texas Rangers - Texas Monthly

narrative: Henry Lee Lucas (1936-2001) occupies a singular and cautionary place in American criminal history: a man who confessed to hundreds of murders across the country, most of which investigators later concluded he did not commit. Untangling his small number of confirmed killings from his vast catalogue of discredited confessions remains the central difficulty of the case, and it is why so many genuinely unsolved homicides were, for a time, wrongly closed.

Lucas's earliest documented killing was that of his mother, Viola Lucas, in Tecumseh, Michigan, in January 1960; he was convicted and served roughly a decade in prison. After his release he drifted through the South, and by the early 1980s was living in Texas with an accomplice, Ottis Toole. Following an arrest on a weapons charge in June 1983, Lucas confessed to the murders of Kate (Katie Pearl) Rich, an elderly woman in Ringgold, Texas, and of Frieda 'Becky' Powell, Toole's teenage niece and Lucas's companion. These killings, together with his mother's death, are the murders most reliably attributed to him. Reporting has often summarized his verifiable toll as roughly three victims, though he was ultimately convicted of eleven homicides.

What made Lucas notorious was not those crimes but what followed. In custody he began confessing to a staggering number of murders, eventually claiming responsibility for some 600 killings nationwide. The Texas Department of Public Safety and Texas Rangers organized a 'Lucas Task Force' to coordinate the flood of inquiries, and detectives from many jurisdictions traveled to interview him about their unsolved cases. Critics later charged that Lucas was frequently shown case files, crime-scene photographs, and details before interviews, and was rewarded with privileges such as food, cigarettes and attention, all of which gave him incentive and material to fabricate convincing admissions.

The confessions began to collapse under scrutiny. A 1985 Dallas Times Herald investigation demonstrated that Lucas could not physically have been present for many of the murders he claimed, given documented travel and work records. Waco prosecutor Vic Feazell and Texas Attorney General Jim Mattox pursued their own review; Mattox's office concluded that Lucas was a fabricator and warned that some officials appeared to have 'cleared cases just to get them off the books.' The episode became one of the most-cited examples of the dangers of false confessions and prompted reassessment of interrogation practices.

Lucas had meanwhile been sentenced to death for the murder of an unidentified woman known as 'Orange Socks,' found in Williamson County, Texas, on Halloween 1979 and later reported to be identified as Debra Jackson. Doubts about that conviction were serious: evidence suggested Lucas may have been in another state, and details of his confession appeared to trace back to material he had been shown. In 1998, Governor George W. Bush commuted Lucas's death sentence to life imprisonment, the only death sentence Bush commuted during his tenure as governor, citing doubt about his guilt in that case.

Lucas died of heart failure in a Texas prison on March 12, 2001, at age 64. The lasting legacy of his case is twofold: a handful of genuine murders for which he was justly held responsible, and a far larger number of real, still-unsolved homicides that were improperly marked as closed on the strength of confessions now widely regarded as false. Because of this, the true fate of many of the victims once attributed to Lucas remains uncertain, which is why the case is best described as only partially solved.

name: Boston Strangler Victims
summary: Thirteen women were strangled in the Boston area between 1962 and 1964. Albert DeSalvo confessed to all 13 murders but was never tried for them. DNA evidence collected in 2013 linked DeSalvo to the last victim, Mary Sullivan. Questions remain about whether DeSalvo committed all the murders.
lastSeen: N/A

sources.title: Boston Strangler - Wikipedia
Albert DeSalvo - Wikipedia
Solving Cold Cases with DNA: The Boston Strangler Case - Office of Justice Programs
Lab: Confessed Boston Strangler's DNA on slain woman's body - CNN
Police Find First Victim of 'Boston Strangler' - Mass Moments
Who was the Boston Strangler? New evidence may point to a different suspect - CBS Boston

narrative: Between June 14, 1962, and January 4, 1964, at least 13 women were killed in the Greater Boston area in a series of murders that came to be attributed to a single offender the press dubbed the "Boston Strangler." The victims ranged in age from 19 to 85 and were generally attacked in their own apartments; most were sexually assaulted and strangled, frequently with articles of their own clothing left knotted around the neck. The first known victim was 55-year-old Anna Slesers, found on June 14, 1962, and the last widely counted victim was 19-year-old Mary Sullivan, killed on January 4, 1964, in her Charles Street apartment.

The killings generated one of the largest manhunts in Massachusetts history, and the state assembled a special "Strangler Bureau" to coordinate the investigation. Investigators were never certain that a single person was responsible: the victims varied widely in age and circumstance, and the methods differed enough that some detectives and later analysts believed more than one killer may have been involved. No one was ever charged with the stranglings during the years the cases were actively worked, and much of the physical evidence predated modern forensic techniques.

The case became linked to Albert DeSalvo, who was in custody on unrelated sexual-assault charges connected to the "Green Man" and "Measuring Man" offenses. While held, DeSalvo confessed in detail to being the Boston Strangler, initially to a fellow inmate and then to authorities through his attorney, F. Lee Bailey. His account included details that drew attention, but it also contained errors, and skeptics noted that some information could have come from press coverage or from investigators. His confession was never used to try him for the murders; a judge ruled it inadmissible, and DeSalvo was instead convicted and sentenced to life in 1967 for the earlier sexual offenses. He later recanted. DeSalvo was never tried for any of the stranglings and was stabbed to death in the Walpole State Prison infirmary in 1973; his killing was never solved.

For decades DeSalvo's guilt remained disputed. Former FBI profiler John Douglas and others questioned whether one man committed all the crimes, and some victims' families and researchers argued that the confession was unreliable. A partial resolution came in July 2013, when Massachusetts authorities announced that DNA recovered from the scene of Mary Sullivan's murder produced a familial match to DeSalvo through a relative. Investigators then exhumed DeSalvo's remains, and testing of the recovered DNA was reported as a definitive match, which officials said established that DeSalvo raped and killed Sullivan.

The 2013 DNA evidence directly ties DeSalvo to only one of the 13 deaths. The other cases were not resolved by that testing, and questions remain about whether DeSalvo was responsible for all, some, or none of the remaining murders, and whether one or more other offenders were involved. As a result, the Boston Strangler killings are best described as partially solved: forensically confirmed in the Sullivan case, but still uncertain as to the other victims.

name: William 'Billy' Jones Jr.
summary: Three-year-old William "Billy" Jones Jr. disappeared on December 17, 1962, while playing outside with his younger sister in Vineland, New Jersey. He was last seen near a neighbor's house at about 11:45 a.m. Searches by volunteers and the National Guard found nothing. Vineland police reopened the case in 2009, and the FBI still lists him as missing.
lastSeen: December 17, 1962, about 11:45 a.m., outside a neighbor's house in Vineland, NJ

narrative: William Ebeneezer Jones Jr., called Billy, was born on March 5, 1959, and was three years old when he went missing from his neighborhood in Vineland, in southern New Jersey. His case is described by Fox News as believed to be the longest unsolved case of a missing child under five in the state, and it is carried on the FBI's kidnappings and missing persons list.

According to the FBI, Billy was last seen outside a neighbor's house at around 11:45 a.m. on December 17, 1962. He had gone out to play with his younger sister, Jill. Sources differ slightly on the exact spot: the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children says he was last seen in the back yard of his residence, while Fox News reported that he vanished from the front yard. The FBI describes him as wearing a light blue or grayish snowsuit with a navy collar and silver buttons, a matching hat, and tan high-top shoes with yellow laces, and says he reportedly had a dime in his pocket given to him by his mother.

A search began within about an hour. New Jersey 101.5 reports that it grew to involve more than 100 people and the New Jersey National Guard, and Fox News reported that hundreds of volunteers eventually took part. Investigators also excavated ground near an abandoned automobile dump. Nothing connected to Billy was found.

At the time he disappeared Billy was 3 feet 6 inches tall and weighed 35 pounds, with brown or blond hair and blue eyes. The FBI notes a distinctive vaccination scar on the back of his left arm that was said to resemble a giraffe. The bureau has also published photographs of the family home and neighborhood, and an image age-progressed to 50.

Vineland Police Detective Kristian Kirchner reopened the investigation in 2009, and in 2012, on the fiftieth anniversary, an FBI special agent told Fox News the bureau hoped to develop new leads. By then both of Billy's parents had died. His sister told Fox News she has no memory of the day and believes her brother may have been taken by someone who had lost a child and raised as their own; that is her personal view and has not been established by investigators. The National Center for Missing and Exploited Children continues to circulate an age-progressed image. No one has been charged, and Billy has never been found. The FBI asks anyone with information to contact the Vineland Police Department or the bureau's Newark field office.

name: 16th Street Baptist Church Bombing Victims
summary: A dynamite bomb planted by Ku Klux Klan members killed Addie Mae Collins, Carole Robertson and Cynthia Wesley, all 14, and Denise McNair, 11, at Birmingham's 16th Street Baptist Church on September 15, 1963. Robert Chambliss was convicted in 1977, Thomas Blanton Jr. in 2001 and Bobby Frank Cherry in 2002. All three died in prison.
lastSeen: September 15, 1963, 16th Street Baptist Church, Birmingham, AL

sources.title: FBI - Famous Cases: Baptist Street Church Bombing (archived)
National Park Service - 16th Street Baptist Church Bombing (1963)
The New York Times - Thomas Blanton, Who Bombed a Birmingham Church, Dies at 82 (archived)
The Guardian - Former Klansman convicted of 1963 church bombing
NPR - 16th Street Baptist Church Bombing: Forty Years Later
Wikipedia - 16th Street Baptist Church bombing

narrative: On the morning of Sunday, September 15, 1963, a dynamite bomb exploded at the 16th Street Baptist Church in downtown Birmingham, Alabama. The FBI places the blast at about 10:24 a.m., in a back stairwell of the building. It killed four girls who were in a basement room on the other side of the wall: Addie Mae Collins, Carole Robertson and Cynthia Wesley, all 14, and Carol Denise McNair, 11. More than 20 other people were injured, among them Addie Mae's sister Sarah, who lost an eye.

The church was the largest Black congregation in the city and a central meeting place for the civil rights movement, and it had received bomb threats before. According to the National Park Service, more than 8,000 people attended the funeral service for the girls, and the attack drew national and international attention to the violence surrounding desegregation in Birmingham.

The FBI states that dozens of agents worked the case and that by 1965 the bureau had identified four suspects, all Klan members: Robert E. Chambliss, Bobby Frank Cherry, Herman Frank Cash and Thomas E. Blanton Jr. No federal charges were brought in the 1960s. The bureau's own account attributes this to reluctant witnesses, a lack of physical evidence and surveillance material that was then inadmissible. Other accounts, including The New York Times, say FBI Director J. Edgar Hoover blocked efforts by the Birmingham office to bring charges, a claim the FBI disputes.

Alabama Attorney General Bill Baxley reopened the case in the 1970s. On November 18, 1977, a jury convicted Chambliss of the murder of Denise McNair, and he was sentenced to life imprisonment. He died in 1985. Herman Cash died in 1994 without ever being charged.

The FBI reopened its investigation in the mid-1990s, and Blanton and Cherry were indicted in May 2000. Blanton was convicted of four counts of first-degree murder on May 1, 2001, and received four life sentences. Cherry was convicted of the same charges on May 22, 2002, after a trial in which, The Guardian reported, members of his own family testified that he had boasted of taking part. He denied involvement. Cherry died in prison in November 2004. Blanton was denied parole in 2016 and died on June 26, 2020, at age 82, at the Donaldson Correctional Facility in Bessemer, Alabama, according to The New York Times. He was the last survivor of the three men convicted.

name: Frank Sinatra Jr. Kidnapping
summary: Singer Frank Sinatra Jr., 19, was abducted at gunpoint from Harrah's Club Lodge at Lake Tahoe on December 8, 1963. His father paid a $240,000 ransom and he was freed unharmed in Los Angeles on December 11. Barry Keenan, Joe Amsler and John Irwin were arrested within days, and all three were convicted in 1964. Nearly all the ransom was recovered.
lastSeen: December 8, 1963, Harrah's Club Lodge, Lake Tahoe, NV

sources.title: FBI - Famous Cases: Frank Sinatra, Jr., Kidnapping (archived)
CBS News / AP - Frank Sinatra Jr. dies at 72
The Guardian - Frank Sinatra Jr obituary
Wikipedia - Frank Sinatra Jr.

narrative: Frank Sinatra Jr., the 19-year-old son of the singer Frank Sinatra, was at the start of his own music career in December 1963 and was performing at Harrah's Club Lodge at Lake Tahoe, on the Nevada-California border. According to the FBI, two 23-year-old former high school classmates from Los Angeles, Barry Keenan and Joe Amsler, had been following him from city to city for several weeks with a plan to abduct him and demand money from his father.

At about 9 p.m. on December 8, 1963, the FBI's account states, Sinatra was resting in his dressing room with a friend when Keenan knocked, pretending to deliver a package. The two men tied up the friend with tape, blindfolded Sinatra and took him out a side door to a waiting car. The friend freed himself and raised the alarm. Roadblocks were set up and police actually stopped the car, but the men talked their way through and drove to a house in the Canoga Park area of Los Angeles.

The FBI's Reno office joined the case within the hour, and agents advised the elder Sinatra to wait for a demand, pay it and let the bureau trace the money. A third participant, John Irwin, acted as the contact. On December 10 he passed on a demand for $240,000. The FBI photographed the bills and left them, as instructed, between two school buses in Sepulveda, California, in the early hours of December 11.

While Keenan and Amsler collected the money, the FBI says, Irwin became nervous and released the victim. Sinatra walked a few miles and alerted a security guard in Bel Air, who drove him to his mother's home hidden in the trunk of a patrol car to avoid the press. He was not physically harmed.

Agents traced the hideout in Canoga Park and gathered evidence there. Irwin then confided in his brother, who called the FBI's San Diego office, and Keenan and Amsler were arrested within hours. Nearly all of the ransom was recovered. At trial the defense argued that Sinatra had staged the kidnapping for publicity; the FBI says the evidence, including a confession letter Keenan had left in a safe-deposit box, contradicted that claim. All three men were convicted in March 1964, The Guardian reported. According to CBS News and the Associated Press, Keenan was sentenced to life plus 75 years, but his sentence was later reduced after he was found to have been legally insane at the time, and he was paroled in 1968 after about four and a half years. Frank Sinatra Jr. continued performing and died on March 16, 2016, aged 72.

name: John F. Kennedy Assassination
summary: President John F. Kennedy, 46, was shot dead in his motorcade in Dealey Plaza, Dallas, on November 22, 1963. Lee Harvey Oswald was charged but was killed by Jack Ruby two days later and never tried. The Warren Commission found Oswald acted alone; a 1979 House committee agreed he fired the fatal shots but said a conspiracy was probable.
lastSeen: November 22, 1963, Dealey Plaza, Dallas, TX

narrative: President John F. Kennedy arrived at Love Field in Dallas at 11:40 a.m. on Friday, November 22, 1963, on the second day of a Texas trip, according to the Warren Commission's report. A motorcade was to take him through downtown Dallas to a luncheon at the Trade Mart. At about 12:30 p.m., as the open presidential limousine passed through Dealey Plaza, rifle shots struck the president and seriously wounded Texas Governor John Connally, who was riding in the same car. Kennedy was taken to Parkland Memorial Hospital and pronounced dead at 1:00 p.m. He was 46.

Dallas police arrested Lee Harvey Oswald, an employee of the Texas School Book Depository overlooking the plaza, in a movie theater that afternoon. He was charged under Texas law with the murder of the president and of Dallas police officer J.D. Tippit, who was shot dead about 45 minutes after the assassination. Oswald denied the charges. On November 24, while being moved through the basement of Dallas police headquarters, he was shot by nightclub operator Jack Ruby and died at Parkland. Ruby was convicted of murdering Oswald; the conviction was overturned on appeal, and Ruby died in 1967 while awaiting a new trial.

Because Oswald was never tried, no court ruled on his guilt. President Lyndon Johnson appointed a commission chaired by Chief Justice Earl Warren on November 29, 1963. Its report, delivered on September 24, 1964, concluded that Oswald fired the shots from the sixth floor of the depository and that there was no evidence that he or Ruby was part of a conspiracy.

The House Select Committee on Assassinations re-examined the case in the late 1970s. Its findings, published by the National Archives, state that Oswald fired three shots and that the third killed the president. Relying on acoustic evidence, the committee also concluded that there was a high probability that two gunmen fired and that Kennedy was probably assassinated as a result of a conspiracy, though it could not identify another gunman. It found that the Soviet and Cuban governments, the Secret Service, the FBI and the CIA were not involved. A later National Academy of Sciences panel disputed the acoustic analysis, and the Justice Department concluded that no persuasive evidence supported a conspiracy.

Congress passed a records act in 1992 requiring release of assassination files. After staged releases, President Donald Trump signed an executive order on January 23, 2025, and on March 18, 2025, the National Archives released the records that had been withheld for classification. Historians told the BBC they did not expect the material to change the basic account.

name: Medgar Evers
summary: Medgar Evers, 37, the NAACP's first field secretary in Mississippi, was shot in the back outside his Jackson home shortly after midnight on June 12, 1963, and died within the hour. Byron De La Beckwith was tried twice in 1964; both all-white juries deadlocked. He was convicted of murder on February 5, 1994, and died in prison in 2001.
lastSeen: June 12, 1963, his home in Jackson, MS

sources.title: FBI - Famous Cases: Medgar Evers (archived)
NAACP - Medgar Evers
PBS NewsHour - Medgar Evers case background
National Park Service - Medgar and Myrlie Evers Home National Monument: History & Culture
Wikipedia - Medgar Evers

narrative: Medgar Evers was born in Decatur, Mississippi, on July 2, 1925, and served in the U.S. Army during the Second World War. As the NAACP's first field secretary in Mississippi, based in Jackson, he set up local chapters, organized voter registration drives and led campaigns to desegregate schools, parks and beaches, according to the NAACP. The organization says there had been several earlier attempts on his life.

At about half past midnight on June 12, 1963, Evers returned home from an NAACP meeting, the FBI's case history states. A few hours earlier President Kennedy had delivered a televised address on civil rights. As Evers walked from his car, carrying T-shirts printed with the slogan "Jim Crow Must Go," a rifle bullet struck him in the back. He reached the steps of the house and collapsed. His wife, Myrlie, and their three children came outside after hearing the shot. He died at a hospital less than an hour later, aged 37, and was buried with full military honors at Arlington National Cemetery.

Jackson police found an Enfield rifle on a wooded rise across the street. A fingerprint recovered from its scope was sent to the FBI, which matched it to Byron De La Beckwith, a white supremacist and segregationist, using his military service prints. He was arrested several days later.

Beckwith was tried for murder twice in 1964, in February and April. Both all-white juries failed to reach a verdict, and he went free. These were mistrials, not acquittals, which left the state able to prosecute again. PBS NewsHour reported that the case was revived after the Jackson Clarion-Ledger examined records of the Mississippi State Sovereignty Commission, unsealed in 1989, that pointed to possible jury tampering and official misconduct in the second trial. Myrlie Evers asked prosecutors to reopen the case, and Hinds County Assistant District Attorney Bobby DeLaughter took it on.

A grand jury indicted Beckwith in December 1990, relying in part on witnesses who said they had heard him boast of the killing, according to the FBI. Evers's body was exhumed for a new autopsy. The third trial began in Jackson in January 1994, and on February 5, 1994, a racially mixed jury found Beckwith guilty of murder. He was sentenced to life in prison. The Mississippi Supreme Court upheld the conviction in 1997, and Beckwith died in custody on January 21, 2001, aged 80. The Evers home in Jackson is now the Medgar and Myrlie Evers Home National Monument, and Evers was posthumously awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2024.

name: James Chaney, Andrew Goodman & Michael Schwerner
summary: Civil rights workers James Chaney, 21, Andrew Goodman, 20, and Michael Schwerner, 24, were killed by Ku Klux Klan members in Neshoba County, Mississippi, on June 21, 1964. Their bodies were found 44 days later. Seven men were convicted of federal conspiracy charges in 1967, and Edgar Ray Killen was convicted of manslaughter in 2005. He died in prison in 2018.
lastSeen: June 21, 1964, leaving the Neshoba County jail in Philadelphia, MS, about 10:30 p.m.

sources.title: FBI - Famous Cases: Mississippi Burning (archived)
The New York Times - Former Klansman Guilty of Manslaughter in 1964 Deaths (archived)
Clarion-Ledger - Klansman who orchestrated Mississippi Burning killings dies in prison
PBS American Experience - Murder in Mississippi
Wikipedia - Murders of Chaney, Goodman, and Schwerner

narrative: James Chaney, a 21-year-old Black Mississippian, and Michael Schwerner, 24, of New York, worked for the Congress of Racial Equality in Meridian, Mississippi. Andrew Goodman, 20, a Queens College student, had just arrived as a volunteer for the 1964 Freedom Summer voter registration project. According to PBS's American Experience, Klan members had beaten congregants and burned Mount Zion Church in Neshoba County on June 16, a church where Schwerner had been organizing.

On Sunday, June 21, 1964, the three men drove to Neshoba County to look into the fire. That afternoon Deputy Sheriff Cecil Price stopped their station wagon and arrested them; Chaney, who was driving, was charged with speeding and the other two were held for investigation. They were released from the jail in Philadelphia, Mississippi, at about 10:30 p.m. and drove off toward Meridian. The FBI's case history states that Klan members followed them according to a plan made in advance. They were not seen alive again.

The Justice Department asked the FBI to investigate the next day. The burned station wagon was found on June 23, leading the bureau to name the case MIBURN, for "Mississippi Burning." Agents, assisted by the National Guard, searched the area for weeks. On August 4, acting on an informant's tip, the FBI recovered the three bodies from beneath an earthen dam on a local farm. They had been shot.

Mississippi brought no murder charges at the time. Federal prosecutors charged 18 men with conspiring to violate the victims' civil rights. On October 20, 1967, a federal jury convicted seven of them: Cecil Price, Klan leader Sam Bowers, Alton Wayne Roberts, Jimmy Snowden, Billy Wayne Posey, Horace Doyle Barnette and Jimmy Arledge. None served more than six years. Others, including Sheriff Lawrence Rainey, were acquitted. The jury deadlocked on Edgar Ray Killen, a part-time preacher, reportedly because one juror would not convict a minister.

The Clarion-Ledger reports that Mississippi authorities reopened the case in 1999. A Neshoba County grand jury indicted Killen for murder in January 2005; The New York Times reported that the grand jury heard evidence concerning the surviving original defendants but indicted only him. On June 21, 2005, the 41st anniversary of the killings, a jury found Killen, then 80, guilty of three counts of manslaughter rather than murder. He was sentenced to 60 years and maintained his innocence. State and federal authorities announced in June 2016 that the investigation was closed. Killen died in prison on January 11, 2018, at 92. No one was ever convicted of murder in the case.

name: Kitty Genovese
summary: Kitty Genovese, 28, was stabbed to death near her apartment in Kew Gardens, Queens, early on March 13, 1964. Winston Moseley confessed, was convicted of murder that June and died in prison in 2016. A New York Times report that 38 neighbors watched and did nothing shaped the idea of the bystander effect but was later found to be greatly exaggerated.
lastSeen: March 13, 1964, Austin Street, Kew Gardens, Queens

sources.title: The New York Times - Winston Moseley, Who Killed Kitty Genovese, Dies in Prison at 81 (archived)
NPR - What Really Happened The Night Kitty Genovese Was Murdered?
The Washington Post - Her shocking murder became the stuff of legend. But everyone got the story wrong. (archived)
Wikipedia - Murder of Kitty Genovese

narrative: Catherine "Kitty" Genovese was born in Brooklyn on July 7, 1935, and in 1964 was managing a bar, Ev's Eleventh Hour, in Queens. She shared an apartment on Austin Street in Kew Gardens with her partner, Mary Ann Zielonko. In the early hours of March 13, 1964, she drove home from work and parked near the Long Island Rail Road station, a short walk from her door, arriving at about 3:15 a.m.

Winston Moseley, a 29-year-old married father of two from South Ozone Park with no criminal record, had been driving around looking for a victim, according to later accounts, and followed her. He stabbed her on the sidewalk. Author Kevin Cook told NPR that her screams woke people on both sides of the street and that a man shouted from a window, after which Moseley retreated. Genovese made her way around the corner, out of sight of most of those who had been woken, and into the vestibule of a building. Moseley returned, found her there, stabbed her again and raped her. The New York Times later reported that the episode lasted about half an hour and that a 70-year-old neighbor came out and held her until police arrived. She died on the way to a hospital.

Moseley was arrested six days later during a burglary and confessed while in custody. He was tried in June 1964, found guilty of murder and sentenced to death. In 1967 an appeals court reduced the sentence to life imprisonment. In 1968 he escaped while being taken to a hospital in Buffalo, raped a woman and held hostages before he was recaptured. He was denied parole 18 times, the last in 2015, and died at the Clinton Correctional Facility in Dannemora, New York, on March 28, 2016, aged 81.

The case became widely known because of a front-page New York Times article published on March 27, 1964, which said that 38 law-abiding citizens had watched the killing over more than half an hour without calling the police. The account prompted national debate and research into what psychologists called the bystander effect, and it is often cited among the factors behind simplified emergency calling; the Times notes that the unified 911 system was established in 1968.

Later reporting found the original account seriously flawed. In Moseley's 2016 obituary, the Times wrote that its article had grossly exaggerated the number of witnesses and what they perceived: no one saw the whole attack, only a few glimpsed parts of it, many believed they were hearing a quarrel, there were two attacks rather than three, and two people did call the police. Genovese's brother Bill examined the case in the 2016 documentary The Witness.

name: Alice Crimmins
summary: Eddie Crimmins Jr., 5, and his sister Alice Marie "Missy" Crimmins, 4, were reported missing from their Queens apartment on July 14, 1965, and were found dead five days apart. Their mother, Alice Crimmins, was tried twice; a manslaughter conviction for Missy's death was reinstated in 1975, while a murder conviction for Eddie's death was overturned and dismissed. She was paroled in 1977.
lastSeen: Reported missing the morning of July 14, 1965, from the family apartment in Kew Gardens Hills, Queens

sources.title: Encyclopedia.com - Alice Crimmins Trials: 1968 & 1971
The Daily Beast - Did Alice Crimmins Kill Her Kids?
Hazlitt - 'Why Can't You Behave?': Revisiting the Case of Alice Crimmins
Murderpedia - Alice Crimmins
Wikipedia - Alice Crimmins

narrative: On the morning of July 14, 1965, Alice Crimmins reported that her two children, five-year-old Eddie Jr. and four-year-old Alice Marie, known as Missy, were missing from their bedroom in the family's garden apartment in Kew Gardens Hills, Queens. According to case summaries compiled by Encyclopedia.com and Murderpedia, Missy's body was found that same afternoon in a vacant lot not far from the apartment; she had been strangled. Eddie's body was found on July 19 on an embankment near the Van Wyck Expressway, about a mile from home. His remains were too decomposed for a cause of death to be established.

The investigation centered on the children's mother. Accounts of the case, including a 2014 Daily Beast review, report that police kept her under surveillance and recorded her conversations for an extended period, and that earlier grand juries did not return an indictment. According to Murderpedia, she was arrested on September 11, 1967, after a neighbor, Sophie Earomirski, came forward to say she had seen a woman carrying a bundle and walking with a child in the early hours of July 14.

Crimmins was tried in May 1968 for Missy's death. The jury found her guilty of first-degree manslaughter and she was sentenced to five to twenty years. In December 1969 an appellate court ordered a new trial, in part because jurors had made an unauthorized visit to the scene, according to Encyclopedia.com; the state's highest court upheld that reversal the following year.

At a second trial, held from March 15 to April 23, 1971, she faced a murder charge in Eddie's death along with a manslaughter charge in Missy's. The jury convicted her on both counts and she received a life sentence plus five to twenty years. In 1973 the Appellate Division overturned both verdicts, dismissing the murder charge on the ground that the prosecution had not proved Eddie's death resulted from a criminal act, and ordering a new trial on the manslaughter count. In February 1975 the New York Court of Appeals let the dismissal of the murder charge stand but reinstated the manslaughter conviction. No third trial took place.

Crimmins returned to prison, later entered a work-release program, and was paroled in 1977; the sources consulted give differing months for the parole date. She married during her work-release period and has since lived privately under her married name.

The case has remained a subject of debate. Writers who have re-examined it, including in Hazlitt and the Daily Beast, argue that the prosecution and press coverage dwelt heavily on Crimmins's personal life and that the physical evidence was limited. Legally, the outcome is a single standing conviction for manslaughter in Missy's death; no one stands convicted in the death of Eddie Crimmins Jr.

Crimmins is released on parole.

name: Jimmie Lee Jackson
summary: Jimmie Lee Jackson, 26, a church deacon and voting rights activist, was shot by Alabama state trooper James Bonard Fowler in Marion on February 18, 1965, and died eight days later. His death prompted the Selma to Montgomery marches. Fowler was indicted for murder in 2007 and pleaded guilty in 2010 to misdemeanor second-degree manslaughter, receiving a six-month jail sentence.
lastSeen: February 18, 1965, Mack's Cafe, Marion, AL

sources.title: National Park Service - Jimmie Lee Jackson
Stanford King Institute - Jackson, Jimmie Lee
WBUR (AP) - Ex-Trooper Pleads Guilty In Civil Rights-Era Slaying
Wikipedia - Murder of Jimmie Lee Jackson
Wikipedia - James Bonard Fowler

narrative: Jimmie Lee Jackson was born in Marion, Alabama, on December 16, 1938. According to the National Park Service and Stanford University's King Institute, he was a former soldier, a laborer who worked in logging and farming, a father, and the youngest deacon at his church. He became active in the local voting rights campaign after seeing his grandfather turned away when trying to register to vote.

On the night of February 18, 1965, demonstrators in Marion set out from Zion United Methodist Church toward the Perry County Jail to protest the arrest of civil rights worker James Orange. The National Park Service account states that the streetlights went dark and state troopers moved against the marchers. Jackson, his mother and other family members took shelter in Mack's Cafe, behind the church. According to the King Institute, Jackson was trying to protect his mother from being beaten when trooper James Bonard Fowler shot him in the abdomen. He was taken to Good Samaritan Hospital in Selma, where he died on February 26, 1965.

Martin Luther King Jr. spoke at Jackson's funeral on March 3. Historians and the National Park Service describe his death as the catalyst for the march from Selma toward Montgomery that began on March 7, 1965, the day known as Bloody Sunday. The marches built support for the Voting Rights Act, which became law later that year.

A grand jury declined to indict Fowler in 1965, and his name was not widely known for decades. In a 2005 interview with the Anniston Star he acknowledged firing the shots and said he had acted in self-defense, asserting that Jackson had tried to take his gun. Perry County District Attorney Michael Jackson, who is not related to the victim, reopened the case, and a grand jury indicted Fowler on murder charges in May 2007.

On November 15, 2010, two weeks before his trial was due to begin, Fowler, then 77, pleaded guilty to misdemeanor second-degree manslaughter. According to the Associated Press report carried by WBUR, he was sentenced to six months in jail in Geneva County, followed by probation, and he apologized to Jackson's family in court while saying he had not intended to kill anyone. Jackson's daughter, Cordelia Billingsley, told reporters that the outcome could not bring real closure.

Fowler was released after about five months because of health problems, according to published accounts, and he died on July 5, 2015. The plea remains the only criminal conviction arising from Jackson's death, which came 45 years after the shooting.

name: Cheri Jo Bates
summary: Cheri Jo Bates, 18, a Riverside City College freshman, was stabbed to death near the campus library on the night of October 30, 1966; her body was found the next morning. Letters once thought to tie the killing to the Zodiac were traced in 2020 to an unrelated hoaxer, and Riverside police said in 2021 that they do not consider the case Zodiac-related. No one has been charged.
lastSeen: October 30, 1966, leaving home for the Riverside City College library, Riverside, CA

sources.title: Riverside Police Department - Cold Case Unit
ABC7 Los Angeles - Who killed Cheri Jo Bates? Cold case continues to haunt Riverside 6 decades later
Patch - Police Refute Claims That Riverside Slaying Was Zodiac Killer
Wikipedia - Murder of Cheri Jo Bates

narrative: Cheri Jo Bates was an 18-year-old freshman at Riverside City College in Riverside, California. According to the Riverside Police Department's Cold Case Unit, her father, Joseph Bates, reported her missing at 5:45 a.m. on October 31, 1966; she had left a note at home the previous day saying she was going to the college library. At about 6:30 that morning a passerby found her body in an alleyway near Terracina Drive and Fairfax Avenue, beside the campus. Her death was ruled a homicide.

Bates had been stabbed and slashed. Published accounts of the investigation state that her Volkswagen Beetle, parked near the library, had been tampered with so that it would not start, and investigators concluded that her attacker had disabled the car in order to approach her. A man's Timex watch with a broken strap was found near her body, along with a shoe print. ABC7 Los Angeles reported that she was found roughly 100 yards from the car.

About a month later, typewritten letters headed as a confession were mailed to the police and to the Riverside Press-Enterprise, and in 1967 handwritten notes followed. Those notes, and a 1971 letter in which the Zodiac referred to activity in Riverside, led to years of speculation that Bates had been an early Zodiac victim.

Riverside police have rejected that theory. According to the department, an anonymous typed letter arrived in April 2016 from someone who admitted writing the handwritten notes as a teenager and called them a sick joke. In 2020, DNA recovered from a stamp identified the author, who police said had no involvement in the murder or in the Zodiac crimes. In August 2021 the Cold Case Unit stated that it does not regard the Bates homicide as Zodiac-related. When a private group publicly named a deceased man as the killer later in 2021, a police spokesman told reporters there was no evidence to support the claim, Patch reported.

The department has said that DNA developed from crime-scene evidence belongs to a male, and that detectives believe the killer was probably someone from the Riverside area. ABC7 reported in June 2026 that a 1982 police report described an unnamed person of interest who has never been arrested or charged, and that an earlier DNA comparison did not produce a match.

The case remains open. Riverside Police Chief Larry Gonzalez told ABC7 in 2026 that evidence is being re-examined with current DNA and fingerprint methods. A privately funded $50,000 reward was announced in 2021, and a friend of Bates has since offered $100,000 for information that resolves the case.

Bates leaves home for the Riverside City College library and is not seen alive by her family again.

name: Richard Speck Victims
summary: Richard Speck broke into a Chicago townhouse and methodically murdered eight student nurses. Corazon Amurao survived by hiding under a bed and later identified Speck. He was convicted and sentenced to death, later commuted to 400 years. He died in prison in 1991.
lastSeen: N/A

sources.title: Richard Speck - Wikipedia
Richard Speck | Serial Killer, Nurses, Prison Video, & Facts | Britannica (archived copy)
A mass murderer leaves eight women dead | July 13, 1966 | HISTORY
How Richard Speck's Rampage 50 Years Ago Changed a Nation | NBC News
Lead Prosecutor Reflects on Richard Speck's Chicago Murders | WTTW

narrative: On the night of July 13-14, 1966, eight student nurses were murdered inside a townhouse at 2319 East 100th Street in the South Deering neighborhood of Chicago, Illinois. The victims were Gloria Davy, Patricia Matusek, Nina Jo Schmale, Pamela Wilkening, Suzanne Farris, Mary Ann Jordan, Merlita Gargullo, and Valentina Pasion. Most were students affiliated with South Chicago Community Hospital who shared the residence as living quarters. The killer, 24-year-old drifter Richard Benjamin Speck, entered the townhouse and, over the course of several hours, systematically stabbed, strangled, and slashed the young women to death.

A ninth resident, 23-year-old Filipino exchange student nurse Corazon Amurao, survived by rolling under a bunk bed and remaining hidden and silent for hours while her friends were killed one by one. After the attacker left, she climbed onto a window ledge and screamed for help, alerting neighbors. Amurao became the central witness for the prosecution. Her account allowed police to establish that a single intruder was responsible and provided a detailed physical description, including that the man had a tattoo reading 'Born to Raise Hell' on his forearm.

The investigation moved quickly. Fingerprints recovered from the crime scene were matched to Speck, who had a prior criminal record. Publicity around the tattoo proved decisive: after Speck attempted suicide by cutting his wrists at a Chicago hotel, an emergency room physician, Dr. LeRoy Smith, recognized the 'Born to Raise Hell' tattoo from news reports and alerted authorities. Speck was arrested and identified while hospitalized in mid-July 1966.

Because of the extraordinary pretrial publicity, the trial was moved to Peoria, Illinois. Proceedings began on April 3, 1967. The emotional high point came when Corazon Amurao stepped down from the witness stand, walked directly to Speck, pointed at him, and declared, 'This is the man.' On April 15, 1967, after the jury deliberated less than an hour, Richard Speck was convicted of all eight murders and sentenced to death. His conviction is a matter of legal record.

Speck's death sentence was never carried out. In 1971 the U.S. Supreme Court set aside his death sentence, and after the Court's 1972 decision in Furman v. Georgia effectively invalidated existing capital-punishment statutes nationwide, Illinois courts resentenced him. He received a term of 400 to 1,200 years in prison and was held at the Stateville Correctional Center. Denied parole repeatedly, Speck remained incarcerated for the rest of his life.

On December 5, 1991, Richard Speck died of a heart attack at a hospital near the prison, one day before his 50th birthday. The case had a lasting impact on American life, widely cited as one of the mass murders that reshaped public perceptions of violent crime in the 1960s. Corazon Amurao completed her nursing career and largely avoided public attention in later decades. The case is closed: Speck was convicted and died in custody.

name: Valerie Percy
summary: Valerie Percy, 21, daughter of U.S. Senate candidate Charles Percy, was beaten and stabbed in her bedroom at the family's lakefront home in Kenilworth, Illinois, early on September 18, 1966. Her stepmother saw an intruder who fled. No one has ever been charged, and Kenilworth police said in September 2026 that they are still pursuing open leads.
lastSeen: September 17, 1966, family home in Kenilworth, IL

sources.title: CBS Chicago - Timeline of the unsolved murder of Valerie Percy in Kenilworth, Illinois
CBS Chicago - 60 years later, the murder of Valerie Percy in Kenilworth, Illinois remains unsolved
Yahoo News / Chicago Tribune - Vintage Chicago Tribune: The cold case of Valerie Percy
WTTW News - The Murder of Valerie Percy: 'Cloud Over Kenilworth' Remains Unsolved
NBC Chicago - 50 Years Later, New Information Puts Mysterious Murder of Valerie Percy Back in Spotlight

narrative: Valerie Percy was 21 and had recently graduated from Cornell University when she was killed in her family's home on the Lake Michigan shore in Kenilworth, a village north of Chicago. Her father, Charles Percy, a former Bell & Howell executive, was then the Republican candidate for the United States Senate, and she had been working on his campaign.

According to a Chicago Tribune retrospective, she went to bed at about 10 p.m. on September 17, 1966, after an evening with campaign colleagues. At around 5 a.m. on September 18 her stepmother, Loraine Percy, was woken by sounds in the house, went to Valerie's room and saw a man standing over the bed holding a flashlight. He ran from the house. Valerie had been beaten about the head and stabbed repeatedly. The Tribune account says the intruder was described as about 5 feet 8 inches tall and around 160 pounds.

Investigators concluded that the intruder had got in by breaking a pane of glass in a French door. The Tribune reported that palm and finger prints were recovered from the bedroom and from the broken glass. WTTW has reported that the weapon was never found and that a $50,000 reward produced no breakthrough. The killing was the first homicide on record in Kenilworth. Both Senate candidates suspended campaigning for a period, and Charles Percy won the election that November; he served in the Senate until 1985.

The inquiry became one of the largest in Illinois history. By 1972 investigators said they had pursued more than 1,300 leads and conducted thousands of interviews. CBS Chicago's timeline of the case notes that by 1973 attention had turned to men associated with a burglary ring, and in later years authors and reporters have put forward other theories. None of these resulted in charges, and no suspect has been officially identified as the killer.

The Illinois State Police led the case until 2002, when it passed to the Kenilworth Police Department and a regional major crimes task force. In 2016 a lawsuit sought release of the roughly 20,000-page file, according to NBC Chicago and WTTW; police opposed disclosure on the ground that the investigation was still active, and the records have remained largely withheld.

Charles Percy died in 2011. As the sixtieth anniversary approached in September 2026, Kenilworth police Commander Ryan Glew said in a statement reported by CBS Chicago and the Tribune that the department is investigating open and active leads and that resolving the case for the family and the community remains a priority. The murder is still unsolved.

name: Barbara Jane Mackle
summary: Barbara Jane Mackle, 20, an Emory University student, was abducted at gunpoint from a Decatur, Georgia, motel on December 17, 1968, and buried in a ventilated box while a $500,000 ransom was demanded. FBI agents found her alive on December 20 after more than three days underground. Gary Steven Krist was convicted and sentenced to life; Ruth Eisemann-Schier pleaded guilty.

narrative: Barbara Jane Mackle was a 20-year-old student at Emory University and the daughter of Robert Mackle, a Florida property developer and co-founder of the Deltona Corporation. In December 1968 she and her mother, Jane, were staying at the Rodeway Inn in Decatur, near the campus.

At about 4 a.m. on December 17, 1968, a man and a woman knocked on the door of the room. According to Time magazine's report that month, the man claimed to be a detective. The pair forced their way in, bound Jane Mackle and took Barbara away at gunpoint. She was driven to a remote stand of pines off South Berkeley Lake Road in Gwinnett County, northeast of Atlanta, and placed in a fiberglass-reinforced box buried in a shallow trench. Accounts of the case say the box was fitted with two air tubes, an air pump and a lamp, and stocked with water and food.

The kidnappers demanded $500,000 from her father. Time reported that a first attempt to deliver the money in Florida failed when local police happened upon the scene, and that the kidnappers abandoned a car which gave the FBI their identities. A second delivery succeeded. On December 20 the FBI received a telephone call giving rough directions to the burial site, and agents searching the woods found and dug out the box. Mackle had been underground for more than three days, a period usually given as about 83 hours, and was dehydrated but otherwise in good condition.

The FBI identified the kidnappers as Gary Steven Krist, an escaped California prisoner, and Ruth Eisemann-Schier, a graduate student from Honduras. Krist was captured within days in a swampy area on Florida's Gulf coast after fleeing by boat, and most of the ransom was recovered, according to published accounts. Eisemann-Schier became the first woman placed on the FBI's Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list on December 28, 1968. She was arrested in Norman, Oklahoma, on March 5, 1969.

Krist was convicted in 1969 and sentenced to life in prison. Eisemann-Schier pleaded guilty and was sentenced to seven years; she was paroled after about four years and deported to Honduras. Krist was paroled after ten years, later received a pardon and qualified as a physician, but his Indiana medical license was revoked in 2003. He was arrested in 2006 in a cocaine-smuggling case off Alabama and served further federal prison time.
Mackle described her experience in the book 83 Hours Till Dawn, written with Miami Herald reporter Gene Miller, and has otherwise lived privately.

name: David Faraday & Betty Lou Jensen
summary: David Faraday, 17, and Betty Lou Jensen, 16, were shot with a .22-caliber pistol at a turnout on Lake Herman Road, just outside Benicia, California, late on December 20, 1968. Jensen died at the scene and Faraday died soon afterward. In letters sent to Bay Area newspapers in 1969, the writer known as the Zodiac claimed the killings. No one has been charged.
lastSeen: December 20, 1968, Lake Herman Road, near Benicia, CA

narrative: David Arthur Faraday, 17, and Betty Lou Jensen, 16, were out on a date on the evening of Friday, December 20, 1968. According to accounts of the case, Faraday called for Jensen at her home in the area and had promised to have her back by 11 p.m. The pair drove in Faraday's station wagon to a gravel turnout on Lake Herman Road, a rural road just beyond the Benicia city limits in Solano County that was known locally as a lovers' lane.

Several people drove past the turnout that night. Timelines assembled from the police reports indicate that passers-by saw the couple sitting in the parked car at about 11 p.m., and that another motorist passed a few minutes before 11:15 p.m. and noticed two vehicles at the spot. Shortly afterward a local resident, Stella Borges, came upon the two teenagers lying on the ground at the turnout and alerted police.

Faraday had been shot once in the head at close range. Jensen had been shot five times in the back, apparently as she tried to get away from the gunman. According to Wikipedia's account she died at the scene, while Faraday was taken to a hospital and did not survive. Spent .22-caliber casings were recovered, and the ammunition was identified as copper-coated Winchester Western Super X. There was no sign of robbery or sexual assault.

Investigators found no motive and no suspect, and the inquiry had stalled by the following summer. Then, on July 31, 1969, three Bay Area newspapers received letters from a writer who claimed responsibility for the Lake Herman Road shootings and for a July 4, 1969 shooting in Vallejo, and who supplied details about the crimes to support the claim. The writer became known as the Zodiac. After a stabbing at Lake Berryessa that September, the attacker wrote the date of the Lake Herman Road killings on a victim's car door.

Law enforcement agencies treat Faraday and Jensen as the first of the confirmed Zodiac victims. The series also includes the Vallejo shooting, the Lake Berryessa attack and the murder of a San Francisco cab driver named Stine later in 1969.

Despite decades of work by local, state and federal investigators, and the examination of many named individuals, no one has been charged with any of the crimes. According to Wikipedia's summary of the case, it remains open with several agencies, including the Solano County Sheriff's Office, and the California Department of Justice and the FBI. The decoding of one of the ciphers by private researchers in December 2020 did not reveal the writer's identity.

name: Jane Durrua
summary: Jane Durrua, 13, of Keansburg, New Jersey, disappeared on November 4, 1968, and was found dead in a field in Middletown the next morning. In March 2008 a grand jury indicted Robert Zarinsky for her murder on the basis of DNA evidence. Zarinsky, already serving a life sentence for a 1969 murder, died in prison in November 2008 before he could be tried.

narrative: Jane Durrua was a 13-year-old girl from Keansburg, in Monmouth County, New Jersey. She disappeared on the evening of November 4, 1968. According to the case summary published by Murderpedia, she had been making her way home and took a shortcut across a grassy field beside railroad tracks.

Her body was found the following morning in a field in the neighboring township of Middletown. She had been sexually assaulted and had died from blows to the head, according to the same account. The investigation at the time did not lead to an arrest, and the case went unsolved for decades.

When the evidence was later re-examined with DNA testing, the first result led investigators in the wrong direction. Murderpedia reports that another man was arrested in error because of a mix-up in the handling of DNA evidence, a mistake attributed to the Monmouth County Prosecutor's Office. That man was not responsible for the crime.

Further testing pointed to Robert Zarinsky, who was then a New Jersey state prisoner. Zarinsky had been convicted in 1975 of murdering Rosemary Calandriello, a 17-year-old from Atlantic Highlands who vanished on August 25, 1969 and whose body has never been found, and he was serving a life sentence for that crime. According to published accounts, genetic material recovered from Durrua's clothing matched his profile. On March 11, 2008, a grand jury indicted him for her murder.

The charge was never tested in court. Zarinsky died on November 28, 2008, at South Woods State Prison in Bridgeton, at the age of 68, before a trial could be held. Because he was not tried, he was never convicted of killing Jane Durrua, and the indictment ended with his death.

Zarinsky has been connected by investigators to other crimes. In 2001 a jury acquitted him of the 1958 murder of Rahway police officer Charles Bernoskie. In February 2016, WABC-TV reported that authorities had announced DNA evidence linking him to the 1965 killing of Mary Agnes Klinsky, an 18-year-old whose body was found beside the Garden State Parkway; that finding also came after his death and did not result in a prosecution. He had additionally been regarded as a suspect in several other killings of young women in New Jersey between 1969 and 1974, according to Wikipedia's summary, but was not charged in those cases. The 2008 indictment, returned forty years after Jane Durrua's death, is the closest her case came to a formal resolution.

name: Robert F. Kennedy Assassination
summary: Senator Robert F. Kennedy, 42, was shot in the kitchen pantry of the Ambassador Hotel in Los Angeles shortly after midnight on June 5, 1968, after winning the California Democratic primary; he died on June 6. Sirhan Sirhan was convicted of first-degree murder in April 1969. His death sentence was commuted to life in 1972, and he remains in prison after repeated parole denials.
lastSeen: June 5, 1968, Ambassador Hotel, Los Angeles, CA

narrative: Senator Robert F. Kennedy was campaigning for the Democratic presidential nomination in the spring of 1968. On the night of June 4 he won the California primary and spoke to supporters at the Ambassador Hotel in Los Angeles.

At about 12:15 a.m. on June 5, as he left through a kitchen pantry, Kennedy was shot. Five other people were wounded: Paul Schrade, William Weisel, Elizabeth Evans, Ira Goldstein and Irwin Stroll; all survived. Bystanders, among them the athletes Rafer Johnson and Roosevelt Grier, restrained 24-year-old Sirhan Bishara Sirhan, who was holding a .22-caliber Iver Johnson revolver, and he was arrested at the scene. Kennedy was taken to Good Samaritan Hospital, where he died at 1:44 a.m. on June 6, 1968. He was 42.

Sirhan's trial opened in Los Angeles in early 1969. On April 17, 1969, the jury convicted him of first-degree murder and of assaulting the five wounded victims, and he was sentenced to death later that month. In 1972 the sentence was commuted to life imprisonment with the possibility of parole after the California Supreme Court, in People v. Anderson, invalidated the death sentences then in force.

Questions about whether Sirhan acted alone have persisted. The Los Angeles County medical examiner, Thomas Noguchi, concluded that the fatal shot was fired from very close range behind Kennedy's right ear, a finding that has fed debate about the positions of those in the pantry, and a later analysis of an audio recording was argued by some experts to show more shots than Sirhan's eight-round revolver could have fired; other experts dispute that reading. A court-ordered re-examination of the firearms evidence in 1975 found, according to Wikipedia's summary of the panel's report, little or no evidence of a second gun. No other person has been charged.

Sirhan has been denied parole many times. On August 27, 2021, a two-member panel of the California parole board found him suitable for release, with two of Kennedy's sons supporting parole and other family members opposed. Governor Gavin Newsom reversed that decision on January 13, 2022, writing that Sirhan had not shown the accountability and insight needed for safe release. The board denied parole again on March 1, 2023. NBC San Diego reported a further denial following a hearing in August 2024, with reconsideration possible after three years.

Sirhan is held at the Richard J. Donovan Correctional Facility near San Diego. In January 2025 President Donald Trump signed an executive order directing the declassification of remaining federal records on the assassination, and batches of files have since been released.

name: Zodiac Killer Victims
summary: At least five confirmed victims were killed by an unidentified serial killer in Northern California between 1968 and 1969. The killer taunted police and newspapers with cryptic letters and ciphers signed with a crosshair symbol. Despite thousands of suspects being investigated over decades, the Zodiac was never identified or arrested.
lastSeen: N/A
