narrative: James Riddle "Jimmy" Hoffa, the former president of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, was last seen on the afternoon of Wednesday, July 30, 1975, outside the Machus Red Fox restaurant in Bloomfield Township, an affluent suburb north of Detroit, Michigan. Hoffa left his home in Lake Orion early that afternoon expecting to meet two men connected to organized crime: Detroit mob figure Anthony "Tony Jack" Giacalone and New Jersey Teamsters official and Genovese-family capo Anthony "Tony Pro" Provenzano. According to his family, Hoffa called his wife, Josephine, from a nearby payphone in the mid-afternoon to complain that no one had arrived to meet him. He was never heard from again. His unlocked car was found in the restaurant parking lot the following morning.

Hoffa had built the Teamsters into one of the most powerful labor unions in the United States during his presidency from 1957 to 1971, but his career was intertwined with figures in the Mafia and with control of the union's large pension fund. He was convicted in the mid-1960s on charges including jury tampering and fraud and began serving a prison sentence in 1967. President Richard Nixon commuted the sentence in December 1971, on the condition, later contested by Hoffa, that he stay out of union activity until 1980. At the time of his disappearance, Hoffa was reportedly working to reclaim leadership of the Teamsters, a campaign that investigators believed some organized-crime figures viewed as a threat.

The FBI opened an extensive investigation and quickly focused on the theory that Hoffa had been lured to the restaurant and killed. Police tracking dogs were reported to have detected Hoffa's scent in a maroon 1975 Mercury linked to associates of Giacalone. In a 56-page internal briefing document known as the "Hoffex Memo," prepared for a January 1976 FBI conference and later made public, agents laid out their belief that Hoffa had been murdered at the direction of organized-crime figures. The memo named several reputed mob associates as suspects and discussed the movements of Charles "Chuckie" O'Brien, a Hoffa protege, on the day of the disappearance. No one, however, was ever charged in connection with the case, and the specific circumstances were never conclusively established.

Over the decades, numerous tips and theories prompted searches for Hoffa's remains, none of which succeeded. A long-repeated rumor that he was buried beneath Giants Stadium in New Jersey was never substantiated and was undercut when the stadium was later demolished. Investigators dug beneath a Roseville, Michigan, driveway in 2012 and searched a field in Oakland Township, Michigan, in 2013 based on informant accounts, both without result. In October 2021 the FBI surveyed and later excavated a site beneath the Pulaski Skyway at a former Jersey City, New Jersey, landfill after a deathbed account claimed Hoffa's body had been buried there; in 2022 the bureau announced that nothing of evidentiary value had been found.

Hoffa was declared legally dead by an Oakland County, Michigan, probate court, with the death recorded as of July 30, 1982, seven years after he vanished. As of 2026, his body has never been recovered, no one has been criminally charged in his disappearance, and the case is officially unsolved. It endures as one of the most enduring mysteries in American organized-labor and organized-crime history, revisited periodically as witnesses age and new tips surface, but without a definitive, proven resolution.

name: Myrna Opsahl
summary: Myrna Opsahl, 42, was fatally shot on April 21, 1975, while depositing church collection money during a Symbionese Liberation Army robbery of the Crocker National Bank in Carmichael, California. In November 2002 four former SLA members pleaded guilty to second-degree murder; a fifth, James Kilgore, pleaded guilty later. Sentences ranged from six to eight years.
lastSeen: April 21, 1975, Crocker National Bank, Carmichael, CA

narrative: Myrna Lee Opsahl was a 42-year-old mother of four whose husband was a surgeon. On April 21, 1975, she went to the Crocker National Bank branch in Carmichael, a suburb of Sacramento, with other members of her Seventh-day Adventist church to deposit the weekend collection, according to PBS's American Experience.

Armed members of the Symbionese Liberation Army entered the bank and announced a robbery. Opsahl was hit by a shotgun blast and died of her wounds. The group left with about $15,000. The killing was not publicly tied to the SLA at first, and it drew far less attention than the group's kidnapping of Patricia Hearst the previous year.

For more than two decades nobody was held responsible for the death. The Seattle Times reported that Steven Soliah, an SLA associate, was tried for the robbery and acquitted, and that prosecutors said they lacked the evidence to charge anyone with murder. Hearst's 1982 memoir described the robbery and said that Emily Harris had admitted firing the shot. Harris denied any involvement for years.

The case was revived after the 1999 arrest in Minnesota of Sara Jane Olson, formerly Kathleen Soliah, who had been a fugitive on charges of placing bombs under Los Angeles police cars. In January 2002, Sacramento County authorities arrested William Harris, Emily Montague (the former Emily Harris) and Michael Bortin and charged them, together with Olson and the fugitive James Kilgore, with murder.

On November 7, 2002, the four defendants in custody or on bail pleaded guilty to second-degree murder in Sacramento County Superior Court, the San Francisco Chronicle reported. Each apologized to the Opsahl family in court. Under the agreement Montague received eight years, William Harris seven, and Bortin and Olson six each; they were sentenced on February 14, 2003. According to later reporting by Fox News, Montague said the shotgun went off accidentally, and William Harris had acted as a lookout.

Kilgore was arrested in Cape Town, South Africa, in November 2002 and was returned to the United States. He also pleaded guilty to second-degree murder and was sentenced in 2004. Bortin was paroled in February 2006, William Harris in September 2006 and Montague in February 2007. Olson was released in March 2009. Kilgore, the last of the five in custody, was paroled in May 2009, according to Wikipedia's account of his case.

A Pierce County jury convicted him of two more murders in 2002 and sentenced him to death; that sentence became life without parole after Washington's Supreme Court struck down the death penalty in 2018.

narrative: Robert Lee Yates Jr. was born in 1952 and graduated from high school in Oak Harbor, Washington. He enlisted in the Army in 1977, became a helicopter pilot and served overseas before leaving active duty in 1996; he then flew for the Army National Guard until 2000, according to Wikipedia's summary of his service record.

Beginning in the 1990s, women who worked in prostitution along East Sprague Avenue in Spokane were found shot to death and left in rural areas, several with plastic bags over their heads. A task force investigated the killings for years. On April 18, 2000, Yates was arrested and charged with the murder of 16-year-old Jennifer Joseph. The Seattle Times reported the following month that the Spokane County sheriff said DNA evidence tied Yates to other deaths in Spokane and Tacoma.

In 2000 Yates pleaded guilty in Spokane County Superior Court to 13 counts of murder and one count of attempted murder under an agreement that spared him a death sentence in that county, and he was sentenced to 408 years in prison, the Spokesman-Review reported. The plea covered more than the Spokane killings. It included the deaths of Patrick Oliver, 21, and Susan Savage, 22, who were shot near Walla Walla in July 1975, and, according to Wikipedia, Stacy Hawn, whose remains were found in Skagit County in 1988. The remains of one victim, Melody Murfin, were found buried at Yates's home after his confession.

Pierce County prosecutors separately charged Yates with killing Melinda Mercer in 1997 and Connie Ellis in 1998. A jury convicted him in September 2002, and he was sentenced to death on October 3, 2002. The Washington Supreme Court upheld the sentence on appeal, and Courthouse News reported that the court rejected his argument that the sentence was disproportionate.

Yates also argued that his Spokane County sentence was calculated incorrectly for the 1975 murders, which predated the state's sentencing reforms. The Spokesman-Review reported in 2016 that the state Supreme Court had found no practical difference between the sentence he agreed to and the one he said he should have received.

In October 2018 the Washington Supreme Court ruled that the state's death penalty was applied in an arbitrary and racially biased way. The decision converted the sentences of everyone on death row, including Yates, to life without the possibility of parole. Sources reviewed for this entry describe him as still serving his sentences in a Washington prison.

narrative: Anna Mae Pictou Aquash was born in 1945 in Nova Scotia and was a member of the Mi'kmaq nation. In the early 1970s she became a prominent member of the American Indian Movement, which had been founded to protest the treatment of Native Americans and which occupied Wounded Knee, South Dakota, for 71 days in 1973.

On February 24, 1976, a body was found at the bottom of a ravine along Highway 73 near Wanblee, on the Pine Ridge Indian Reservation. According to Wikipedia's summary of the record, the first autopsy attributed the death to exposure and the woman was buried without being identified. Her hands had been removed and sent to the FBI for fingerprinting, which led to her identification. A second autopsy, performed after exhumation, found that she had been shot in the back of the head.

Nearly three decades passed before anyone was charged. In 2003 a federal grand jury indicted Arlo Looking Cloud and John Graham. Looking Cloud was arrested in Denver that March. At his trial in Rapid City in February 2004, witnesses testified that Aquash had been taken from a house in Denver in December 1975 by Looking Cloud, Graham and Theda Clark, driven to Rapid City and then to the reservation, because some in the movement suspected she was a government informant. AIM leaders have denied involvement. The jury convicted Looking Cloud of first-degree murder and he was sentenced to life in prison.

Graham, a Southern Tutchone man from the Yukon, was arrested in Vancouver in December 2003 and fought extradition until December 2007. A federal murder charge against him was dismissed in 2009, and he was then tried in state court in Rapid City. Looking Cloud testified that he saw Graham shoot Aquash. On December 10, 2010, the jury found Graham guilty of felony murder in the course of a kidnapping and not guilty of premeditated murder, Native Sun News reported. He was sentenced on January 24, 2011, to life without parole, and the South Dakota Supreme Court upheld the conviction in 2012.

Two other people were charged. Vine Richard Marshall was indicted in 2008 on a federal charge of aiding and abetting the murder, accused of supplying the handgun; he pleaded not guilty and was acquitted. Thelma Rios pleaded guilty in state court in November 2010 to being an accessory to kidnapping and died in 2011. Clark, by then 87 and living in a nursing home, was called at Graham's trial but declined to testify.

In 2011 a federal judge reduced Looking Cloud's sentence to 20 years in recognition of his testimony, and he was released in November 2020, according to Wikipedia. Aquash was reburied in Nova Scotia in June 2004. CBS News reported at Graham's sentencing that officials still considered the investigation open.

name: Oakland County Child Killer Victims
summary: A serial killer known as the 'Babysitter' abducted and murdered four children in Oakland County, Michigan. The victims ranged in age from 10 to 12 years old. The killer washed and redressed victims before leaving them in plain sight. Despite one of the largest investigations in Michigan history, the killer was never identified.
lastSeen: Various dates, Oakland County, MI

sources.title: Oakland County Child Killer - Wikipedia

narrative: Between February 1976 and March 1977, four children were abducted and murdered in Oakland County, Michigan, in a series of killings attributed to an unidentified offender the press dubbed the Oakland County Child Killer (OCCK). The confirmed victims were Mark Stebbins, 12, of Ferndale; Jill Robinson, 12, of Royal Oak; Kristine Mihelich, 10, of Berkley; and Timothy King, 11, of Birmingham. In each case the child vanished from an ordinary errand and was held for several days before being killed; several of the bodies were found deliberately placed in plain view along roadsides in the snow, a detail that fed intense public fear across metropolitan Detroit.

The killings prompted one of the largest homicide investigations in U.S. history to that point. A multi-agency task force led by the Michigan State Police and drawing on officers from Oakland County communities was assembled, and investigators fielded tens of thousands of tips. The task force disbanded in December 1978, with responsibility for the still-open case reverting to the Michigan State Police, which continues to hold the investigation. No one has ever been charged or convicted, and the case remains officially unsolved.

Over the decades investigators have publicly identified several persons of interest, none of whom has been charged in the killings. Christopher Busch, a convicted child molester and the son of a General Motors executive, was investigated as a possible suspect; he died in 1978 in what was ruled a suicide, and authorities have said DNA testing in 2012 did not link him to the murders. Arch Sloan, a convicted sex offender serving life sentences on unrelated charges, drew scrutiny after hair evidence recovered from his car was reported to match hairs found on two of the victims, though the hair was not Sloan's own. Ted Lamborgine, described by some investigators in 2007 as a leading suspect, pleaded guilty to unrelated sex offenses and declined a polygraph on the OCCK case. James Gunnels was identified as a person of interest after a hair on Kristine Mihelich's body was reported as a mitochondrial DNA match to him or a maternal relative. Authorities have repeatedly cautioned that these developments have not established the identity of the killer.

The investigation has been shadowed by a long controversy over how physical evidence and case files were handled. Timothy King's father, Barry King, pursued litigation and public-records efforts that led to the release of thousands of pages of documents, alleging investigative mistakes, inter-agency conflict, and potential obstruction; he died in 2020 without seeing the case resolved. A DNA profile developed from crime-scene material reportedly does not match any named suspect, and officials including Oakland County Sheriff Michael Bouchard have acknowledged that portions of the surviving evidence have degraded or were consumed in earlier testing.

As of 2026, roughly 50 years after the murders, the case remains open and unsolved. The Michigan State Police and Oakland County Prosecutor's Office describe the investigation as active, while surviving family members have publicly pressed for retesting of evidence, digitization of case files, and a dedicated cold-case effort. Investigators have expressed hope that advances in DNA and forensic genealogy, or a new witness account, could eventually identify the person or people responsible.

name: Son of Sam Victims
summary: David Berkowitz, known as 'Son of Sam,' murdered six people and wounded seven others in New York City over 13 months. He terrorized the city with taunting letters to police and media. He was caught in August 1977 after a parking ticket near the last murder scene. He pleaded guilty and is serving six consecutive 25-years-to-life sentences.

narrative: Between the summer of 1976 and the summer of 1977, a series of nighttime shootings terrorized New York City. Using a .44 caliber Bulldog revolver, the gunman targeted young people, most often women with long dark hair and couples sitting in parked cars in the Bronx, Queens, and Brooklyn. The first fatal attack came on July 29, 1976, when 18-year-old Donna Lauria was killed and her friend Jody Valenti wounded as they sat in a car in the Bronx. Over the following year the attacks continued, ultimately leaving six people dead and several others wounded. The dead included Christine Freund, Virginia Voskerichian, Valentina Suriani, Alexander Esau, and Stacy Moskowitz, along with Donna Lauria.

As the shootings mounted, police connected them through ballistics matching the same .44 caliber weapon, and the case drew intense press coverage under nicknames such as the ".44 Caliber Killer." The gunman began communicating with authorities and the media through taunting handwritten letters. A note left at one crime scene and a later letter to Daily News columnist Jimmy Breslin, dated May 30, 1977, signed the name "Son of Sam." Berkowitz later said the name referred to a demon he claimed spoke to him through a dog owned by his neighbor Sam Carr, a story he subsequently admitted was a fabrication.

The killings triggered one of the largest manhunts in the city's history, involving a dedicated task force known as Operation Omega and heavy patrols of areas where couples parked. The decisive break came after the final shooting in Brooklyn on July 31, 1977, which killed Stacy Moskowitz and blinded Robert Violante. A witness had noticed police ticketing cars near the scene, and investigators traced a parking ticket issued that night to a vehicle registered to David Berkowitz of Yonkers. On August 10, 1977, officers arrested Berkowitz outside his apartment; a .44 revolver was found in his car, and he quickly confessed.

Berkowitz, a 24-year-old former postal worker, was found mentally competent to stand trial. On May 8, 1978, he pleaded guilty to the shootings, and on June 12, 1978, he was sentenced to six consecutive terms of 25 years to life in prison. He remains incarcerated in the New York State prison system, most recently at Shawangunk Correctional Facility, and has repeatedly been denied or has declined parole. These facts—his guilty plea and continued imprisonment—are established and undisputed.

The case had a lasting legal legacy. Anticipating that Berkowitz might profit from selling his story, New York enacted the first "Son of Sam" law to divert such earnings to victims; the U.S. Supreme Court struck down the original statute on First Amendment grounds in Simon & Schuster v. Members of the New York State Crime Victims Board (1991), after which New York and many other states passed revised versions. Beginning in the 1990s, Berkowitz claimed he had not acted alone, alleging that a Satanic cult he called "the Twenty-Two Disciples of Hell" was involved and naming associates including John and Michael Carr. These conspiracy claims have never been proven; official reviews were inconclusive, and Berkowitz alone was convicted of the crimes.

name: Bonnie Garland
summary: Bonnie Garland, a 20-year-old Yale student, was fatally beaten with a hammer as she slept in her parents' Scarsdale, New York, home on July 7, 1977. Her former boyfriend Richard Herrin, a Yale graduate, confessed to a priest hours later. A Westchester County jury convicted him of first-degree manslaughter on June 18, 1978; he was released in January 1995.
lastSeen: July 7, 1977, parents' home in Scarsdale, NY

sources.title: Casemine - Garland v. Herrin, 554 F. Supp. 308 (S.D.N.Y. 1983)

narrative: Bonnie Joan Garland, whose family lived in Scarsdale, New York, was a student at Yale University. According to the facts set out by a federal judge in Garland v. Herrin, a civil suit later brought by her parents, she met Richard Herrin in the fall of 1974 when both were Yale undergraduates. Herrin graduated in 1975 and began graduate study at Texas Christian University, while Garland remained at Yale. He visited her family's home and came to know her parents.

By the summer of 1977 the relationship was ending. Herrin travelled to Scarsdale in early July and stayed at the Garland house. According to Wikipedia's account of the trial evidence, Garland told him on July 6 that she wanted to end the relationship.

In the early hours of July 7, 1977, after Garland had fallen asleep, Herrin went downstairs to find a weapon. The court's summary of his own trial testimony states that he chose a hammer, wrapped it in a towel so that family members would not notice it, returned to her bedroom and struck her repeatedly on the head. Her parents were in the house at the time. Herrin testified that he had decided to kill both Garland and himself.

Herrin left in the family's car and drove north. He stopped in Coxsackie, about 100 miles away, where he found a church and told a priest what he had done. Police went to the Garland home and found her gravely injured. She died later that day. She was 20 years old.

Herrin was prosecuted in Supreme Court, Westchester County, before Judge Richard Daronco. He was tried on a murder charge. Members of the Catholic community at Yale had supported his release on bail before trial, which drew public criticism. On June 18, 1978, the jury convicted him of first-degree manslaughter rather than second-degree murder. He received the maximum sentence available for that offense, reported as eight and one-third to 25 years.

Garland's parents sued Herrin in federal court. He conceded liability for wrongful death, and after a trial in October 1982 a jury set those damages at $10,000; the court also addressed the parents' claims for emotional distress. Herrin was released from a New York state prison on January 12, 1995, after about 17 years in custody, according to Wikipedia.

name: Hillside Strangler Victims
summary: Cousins Angelo Buono and Kenneth Bianchi posed as police officers, kidnapped, raped, and murdered 10 women in Los Angeles. Their victims were found on hillsides, giving rise to the 'Hillside Strangler' name. Both were convicted: Bianchi in 1979 and Buono in 1983.
lastSeen: N/A

narrative: Between October 1977 and February 1978, the Los Angeles area was gripped by a series of killings in which the bodies of young women and girls were found discarded, often nude, on hillsides and roadside slopes across the city and surrounding foothills. Because the earliest victims were left in elevated, exposed locations, the press dubbed the unknown killer the "Hillside Strangler," and investigators initially believed they were hunting a single man. The victims ranged in age from 12 to 28 and were typically abducted, sexually assaulted, tortured, and strangled before their bodies were posed in visible places, in several instances near police facilities.

As the investigation progressed, evidence suggested that two people were working together rather than one. The perpetrators were eventually identified as cousins Kenneth Bianchi and Angelo Buono Jr., an auto-upholstery worker. The pair frequently posed as police officers to lure women into their vehicle, then drove them to Buono's home and shop in the Glendale area, where the assaults and murders took place. By the time they stopped, ten women and girls in the Los Angeles region had been killed, including 12-year-old Dolores Cepeda and 14-year-old Sonja Johnson, whose disappearances heightened public alarm.

The case broke open outside California. In January 1979, Bianchi, who had moved to Bellingham, Washington, was arrested for the murders of two women there. Investigators linked him to the Los Angeles killings, and Bianchi at first mounted an insanity defense, claiming he suffered from multiple personality disorder and that an alternate personality named "Steve" had committed the crimes. Court-appointed and prosecution experts, including hypnosis specialist Dr. Martin Orne, concluded that Bianchi was faking the disorder; the courts rejected the insanity and multiple-personality claims, and Bianchi ultimately admitted the alter egos were fabricated.

To avoid the death penalty, Bianchi pleaded guilty to several of the murders and agreed to testify against Buono, naming his cousin as his accomplice. Buono was arrested in October 1979. His prosecution was long and difficult, at one point nearly collapsing over doubts about Bianchi's reliability as a witness, but the case proceeded to a lengthy trial featuring hundreds of witnesses. In November 1983 Buono was convicted of nine of the murders, and in January 1984 he was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole.

Both men were convicted and imprisoned. Angelo Buono died of a heart attack on September 21, 2002, at age 67, while serving his sentence at Calipatria State Prison in California. Kenneth Bianchi received life sentences for both the Washington and California murders and remains incarcerated, most recently reported at the Washington State Penitentiary, where he has repeatedly been denied parole. The Hillside Strangler case remains one of the most studied examples of two offenders killing in tandem, and of a defendant's disputed insanity claim being tested and rejected in court.

summary: Roger Reece Kibbe, called the I-5 Strangler, was convicted of murdering seven women and girls in Northern California between 1977 and 1987. A jury convicted him of one killing in 1991, and after DNA linked him to six more he pleaded guilty in 2009 and received life terms without parole. Kibbe, 81, was strangled by his cellmate at Mule Creek State Prison on February 28, 2021.

narrative: Between 1977 and 1987, a series of women were abducted, sexually assaulted and strangled in the Sacramento and Stockton areas, and their bodies were left along highways and in remote places across Northern California. The Los Angeles Times reported that two of the victims were taken from Interstate 5 after their cars broke down, which gave the unidentified killer the name I-5 Strangler. The victims' clothing had been cut in unusual patterns.

The earliest known victim was Lou Ellen Burleigh, 21, of Walnut Creek, who disappeared in September 1977. The others, according to Wikipedia's list drawn from court and news records, were Lora Heedick, 21, Barbara Ann Scott, 29, Stephanie Brown, 19, Charmaine Sabrah, 26, and Katherine Kelly Quinones, 25, all killed in 1986, and Darcie Frackenpohl, 17, of Seattle, who was killed in 1987 and found near Echo Summit in the Sierra Nevada.

Roger Kibbe, who lived in the Sacramento suburbs, became a suspect on the basis of a composite sketch, the vehicle he drove and an attempt to abduct a woman in Sacramento, the Los Angeles Times reported. Without DNA technology, prosecutors charged him only with the Frackenpohl killing. A jury convicted him of first-degree murder, and in May 1991 he was sentenced to 25 years to life.

DNA testing later tied Kibbe to six more killings. Investigators confronted him in prison, and the Times reported that he admitted to the murders in 2003. A grand jury indicted him in 2008. In 2009 he pleaded guilty to six murders in exchange for prosecutors not seeking the death penalty, and he received six life sentences without the possibility of parole. As part of the agreement he agreed to help locate Burleigh's body, the only one that had not been found.

Repeated searches near Lake Berryessa with Kibbe present were unsuccessful. In early 2011 Napa County Deputy Sheriff Michael Bartlett, searching on his own time, found a bone in a creek bed in the area Kibbe had described. DNA testing confirmed in June 2011 that the remains were Burleigh's.

On February 28, 2021, a corrections officer found Kibbe unresponsive in his cell at Mule Creek State Prison in Ione, with his cellmate, Jason Budrow, standing nearby, CBS San Francisco reported. Kibbe was 81. An autopsy found that he had been strangled. KTVU later reported that Budrow, who was already serving life without parole for a 2010 murder, received an additional consecutive life sentence for killing Kibbe.

name: Bob Crane
summary: Actor Bob Crane, 49, star of Hogan's Heroes, was found bludgeoned to death in his Scottsdale, Arizona, apartment on June 29, 1978. His friend John Carpenter was charged in 1992 and acquitted by a jury in 1994; he died in 1998. DNA retesting in 2016 of blood from Carpenter's rental car did not match Crane, and the case remains unsolved.
lastSeen: Night of June 28, 1978, after a performance at the Windmill Dinner Theatre, Scottsdale, AZ

narrative: Bob Crane was born in Waterbury, Connecticut, in 1928 and worked as a radio host before starring as Colonel Robert Hogan in the CBS comedy Hogan's Heroes from 1965 to 1971. In June 1978 he was in Scottsdale, Arizona, appearing in the play Beginner's Luck at the Windmill Dinner Theatre and living at the Winfield Apartments.

According to a 1993 Phoenix New Times investigation, actress Victoria Berry, who was in the play with him, went to the apartment at about 2 p.m. on June 29, 1978, for an appointment. No one answered, the door was unlocked, and she found a body in the bed with an electrical cord tied around the neck. The victim was identified as Crane. He had been struck on the head with a heavy object. Investigators came to believe the weapon was a camera tripod, but no weapon was ever recovered.

Police attention turned to John Henry Carpenter, a video equipment salesman and friend of Crane who had been in the theatre audience the night before and had left with him after the show. Carpenter flew home to Los Angeles on the morning of June 29 and telephoned the apartment twice that afternoon while officers were there, New Times reported. He told police he had been with Crane until the early morning hours. Blood of Crane's type was found on the door of Carpenter's rental car, but testing available in 1978 could not go further, and the county attorney declined to file charges.

The case was re-examined around 1990, and Carpenter was arrested and charged with murder in June 1992. At trial in 1994 the defense emphasized that the evidence was circumstantial, that no weapon had been found and that evidence had been handled poorly. The jury acquitted him. Carpenter maintained his innocence until his death in 1998.

In November 2016, Phoenix television journalist John Hook announced the results of new DNA testing he had arranged on the surviving blood samples from the rental car. According to CNN and Fox News, the tests produced two profiles: one from an unidentified man and one partial profile too degraded to interpret. Neither was Crane's. Carpenter's trial lawyer said the result vindicated his client.
USA Today reported that Hook cautioned against treating the result as conclusive in either direction. No one else has been charged, and the killing remains unsolved.

name: FSU Chi Omega Murders
summary: Margaret Bowman, 21, and Lisa Levy, 20, were killed and two sorority sisters badly injured when Ted Bundy attacked the Chi Omega house at Florida State University early on January 15, 1978. A fifth student was attacked nearby the same night. Bundy was convicted on July 24, 1979, sentenced to death, and executed in 1989 for a separate Florida murder.

narrative: In the early hours of Sunday, January 15, 1978, an intruder entered the Chi Omega sorority house near the Florida State University campus in Tallahassee. According to a Rolling Stone account based on interviews with survivor Kathy Kleiner, the man came in through a back door with a broken combination lock at about 2:45 a.m., carrying a piece of firewood he had picked up outside.

Margaret Bowman, 21, was beaten and strangled in her bed. Lisa Levy, 20, was beaten, sexually assaulted and strangled in a room across the hall; the Seattle Times reported that she died on the way to the hospital. The attacker then entered the room shared by Kleiner and Karen Chandler and struck both women with the club. Both suffered broken jaws and other serious injuries but survived. Kleiner has said the attack stopped when headlights from a car outside lit up the room.

Those headlights belonged to the car bringing sorority member Nita Neary home from a date. She saw a man leaving the house and later gave the only eyewitness identification at trial. Shortly afterward, several blocks away, FSU student Cheryl Thomas was attacked in her apartment. ABC News reported that her neighbors heard noises, telephoned her and then called police; the attacker fled and Thomas survived with severe injuries.

Ted Bundy, who had escaped from a Colorado jail on December 30, 1977, had rented a room near the campus earlier in January. On February 9 he abducted and killed 12-year-old Kimberly Leach in Lake City. A Pensacola police officer arrested him on February 15, 1978, after stopping a stolen car. He was indicted in July 1978 for the Chi Omega murders and the three attempted murders.

According to ABC News, Bundy rejected a plea agreement in May 1979 that would have spared him the death penalty. At the trial, which was televised nationally, forensic dentists testified that bite marks on Levy's body matched casts of Bundy's teeth. On July 24, 1979, the jury found him guilty of both murders and of the attempted murders of Kleiner, Chandler and Thomas, and he was sentenced to death about a week later.

A second jury convicted Bundy of the Leach murder in February 1980, and he received a third death sentence. After years of appeals, he was executed at Florida State Prison on January 24, 1989. The Los Angeles Times noted that the execution was technically carried out for the Leach murder, while he remained under sentence of death for the Chi Omega killings.

narrative: Jeffrey Dahmer, often called the "Milwaukee Cannibal," murdered 17 men and boys between 1978 and 1991. His victims were predominantly young men, and many were Black, Asian, or Latino. Dahmer committed his first killing on June 18, 1978, in Bath Township, Ohio, when he killed 18-year-old Steven Hicks. He did not kill again for nearly nine years, resuming in 1987 after moving to the Milwaukee, Wisconsin, area. There he typically approached victims in bars, malls, and other public places, lured them to his apartment with offers of money or company, drugged them, and killed them. He dismembered the bodies and, in some cases, engaged in acts he later confessed to investigators.

Dahmer's crimes came to light on July 22, 1991, when a man named Tracy Edwards escaped from Dahmer's Milwaukee apartment and, still partially handcuffed, flagged down police. When officers accompanied Edwards back to the apartment, they discovered photographs of dismembered bodies and then found human remains stored in the refrigerator, freezer, and elsewhere in the residence. Dahmer was arrested that night and soon confessed to the killings. Forensic investigators eventually connected the remains and evidence to numerous victims.

Reporting and later official reviews highlighted earlier missed opportunities to stop Dahmer. In one widely cited case in May 1991, 14-year-old Konerak Sinthasomphone escaped Dahmer's apartment and was found on the street, but police returned the injured, disoriented boy to Dahmer after Dahmer described him as an intoxicated adult partner; the boy was killed after officers left. Neighbor Glenda Cleveland and others had raised concerns at the time. According to news accounts, the episode drew intense criticism of the Milwaukee Police Department's handling of the encounter, and two officers were fired, though they were later reinstated following appeals.

Dahmer was charged with multiple counts of murder in Wisconsin. He pleaded guilty but insane, and the central question at his 1992 trial was whether he was legally sane. On February 15, 1992, a jury rejected the insanity defense and found him legally sane and guilty on 15 counts of murder. On February 17, 1992, he was sentenced to 15 consecutive life terms in prison. He was later extradited to Ohio and received an additional life sentence for the 1978 murder of Steven Hicks. At sentencing, relatives of the victims confronted Dahmer directly, describing their grief and anger.

On November 28, 1994, Dahmer was beaten to death by a fellow inmate, Christopher Scarver, at the Columbia Correctional Institution in Portage, Wisconsin; he was 34. Scarver, who was already serving a life sentence, also killed another inmate in the same attack. The case left a lasting mark on Milwaukee, particularly on the families of the victims and on the city's Black and immigrant communities, and it prompted scrutiny of how police responded to complaints. The case is closed: Dahmer was convicted and is deceased.

name: Judy Chartier
summary: Judith "Judy" Chartier, 17, of Chelmsford, Massachusetts, vanished after leaving a party in Billerica around 2 a.m. on June 5, 1982. In November 2021 divers found her 1972 Dodge Dart and human remains in the Concord River in Billerica; dental records confirmed the remains were hers. Officials said then that the cause of death was undetermined.
lastSeen: June 5, 1982, about 2 a.m., leaving a party in Billerica, Massachusetts

sources.title: WBUR - DA: Remains found in river belong to Chelmsford teen missing 40 years
NBC Boston - Human Remains in Concord River Identified as Long-Missing Teen Judith Chartier
Boston.com - Remains found in Concord River that of teenage girl missing for decades
CBS Boston - Judith Chartier Case: Human Remains Found In Concord River Identified

narrative: Judith Chartier, known as Judy, was 17 and lived in Chelmsford, Massachusetts. On the night of June 4, 1982, she went to an outdoor party in the neighboring town of Billerica. She left at about 2 a.m. on June 5, driving a 1972 Dodge Dart Swinger, and was not heard from again. Neither she nor the car could be found, and her disappearance remained one of the region's long-running missing person cases.

Nearly 40 years later, the Middlesex District Attorney's Office reviewed the file again. District Attorney Marian Ryan said the decision to search the Concord River in Billerica came from that fresh review and not from a new tip, CBS Boston reported. Two civilian specialists in underwater sonar, Bruce Stebbins and Hans Hug, assisted investigators, and the district attorney's office described their work as critical, according to Boston.com.

On Tuesday, November 2, 2021, divers recovered pieces of a car from the river. The vehicle identification number matched the Dodge Dart that Chartier had been driving. The next day divers found human remains in about 10 feet of water, roughly 15 to 20 yards from shore. They also recovered clothing, a small purse or card case and a laminated work identification card. The location was close to where the party had been held.

On November 5, 2021, Ryan, Chelmsford Police Chief James Spinney and Billerica police announced that the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner had identified the remains as Chartier's through dental records. Chartier's parents had died before the discovery; her siblings were informed of the findings.

Officials said at the time that the cause and manner of death had not been determined. The medical examiner's office and a forensic anthropologist, Dr. James Pokines, were to reconstruct the remains, a process Ryan said would take weeks or months. WBUR reported that Ryan said it was too early to say whether foul play was involved. Investigators also said they wanted to speak again with people who had been at the party.

The sources reviewed for this entry do not report a final ruling on how Chartier died, and no one has been charged in connection with her death. The case is therefore best described as a resolved disappearance with the circumstances of death still not publicly explained.

name: Kimberly Leach
summary: Twelve-year-old Kimberly Leach was abducted from Lake City Junior High School in Florida on February 9, 1978. Her remains were found in April 1978 in a shed near Suwannee River State Park. Ted Bundy was convicted of her kidnapping and murder in 1980 and sentenced to death; he was executed in Florida's electric chair on January 24, 1989.
lastSeen: February 9, 1978, Lake City Junior High School, Lake City, FL

sources.title: ABC News - Remembering Kimberly Leach, 12, Ted Bundy's last victim
Yahoo / Women's Health - Ted Bundy Kidnapped And Murdered His Last Victim In The Middle Of A School Day
Wikipedia - Murder of Kimberly Leach

narrative: Kimberly Dianne Leach was a 12-year-old seventh-grader at Lake City Junior High School in Lake City, Florida. According to the Wikipedia article on the case, she was born on October 28, 1965. She is widely described, including by ABC News, as the last known victim of Ted Bundy and the youngest of his known murder victims.

On the morning of February 9, 1978, Kimberly disappeared from her school during the school day. According to the Wikipedia account, she had been sent during first period to fetch a purse she had left in her homeroom and did not come back. Witnesses later described a white van near the school, and ABC News reported that a firefighter gave an account of seeing a man leading a young girl toward a white van.

Bundy was arrested in Pensacola on February 15, 1978, while driving a stolen vehicle, according to the Wikipedia article. ABC News reported that he was taken into custody before Kimberly had been found, and described him as a fugitive and convicted kidnapper who was on the FBI's Most Wanted list at the time. A large search followed her disappearance and lasted roughly two months.

Her remains were located in April 1978; the Wikipedia article gives the date as April 7. ABC News and Women's Health both reported that her body was found in a shed behind Suwannee River State Park, and the Wikipedia article describes the structure as an abandoned hog shed about 30 miles west of Lake City. The body was badly decomposed by the time it was found.

Bundy was tried for Kimberly's kidnapping and murder in Orlando in early 1980. According to ABC News, the evidence presented included eyewitness testimony, fiber evidence and hotel receipts that placed him in Lake City. The Wikipedia article states that the trial ran from January 7 to February 9, 1980, that the jury deliberated for about seven hours before finding him guilty of both kidnapping and murder, and that he was sentenced to death. Women's Health reported that it was the third death sentence he had received in Florida.

Bundy spent nearly nine years on Florida's death row. He was executed in the electric chair at Florida State Prison on January 24, 1989. ABC News reported that in the days before his execution he confessed to 30 murders, and that investigators have long suspected the true number may be higher.

name: Rep. Leo Ryan & Jonestown Victims
summary: U.S. Congressman Leo Ryan was shot dead at the Port Kaituma airstrip in Guyana on November 18, 1978, along with four others, while investigating Jim Jones's Peoples Temple. Hours later more than 900 Temple members died at Jonestown in a mass murder-suicide, bringing the day's death toll to 918. Larry Layton, the only person convicted in U.S. courts over the attack, was found guilty in 1986 of conspiracy and aiding and abetting Ryan's murder, sentenced to life, and paroled in 2002 after about 18 years in custody.
lastSeen: November 18, 1978, Port Kaituma airstrip, Guyana

sources.title: Jonestown - Wikipedia

Mass suicide at Jonestown | November 18, 1978 - HISTORY

narrative: In November 1978, U.S. Representative Leo Ryan, a Democrat from California, led a fact-finding delegation to Guyana to investigate reports that members of Jim Jones's Peoples Temple were being held against their will at Jonestown, the church's agricultural settlement in the South American jungle. According to the historical record, Ryan traveled as chairman of a congressional oversight subcommittee and was accompanied by aides, several journalists, an NBC television crew, and a group of relatives of Temple members known as the Concerned Relatives. The delegation arrived in the Guyanese capital of Georgetown on November 14 and reached Jonestown on November 17.

During the visit, a number of Temple members indicated they wished to leave, and Ryan agreed to escort them out. On November 18, 1978, as the group prepared to depart from the airstrip at nearby Port Kaituma, gunmen who had followed the delegation from Jonestown opened fire on the party and the waiting aircraft. Congressman Ryan was killed, shot more than twenty times, along with four others: NBC reporter Don Harris, NBC cameraman Bob Brown, San Francisco Examiner photographer Greg Robinson, and Temple defector Patricia Parks. Roughly nine to eleven others were wounded, including Ryan's legislative aide Jackie Speier, who survived and later became a U.S. congresswoman. Ryan is the only sitting member of the U.S. Congress to be killed in the line of duty.

Later that same day at the Jonestown settlement, more than 900 Peoples Temple members died in what the historical record describes as a mass murder-suicide carried out at Jones's direction. Members drank or were forced to consume grape Flavor Aid laced with cyanide and sedatives; the poison was administered to infants and children first, some by syringe, before adults consumed it. Reported figures place the death toll at Jonestown at 909, including some 304 children, with additional deaths in Georgetown bringing the overall total to 918. Jim Jones himself was found dead in the settlement's central pavilion with a gunshot wound to the head, determined by investigators to be self-inflicted. It remained one of the largest losses of American civilian life in a single non-natural event prior to September 11, 2001.

Larry Layton, a Peoples Temple member who had posed as a defector and boarded one of the aircraft, drew a weapon and fired at members of the departing group, wounding two people before being subdued. He was the only person tried and convicted in U.S. courts in connection with the airstrip attack. Layton was initially acquitted in a Guyanese court. In the United States, his first federal trial in 1981 ended in a mistrial; he was retried and convicted in 1986 by a federal jury in San Francisco of conspiracy and aiding and abetting in the murder of Congressman Ryan and the attempted murder of U.S. deputy chief of mission Richard Dwyer. He was sentenced in March 1987 to life in prison and was released on parole in 2002.

The Jonestown tragedy left a lasting imprint on American culture, giving rise to the phrase 'drinking the Kool-Aid' and prompting congressional and public scrutiny of new religious movements. The case is considered closed. Larry Layton's conviction stands as the sole criminal conviction obtained; the other identified gunmen died at Jonestown, and no further prosecutions followed. Jackie Speier's survival and later political career, along with continued scholarship and the recovery of unclaimed victims' remains decades afterward, have kept the events in public memory.

name: Frank Hilley
summary: Frank Hilley died on May 25, 1975, in a death first attributed to infectious hepatitis. After his daughter Carol was found to have been poisoned with arsenic in 1979, his body was exhumed and arsenic was detected. His wife, Audrey Marie Hilley, was convicted in 1983 of his murder and of Carol's attempted murder. She fled during a 1987 prison furlough and died of hypothermia.
lastSeen: May 25, 1975, Anniston, AL (died in hospital)

sources.title: UPI Archives - Fugitive killer Audrey Marie Hilley, dubbed 'The Black Widow'
UPI Archives - Death of 'Black Widow' as mysterious as her life
Oxygen - Audrey Marie Hilley Poisons Husband, Daughter Before Escaping Prison
EBSCO Research Starters - Marie Hilley

narrative: Frank Hilley married Audrey Marie Frazier in 1951, and the couple lived in the Anniston, Alabama, area. In the spring of 1975 he became ill with nausea and abdominal pain. According to the Wikipedia article on Marie Hilley, he was first thought to have a stomach virus, was later admitted to hospital, and died on May 25, 1975. EBSCO's research summary states that doctors attributed the death to infectious hepatitis and kidney failure. His wife collected on a life insurance policy worth about $31,000, according to Oxygen.

The death was not treated as suspicious for more than four years. In 1979 the couple's daughter, Carol, became seriously ill with nausea and numbness in her limbs. Testing found high levels of arsenic in her system, and Oxygen reported that her mother had taken out a life insurance policy on her. Marie Hilley was arrested in October 1979 on a charge of attempting to murder her daughter.

Carol's poisoning led authorities to exhume Frank Hilley's body on October 3, 1979. According to the Wikipedia article, tests found arsenic at between ten and 100 times the normal level, and investigators concluded that he had died of arsenic poisoning. Marie Hilley was released on bond in November 1979 and disappeared. EBSCO and Wikipedia both state that she was indicted for her husband's murder on January 11, 1980, while she was a fugitive.

She remained at large for more than three years, living under assumed names. UPI reported that she had married in Florida under one name and later posed as that woman's sister. Authorities found her in New England in January 1983; Oxygen reported that she was located in Keene, New Hampshire, and acknowledged her identity under questioning. She was returned to Alabama for trial.

At a trial in 1983, a jury found her guilty of the murder of Frank Hilley and the attempted murder of Carol. She was sentenced to life imprisonment for the murder plus 20 years for the attempted murder, according to UPI, Oxygen and EBSCO.

In February 1987 she was granted a three-day furlough from Tutwiler Prison, her first since sentencing, and did not return. UPI reported that Anniston police found her four days later, on February 26, 1987, unconscious on the back porch of a house, and that she died that afternoon at a hospital. A hospital official attributed her death to hypothermia and exposure.

name: Atlanta Child Murders Victims
summary: At least 28 young Black children and adults were murdered in Atlanta between 1979 and 1981, causing citywide panic. Wayne Williams was convicted of two adult murders and sentenced to life. Authorities attributed the child murders to him but never charged him with those. Investigations were reopened in 2019 amid questions about the evidence.
lastSeen: Various dates, Atlanta, GA

sources.title: Wayne Williams - Wikipedia

narrative: Between the summer of 1979 and the spring of 1981, at least 28 Black children, teenagers, and young adults were murdered in Atlanta, Georgia, in a wave of killings that came to be known as the Atlanta Child Murders. Most of the victims were young Black males from poor neighborhoods; many were abducted while running errands or walking through the city, and their bodies were later recovered in wooded areas, along roadsides, or in the Chattahoochee and South rivers. The steady accumulation of deaths spread fear through Atlanta's Black communities, prompted curfews and volunteer search parties, and drew intense national attention, including federal involvement and the eventual formation of a dedicated police task force.

Attention turned to Wayne Bertram Williams, a 23-year-old Atlanta music promoter and freelance photographer, after officers staking out a bridge over the Chattahoochee River reported hearing a splash in the early hours of May 22, 1981. Two days later, the body of Nathaniel Cater, a 27-year-old man, was recovered downstream. Williams was arrested on June 21, 1981. His trial began on January 6, 1982, and on February 27, 1982, a jury convicted him of murdering two adult men, Cater and 21-year-old Jimmy Ray Payne. He was sentenced to two consecutive life terms.

It is important to state precisely: Williams was convicted only of the two adult murders. He was never tried for the killing of any of the children. After his conviction, the police task force concluded there was sufficient evidence to link Williams to many of the other cases, and Atlanta authorities administratively 'cleared' roughly two dozen of the child and teen killings by attributing them to him and closing them. Those cases were never presented to a jury or tested in court. Prosecutors relied heavily on hair and fiber analysis, arguing that unusual carpet and other fibers recovered from victims matched fibers from Williams's home, car, and dog. Defense experts and later critics have questioned the statistical strength and interpretation of that fiber evidence.

The case remains genuinely disputed. Williams has consistently maintained his innocence and has alleged that Atlanta officials covered up evidence pointing elsewhere. Alternative theories have circulated for decades, most prominently the claim that members of the Ku Klux Klan were involved in some of the killings; an early suspect, a white supremacist named Charles T. Sanders, was reportedly recorded making hostile remarks about the victims. These alternative theories have not been proven, and no one else has been charged. Skeptics, including some victims' relatives, have argued that a single-perpetrator conclusion was reached too readily, while others point to the drop in similar killings after Williams's arrest as circumstantial support for his guilt.

In March 2019, Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms, together with the Atlanta Police Department, the Fulton County District Attorney, and the Georgia Bureau of Investigation, announced that authorities would re-examine the murders using modern forensic methods and genetic databases unavailable in the 1980s. Investigators re-analyzed fiber evidence across the roughly 30 cases and sent selected samples to a private laboratory in the Salt Lake City, Utah, area that specializes in recovering DNA from old, degraded material. By 2021, officials said DNA had been extracted and processed in connection with two cases, and the review timeline had been broadened to 1970 through 1985 to check for additional possible victims. As of this writing, the re-investigation has not publicly overturned the original findings; Williams remains imprisoned and continues to assert his innocence.

name: Etan Patz
summary: Six-year-old Etan Patz was one of the first missing children to appear on a milk carton when he disappeared walking to school in SoHo. The case transformed child safety in America. Pedro Hernandez confessed to the murder in 2012 and was convicted in 2017, ending a 38-year mystery.
lastSeen: May 25, 1979, walking to school bus in SoHo, New York City

sources.title: Disappearance of Etan Patz - Wikipedia
Court reimposes conviction of man found to have killed Etan Patz - SCOTUSblog
Supreme Court reinstates murder conviction for Pedro Hernandez in case of Etan Patz - NBC News

narrative: On the morning of May 25, 1979, six-year-old Etan Kalil Patz left his family's loft on Prince Street in the SoHo neighborhood of Lower Manhattan to walk to his school bus stop alone for the first time. According to news accounts and later court records, he never boarded the bus and never arrived at school; he was reported missing that afternoon. His disappearance triggered one of the largest missing-child searches New York City had seen, and his face became one of the first to appear on milk cartons during the 1980s missing-children campaigns. In 1983, President Ronald Reagan designated May 25, the anniversary of Etan's disappearance, as National Missing Children's Day, cementing the case as a landmark in the American missing-children movement.

For decades the case went unsolved. The most prominent early suspect was Jose Ramos, a convicted child molester who had been acquainted with a woman who briefly walked Etan and other children to the bus stop. Federal prosecutor Stuart GraBois pursued Ramos in the late 1980s and 1990s, and reporting notes Ramos made ambiguous statements about being with a boy the day Etan vanished, but he was never charged with the murder. In 2001 Etan was declared legally dead, and in 2004 a civil court awarded his parents a $2 million wrongful-death judgment against Ramos that was never collected. Manhattan District Attorney Cyrus Vance Jr. reopened the investigation on May 25, 2010.

The case shifted in May 2012, when police announced the arrest of Pedro Hernandez, who had worked at a SoHo convenience store in 1979. Authorities said Hernandez confessed to luring Etan with the promise of a soda, strangling him, and disposing of the body. A grand jury indicted him on second-degree murder and first-degree kidnapping charges in November 2012. His first trial ended in a mistrial in May 2015 after jurors deadlocked, reported as 11-to-1 in favor of conviction. After a retrial, a jury found Hernandez guilty on February 14, 2017, and he was sentenced in April 2017 to 25 years to life. His defense argued throughout that his confession was false and unreliable, pointing to his low IQ and mental-health history.

On July 21, 2025, a three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit overturned the conviction, ruling that the trial judge had given a legally erroneous answer to a jury note during deliberations. Jurors had asked whether they must disregard Hernandez's later confessions if they found his initial, pre-Miranda statements involuntary; the judge answered simply, "No." The appeals court found this response "clearly wrong" and "manifestly prejudicial" and ordered that Hernandez be retried or released.

The legal outcome then reversed again. After the Manhattan District Attorney signaled an intent to retry Hernandez, the U.S. Supreme Court took up the matter and, on June 22, 2026, reinstated the conviction in a 6-3 unsigned opinion. The majority held that it was not "clearly established" federal law requiring the challenged jury instruction, and that the Second Circuit had exceeded its authority under federal habeas standards; Justices Sotomayor, Kagan, and Jackson dissented. As of 2026, Hernandez's murder and kidnapping conviction and his 25-years-to-life sentence stand as reinstated. The DA's office had considered the matter resolved as a conviction; Etan Patz's remains have never been found.

name: Susan Reinert
summary: Teacher Susan Reinert of Ardmore was last seen on June 22, 1979; her body was found three days later in the trunk of her car at a hotel near Harrisburg. Her children, Karen, 11, and Michael, 10, were never found. Colleague William Bradfield was convicted in 1983 and died in prison. Former principal Jay C. Smith was convicted in 1986, but the conviction was overturned in 1992.
lastSeen: June 22, 1979, Ardmore, PA

sources.title: UPI Archives - Former principal sentenced to die for slayings of teacher, children

narrative: Susan Reinert, 36, taught English at Upper Merion High School in Montgomery County, Pennsylvania, and lived in Ardmore with her two children, Karen, 11, and Michael, 10. According to the Wikipedia article on Jay C. Smith, the three were last seen on the evening of June 22, 1979.

On June 25, 1979, Reinert's body was found in the trunk of her own car in the parking lot of a hotel in suburban Harrisburg, more than an hour from her home. UPI reported that the body was unclothed and bruised. The Philadelphia Inquirer reported that she died of a massive overdose of morphine. Her children were not with her and have never been located; according to the Unresolved podcast's account of the case, they were declared legally dead in 1986.

Investigators focused on William Bradfield, a fellow Upper Merion teacher who had been romantically involved with Reinert and who was the beneficiary of life insurance on her, which the Inquirer put at about $730,000. According to Wikipedia, Bradfield was convicted in 1981 of fraud for taking $25,000 from Reinert. In 1983 he was convicted in connection with the killings of Reinert and her children and sentenced to life in prison. He died in Graterford prison in January 1998, according to the Inquirer.

Jay C. Smith, the former principal of Upper Merion High School, was charged in 1985. Prosecutors alleged that he and Bradfield had plotted the killing to collect the insurance money, UPI reported. A jury convicted Smith in 1986 of three counts of murder, and he was sentenced to death. Smith denied involvement throughout; UPI quoted him as saying at sentencing that he had no Reinert blood on his hands.

In 1992 the Pennsylvania Supreme Court overturned Smith's conviction and barred a retrial, citing what the Inquirer described as egregious prosecutorial misconduct, including the concealment of evidence. He was released after about six years on death row. According to Wikipedia, his later civil suits against police and against author Joseph Wambaugh, whose 1987 book Echoes in the Darkness covered the case, were unsuccessful. Smith died on May 12, 2009, at age 80, still maintaining his innocence.

Bradfield's 1983 conviction was the only one in the case that was left standing, and both men convicted at trial have since died. The bodies of Karen and Michael Reinert have never been found, and what happened to them after June 22, 1979, has not been established.

name: Betty Gore
summary: Betty Gore, 30, was killed with an axe at her home in Wylie, Texas, on June 13, 1980, sustaining 41 blows. Her friend Candy Montgomery was charged with murder and testified that she acted in self-defense after Gore confronted her. A jury in McKinney acquitted Montgomery on October 30, 1980. No one has been convicted in Gore's death.
lastSeen: June 13, 1980, her home in Wylie, TX

sources.title: Oxygen - How Candy Montgomery, Betty Gore Case Divided Wylie, Texas
Newsweek - What Happened to Candy Montgomery and Where Is She Now?
Wikipedia - Candy Montgomery

narrative: Betty Gore, 30, lived in Wylie, Texas. She was killed at her home on Friday, June 13, 1980. According to the Wikipedia article on the case and reporting by Oxygen, she was struck 41 times with a wood-splitting axe.

Suspicion turned to Candace "Candy" Montgomery, a friend of Gore's and an active member of a local church. Montgomery had had an affair with Gore's husband, a fact that became central to the trial. According to Wikipedia, Montgomery was taken into custody on June 26, 1980, and Wylie police charged her with murder.

Montgomery pleaded not guilty and stood trial in McKinney in the fall of 1980. She did not dispute that she had struck Gore with the axe. Her defense was that she had acted to protect herself: as Oxygen summarized her testimony, the two women were talking about the affair when Gore picked up an axe and became violent. Newsweek reported that Montgomery had undergone hypnosis sessions with a psychiatrist, Dr. Fred Fason, before giving her account in court. Newsweek also reported testimony that Gore was still alive when 40 of the 41 blows were delivered.

The trial lasted eight days, according to Wikipedia. On October 30, 1980, a jury of nine women and three men deliberated for a little more than three hours and found Montgomery not guilty. The acquittal ended the criminal case, and the sources reviewed describe no other person being charged in connection with Gore's death.

The verdict was poorly received by many in the community. Wikipedia describes a crowd outside the courthouse shouting at Montgomery as she left, and quotes Gore's father as saying that the family did not know what had happened and never would. Oxygen reported that the case split Wylie, where a number of fellow church members had supported Montgomery. Newsweek reported that Montgomery and her husband moved to Georgia after the trial and later divorced, and that she has kept out of public view.

The case has been retold several times on screen. Wikipedia lists the 1990 CBS television film A Killing in a Small Town, the 2022 Hulu series Candy, starring Jessica Biel, and the 2023 HBO Max series Love & Death, starring Elizabeth Olsen. Renewed attention from these productions has not changed the legal status of the case: Betty Gore's death was a homicide for which the person tried was acquitted on grounds of self-defense.

timeline.event: Betty Gore, 30, is killed with an axe at her home in Wylie, Texas.
Candy Montgomery is taken into custody and charged with murder.

Hulu releases the series Candy.
HBO Max releases the series Love & Death.

name: Herman Tarnower
summary: Dr. Herman Tarnower, 69, author of the Scarsdale Diet, was shot dead at his home in Purchase, New York, on March 10, 1980, by his longtime companion Jean Harris. Harris said she had meant to kill herself and that the gun went off in a struggle. She was convicted of second-degree murder in February 1981 and sentenced to 15 years to life. Governor Mario Cuomo commuted the sentence in December 1992.
lastSeen: March 10, 1980, his home in Purchase, NY

sources.title: Encyclopedia.com - Jean Harris Trial: 1980-81
Wikipedia - Jean Harris
Wikipedia - Herman Tarnower

narrative: Herman Tarnower was a physician in Westchester County, New York, who became widely known as the author of the best-selling Scarsdale Diet book. According to his Wikipedia biography, he was born in New York City on March 18, 1910, and was 69, a week short of his 70th birthday, when he died.

On March 10, 1980, Tarnower was shot at his home in Purchase, New York. The shooter was Jean Harris, a school headmistress, who had been in a relationship with him for many years. According to the Wikipedia articles on both Tarnower and Harris, he was hit four times at close range by rounds from a .32-caliber revolver. Harris was arrested shortly afterward.

Harris was charged with second-degree murder and tried at the Westchester County Courthouse in White Plains before Judge Russell R. Leggett. According to Encyclopedia.com's account of the trial, proceedings ran from November 21, 1980, to February 24, 1981. Harris did not deny firing the gun. Her account was that she had driven to Tarnower's house intending to take her own life and that he was shot accidentally as the two struggled over the weapon. The jury, in convicting her of second-degree murder, did not accept that account.

The trial lasted about 14 weeks, and the jury deliberated for eight days, according to Wikipedia. Harris was found guilty of second-degree murder, and Judge Leggett imposed the sentence of 15 years to life. She served her sentence at the Bedford Hills Correctional Facility for Women in Westchester County. Encyclopedia.com notes that her appeals continued through the 1980s and that an earlier clemency request was turned down as premature.

On December 29, 1992, Governor Mario Cuomo commuted Harris's sentence. According to Wikipedia, the decision came as she was about to undergo quadruple bypass heart surgery, and she had by then served about 11 years. She was paroled in early 1993.

Following her release, Harris spoke publicly on behalf of women in prison; Encyclopedia.com describes her as a vocal advocate for better treatment of female prisoners. She lived for a time in a retirement community in Hamden, Connecticut, and died of natural causes on December 23, 2012, at age 89, at an assisted-living facility in New Haven, according to Wikipedia. Her conviction was never overturned.

name: Jeannie Mills Family
summary: Peoples Temple defectors Jeannie Mills, 40, and Al Mills, 51, were shot dead with their daughter Daphene, 15, at their Berkeley home on February 26, 1980. The couple had co-founded the Concerned Relatives group. Their son was arrested in December 2005, but prosecutors declined to file charges for lack of evidence and he was released. The killings remain unsolved.
lastSeen: February 26, 1980, family home in Berkeley, CA

sources.title: The Press Democrat / AP - Man arrested in shooting of ex-Peoples Temple members
Cult Education Institute / AP - No charges filed against son in 1980 murders
Wikipedia - Jeannie Mills

narrative: Jeannie and Al Mills, born Deanna and Elmer Mertle, were among the best-known defectors from Peoples Temple, the group led by Jim Jones. According to an Associated Press report carried by the Press Democrat, the couple joined the Temple in 1969 and left in 1975 after their daughter was beaten with a paddle. They changed their names after leaving. According to Wikipedia, they helped found the Concerned Relatives organization in 1977 and ran the Human Freedom Center in Berkeley, and Jeannie Mills published a memoir, Six Years with God.

On February 26, 1980, a little more than a year after the deaths at Jonestown in November 1978, Al Mills, 51, Jeannie Mills, 40, and their daughter Daphene, 15, were found shot in the head at the family's home on Woolsey Street in Berkeley, California. The ages and date are given in the Associated Press report and in a San Francisco Chronicle article archived by San Diego State University's Jonestown project.

Because of the family's history, the killings prompted speculation about retaliation by surviving Temple loyalists. The Chronicle noted that the couple had asked for police protection after leaving the Temple. Wikipedia states that the theories about Temple "hit squads" were never substantiated. No arrests were made at the time, and the investigation eventually went cold.

The couple's son, Edward Mills, then 17, was in the house at the time. According to the Associated Press and the Chronicle, he told police he had been unaware of the shootings and denied any involvement. Police reported finding gunshot residue on his hands, but he was not arrested in 1980.

Berkeley police reopened the case in about 2003 as part of a cold case review. In early December 2005, Edward Mills, then 43 and living in Japan, was arrested on a Berkeley police warrant when he arrived at San Francisco International Airport. Within days, the Alameda County District Attorney's Office declined to file charges. The Associated Press quoted prosecutor Chris Carpenter as saying the evidence was not sufficient to meet the required standard. Mills was released and, according to the Jonestown project, returned to Japan. He has not been charged with any crime in connection with the deaths, and the Jonestown project states that family members maintain he is innocent.

At the time of the 2005 arrest, a Berkeley police spokesperson said investigators had looked at Peoples Temple but that it did not appear to have been a motive. No one has been charged in the deaths of Al, Jeannie and Daphene Mills, and the case remains unsolved.

name: Tammy Terrell
summary: The body of a teenage girl found in the desert in Henderson, Nevada, on October 5, 1980, was identified in 2021 as Tammy Terrell, 17, of Roswell, New Mexico. Known for 41 years as Arroyo Grande Jane Doe, she had been stabbed and beaten. She was last seen in Roswell on September 28, 1980. Henderson police identified her through genetic genealogy; her killing remains unsolved.
lastSeen: September 28, 1980, Roswell, NM

sources.title: KTVZ / CNN - Nevada police identify victim of 41-year-old cold case homicide using genealogy and DNA testing
KOLO-TV / AP - Henderson police ID girl from New Mexico found dead in 1980
Wikipedia - Murder of Tammy Terrell

narrative: On the evening of October 5, 1980, a passing driver found the body of a teenage girl in a desert area of Henderson, Nevada, near what is now Arroyo Grande Boulevard and Lake Mead Parkway, according to a CNN report republished by KTVZ. With no identification, she became known as Arroyo Grande Jane Doe, a name taken from the place where she was found.

The death was ruled a homicide. KOLO-TV, citing Henderson police, reported that she had been stabbed and beaten, possibly with a hammer. According to the Wikipedia article on the case, she had multiple head wounds and several puncture wounds in her upper back, and investigators estimated that she had died roughly a day before she was found.

For 41 years, efforts to learn her name were unsuccessful. According to Wikipedia, hair samples were sent to a specialist laboratory in 2019, and the resulting DNA profile was uploaded to a genealogy database for comparison with potential relatives, in work overseen by genetic genealogist Barbara Rae-Venter. Police described the technique as investigative genetic genealogy, in which DNA testing is used to find possible relatives of an unidentified person. The identification was confirmed with DNA from two of her sisters.

On December 2, 2021, the Henderson Police Department announced that the victim was Tammy Corrine Terrell, 17, of Roswell, New Mexico. The CNN report states that the identification itself was made on November 10, 2021. Wikipedia gives her date of birth as July 4, 1963.

Police said Tammy was last seen on September 28, 1980, in Roswell. According to the accounts summarized by Wikipedia, she had been dropped off at the state fair in Roswell that day and was later seen at a restaurant in the city in the company of a white man and woman who have not been identified; there were indications they may have been traveling toward California. Her body was found in Nevada one week later.

No suspect has been publicly identified and no one has been charged. KOLO-TV reported that, with a name now attached to the victim, Henderson police were treating the case as an active murder investigation. As of the sources reviewed, the killing remains unsolved and the investigation is described by police as ongoing.

timeline.event: Tammy Corrine Terrell is born, according to Wikipedia.

name: Adam Walsh
summary: Six-year-old Adam Walsh was abducted from a Sears store in Hollywood, Florida, on July 27, 1981. His severed head was found two weeks later. The case transformed his father John Walsh into a victims' rights advocate who went on to host America's Most Wanted. Ottis Toole confessed to the murder and later recanted; he died in prison in 1996 without being charged, and police named him as the killer when they closed the case in 2008.
lastSeen: July 27, 1981, Sears store, Hollywood, FL

sources.title: Murder of Adam Walsh - Wikipedia
Ottis Toole - Wikipedia
Police Name Killer, Close Adam Walsh Murder Case - NPR
Six-year-old Adam Walsh is abducted, July 27, 1981 - HISTORY
Adam Walsh Murder: The Missing Child Who Changed America - TIME

narrative: On July 27, 1981, six-year-old Adam Walsh vanished from a Sears department store at the Hollywood Mall in Hollywood, Florida. His mother, Reve Walsh, had briefly left him near a display of Atari video games while she shopped a short distance away; when she returned a few minutes later, Adam was gone. A security guard is reported to have ushered a group of boys out of the store after a dispute at the game kiosk, and Adam was not seen again by his family. Two weeks later, on August 10, 1981, fishermen discovered the child's severed head in a drainage canal off the Florida Turnpike near Vero Beach in Indian River County, roughly 120 miles north of the mall. The rest of his remains were never found.

Adam's murder devastated his parents, John and Reve Walsh, and transformed John Walsh into one of the most prominent victims' advocates in the United States. Just days after their son's funeral, the couple founded what became the Adam Walsh Outreach Center for Missing Children, and John Walsh went on to lobby Congress for reforms in how missing children were tracked and searched for. His advocacy helped drive passage of the Missing Children Act of 1982 and the Missing Children's Assistance Act of 1984, which led to the creation of the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children. In 1988 he became the host of the television program America's Most Wanted. In 2006, the Adam Walsh Child Protection and Safety Act was signed into law, establishing a national sex-offender registry and other measures in Adam's name.

The investigation stretched over more than two decades and drew intense national attention, but it was hampered by mistakes. Drifter and convicted serial killer Ottis Toole became the prime suspect after he told investigators in 1983 that he had abducted and killed a boy from a South Florida mall, later specifically confessing to Adam's murder. Toole repeatedly confessed and then recanted over the years, and the physical case against him was undermined when Hollywood police lost key evidence, including bloodstained carpeting and a machete from Toole's car, and eventually the vehicle itself. Toole was never charged with Adam's killing. He died in prison of cirrhosis of the liver on September 15, 1996, while serving time for unrelated crimes.

On December 16, 2008, Hollywood Police Chief Chad Wagner, appearing alongside John and Reve Walsh, announced that the department was administratively closing the case and that its review of the file had satisfied investigators that Ottis Toole was Adam's killer. Police acknowledged they had no DNA or surviving physical evidence tying Toole to the crime and declined to detail their reasoning, resting the conclusion largely on an external review of the existing case file. The closure brought the Walsh family a measure of resolution but no courtroom verdict.

It is important to note that Ottis Toole was never convicted, and never even charged, in connection with Adam Walsh's murder. The 2008 announcement was a police administrative decision to close the case naming Toole as the perpetrator, not a criminal conviction, and Toole had already been dead for twelve years by that point. No living person has ever been prosecuted for the crime, and the case remains formally closed by police rather than resolved through the courts.
