name: Dean and Tina Clouse
summary: The remains of Harold Dean Clouse Jr. and his wife, Tina Linn Clouse, were found in woods in the Houston area on January 12, 1981, and were not identified until 2021 through genetic genealogy. Their infant daughter, Holly, was missing until June 2022, when she was located alive in Oklahoma. No suspect has been named, and the homicides remain unsolved.
lastSeen: Late 1980, Lewisville, TX

sources.title: Texas Observer - Who Killed Dean and Tina Clouse?
ABC13 Houston - Baby Holly cold case: Woman found alive 40 years after her parents were killed
FOX 7 Austin - 'Baby Holly' found alive 40 years later; still no suspect in parents' murders
Wikipedia - Murders of Dean and Tina Clouse
NBC News - 'Baby Holly,' missing child of Florida couple murdered in 1981, found alive at age 42
NPR - 'Baby Holly' found alive over 40 years after parents turned up dead in Houston
ABC News - 'Baby Holly' speaks out for the 1st time after being missing for over 40 years
NBC News - Couple murdered in Houston in 1981 identified; daughter, now 41, still missing

narrative: Harold Dean Clouse Jr. and Tina Gail Linn married in June 1979 and had a daughter, Holly Marie, in January 1980. According to the Texas Observer, the family moved from Florida to Lewisville, Texas, in 1980 after Dean found construction work there. Relatives stopped hearing from them late that year. Wikipedia gives Dean's age at death as 21 and Tina's as 17.

On January 12, 1981, the remains of a man and a woman were found in a wooded area off Wallisville Road in Harris County, in the Houston area. According to the Texas Observer, the bodies lay several feet apart. The man had been beaten to death and the woman had been strangled. Investigators believe they were killed between December 1980 and early January 1981, FOX 7 Austin reported. No child was found at the scene, and the two victims could not be identified.

In the months after the couple fell out of contact, their families had an unusual encounter. FOX 7 reported that relatives received a call from a woman calling herself "Sister Susan," who said the couple had joined a religious group and were giving up their possessions. The Texas Observer reported that women in white robes returned the couple's car to Florida and asked for money. The families did not know that Dean and Tina were dead.

The remains stayed unidentified for four decades. In 2021, Identifinders International, a firm that performs genetic genealogy for law enforcement, identified them as Dean and Tina Clouse, according to ABC13 Houston. The identification raised a new question: what had happened to Holly.

In June 2022, the Texas Attorney General's Cold Case and Missing Persons Unit announced that Holly had been found alive, aged 42, living in Oklahoma. ABC13 reported that as a baby she had been left at a church in Arizona by two barefoot women in white robes who belonged to a nomadic religious group, and that she was subsequently raised by an adoptive family. Officials said the family that raised her is not suspected of any involvement. ABC13 noted that she was located on what would have been her father's birthday.

No one has been arrested or publicly named as a suspect in the killings. FOX 7 reported that the Texas Attorney General's Office was asking members of the public with information to contact its cold case unit. Authorities have not publicly linked any individual to the deaths, and the investigation remains open.

name: Keddie Cabin Murders
summary: Glenna "Sue" Sharp, her son John, and his friend Dana Wingate were bound, stabbed, and bludgeoned in Cabin 28 at the Keddie Resort on the night of April 11-12, 1981. Three younger boys in an adjacent bedroom were unharmed, while Sue's 12-year-old daughter Tina vanished; her remains were found in 1984 in Butte County. No one has ever been charged, and the case remains unsolved; persons of interest Martin Smartt and John Boubede both died without being charged.
lastSeen: April 11, 1981, Cabin 28, Keddie Resort, CA

sources.title: Keddie murders - Wikipedia
Keddie murders revisited part 1: New evidence discovered - Plumas News
35 Years Later, New Clues May Solve Keddie Murder Mystery - CBS Sacramento
Keddie murders revisited - following the clues - Plumas News
Are Martin Smartt and John 'Bo' Boubede Dead or Alive? - The Cinemaholic

narrative: On the night of April 11-12, 1981, four people were killed inside Cabin 28 of the Keddie Resort, a small mountain community in Plumas County, California. The victims were Glenna Susan "Sue" Sharp, a 36-year-old single mother who had recently moved to Keddie; her 15-year-old son John Steven Sharp; and John's 17-year-old friend Dana Hall Wingate. Sue's 12-year-old daughter, Tina Louise Sharp, was missing from the cabin and would remain unaccounted for. The three bodies were discovered on the morning of April 12 by Sue's 14-year-old daughter Sheila, who had spent the night at a neighbor's home. Three younger children -- Sue's sons Rick and Greg and their friend Justin Smartt -- were found unharmed in an adjacent bedroom.

The victims had been bound with medical tape and electrical wire and killed with a combination of knives and a hammer or similar blunt instrument, an unusually violent scene that drew regional attention. The initial investigation, handled by the Plumas County Sheriff's Office with assistance from state and federal agencies, was later widely criticized for mishandled leads and evidence. Tina Sharp's fate remained unknown until April 1984, when a bottle collector found a human skull and other bones at Camp 18 near Feather Falls in Butte County, roughly 60 miles from Keddie. The remains were confirmed to be Tina's in June 1984. No one was arrested, and the case went cold for decades.

Over the years, attention focused on two men who were publicly reported as persons of interest but who were never charged: Martin "Marty" Smartt, a neighbor who lived nearby, and his houseguest and associate Severin John "Bo" Boubede. According to later reporting, Smartt had told investigators that a claw hammer went missing from his home around the time of the killings, and Boubede reportedly gave authorities false claims about his background. Both men died before any charges were considered -- Boubede in 1988 and Smartt, reportedly of cancer, in 2000. It is important to stress that neither man was ever charged or convicted, and their identification as suspects rests on investigative reporting and reopened-case statements rather than any adjudicated finding of guilt.

The Plumas County Sheriff's Office reopened the case in 2013 under Sheriff Greg Hagwood, with special investigator Mike Gamberg leading much of the renewed work. In March 2016 a hammer matching the description of the one Smartt had reported missing was recovered from a pond near the crime scene, after a relative of Boubede reportedly provided information; the hammer and a knife were slated for forensic testing. Investigators subsequently reported that DNA recovered from medical tape used at the scene matched what Gamberg described as a "known living suspect," a claim officials made publicly but which has not resulted in charges. Reports have also circulated of a claimed confession by Smartt to a Veterans Affairs counselor in Reno; this account is attributed to the counselor and remains an unproven claim that was reportedly treated as hearsay.

As of this writing the Keddie murders remain officially unsolved, with no one ever convicted in the deaths of Sue, John, Tina, and Dana. Investigators have suggested that several people may have been involved in the crimes or a subsequent cover-up, but those statements have not been tested in court. The case continues to be listed as active, and any characterization of specific individuals as responsible should be understood as unproven and never established through prosecution.

name: Marcia King (Buckskin Girl)
summary: Marcia King, 21, of Arkansas, was found strangled beside Greenlee Road near Troy, Ohio, on April 24, 1981. Unidentified for nearly 37 years, she was known as Buckskin Girl for her fringed jacket. The DNA Doe Project identified her through genetic genealogy, and her identity was confirmed on April 9, 2018. No suspect has been identified in her killing.
lastSeen: 1980, Little Rock, AR (last contact with family)

sources.title: DNA Doe Project - Buckskin Girl
DNA Doe Project - Buckskin Girl Press Release
KATV - Arkansas woman identified as victim in 37-year-old Ohio case
FOX19 - Jane 'Buckskin Girl' Doe identified after 37 years
Wikipedia - Murder of Marcia King

narrative: On April 24, 1981, the body of a young woman was found in a ditch beside Greenlee Road in Miami County, Ohio, near Troy and about 20 miles north of Dayton, according to FOX19 and KATV. She was fully clothed in jeans and a distinctive fringed buckskin jacket, but was barefoot and carried no identification. The jacket gave rise to the name by which she was known for decades, Buckskin Girl.

KATV reported that the cause of death was strangulation, along with blunt force trauma. The DNA Doe Project states that she had been dead for only a day or two when she was found. Fingerprints were taken but matched no records, according to the organization's press release.

Investigators returned to the case repeatedly as forensic methods advanced. According to the DNA Doe Project, a nuclear DNA profile was developed in 2001, the case was entered into the National Missing and Unidentified Persons System in 2008, and mitochondrial DNA was submitted to the FBI's CODIS database in 2009. Pollen analysis of her clothing and isotope testing of her hair suggested she had spent time in the southwestern United States and in northern Texas in the year before her death. None of this produced a name.

The case became one of the first taken on by the DNA Doe Project, a nonprofit founded in 2017 to apply genetic genealogy to unidentified remains. A blood sample preserved since 1981 was processed and the profile uploaded to the GEDmatch database. According to the organization, its volunteers found a candidate within about four hours on March 29, 2018. The identification was confirmed on April 9, 2018, by comparison with a relative's DNA, and was announced by the Miami County Sheriff's Office that month.

The victim was Marcia Lenore King, born Marcia Sossoman on June 9, 1959, in Arkansas. She was 21. According to the DNA Doe Project, she often hitchhiked and had left home in Arkansas in 1980, after which her family did not hear from her. The organization's press release notes that her mother kept the same home and telephone number throughout the 37 years in the hope that she would return.

With a name established, the sheriff's office said it would go forward with the homicide investigation. FOX19 reported that detectives were concentrating on the last month of King's life and on connections to Pittsburgh and Louisville, Kentucky. No suspect has been publicly identified, and the Miami County Sheriff's Office has continued to ask for tips.

name: Philip Testa
summary: Philip "Chicken Man" Testa, 56, reputed head of the Philadelphia crime family, was fatally injured on March 15, 1981 when a nail-packed bomb exploded on the porch of his South Philadelphia home. Theodore DiPretoro pleaded guilty to the murder in 1983 and received a life sentence. Rocco Marinucci, whom police sources said triggered the device, was found shot dead a year later.
lastSeen: March 15, 1981, front porch of his home on Porter Street, South Philadelphia, PA

narrative: Philip Testa, widely known by the nickname "Chicken Man," was described by law enforcement and in press reports as the man who took over leadership of Philadelphia's organized crime family after longtime boss Angelo Bruno was shot dead in March 1980. According to United Press International, Testa had been indicted on federal racketeering charges along with Frank Narducci and eight others in February 1981, only weeks before his own death.

At about 3 a.m. on Sunday, March 15, 1981, Testa was returning to his twin home on Porter Street in the Girard Estates section of South Philadelphia when an explosive device packed with nails went off at the front porch. According to the organized crime history site The Writers of Wrongs, which summarizes contemporary newspaper coverage, the blast tore through the concrete porch floor and drove the front door into the house, and investigators concluded that the bomb had been set off by remote control by someone who could see the porch. Testa was taken to St. Agnes Hospital and died roughly an hour later. He was 56. UPI reported that he was buried on March 20, 1981 at Holy Cross Cemetery in Yeadon, close to Bruno's grave.

The investigation led to two young men from South Philadelphia. UPI reported in June 1982 that Theodore DiPretoro, then 21, had been charged with Testa's murder, with police alleging that he built and planted the device. Police sources cited in the same report said that Rocco Marinucci, 30, was present and triggered the bomb from a van parked nearby. Marinucci was never tried: he was found dead on March 15, 1982, the first anniversary of the bombing, with firecrackers in his mouth, in what investigators regarded as retaliation.

DiPretoro pleaded guilty to the murder on September 20, 1983. According to UPI, he told the court he had helped Marinucci because he feared he would be killed if he refused. In November 1983 Common Pleas Judge Lisa Richette sentenced him to life in prison, to run concurrently with a life term he was already serving for an unrelated 1980 killing.

Who ordered the bombing has never been established in court. Published accounts, including Testa's Wikipedia biography, state that the plot was allegedly directed by his underboss Peter Casella and by Narducci; neither man was convicted of it. Narducci was shot dead in January 1982, and Casella was reportedly forced out of the organization and moved to Florida. Testa's killing is generally described as one of the opening events of a violent struggle inside the Philadelphia crime family during the early 1980s. His son Salvatore Testa was himself shot dead in 1984.

Some reference lists still classify the Testa bombing as unsolved, apparently because the people alleged to have ordered it were never prosecuted. The court record, however, shows that one participant admitted his role and was sentenced for the murder.

name: Sebastian Russo
summary: Dr. Sebastian Russo, 56, a Baltimore family physician known for charging patients $5 or less, was shot dead in his Harford Road office on the evening of February 27, 1981. An open drug cabinet led detectives to suspect the killer wanted drugs. Two people seen in the waiting room were never identified, and no one has been charged.
lastSeen: February 27, 1981, his medical office on Harford Road in the Hamilton neighborhood of Baltimore, MD

sources.title: Dan Rodricks - The unsolved murder of the five-dollar doc
Wikipedia - Sebastian Russo
Wikipedia - List of unsolved murders (1980-1999)

narrative: Sebastian Russo was born in Riposto, Sicily, on November 15, 1924, according to his Wikipedia biography, and later settled in Baltimore, where he worked as a primary care physician. He practiced out of a rowhouse office on Harford Road in the Hamilton neighborhood of northeast Baltimore. Columnist Dan Rodricks, who has written about the case several times, describes him as an old-fashioned doctor who opened his office early in the morning, saw dozens of patients a day and still made house calls. Because he usually charged $5 or less for a visit, he was remembered after his death as the last of Baltimore's "$5 doctors."

On the evening of Friday, February 27, 1981, a neighbor heard a noise coming from the office and called police. According to the account summarized on Wikipedia, officers arrived some time after 9:30 p.m. and found Russo lying on his back with a single gunshot wound to the upper left chest. His keys were on the floor beside him and the door of a drug cabinet was open. Those details led Baltimore homicide detectives to suspect that the person responsible had been looking for drugs.

Patients who had been in the waiting room that evening gave investigators their best lead. They said a man had come into the office, left, then come back a few minutes later and waited about an hour to be seen. When the last of those witnesses left, the man and a woman were still in the office; it was not clear whether the two had arrived together. Rodricks reports that police circulated descriptions of a man in a green jacket and a woman in a tan coat, and that the two were believed to have left in a blue van. Neither person was ever identified.

The investigation was led by Sergeant Dick Ellwood of the Baltimore Police homicide unit. No arrest was made. According to Wikipedia, a reward fund set up for information about the killing went unclaimed, and part of the money was later used to help pay for a memorial clock erected in the doctor's honor in 1983.

More than four decades later the case has not been solved. Rodricks wrote in 2023 that it remains open but is not being actively investigated, and he published the Baltimore Police Department's homicide tip contacts for anyone with information. No suspect has ever been publicly named or charged in connection with Dr. Russo's death.

timeline.event: Sebastian Russo is born in Riposto, Sicily.

name: Tammy Mahoney
summary: Tammy Mahoney, a 19-year-old SUNY Morrisville student, vanished on May 8, 1981 after hitchhiking near Route 46 in Oneida, New York. The FBI says she was taken to a party on Territory Road on Oneida Indian Nation land and was last seen leaving on foot after an altercation. Investigators believe she was killed, but she has never been found and no one has been charged.
lastSeen: May 8, 1981, leaving a party at a residence on Territory Road, off Route 46, in Oneida, NY

sources.title: Spectrum News - FBI confirms last-known whereabouts of Tammy Mahoney, missing since 1981
Spectrum News - 40 years since Tammy Mahoney's disappearance, mysteries and hope remain
CNY Central - FBI, NYS Police provide update on Tammy Mahoney case, exactly 42 years after disappearance

narrative: Tammy Mahoney was 19 years old and a student at SUNY Morrisville in central New York when she disappeared on Friday, May 8, 1981. According to CNY Central, she was hitchhiking on State Route 46 near the city of Oneida that evening. Her family and friends never heard from her again, and no trace of her has been found in the decades since.

For many years the public account of her last movements was limited to the fact that she had been seen hitchhiking. Investigators long believed that she had been picked up and taken to a gathering on territory of the Oneida Indian Nation. Spectrum News reported in 2021 that investigators believe she was killed the night she disappeared, and CNY Central has reported that law enforcement believes she was kidnapped, sexually assaulted and murdered. No one has been charged, and those beliefs have not been tested in court.

The case is being investigated by the FBI together with the New York State Police. In 2016, searches of wooded areas and of a property on Chestnut Ridge Road produced no evidence, according to CNY Central. In 2019 the reward for information was increased, with the Oneida Indian Nation matching the federal contribution for a reported total of $40,000.

In October 2020 the FBI made a public appeal about a wallet that had been handed in at the Oneida police station about a week after Mahoney vanished. Agents said they wanted to speak with the unidentified person who turned it in, believing that person might have knowledge of what happened. FBI Special Agent Thomas Relford told Spectrum News in 2021 that the appeal had produced promising leads and that investigators needed someone who had been at the party, or who had heard about it afterward, to come forward.

In March 2022 the FBI publicly confirmed key details for the first time: that Mahoney was taken to a party at a residence on Territory Road, and that she was last seen leaving on foot following an altercation. On May 8, 2023, the 42nd anniversary of her disappearance, the FBI and State Police announced that more investigators and resources were being assigned to the case. Officials said additional witnesses had gone on the record during the previous year and that their accounts corroborated what earlier witnesses had reported.

Mahoney's mother died without learning what happened to her daughter, her sister told Spectrum News. As of the most recent reports located, the case remains open, no remains have been recovered and no arrests have been made. The FBI asks anyone with information to contact its Albany field office.

name: Chicago Tylenol Murders Victims
summary: Seven people in Chicago died after taking cyanide-laced Tylenol capsules in 1982. The deaths prompted a nationwide recall and led to tamper-resistant packaging regulations. James W. Lewis was convicted of extortion related to the case but was never charged with the murders. The killer has never been identified.
lastSeen: September 29, 1982, Chicago area, IL

sources.title: Chicago Tylenol murders - Wikipedia
The 1982 Tylenol murders: Who did it? No one has ever been charged - CBS News Chicago
How the Tylenol murders of 1982 changed the way we consume medication - PBS NewsHour
Changes in the Law Result From OTC Drug Product Tampering - Pharmacy Times

narrative: In late September and early October 1982, seven people in the Chicago metropolitan area died after taking Extra-Strength Tylenol capsules that had been secretly laced with potassium cyanide. The first known victim was 12-year-old Mary Kellerman of Elk Grove Village, who collapsed on September 29, 1982, after her parents gave her a capsule for a cold. Within days, postal worker Adam Janus, 27, died, followed by his brother Stanley, 25, and Stanley's wife Theresa, 19, who had taken capsules from the same bottle while grieving. The other victims were Mary McFarland, 31, Paula Prince, 35, and Mary Reiner, 27. Investigators determined the capsules had not been contaminated at the factories in Pennsylvania and Texas but had been tampered with after distribution, most likely on or near store shelves, then returned to pharmacies and supermarkets across the area.

The deaths triggered one of the largest product recalls in U.S. history. Johnson & Johnson, through its McNeil Consumer Products subsidiary, pulled roughly 31 million bottles of Tylenol from shelves nationwide at a cost estimated to exceed 100 million dollars, and warned the public against consuming the product. The company's transparent, consumer-first response is still cited as a model of corporate crisis management; it later reintroduced the product in triple-sealed, tamper-resistant packaging. The case reshaped consumer safety in the United States: manufacturers adopted tamper-evident seals and shifted from easily opened powder capsules toward solid caplets, and in 1983 Congress passed the Federal Anti-Tampering Act (codified at 18 U.S.C. 1365), making it a federal crime to tamper with consumer products. The FDA followed with tamper-resistant packaging regulations, later strengthened in 1989.

The investigation drew federal and local agencies but never produced a murder charge. James W. Lewis became the central figure after he mailed Johnson & Johnson a letter demanding 1 million dollars to 'stop the killing.' Lewis was convicted in 1983 of extortion for that demand and served roughly 13 years in federal prison, but he was never charged with the poisonings and consistently denied committing them. Court filings unsealed in early 2009 showed Justice Department investigators believed Lewis was responsible, though they lacked evidence to charge him. Other people were examined and ruled out, including Roger Arnold, a warehouse worker who possessed cyanide and who in 1983 fatally shot a man he wrongly believed had informed on him.

Authorities revived the case around its 25th anniversary. In 2009, the FBI searched Lewis's Cambridge, Massachusetts, home, and in 2010 investigators collected DNA from Lewis and exhumed Arnold's remains for comparison; the samples did not match evidence recovered from the tampered bottles. Lewis died on July 9, 2023, at age 76 in Cambridge; the Massachusetts medical examiner attributed his death to heart and liver disease and found no foul play. As of 2026, no one has ever been charged or convicted of the murders. The case remains open, overseen by the Arlington Heights Police Department, and is officially unsolved more than four decades after the deaths.

name: Diane Suzuki
summary: Diane Suzuki, a 19-year-old University of Hawaii student, disappeared on July 6, 1985 from the Rosalie Woodson Dance Academy in Aiea, where she taught part-time. Her purse, keys and car were left behind. Honolulu police later found apparent blood in a studio bathroom and classified the case as a homicide, but her body was never found and a 1993 investigative grand jury led to no charges.
lastSeen: July 6, 1985, Rosalie Woodson Dance Academy in Aiea, Hawaii

sources.title: Honolulu Star-Bulletin - Lack of evidence halts Suzuki case (May 3, 2000)
Wikipedia - Disappearance of Diane Suzuki
iHeart - Beneath the Palms podcast: The Disappearance of Diane Suzuki (episode page)

narrative: Diane Yayoe Suzuki was a 19-year-old student at the University of Hawaii at Manoa who also worked as a part-time instructor at the Rosalie Woodson Dance Academy in Aiea, on the island of Oahu. According to Wikipedia's summary of the case, she was born on May 14, 1966, and stood just under five feet tall.

On Saturday, July 6, 1985, Suzuki finished teaching a class at the studio and was expected to leave at around 5 p.m. She was not seen again. Her purse, her keys and her car were all still at the dance academy, which suggested to her family and to police that she had not left voluntarily. An extensive search of Oahu followed, but no trace of her was located.

The Honolulu Police Department initially handled the matter as a missing person case. Attention turned early to an acquaintance of Suzuki's who worked as a photographer at the dance school. According to a 2000 report in the Honolulu Star-Bulletin, he was questioned soon after she vanished and reportedly failed a polygraph examination, but he was released without charges after his family retained an attorney. Police also searched a marsh area behind his home. He has never been charged with any offense connected to the disappearance.

Several years later, investigators returned to the studio and applied luminol, a chemical that reacts with traces of blood, in an upstairs bathroom. The test indicated what police believed to be blood, and the case was reclassified as a homicide. Wikipedia notes that this was the first Honolulu Police Department investigation to make use of luminol. The Star-Bulletin reported, however, that there was no record of Suzuki's blood type available for comparison, which limited what the finding could prove.

In November 1993, Honolulu Prosecuting Attorney Keith Kaneshiro convened an investigative grand jury to put witness statements on the record under oath. The Star-Bulletin quoted him as saying that many people were called, including some who were regarded as suspects. No indictment followed. Kaneshiro explained that without a body it was not possible to establish a cause of death, which made it difficult to build a prosecution. The newspaper reported that the case had not been actively investigated since that time.

Suzuki's family held a memorial service for her on July 6, 1997, twelve years to the day after she disappeared. Her mother, Yuri Suzuki, died in December 1998. The case has continued to draw attention in Hawaii, including a podcast episode released in 2025 marking forty years since the disappearance. Diane Suzuki has never been found, and the case remains unsolved.

name: Dorothea Puente Victims
summary: Dorothea Puente was a Sacramento boardinghouse operator who poisoned elderly tenants and continued cashing their Social Security checks. Seven bodies were found buried in her yard in 1988. She was convicted of three murders and died in prison in 2011. She remains one of history's most notorious female serial killers.
lastSeen: N/A

sources.title: Dorothea Puente - Wikipedia
The Life and Deaths of Dorothea Puente - Sactown Magazine
Dorothea Puente - Crime Museum

Casetext (Internet Archive copy) - Puente v. Mitchell, N.D. Cal. 2006

narrative: Dorothea Puente operated a boarding house at 1426 F Street in downtown Sacramento, California, presenting herself as a caring landlady who took in elderly, disabled, and marginalized tenants, many of them referred to her through social services. Behind that reputation, she systematically murdered residents and continued to collect their Social Security and other government benefit checks after their deaths, forging signatures and diverting the funds for her own use.

Between 1982 and 1988, Puente is believed to have killed at least nine people, typically by drugging them with sedatives before they died. Her earliest identified victim was Ruth Munroe, a business associate who died of a codeine overdose in April 1982. Another early victim was her boyfriend Everson Gillmouth, 77, whose remains were found in a box along the Sacramento River in January 1986 but not identified for years. Most of her later victims were tenants at the F Street house, and their bodies were buried in the yard of the property.

The scheme unraveled in November 1988. Social workers and family had grown concerned about a missing developmentally disabled tenant, Alvaro 'Bert' Montoya, and on November 11, 1988, police and a federal probation agent came to the boarding house and began digging in the yard. They uncovered human remains, and over the following days investigators exhumed a total of seven bodies buried on the property. Puente, questioned but not immediately detained, fled Sacramento and was arrested days later in Los Angeles after a man she met at a bar recognized her from news reports.

Puente was ultimately charged with nine counts of murder. Her trial, moved to Monterey on a change of venue, began in early 1993 and featured lengthy jury deliberations that became among the longest in California history to that point. On August 26, 1993, the jury convicted her of three murders: first-degree murder in the deaths of tenants Dorothy Miller and Benjamin Fink, and second-degree murder in the death of Leona Carpenter. The jury deadlocked on the remaining six counts, which resulted in a mistrial on those charges; prosecutors did not retry them.

The jury declined to impose the death penalty, and on December 10, 1993, Puente was sentenced to two life terms in prison without the possibility of parole. She was incarcerated at the Central California Women's Facility in Chowchilla, where she consistently maintained her innocence and denied killing anyone, insisting the deaths were natural.

Dorothea Puente died in prison on March 27, 2011, at the age of 82. Because the case ended in conviction, it is not an unsolved matter; the recorded status reflects her 1993 convictions on three counts of murder. The six deadlocked counts, along with earlier suspected victims such as Ruth Munroe and Everson Gillmouth, were never adjudicated, leaving the full number of her victims a matter of historical estimate rather than legal finding.

name: Green River Killer Victims
summary: Gary Ridgway, the Green River Killer, murdered at least 49 women in Washington State. He targeted mostly sex workers and runaways. Ridgway was convicted in 2003 after DNA evidence linked him to four victims. He pleaded guilty and led investigators to several bodies in exchange for avoiding the death penalty.
lastSeen: N/A

Green River homicides investigation - King County Sheriff's Office
Green River Killer Gary Ridgway returned to King County to locate more victim remains - KOMO News

narrative: Beginning in the summer of 1982, the bodies of young women and girls started appearing in and around the Green River in King County, Washington. The first confirmed victim, 16-year-old Wendy Lee Coffield, was discovered in the river on July 15, 1982. Within about a month, four more bodies were found along the riverbank, including Debra Lynn Bonner, Marcia Faye Chapman, Opal Charmaine Mills, and Cynthia Jean Hinds. Many of the victims were vulnerable women, including runaways and those involved in sex work, whom the killer targeted before disposing of their remains in wooded and rural sites across the region. The cluster of killings prompted the King County Sheriff's Office to form the Green River Task Force in 1982, launching one of the longest and most resource-intensive serial-murder investigations in U.S. history.

The killings continued through the 1980s and, by some accounts, into the 1990s, while the task force struggled to identify a suspect despite thousands of tips. Gary Leon Ridgway, a truck painter at the Kenworth plant in Renton, first drew investigators' attention in 1983 after the disappearance of Marie Malvar, whose companions reported seeing his truck. Ridgway was questioned and, in 1984, passed a polygraph examination, and for years there was insufficient evidence to charge him. The case remained largely stalled until advances in forensic DNA analysis allowed investigators to re-examine biological evidence preserved from the crime scenes and from samples taken from Ridgway years earlier.

In 2001, DNA testing linked Ridgway to several of the victims, and he was arrested on November 30, 2001, at the Kenworth factory. Prosecutors reached a plea agreement that spared Ridgway the death penalty in exchange for his full cooperation in locating victims' remains and detailing his crimes. On November 5, 2003, Ridgway pleaded guilty to 48 counts of aggravated first-degree murder, and on December 18, 2003, he was sentenced to 48 consecutive life terms without the possibility of parole, plus additional time for evidence tampering. At the time he was the most prolific convicted serial killer in American history. He later pleaded guilty to a 49th murder after the remains of Rebecca Marrero were identified.

Even after Ridgway's convictions, the case has never fully closed. He admitted to killing far more women than he was charged with, at times claiming a total that authorities could not fully corroborate, and some presumed victims have never been recovered. According to the King County Sheriff's Office, several women linked to the case remain missing and some recovered remains long went unidentified. Modern genetic testing has since produced new identifications: investigators identified Lori Anne Razpotnik, previously known only as 'Bones 17,' in December 2023, and remains cataloged as 'Bones 20' were identified as Tammie Liles.

As of 2026, Ridgway remains incarcerated in the Washington state prison system, serving his life sentences, and investigators continue to work the case. In September 2024, court records show Ridgway was briefly returned from prison to King County, where he was booked into the county jail from September 9 to September 13 and taken to sites where he believed additional remains might be found, after earlier attempts based on his verbal descriptions had failed. The King County Sheriff's Office states that the investigation continues in order to identify unnamed victims, locate other missing women, and confirm additional potential victims, and it continues to seek information from the public.

name: Kathleen McCormack Durst
summary: Kathleen McCormack Durst, a 29-year-old medical student, disappeared on January 31, 1982 from South Salem, New York, and has never been found. A Westchester County grand jury indicted her husband, real estate heir Robert Durst, for second-degree murder on November 1, 2021. He died in custody in California on January 10, 2022 before he could be tried, so the charge was never adjudicated.
lastSeen: January 31, 1982, South Salem, NY, after leaving a friend's gathering in Newtown, CT

narrative: Kathleen McCormack, known as Kathie, married New York real estate heir Robert Durst in 1972. By early 1982 she was 29 years old and in her final year at the Albert Einstein College of Medicine, a few months from graduating, according to NBC's Dateline. Relatives and friends have said the marriage was troubled and that she was preparing to seek a divorce; her brother has said publicly that Durst was abusive toward her.

She was last seen on Sunday, January 31, 1982. According to Wikipedia's account, she arrived that evening at a gathering at a friend's house in Newtown, Connecticut, and then left to return to the couple's cottage in South Salem, in Westchester County. Robert Durst told police that he later drove her to a train station so she could travel to Manhattan, and the early investigation focused on the city. No body has ever been found.

The New York State Police reopened the investigation in 1999. Durst was never charged during that period and denied any involvement. At the request of her family, a court declared Kathleen Durst legally dead in 2017.

In two other cases Durst did face trial. According to Wikipedia, a Texas jury acquitted him in November 2003 of murdering his Galveston neighbor Morris Black. In September 2021 a Los Angeles jury convicted him of the first-degree murder of his friend Susan Berman, who was shot in 2000, and he was sentenced in October 2021 to life without parole. ABC News reported that prosecutors in that case argued he killed Berman because he feared what she might tell investigators about Kathleen's disappearance.

After taking office in January 2021, Westchester County District Attorney Miriam Rocah set up a Cold Case Bureau that took up the matter again. A criminal complaint was filed against Durst in October 2021, and on November 1, 2021 a grand jury indicted him for murder in the second degree. Durst, then 78 and in poor health, died on January 10, 2022 while in the custody of California corrections authorities, before he could be brought to New York. The charge was therefore never tried, and he is presumed innocent of it as a matter of law. Wikipedia notes that his conviction in the Berman case was vacated because his appeal was pending when he died.

Later in January 2022 the District Attorney's Office released a report on its investigation. It said that witness statements had discredited the account that Kathleen was last seen in Manhattan and that investigators had been misled by it for years, and it described evidence of domestic violence and a handwritten note found in the South Salem home. In May 2026, News 12 reported that a federal judge dismissed a wrongful death lawsuit her family had filed against Durst's widow.

name: Kellie Poppleton
summary: Kellie Jean Poppleton, a 14-year-old Fremont student, was found dead beside Kilkare Road in Sunol, California on December 2, 1983. She had been beaten and strangled. A 13-year-old girl's confession led to several arrests that month, but the account did not hold up and all charges were dropped. The Alameda County Sheriff's Office cold case unit still seeks leads, including on a black Pontiac Trans Am.
lastSeen: December 2, 1983, near Darwin Drive and Fremont Boulevard in Fremont, California

sources.title: Pleasanton Weekly - Alameda County Sheriff's Office brings cold cases back to light
Pleasanton Weekly - Sunol: Sheriff's office commemorates cold-case homicide victim's death
Patch - Who Killed Kellie Poppleton? Deputies Are Still Searching For Answers Decades Later
UPI Archives - 13-year-old girl charged with teen's brutal death (Dec. 15, 1983)
The Deck - Kellie Poppleton (9 of Hearts, California)

narrative: Kellie Jean Poppleton was 14 years old and attended Conrad Noll School in Fremont, California. According to the Alameda County Sheriff's Office, she was last seen near the corner of Darwin Drive and Fremont Boulevard in Fremont. The podcast The Deck, which covered the case with the cooperation of investigators, reports that she had stopped at a nearby liquor store, where she bought matches and used a payphone to call her boyfriend.

On Friday, December 2, 1983, her body was found at a pullout on the side of Kilkare Road in Sunol, a rural community several miles from Fremont. Sheriff's Detective Ed Chicoine told Patch that she died of asphyxiation caused by strangulation and that she also had multiple head wounds; a necktie had been placed around her neck. A 1983 United Press International report stated that authorities said she had also been sexually assaulted. Items recovered at the scene included a man's gray sweater, a red necktie, a length of coaxial wire and a bag printed with the words "Welcome to Korea," according to The Deck.

Within two weeks the case appeared to have been solved. A 13-year-old Fremont girl told police that she and others had taken Poppleton on a drive, beaten and strangled her, because they thought she had informed on a drug ring operating in local junior high schools. Four people were arrested. UPI reported on December 15, 1983 that investigators had serious doubts about the story: school officials said no such drug ring existed, people who knew Poppleton described her as a good student with no involvement in drugs, and one of the girls named was shown to have been somewhere else at the time. Charges against a second 13-year-old girl, a 17-year-old boy and a 27-year-old man were dropped that month. According to The Deck, the confession was false and the charge against the girl who made it was dropped by February 1984.

No one else has been charged. The Sheriff's Office has said that witnesses reported seeing a black Pontiac Trans Am near the place where the body was found, before it was discovered. The vehicle and its driver have not been publicly identified.

The Deck reports that investigators have since had evidence examined by Parabon NanoLabs, which produced DNA-based composite images estimating what an unknown suspect may have looked like at different ages. The case was also featured on the television series On the Case with Paula Zahn.

The Alameda County Sheriff's Office marks the anniversary of the killing each December with a public appeal, most recently reported by Patch in December 2025. The investigation is filed under case number 83-13639, and the office asks anyone with information to call its Cold Case Homicide Unit at 510-667-3661.

name: Wah Mee Club Massacre
summary: Thirteen people were robbed and murdered at the Wah Mee private gambling club in Seattle's Chinatown-International District on February 19, 1983; a fourteenth victim survived. Kwan Fai "Willie" Mak and Keung Kin "Benjamin" Ng were convicted of 13 counts of aggravated first-degree murder: Mak was sentenced to death, later reduced to life without parole, and Benjamin Ng to life without parole. Wai-Chiu "Tony" Ng was acquitted of murder but convicted of robbery and assault, paroled in 2013 and deported to Hong Kong in 2014. It remains the deadliest mass murder in Washington State history.
lastSeen: February 19, 1983, Wah Mee Club, Seattle, WA

sources.title: Wah Mee massacre - Wikipedia
Wah Mee Massacre leaves 13 dead in Seattle's Chinatown International District on February 19, 1983 - HistoryLink.org
Man convicted in Wah Mee Massacre granted parole - The Seattle Times
'Wah Mee Massacre' remains Washington's deadliest mass shooting - KING 5 (archived copy)
Feb. 19, 1983: The Wah Mee Massacre in Seattle - HeraldNet
Wah Mee: A look back at the deadliest mass shooting in Washington history - KIRO 7 News

narrative: During the early morning hours of February 19, 1983, three armed men entered the Wah Mee Club, an illegal gambling parlor in the basement of the Louisa Hotel at 665 South King Street in Seattle's Chinatown-International District. The club, known within the community for high-stakes gambling, was frequented by patrons carrying large sums of cash. The gunmen, admitted as regulars, gained entry near closing time and proceeded to bind the occupants at gunpoint before robbing them.

The attackers hogtied fourteen people with nylon cord and shot each of them, most in the head and some repeatedly, in what investigators concluded was a deliberate attempt to leave no witnesses. Thirteen victims died, making it the deadliest mass murder in Washington state history. The dead ranged in age and included gamblers, club employees, and community members; the killings devastated the tight-knit Chinatown-International District.

One man survived. Wai Yok Chin, a 61-year-old pai gow dealer and former U.S. Navy sailor, was shot but managed to loosen his bindings, crawl up the stairs, and reach South King Street, where he flagged down help and alerted police. Despite his wounds, Chin lived to identify the assailants and became the prosecution's central eyewitness across the trials. He died in May 1993 at age 71.

Police quickly identified three suspects: Kwan Fai "Willie" Mak, 22; Keung Kin "Benjamin" Ng, 20; and Wai Chiu "Tony" Ng, 25 (no relation to Benjamin). Investigators concluded the robbery was primarily planned by Mak, reportedly to pay off gambling debts. Mak and Benjamin Ng were arrested in Seattle within days. Tony Ng fled the country and remained a fugitive until he was arrested in Calgary, Alberta, Canada, on October 4, 1984, and later extradited.

All three men were convicted, but their outcomes differed significantly. Benjamin Ng was convicted on August 25, 1983, of 13 counts of aggravated first-degree murder; jurors declined to impose death, and he was sentenced the following day to life in prison without the possibility of parole. Willie Mak was convicted on October 6, 1983, and sentenced on October 22 to death by hanging. His death sentence was overturned on appeal in 1988 due to flawed sentencing-phase instructions, and after further proceedings he was resentenced on April 29, 2002, to life in prison without parole.

Tony Ng, whose defense argued he participated under duress from Mak and did not fire the fatal shots, was tried separately in 1985. On April 19, 1985, a jury found him guilty of 13 counts of first-degree robbery and one count of first-degree assault, but acquitted him of the murder charges. He was sentenced on July 3, 1985, to consecutive terms totaling a lengthy prison sentence with the possibility of parole.

As of the most recent reporting, both Willie Mak and Benjamin Ng remain incarcerated in Washington state, serving life sentences without parole. Tony Ng was granted parole in October 2013 after serving roughly 28 years and was deported to his native Hong Kong on May 13, 2014. The massacre remains a defining tragedy in the history of Seattle's Chinatown-International District, memorialized on its anniversaries.

name: Angela Samota
summary: Angela Samota, a 20-year-old Southern Methodist University student, was raped and stabbed to death in her Dallas home in the early hours of October 13, 1984. The case went unsolved until DNA testing in 2008 matched Donald Andrew Bess Jr., who was on parole at the time of the killing. He was convicted of capital murder and sentenced to death in 2010, and died on death row in October 2022.
lastSeen: October 13, 1984, her condominium in Dallas, TX

sources.title: Texas Department of Criminal Justice - Death Row Information: Donald Andrew Bess
Wikipedia - Murder of Angela Samota
The Cinemaholic - Who Killed Angela Samota? Where is Donald Andrew Bess Now?

narrative: Angela Marie Samota, known as Angie, was born on September 19, 1964 and was a 20-year-old student at Southern Methodist University in Dallas in the fall of 1984. According to Wikipedia's account of the case, she spent the evening of Friday, October 12 at the State Fair of Texas and at a dance club with friends before returning to her condominium at about 1:45 a.m. on October 13.

Shortly afterward she telephoned her boyfriend and told him that a man was in her home who had asked to use the telephone and the bathroom. When she did not call back as expected, he became alarmed and contacted the police. Officers reached the residence at 2:17 a.m. and found her dead on her bed. An autopsy determined that she had been raped and stabbed 18 times in the chest, with the wounds to her heart proving fatal.

Dallas police looked at several men who knew her in the weeks that followed, but none was charged and, according to published accounts, all were eventually cleared. The investigation stalled and the case stayed unsolved for more than twenty years. A friend and former roommate, Sheila Wysocki, repeatedly pressed the police department to re-examine the evidence, and she later became a licensed private investigator.

In 2006 Dallas Police Detective Linda Crum took up the case and submitted preserved biological evidence, including blood, semen and fingernail samples, for DNA testing. In 2008 the resulting profile was matched to Donald Andrew Bess Jr. By then Bess was in a Texas prison serving a life sentence for a separate sexual assault and kidnapping. Records of the Texas Department of Criminal Justice show that he had earlier been imprisoned for aggravated rape, aggravated kidnapping and sexual assault, and that he had been released on parole on March 23, 1984, less than seven months before Samota was killed.

Bess was tried in Dallas County in 2010. The jury found him guilty of capital murder, and he was sentenced to death in June of that year after hearing testimony from other women who said he had assaulted them. The Department of Criminal Justice recorded his arrival on death row on September 27, 2010. According to Wikipedia, the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals upheld the conviction and sentence in March 2013, the United States Supreme Court declined to hear the case in January 2014, and a further appeal was rejected in 2016.

The sentence was never carried out. Wikipedia reports that Bess died of a heart attack on October 8, 2022 while still on death row, at the age of 74. Samota's mother had died the previous year, having seen the man responsible for her daughter's death identified and convicted.

name: Night Stalker Victims
summary: Richard Ramirez, the Night Stalker, terrorized Southern California and the San Francisco Bay Area in 1984-1985 with a series of home-invasion murders, rapes, and burglaries. He was captured on August 31, 1985, when residents of East Los Angeles recognized him from published photographs and held him until police arrived. He was convicted in 1989 on 43 counts, including 13 murders, and sentenced to death; DNA later linked him to a fourteenth killing. He died of cancer on death row in 2013.
lastSeen: N/A

sources.title: Richard Ramirez - Wikipedia
DNA Links "Night Stalker" Richard Ramirez to 1984 Killing of 9-Year-Old Mei Leung - CBS News
'Night Stalker' tied to SF victim through DNA - San Francisco Examiner

narrative: Between the spring of 1984 and the summer of 1985, a string of nighttime home-invasion attacks spread terror across Greater Los Angeles and, later, the San Francisco Bay Area. An intruder entered homes through unlocked windows and doors, shooting or beating sleeping residents, sexually assaulting victims, and ransacking the properties. Because there was no consistent victim profile and no single method, investigators were slow to connect the crimes; the press eventually dubbed the unknown assailant the "Night Stalker." The attacks left at least thirteen people dead and many more wounded or assaulted, and the seemingly random nature of the violence fueled widespread public fear during the summer of 1985.

The attacker's earliest confirmed killing was the April 10, 1984 rape and murder of nine-year-old Mei Leung in the basement of a San Francisco apartment building, though this link was not established until years later. The principal spree ran through 1984 and into 1985, striking victims in communities across Southern California before extending to the Bay Area. Survivors' accounts and physical evidence gradually convinced detectives that a single offender was responsible, and a multi-agency task force was assembled as the death toll rose through the summer of 1985.

The investigation broke open in late August 1985. After an attack on August 24, 1985 in Mission Viejo, a witness recorded a license plate, and police recovered a stolen Toyota that had been abandoned. A fingerprint lifted from the vehicle was run through California's newly installed computerized fingerprint database, which returned a match to Richard Ramirez, a drifter originally from El Paso, Texas. Authorities publicly released his name and photograph. On August 31, 1985, Ramirez was recognized by residents in East Los Angeles after his picture appeared in newspapers; a group of citizens chased and subdued him on the street until police arrived and took him into custody.

Ramirez was charged with a series of crimes committed during the spree. After a lengthy trial, on September 20, 1989 a Los Angeles jury convicted him of thirteen counts of murder, along with five attempted murders, eleven sexual assaults, and fourteen burglaries. On November 7, 1989 he was sentenced to death. Ramirez remained on California's death row for more than two decades. He died in custody on June 7, 2013, at age 53, from complications of B-cell lymphoma while awaiting execution.

In 2009, DNA testing linked Ramirez to the 1984 murder of Mei Leung, the case now regarded as his first known killing, though he was never charged in that death because he had already been convicted and sentenced. In 2016, San Francisco authorities disclosed that a second DNA profile had been recovered from the Leung crime scene, indicating another person may have been present, a thread that remains unresolved. Ramirez stands convicted of the Night Stalker murders, and his case is closed by his conviction and death, while the full scope of the Leung investigation continues to be examined.

name: Vicki Lynne Hoskinson
summary: Eight-year-old Vicki Lynne Hoskinson vanished on September 17, 1984 while riding her bicycle to mail a birthday card near her Tucson home. Her remains were found in the desert northwest of the city on April 12, 1985. Frank Jarvis Atwood was convicted of first-degree murder in 1987 and sentenced to death. He maintained his innocence and was executed by lethal injection on June 8, 2022.
lastSeen: September 17, 1984, riding her bicycle near her home in Tucson, AZ

sources.title: Wikipedia - Murder of Vicki Lynne Hoskinson
ABC15 Arizona - Arizona death row inmate unanimously denied clemency ahead of June execution
KJZZ - Arizona plans to seek warrants for first executions in years
KGUN 9 - Death row inmate denied appeal

narrative: Vicki Lynne Hoskinson was born on February 2, 1976 and lived with her family in Tucson, Arizona. On the afternoon of Monday, September 17, 1984, the eight-year-old set out on her bicycle to mail a birthday card to an aunt. She did not come home. According to Wikipedia's account of the case, her bicycle was found lying in the street a few blocks away.

A coach at a nearby elementary school had noticed a man sitting in a car in an alley that day and thought the driver's behavior was suspicious. He memorized the license plate, wrote it down and gave it to police. The plate was traced to a car belonging to Frank Jarvis Atwood, a 28-year-old from Los Angeles who was on parole in California following a conviction for a sexual offense against a child. Atwood was detained within days in Kerrville, Texas, where his car was being repaired, and was returned to Arizona on a kidnapping charge, to which he pleaded not guilty.

On April 12, 1985, a hiker found a child's skull in the desert northwest of Tucson, roughly 20 miles from where the bicycle had been recovered. Dental records confirmed that the remains were Vicki's. Because of the condition of the remains, the cause of death could not be determined.

The trial was moved to Phoenix because of the publicity the case had received in Tucson, and it began in January 1987. Prosecutors relied largely on physical evidence from the vehicle and the bicycle. Experts testified that pink paint on the bumper of Atwood's car was consistent with the bicycle, that nickel plating from the bumper was found on the bicycle, and that damage under the car corresponded to one of its pedals. On March 26, 1987 the jury found Atwood guilty of first-degree murder, and on May 8, 1987 he was sentenced to death.

Atwood consistently maintained that he was innocent. In appeals that lasted 35 years, he argued that police had tampered with the evidence on his car and pointed out that nothing was found inside the vehicle linking the child to it. State and federal courts rejected these claims; KGUN reported that the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals denied his appeal, a ruling Wikipedia dates to September 2017. In April 2021 the Arizona Attorney General's office notified the state Supreme Court that it would seek an execution warrant, according to KJZZ. The clemency board unanimously declined to recommend clemency in May 2022, ABC15 reported.

Atwood was executed by lethal injection at the state prison in Florence on June 8, 2022. Vicki's mother, Debbie Carlson, became an advocate for crime victims; Wikipedia credits her with helping to establish Arizona's Victims' Bill of Rights in 1990 and the Amber Alert system for southern Arizona.

name: Grim Sleeper Victims
summary: Lonnie Franklin Jr., known as the Grim Sleeper, was convicted of killing 10 women in Los Angeles between 1985 and 2007. He appeared to stop killing for years (hence 'Grim Sleeper') and was identified through familial DNA from his son. He was convicted in 2016 and died on death row in 2020.
lastSeen: N/A

sources.title: Grim Sleeper - Wikipedia
Condemned Inmate Lonnie Franklin Dies - California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation
Brown's Forensic Experts Identify Grim Sleeper Serial Killer Suspect Through Unprecedented Use of Familial DNA - California Department of Justice
'Grim Sleeper' serial killer Lonnie Franklin Jr. found dead in prison cell - NBC News
'Grim Sleeper' killer sentenced to death - CNN
Familial DNA Searching and Abandoned DNA Identify the Grim Sleeper Serial Killer - Stanford Law School

narrative: Beginning in the mid-1980s, a series of murders targeting young women unfolded across the impoverished neighborhoods of South Los Angeles. The first confirmed killing linked to the case was that of Debra Jackson in August 1985; over the following two decades the same offender would be tied to the deaths of at least ten people, most of them Black women, several of whom struggled with addiction during the era's crack-cocaine epidemic. Many victims were shot with a small-caliber handgun and their bodies discarded in alleys, dumpsters, and abandoned lots. Because the killings appeared to pause for roughly 14 years, from 1988 until 2002, the press later nicknamed the unidentified suspect the 'Grim Sleeper.'

For years the cases drew comparatively little public attention or investigative urgency, a neglect that community activists and victims' families attributed to the victims' race, poverty, and marginalized circumstances. DNA evidence eventually connected many of the killings to a single perpetrator, but the profile matched no one in California's offender database, and the investigation stalled. The final confirmed victim, Janecia Peters, was found on January 1, 2007.

The break came in 2010 through a pioneering forensic technique. Investigators conducted a familial DNA search, scanning the state database not for an exact match but for a close partial match that could indicate a blood relative. The search flagged Christopher Franklin, who had been entered into the database after a 2008 felony conviction and was too young to have committed the earlier murders. The near-match pointed investigators to his father, Lonnie David Franklin Jr. Detectives then covertly collected discarded 'abandoned DNA' from a slice of pizza Franklin left at a restaurant, and it matched the crime-scene evidence. It was the first time California's familial-search protocol had led to an arrest in a criminal case, marking a significant moment in forensic practice.

Franklin, a former city sanitation worker and police garage attendant, was arrested on July 7, 2010. When police searched his home, they recovered hundreds of photographs and videos of women, prompting authorities to release the images publicly and raising concern that he may have had many additional, uncharged victims. A Los Angeles Police Department task force reviewed the material for possible further cases. On May 5, 2016, a jury convicted Franklin of ten counts of first-degree murder and one count of attempted murder. The same jury recommended a death sentence on June 6, 2016, and on August 10, 2016, a Los Angeles County judge formally sentenced him to death.

Franklin was sent to death row at San Quentin State Prison. On March 28, 2020, corrections officers found him unresponsive in his cell; he was pronounced dead that evening at age 67, with authorities reporting no signs of trauma. His death ended the appeals process before any execution. Investigators have said they believe the true number of victims may be considerably higher than the ten for which he was convicted, given the gap years and the trove of photographs recovered from his home, though those additional cases were never formally charged.

name: Shari Smith
summary: Seventeen-year-old Shari Faye Smith was abducted at gunpoint from the end of her family's driveway in Lexington County, South Carolina, on May 31, 1985, and her body was found days later in Saluda County. Larry Gene Bell, who telephoned her family repeatedly after the abduction, was convicted of her kidnapping and murder in 1986 and executed on October 4, 1996.
lastSeen: May 31, 1985, at the mailbox at the end of her family's driveway, Lexington County, SC

sources.title: FindLaw - Bell v. Evatt (4th Cir. 1995)
UPI Archives - Man who killed two executed
Forensic Files Files - Larry Gene Bell & Shari Faye Smith: Kidnapping, Murder
Wikipedia - Larry Gene Bell

narrative: Shari Faye Smith, 17, disappeared on the afternoon of Friday, May 31, 1985, from the end of the driveway of her family's home in Lexington County, South Carolina. According to the facts summarized by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit in Bell v. Evatt, she was taken at about 3:15 p.m. United Press International reported that she had stopped to check the mail, and other accounts say her car was found at the roadside near the mailbox.

In the days that followed, a man telephoned the Smith family several times. The appeals court wrote that the caller gave details only the abductor would know and eventually directed authorities to her body, which was recovered on June 5, 1985. Accounts of the case place the recovery site in neighboring Saluda County. The family also received a letter in Shari's handwriting headed "Last Will and Testament," which the court record says was intercepted in the mail.

Two weeks after the Smith abduction, on June 14, 1985, Debra May Helmick was taken from outside her home in Richland County. Most news accounts give her age as nine, while the federal appeals opinion describes her as ten. According to the court record, the caller told the Smith family where her body could be found as well.

Larry Gene Bell, an electrician, was arrested on June 27, 1985. The court record and news reports say investigators reached him through a tip and through a telephone number whose impression had been left on the paper of the letter; the number led to a couple for whom Bell had been house-sitting. In February 1986 a jury convicted Bell of kidnapping and murdering Shari Smith and recommended a death sentence, which the trial judge imposed. The South Carolina Supreme Court affirmed the conviction and sentence in 1987. Bell was also convicted and sentenced to death for the kidnapping and murder of Debra May Helmick.

Bell's mental state was raised repeatedly during the proceedings; UPI reported that he gave rambling testimony at trial and made bizarre claims during psychiatric evaluation. The courts nonetheless upheld his convictions, and on December 18, 1995, the Fourth Circuit affirmed the denial of federal habeas relief.

Bell was executed in South Carolina's electric chair on October 4, 1996, having chosen electrocution over lethal injection, according to UPI and execution records. In February 2025, Charlotte-Mecklenburg police in North Carolina announced that they had also identified Bell as responsible for the 1984 disappearance of Sandee Cornett, according to the Wikipedia summary of that department's statement. The Smith case was dramatized in a 1991 television film and has been covered in several documentary series.

name: Steve Christensen & Kathy Sheets
summary: Steven Christensen and Kathleen Sheets were killed by package pipe bombs in the Salt Lake City area on October 15, 1985. Document dealer Mark Hofmann, injured the next day when a third bomb exploded in his car, pleaded guilty in January 1987 to two counts of second-degree murder and to fraud-related charges tied to forged historical documents. He remains in a Utah prison.
lastSeen: October 15, 1985, Salt Lake City, UT

The Salt Lake Tribune - 30 years after Mormon bombings, Mark Hofmann's ex-wife finds peace and herself

narrative: On October 15, 1985, two pipe bombs disguised as packages killed two people in the Salt Lake City area. Steven Christensen, a businessman and collector of historical documents, was fatally injured by the first device; The Salt Lake Tribune later described testimony from a witness who found him lying in a hallway. Later the same day a second device, left outside her home, killed Kathleen "Kathy" Sheets. She was the wife of J. Gary Sheets, Christensen's business partner. According to Wikipedia's account, a secretary was also hurt by shrapnel in the first blast.

The following day, October 16, a third bomb exploded in a car belonging to Mark Hofmann, a dealer in rare documents who had sold items relating to early Latter-day Saint history. Hofmann was seriously injured. Investigators at first considered whether the bombings were connected to the troubled investment business run by Gary Sheets, which the Los Angeles Times reported was the impression Hofmann had intended to create.

Hofmann was arrested in early 1986 and charged with murder, bomb offenses, theft by deception and fraud. At a preliminary hearing in April 1986, prosecutors presented evidence linking him to the bombs and to a long series of forgeries. In January 1987 he pleaded guilty to two counts of second-degree murder and to fraud-related counts involving the so-called Salamander Letter and a purported collection of papers of early church leader William McLellin. As part of the plea he agreed to answer prosecutors' questions about his crimes.

The Los Angeles Times reported on the resulting 544-page interview transcript, released in July 1987. In it Hofmann said he killed Christensen to stop a pending document transaction from exposing his frauds and that the Sheets bomb was meant as a diversion. He claimed the third bomb was a suicide attempt, a claim prosecutors and the Salt Lake City police chief publicly doubted.

Judge Kenneth Rigtrup sentenced Hofmann to five years to life and recommended that he never be released. In 1988 the Utah Board of Pardons, after hearing Hofmann describe the bombing, decided that he would spend the rest of his natural life in prison, according to published accounts cited by Wikipedia. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints subsequently published a list of documents it had acquired or used that were now known to be Hofmann forgeries.

Hofmann was held for decades at the Utah State Prison in Draper. In September 2016 the Utah Department of Corrections confirmed to Fox 13 that he had been moved out of maximum security to the Central Utah Correctional Facility in Gunnison. The case was the subject of the Netflix documentary series Murder Among the Mormons, released in March 2021.

name: Anthonette Christine Cayedito
summary: Nine-year-old Anthonette Cayedito vanished from her family's apartment in Gallup, New Mexico, in the early hours of April 6, 1986, after going to answer a knock at the door. About a year later Gallup police received a brief call from a girl who said she was Anthonette; it could not be traced. The FBI, Navajo Nation and Gallup police still list her as missing.
lastSeen: April 6, 1986, family home in Gallup, NM

narrative: Anthonette Christine Cayedito was nine years old when she disappeared from her family's apartment in Gallup, New Mexico. According to NBC News' Dateline, which drew on local newspaper reports from the time, her mother, Penny Cayedito, came home around midnight on the night of April 5-6, 1986, while her three daughters were with a babysitter, and went to sleep sometime before 3 a.m. Not long afterward there was a knock at the door. Anthonette's younger sisters recalled her going to answer it; she did not come back to bed.

Her mother found her missing at about 7 a.m. when she got up to take the children to Bible school, and reported it immediately, NBC reported. One of the sisters told authorities she thought the person at the door had been one of their uncles. Police questioned him and ruled him out. According to Wikipedia's summary of later reporting, one sister said about five years after the disappearance that she had seen two men take Anthonette to a van as the girl shouted to be let go. Another sister has since expressed uncertainty about parts of that account, and it has not been confirmed by investigators.

About a year after the disappearance, Gallup police received a telephone call from a girl who said she was Anthonette and that she was in Albuquerque. NBC reported that a gruff male voice was heard asking who had said she could use the phone before the line went dead, and that the call could not be traced. Whether the caller was really Anthonette has never been established, although Wikipedia notes that her mother said she recognized the voice.

A few years later a waitress in Carson City, Nevada, reported serving a teenage girl she believed might be Anthonette, seated with a couple. After the group left, the waitress said she found a note under the girl's plate asking for help and for someone to call police, according to NBC. That lead also went nowhere.

Penny Cayedito died in 1999. Wikipedia's account, citing a Gallup detective, says she had failed an FBI polygraph and that investigators believed she knew more than she had disclosed; she was never charged with any offense. In 2022 Anthonette's sister Sadie Acevedo told CNN she believes the disappearance may have been connected to a relative.

No one has been charged. In April 2020 the FBI, the Navajo Nation Division of Public Safety and the Gallup Police Department issued a joint reminder that they are still searching for her, and the FBI renewed its appeal on the 35th anniversary in 2021. Tips can be given to the FBI at 505-889-1300 or tips.fbi.gov.

name: Colonial Parkway Murders
summary: Eight young people were killed or disappeared in four incidents along or near Virginia's Colonial Parkway between 1986 and 1989. Using DNA evidence, the FBI and Virginia State Police attributed the 1987 murders of David Knobling and Robin Edwards (announced January 2024) and the 1986 murders of Cathleen Thomas and Rebecca Dowski (announced January 2026) to Alan Wade Wilmer Sr., a commercial fisherman who died in 2017 and was never charged. The 1989 murders of Daniel Lauer and Annamaria Phelps have not been officially attributed to anyone, and the bodies of Keith Call and Cassandra Hailey, who vanished in 1988, have never been found.
lastSeen: Various dates along Colonial Pkwy, VA

narrative: The Colonial Parkway Murders refer to a series of four incidents that killed or claimed eight young people in Virginia's Tidewater region between 1986 and 1989. The victims were mostly young couples who disappeared or were found dead along or near the Colonial Parkway, a scenic National Park Service road linking Jamestown, Williamsburg and Yorktown. Because the crimes shared victim profiles, secluded 'lovers' lane' locations and staged vehicles, investigators long treated them as possibly connected, and together they became one of the most enduring cold cases in Virginia history.

The first incident came in October 1986, when Cathleen Marian Thomas, 27, and Rebecca Ann Dowski, 21, were found dead in a car at a Colonial Parkway overlook near Williamsburg; both had been strangled and their throats cut. In September 1987, David Lee Knobling, 20, and Robin Margaret Edwards, 14, disappeared and were later found shot dead along the James River shoreline. In April 1988, Richard Keith Call, 20, and Cassandra Lee Hailey, 18, vanished after leaving a party; Call's car was recovered at the York River Overlook, but their bodies have never been found. In September 1989, Daniel Lauer, 21, and Annamaria Phelps, 18, disappeared en route to Virginia Beach; their bodies were discovered in October 1989 in woods near an Interstate 64 rest stop in New Kent County.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation and the Virginia State Police led a decades-long joint investigation. Detectives pursued numerous theories, including a widely reported hypothesis that the killer may have worked on or around the water, sometimes described as the 'fisherman' theory, based on physical evidence and the riverside locations of some bodies. For many years no suspect was charged, and the killings remained officially unsolved despite periodic reviews and the preservation of forensic evidence.

The investigation advanced significantly through modern DNA analysis. On January 8, 2024, authorities announced that DNA evidence had linked a deceased man, Alan Wade Wilmer Sr., a Virginia commercial fisherman who died in 2017, to the 1987 murders of Knobling and Edwards, as well as to the separate 1989 Hampton killing of Teresa Lynn Howell. On January 21, 2026, the FBI Norfolk Field Office announced it had resolved the 1986 murders of Thomas and Dowski, also attributing them to Wilmer through forensic testing. Officials have publicly connected Wilmer to at least six killings from the period. Because Wilmer died before any charges were filed, he was never arrested, prosecuted or convicted.

As of 2026, the case is partly resolved but not closed. Two of the four canonical Colonial Parkway incidents, the 1986 Thomas-Dowski and 1987 Knobling-Edwards murders, have been officially attributed to Wilmer by the FBI and Virginia State Police, while the 1988 Call-Hailey disappearance and the 1989 Phelps-Lauer murders remain officially unsolved. Investigators have said they will continue to pursue the remaining cases and to examine whether additional victims or perpetrators are connected.

name: Gary Heidnik Victims
summary: Gary Heidnik abducted six women between November 1986 and March 1987 and held them captive in the basement of his North Philadelphia home, where Sandra Lindsay and Deborah Dudley died. He was arrested after captive Josefina Rivera got away and alerted police. Heidnik was convicted in July 1988 of two counts of first-degree murder and executed on July 6, 1999.

narrative: Between late November 1986 and March 1987, Gary Heidnik abducted six women and imprisoned them in the basement of his house at 3520 North Marshall Street in North Philadelphia. CNN and other outlets identify the women as Josefina Rivera, Sandra Lindsay, Lisa Thomas, Deborah Dudley, Jacqueline Askins and Agnes Adams. All six were Black. Two of them, Lindsay and Dudley, died in captivity.

Rivera, the first to be taken, said in an oral history published by Philadelphia magazine that Heidnik picked her up on the night of November 25, 1986. Lindsay's sister, Tracey Lomax, told CNN that Lindsay, who had an intellectual disability and knew Heidnik from gatherings at his home, went out to a store the day after Thanksgiving 1986 and did not return; her family repeatedly pressed Heidnik and the police about her whereabouts. Thomas was brought to the basement shortly before Christmas, Dudley around New Year's Day and Askins on January 18, 1987, according to Rivera's account.

Survivors testified that the women were chained, kept in a pit dug in the basement floor, starved, beaten and raped. According to 6abc and Wikipedia's summary of the trial evidence, Lindsay died in February 1987 after being left shackled by the wrist to an overhead beam; authorities attributed her death to a combination of starvation and mistreatment. Heidnik dismembered her body. Dudley died in March 1987 when Heidnik applied a live electrical wire to the chains of captives standing in the water-filled pit. Her body was left in the New Jersey Pine Barrens.

Agnes Adams was abducted in late March 1987. The next day Rivera, who had gained a degree of Heidnik's trust, persuaded him to let her out briefly and went to the police. Officers detained Heidnik on March 24, 1987, and freed the remaining women from the basement. Parts of Lindsay's remains were found in the house.

At trial in 1988, defense attorney Charles Peruto Jr. argued that Heidnik was legally insane. The prosecution, led by Charles Gallagher, countered with evidence of planning and of Heidnik's successful management of a large investment account. On July 1, 1988, a jury convicted him of two counts of first-degree murder along with kidnapping, rape, aggravated assault and related charges, and he was sentenced to death.

Heidnik declined to pursue appeals. Lawyers acting for his daughter argued in federal court that he was not mentally competent to be executed, but the courts did not block the sentence, the Associated Press reported. He was executed by lethal injection at the state prison at Rockview on July 6, 1999, and remains the last person executed in Pennsylvania. CNN and 6abc note that the fictional killer Buffalo Bill in The Silence of the Lambs was partly based on him.

name: Jennifer Levin
summary: Jennifer Levin, 18, was found strangled in Central Park behind the Metropolitan Museum of Art on August 26, 1986, hours after leaving an Upper East Side bar with Robert Chambers. With the jury deadlocked after nine days, Chambers pleaded guilty to first-degree manslaughter in March 1988 and served 15 years. He was later imprisoned on drug charges and released in July 2023.
