narrative: Jennifer Levin was 18 when she was killed in Central Park in the early hours of August 26, 1986. She had spent the evening at Dorrian's Red Hand, an Upper East Side bar popular with a private-school crowd. A friend testified at trial that she left Levin at the bar between 1:30 and 2 a.m., United Press International reported. According to Inside Edition, Levin and Robert Chambers, whom she had been seeing that summer, left together at about 4:30 a.m. and walked to the park. About two hours later a cyclist found her partially clothed body near Fifth Avenue and 83rd Street, behind the Metropolitan Museum of Art. She had been strangled, and a medical examiner later testified that her injuries indicated compression of the neck.

Bar patrons told police they had seen Levin leave with Chambers. When detectives went to his home he had fresh scratches on his face, which he first attributed to his cat. According to accounts of the investigation summarized by Wikipedia and Inside Edition, his story changed several times; he ultimately admitted causing her death but said it was an accident that happened when he pushed her off him during a sexual encounter in which, he claimed, she had hurt him. Prosecutors rejected that account, pointing to the difference in size between the two.

Chambers was charged with second-degree murder and released on bail. The case drew intense tabloid coverage, much of it focused on Levin's private life, and the defense strategy was widely criticized as blaming the victim. The trial opened in January 1988 and lasted about three months.

After nine days of deliberation the jury had not reached a verdict. On March 25, 1988, Chambers accepted a plea agreement and pleaded guilty to first-degree manslaughter, admitting that he had intended to cause Levin serious injury. He was sentenced that April to five to 15 years. Because of disciplinary infractions he served the full term and was released from Auburn prison on February 14, 2003.

Levin's parents brought a wrongful-death suit that Chambers did not contest; Wikipedia's account says the judgment entitles the family to a share of his future income, up to $25 million, which the family has said would go to victims' rights groups. They also settled a claim against the owner of the bar.

Chambers was arrested again in October 2007 for selling drugs from his Manhattan apartment. He pleaded guilty in 2008 and was sentenced to 19 years. CBS News, citing state corrections records, reported that he was released from Shawangunk Correctional Facility in late July 2023, about four years early, and remains under post-release supervision for up to five years.

name: Lisa Steinberg
summary: Six-year-old Lisa Steinberg was fatally beaten on November 1, 1987, in the Greenwich Village apartment of Joel Steinberg, a lawyer who had raised her without ever legally adopting her. She was found comatose the next morning and died days later. In January 1989 a jury acquitted Steinberg of murder and convicted him of first-degree manslaughter; he was paroled in 2004.
lastSeen: November 1, 1987, apartment in Greenwich Village, NYC

narrative: Elizabeth "Lisa" Steinberg was six years old when she was fatally injured in the Greenwich Village apartment where she lived with Joel Steinberg, a criminal defense lawyer, and his partner Hedda Nussbaum, a former children's book editor. Lisa had been born in 1981 to Michele Launders, a young single mother who, according to published accounts, paid Steinberg to arrange an adoption. He instead kept the baby. A New York judge ruled after Lisa's death that she had never been legally adopted, the Los Angeles Times reported.

Prosecutors said Steinberg struck the child on the evening of November 1, 1987, and then left the apartment for a dinner engagement. Nussbaum testified that Lisa lay unconscious on the bathroom floor for hours and that after Steinberg returned he smoked cocaine rather than seek help. Nussbaum called 911 at about 6:30 the next morning. Police and paramedics found Lisa comatose; officers also noted that Nussbaum herself had serious facial injuries. A 16-month-old boy, also living in the apartment without a legal adoption, was later returned to his birth mother.

Lisa was taken to St. Vincent's Hospital, where doctors found bleeding in the brain. She was declared brain dead and died after life support was withdrawn several days after she was admitted. Launders went to court for the right to bury her, and more than 1,000 people attended the viewing and funeral in mid-November 1987.

Steinberg and Nussbaum were both arrested and initially charged with second-degree murder. Prosecutors later declined to pursue the case against Nussbaum, concluding, as the Los Angeles Times reported in 1988, that years of beatings by Steinberg had left her unable to act; she became the principal prosecution witness. Her testimony over several days described a long pattern of violence in the household.

On January 30, 1989, after a trial of about twelve weeks, the jury acquitted Steinberg of second-degree murder and convicted him of first-degree manslaughter, according to United Press International. He was sentenced to eight and one-third to 25 years, the maximum then available for that offense. He has continued to deny responsibility for Lisa's death, including in a 2017 interview with the New York Post.

Steinberg was denied discretionary parole several times and was released on June 30, 2004, under the state's conditional-release rules after serving about two-thirds of the maximum term. He had been disbarred. In January 2007 a New York appellate court upheld a $15 million civil award against him in favor of Michele Launders. The case prompted wide public discussion of how schools, neighbors and agencies respond to signs of child abuse.

name: Peggy Hettrick
summary: Peggy Hettrick, 37, was found stabbed and mutilated in a field in Fort Collins, Colorado, on February 11, 1987. Tim Masters, 15 at the time, was convicted in 1999, but the conviction was vacated in January 2008 after DNA testing pointed away from him, and the state attorney general formally exonerated him in 2011. No one else has been charged, and the killing remains unsolved.
lastSeen: February 11, 1987, Fort Collins, CO

narrative: Peggy Hettrick, 37, was found dead on the morning of February 11, 1987, in an open field along the 3800 block of Landings Drive in southern Fort Collins, Colorado. The Larimer County coroner's office records that she had been stabbed in the back. Her body had also been sexually mutilated. A passing cyclist reported the discovery. According to published accounts she had last been seen leaving a nearby bar and restaurant in the early hours of that morning.

Attention quickly turned to Tim Masters, a 15-year-old high school sophomore who lived with his father in a trailer bordering the field. Masters told police he had seen the body on his way to the school bus but thought it was a mannequin. He was questioned at length but was not charged at the time. He went on to serve in the Navy and work as an aircraft mechanic.

More than a decade later Fort Collins police arrested Masters, relying heavily on violent drawings and writings he had produced as a teenager and on the opinion of a forensic psychologist. A jury convicted him of murder in March 1999 and he was sentenced to life in prison.

A new defense team appointed in the mid-2000s alleged that police and prosecutors had withheld evidence. During hearings that began in 2007, a special prosecutor, Adams County District Attorney Don Quick, agreed that material had not been disclosed. Testing commissioned by the defense at a Dutch laboratory, and confirmed by the Colorado Bureau of Investigation, found DNA on Hettrick's clothing that did not match Masters and was consistent with a man who had been considered early in the investigation, CNN reported. That man has not been charged.

On January 22, 2008, a judge vacated the conviction and Masters was released after more than nine years in custody; the charges were dismissed days later. Larimer County and the city of Fort Collins paid a combined $10 million to settle his civil claims. On June 28, 2011, Colorado Attorney General John Suthers announced that Masters had been cleared as a suspect following a review that included more than 170 interviews, further DNA analysis and grand jury testimony.

The lead detective, Lt. Jim Broderick, was indicted for perjury in 2010 and again in 2011; the charges were dismissed and he was not convicted. He resigned from the department in 2013. Two former prosecutors in the case, who had become judges, were censured and lost retention elections in 2010. Responsibility for the homicide investigation was transferred to the Colorado Attorney General's Office, which has used touch-DNA testing on the evidence, Westword reported. No arrest has followed, and the coroner continues to list the case among the county's unsolved homicides.

name: Amber Swartz
summary: Seven-year-old Amber Swartz-Garcia vanished on June 3, 1988, while jumping rope in the front yard of her home in Pinole, California. In 2009 police closed the case on the strength of a confession by convicted child killer Curtis Dean Anderson, who died in 2007, but nothing corroborated it and no remains were found. Pinole police reopened the case in 2013 and it remains active.
lastSeen: June 3, 1988, front yard of her home on Savage Avenue, Pinole, CA

narrative: Amber Jean Swartz-Garcia was seven years old when she disappeared on June 3, 1988, from the front yard of her family's home on Savage Avenue in Pinole, a small city in Contra Costa County, California. She had gone outside to jump rope. Her father, Pinole police officer Bernie Swartz, had been killed in the line of duty in 1980, before she was born, according to KTVU and the Mercury News. Her mother, Kim Swartz, has campaigned on her behalf ever since.
The disappearance drew national attention, but for almost two decades no one was charged and no trace of Amber was found.

In November 2007, Curtis Dean Anderson, who was serving a sentence of about 300 years for the kidnapping and assault of one Vallejo girl and the kidnapping and murder of another, told FBI agents that he had taken Amber. According to statements by Pinole police reported by the Associated Press and the Mercury News, Anderson said he pulled her into his car as he drove through the neighborhood, gave her alcohol to sedate her, drove to Arizona, killed her in a motel in the Tucson area and left her body in the desert. He signed a short handwritten statement. Anderson died of natural causes the following month, before Pinole investigators could interview him again.

On July 6, 2009, Pinole Police Chief Paul Clancy and the FBI announced that they considered the confession truthful and were closing the case. Police acknowledged that they had found no physical evidence linking Anderson to the abduction; they said only that records showed he had been paroled in March 1988 and had been working in the area. Anderson was never charged or tried in connection with Amber. Searches in Arizona found nothing.

Kim Swartz did not accept the confession, noting that Anderson was known for making unreliable statements and that other people had also claimed responsibility over the years. After a family friend's online petition gathered more than 1,300 signatures, Pinole police announced in October 2013 that the case status had been changed from closed to open. The department said it had received no evidence contradicting the confession but that Amber had still not been located, and that newer technology might allow old evidence to be re-examined.

On August 19, 2025, which would have been Amber's 45th birthday, family and residents gathered at Amber Swartz Park, beside her former home. Pinole police told ABC7 and KTVU that detectives were reviewing the file, collecting items that might yield DNA for comparison, and that the department now questions Anderson's involvement. An age-progressed image was released. Amber is still listed as missing.

narrative: Tara Leigh Calico, a 19-year-old University of New Mexico-Valencia student, disappeared on the morning of September 20, 1988, while on her daily bicycle ride along New Mexico State Road 47 near her home in Belen, in Valencia County, New Mexico. She had left home at roughly 9:30 a.m. and reportedly told her mother to come looking for her if she was not back by noon, as she planned to play tennis that afternoon. When Tara failed to return, her mother drove the route but found no sign of her. Searchers later recovered pieces of Tara's Sony Walkman and a cassette tape scattered along the roadside; her bicycle was never found. Several witnesses reported seeing a light-colored pickup truck with a camper shell following closely behind a cyclist that morning, and investigators came to believe she had been abducted.

The case drew national attention in 1989 after a Polaroid photograph surfaced roughly 1,500 miles away. On June 15, 1989, a woman found the photo in the parking lot of a convenience store in Port St. Joe, Florida; it showed a young woman and a boy who appeared bound and gagged, lying on bedding. Family and friends believed the woman resembled Tara, and her mother, Patty Doel, pointed to what she felt was a matching scar. Expert analyses of the image were contradictory and never resolved the question: Scotland Yard reportedly concluded the woman could be Tara, analysts at Los Alamos National Laboratory concluded it was not, and an FBI examination was deemed inconclusive. The connection between the Polaroid and Tara Calico has never been confirmed, and the identities of the people in the photograph remain officially unknown.

Over the following decades the investigation passed through multiple sheriff administrations without resolution. A judge declared Tara legally dead and ruled the case a homicide in 1998. In 2008, then-Valencia County Sheriff Rene Rivera publicly stated that he believed two local young men, who knew Tara, had struck her with a vehicle in an accident, panicked, and killed her, and that her body was then concealed. Rivera said he believed he knew who was involved but that without a body he could not build a prosecutable case; these remarks were his stated theory and were never proven in court or tested at trial. A six-agency task force reexamined the case beginning in October 2013.

The inquiry intensified in later years. The FBI publicized a reward for information, and in the fall of 2021 the Valencia County Sheriff's Office, under Sheriff Denise Vigil, executed a sealed search warrant at a Valencia County residence, drawing on renewed review of old tips, witness accounts, and advances in forensic and DNA analysis. On June 13, 2023, Sheriff Vigil announced that investigators believed there was sufficient evidence to submit the case to the district attorney's office for review of potential charges, while stressing that the identities of persons of interest remained sealed by court order. No one has been charged.

As of 2026 the case remains open and unsolved. Reporting in 2025 indicated that District Attorney Barbara Romo's office had neither filed charges nor formally declined the case, citing a high evidentiary bar given that only offenses such as first-degree murder fall outside the statute of limitations. Investigators, including Lt. Joseph Rowland, have continued physical searches, including examination of an abandoned mine shaft north of Belen thought to have been deliberately collapsed, and have focused on a group of local young adults said to have been seen near the route that morning. Several key witnesses have since died. No remains have been recovered, no one has been convicted, and the disappearance of Tara Calico is officially unsolved.

name: Aileen Wuornos Victims
summary: Aileen Wuornos killed seven men along Florida highways, claiming self-defense. She was convicted of six murders and executed in 2002. She became one of America's most studied female serial killers, with multiple books and the Oscar-winning film 'Monster' depicting her story.
lastSeen: N/A

sources.title: Aileen Wuornos - Wikipedia
What Did Aileen Wuornos Do? Inside The Serial Killer's Crimes And Execution - Forbes (archived copy)

narrative: Between late 1989 and 1990, seven men were shot and killed along the highways of northern and central Florida in a series of murders later attributed to Aileen Carol Wuornos, a woman who supported herself through sex work solicited along interstate roadways. The victims were Richard Charles Mallory, a 51-year-old electronics store owner and her first victim, killed in late November 1989; David Andrew Spears, a construction worker; Charles Edmund Carskaddon, a rodeo worker; Peter Abraham Siems, a retired merchant seaman whose body was never recovered; Troy Eugene Burress, a sausage salesman; Charles Richard 'Dick' Humphreys, a retired Air Force major and former police officer; and Walter Gino Antonio, a trucker and security guard. Each man was shot multiple times, and each was robbed; several were left in wooded areas off Florida roadways.

Wuornos consistently maintained during her first trial that the men had raped or attempted to rape her and that the killings were acts of self-defense. In later statements, according to reporting and court records, she abandoned that account and described the killings as robberies in which she eliminated witnesses, at one point stating that she had killed and robbed the men. The shift between these accounts became a central point of contention in her case and in subsequent public debate. This narrative presents both her self-defense claims and the later statements as reported and attributed, rather than as adjudicated fact.

The investigation gained momentum in July 1990 after Siems's car was found abandoned and wrecked in Orange Springs, Florida; witnesses described two women leaving the vehicle. Investigators linked Wuornos to the crimes through fingerprints recovered from the car and from items pawned under her name. She was arrested on January 9, 1991, at a biker bar in Volusia County. Her former partner, Tyria Moore, cooperated with police, and Wuornos confessed on January 16, 1991, again framing the deaths as self-defense.

Wuornos went to trial for Mallory's murder on January 14, 1992, was convicted on January 27, and was sentenced to death on January 31. She subsequently pleaded guilty or no contest to additional killings and ultimately received six death sentences. She spent more than a decade on Florida's death row. On October 9, 2002, after dropping her appeals and being found competent to be executed, Wuornos was put to death by lethal injection at Florida State Prison near Starke at 9:47 a.m.

Wuornos's case drew intense attention to questions about her mental state and her background. Defense experts reported diagnoses including borderline and antisocial personality disorder, and accounts of her early life described severe abuse and exploitation in childhood; supporters argued these factors, and her account of violence by clients, complicated a simple 'monster' narrative, while prosecutors emphasized the robberies. These interpretations remain debated and are attributed to the parties and experts who advanced them. Her story reached a wide audience through the 2003 film 'Monster,' in which Charlize Theron won the Academy Award for Best Actress for her portrayal of Wuornos, and through multiple documentaries. Her convictions and 2002 execution are established matters of record.

name: Dan & Linda Broderick
summary: Attorney Daniel T. Broderick III, 44, and his wife Linda Kolkena Broderick, 28, were shot in their bed at their San Diego home on November 5, 1989, by his former wife, Betty Broderick. After a first trial ended in a hung jury, she was convicted in 1991 of two counts of second-degree murder and sentenced to 32 years to life. Twice denied parole, she died in custody on May 8, 2026.

narrative: Daniel T. Broderick III, 44, a prominent medical malpractice attorney and former president of the San Diego County Bar Association, and his wife, Linda Kolkena Broderick, 28, were shot to death in their bedroom early on Sunday, November 5, 1989. The shooting took place at their home in the Marston Hills area of San Diego, near Balboa Park. The person who fired the shots was Dan Broderick's former wife, Elisabeth "Betty" Broderick, who at the time lived in La Jolla.

Dan and Betty Broderick married in 1969 and had four children. They separated in 1985 after 16 years of marriage, and the divorce, which was not final until 1989, was bitterly contested, the Los Angeles Times reported. Linda Kolkena had worked as Dan Broderick's legal assistant; the two married in April 1989. In the years before the killings Betty Broderick left abusive messages on her former husband's answering machine, vandalized his home and drove her car into his front door, according to CNN.

On the morning of the shooting she entered the house using a key she had taken from one of her daughters, went upstairs and fired a .38-caliber revolver at the couple as they lay in bed. According to trial testimony summarized by the Times of San Diego, five shots were fired and three struck the victims. According to Wikipedia's account she turned herself in to police that day, and she remained in custody for the rest of her life.

Betty Broderick admitted firing the shots. The contested issue at trial was her state of mind. She was charged with two counts of first-degree murder. Her first trial in 1990 ended in a mistrial when the jury split, with ten jurors favoring a murder conviction and two holding out for manslaughter, the Los Angeles Times reported. At a second trial in 1991, a jury found her guilty of two counts of second-degree murder. She was sentenced to two consecutive terms of 15 years to life plus two years for use of a firearm, a total of 32 years to life, and entered the California Institution for Women in February 1992.
She was denied parole in January 2010, when the board found she had not shown remorse and two of her children opposed release, and again in 2017.

On April 18, 2026, she was moved from the prison in Chino to an outside hospital. She died there at 3:40 a.m. on May 8, 2026, aged 78, the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation said. Her son told reporters she had broken ribs in a fall and later developed infections. The treating doctor attributed the death to natural causes; Oxygen subsequently reported that San Bernardino County records list the manner of death as an accident. The case was dramatized in two 1992 television films and in the 2020 series Dirty John: The Betty Broderick Story.

name: Grissom Family Murders (Danny Rolling Confession)
summary: William "Tom" Grissom, 55, his daughter Julie, 24, and his grandson Sean, 8, were killed in their Shreveport home on November 4, 1989. Danny Rolling was long suspected but never charged in Louisiana. Shortly before his October 2006 execution in Florida for the Gainesville student murders, he gave a minister a handwritten confession to the three killings.
lastSeen: November 4, 1989, Grissom family home, Shreveport, LA

narrative: On November 4, 1989, three members of one family were killed inside a home in Shreveport, Louisiana. According to NBC News and other outlets, the victims were William T. "Tom" Grissom, 55, his daughter Julie Grissom, 24, and his grandson Sean Grissom, 8. Reports state that the three were stabbed as they were getting ready for an evening meal.

Investigators in Shreveport came to suspect Danny Rolling, a local man. According to an ABC report, an investigator noted that Julie Grissom's body had been cleaned and posed in a way that resembled what was later found at crime scenes in Gainesville, Florida, and that the blood type attributed to the Shreveport offender matched that of the Gainesville suspect. News4Jax reported that Shreveport police prepared an arrest warrant for Rolling, but that it was never signed.

In late August 1990, five college students were murdered in Gainesville: Sonja Larson, Christina Powell, Christa Hoyt, Manuel Taboada and Tracy Paules. ABC reported that a Louisiana woman, Cindy Juracich, contacted Crime Stoppers in November 1990 to suggest Rolling as a suspect, and that he was by then being held in the Marion County jail in connection with a supermarket robbery. The same report says Rolling had shot his father during a dispute in May 1990; his father survived.

Rolling pleaded guilty to the Gainesville murders in 1994, before his trial began, and was sentenced to death on April 20, 1994. Louisiana authorities did not prosecute him for the Grissom killings. NBC News reported that officials saw little purpose in a Louisiana trial once he faced execution in Florida. NBC also reported that in 1997 Rolling had sent a detailed written admission to a woman he married while in prison, who passed it to authorities, and that retired detectives said it included descriptions of the crime scene.

Rolling was executed by lethal injection at Florida State Prison on October 25, 2006. Shortly beforehand he gave his spiritual adviser, the Rev. Mike Hudspeth of Shreveport, a handwritten statement taking sole responsibility for the deaths of Julie, Tom and Sean Grissom. Shreveport police subsequently held a news conference about the statement.

Relatives of the Grissom family attended the execution. KSLA reported that Julie Grissom's mother, Joyce Burton, said the family had never had any sense of satisfaction in the years since 1989. Because Rolling was never charged or tried in Louisiana, the Grissom case is resolved on the basis of his confession and the investigative findings rather than a conviction.

name: Ilene Beth Misheloff
summary: Thirteen-year-old Ilene Misheloff vanished on January 30, 1989, while walking home from Wells Middle School in Dublin, California. She was last seen at about 3 p.m. on Amador Valley Boulevard near Village Parkway, and her key fob was later found near John Mape Park. Dublin police and the FBI treat the case as an abduction; no one has been charged.
lastSeen: January 30, 1989, about 3:00 p.m., Amador Valley Boulevard near Village Parkway, Dublin, CA

sources.title: City of Dublin, CA - Ilene Misheloff Disappearance

narrative: Ilene Beth Misheloff was 13 when she disappeared in Dublin, California, on January 30, 1989. According to the City of Dublin's page on the case, she was walking home alone from Wells Middle School and was last seen at about 3:00 p.m. on Amador Valley Boulevard near Village Parkway.

KTVU reported in 2019 that Ilene was a figure skater who had left school early that afternoon so she could collect her skating equipment at home before practice, and that her coaches were due to pick her up at about 3:30 p.m. The station also reported that a family friend had offered her a ride that day and that she chose to keep walking.

According to the City of Dublin, her key fob was later found near the entrance to John Mape Park, which was on the route she usually took home. KTVU described the item as a keychain found in a dry creek bed in the park, which students used as a shortcut. Police describe the case as an abduction, and the FBI lists her among its kidnapping and missing-person cases.

The city's description says Ilene had braces, pierced ears and freckles, and was wearing a charcoal gray Esprit sweater, a pink and gray striped skirt and black Keds sneakers. KTVU reported in 2024 that a $95,000 reward was on offer for information leading to an arrest and conviction.

No arrest has been made and no suspect has been publicly identified in the sources reviewed. A Dublin police detective sergeant told KTVU in 2019 that the matter remained an active investigation rather than a cold case. On the 35th anniversary in January 2024, Dublin police said they were continuing to investigate in the hope that Ilene would return home.

Her parents, Maddi and Mike Misheloff, kept the family home and telephone number unchanged in case she tried to make contact, ABC7 reported in 2019. For more than 30 years the community held an annual walk and candlelight vigil along her route. According to the City of Dublin and KTVU, that tradition ended after Maddi Misheloff died of cancer in 2020. Anyone with information is asked to contact Dublin Police Services or the FBI.

name: Jacob Wetterling
summary: Eleven-year-old Jacob Wetterling was abducted at gunpoint near his home in St. Joseph, Minnesota, on October 22, 1989. His disappearance led to the 1994 Jacob Wetterling Crimes Against Children and Sexually Violent Offender Registration Act. In 2016 Danny Heinrich led investigators to Jacob's remains and confessed in federal court to the abduction and murder under a plea deal; he was not charged with the killing and is serving 20 years on a child-pornography conviction.
lastSeen: October 22, 1989, near his home in St. Joseph, MN

narrative: On the evening of October 22, 1989, 11-year-old Jacob Erwin Wetterling was abducted at gunpoint on a rural road near his home in St. Joseph, Minnesota. Jacob, his younger brother Trevor, and a friend had ridden bicycles to a convenience store to rent a video and were returning home when a masked man armed with a handgun stepped from a driveway and ordered them to stop. The man told the two other boys to run and threatened to shoot if they looked back. When they reached home and turned around, Jacob and the gunman were gone. The abduction, witnessed by the two children, triggered an immediate and massive search that drew national attention and became one of Minnesota's most enduring unsolved cases.

The investigation stretched across nearly 27 years and involved local authorities, the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension, and the FBI. Danny James Heinrich, who lived in nearby Paynesville, was questioned by the FBI on December 16, 1989, but was released without charges at the time. The case remained cold for decades. Jacob's parents, Patty and Jerry Wetterling, became prominent child-safety advocates, and Patty Wetterling helped drive the passage of the Jacob Wetterling Crimes Against Children and Sexually Violent Offender Registration Act, enacted in 1994 as part of the federal Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act. That law required states to establish sex-offender registries and was the first federal statute of its kind, forming the foundation for later measures such as Megan's Law.

The case broke open decades later. Beginning in 2014, investigators reexamined a series of unsolved child assaults in the Paynesville and Cold Spring areas. DNA evidence connected Heinrich to the January 1989 abduction and sexual assault of 12-year-old Jared Scheierl in Cold Spring. In October 2015, authorities publicly named Heinrich a person of interest in Jacob's disappearance, and on October 28, 2015, he was arrested on federal child-pornography charges after investigators found a collection of images at his home.

As part of a federal plea agreement, Heinrich agreed to plead guilty to a single count of receiving child pornography and to disclose what he had done in exchange for prosecutors agreeing not to charge him with Jacob's murder. On September 1, 2016, Heinrich led investigators to a pasture near Paynesville where Jacob's remains were buried; the remains were confirmed as Jacob's through dental records on September 3, 2016. On September 6, 2016, in federal court, Heinrich confessed in detail to abducting, sexually assaulting, and killing Jacob in October 1989, and to the earlier assault on Scheierl.

It is important to state the legal outcome precisely: Heinrich was never charged with or convicted of Jacob Wetterling's murder. Prosecutors said the statute of limitations had expired on the kidnapping and assault charges and that they lacked the evidence to prove murder in court, so they used the child-pornography case as leverage to obtain his confession and locate the remains. In November 2016, Heinrich was sentenced to the maximum 20 years in federal prison on the child-pornography conviction. He was later transferred to the Federal Medical Center in Devens, Massachusetts. As of 2026, the case is considered resolved through Heinrich's confession, though his only criminal conviction in the matter remains the federal child-pornography charge rather than the homicide itself.

name: Lisa Bianco
summary: Lisa Bianco was beaten to death outside her Mishawaka, Indiana, home on March 4, 1989, by her former husband, Alan Matheney, who was on an eight-hour prison furlough. She had not been notified of his release. Matheney was convicted of murder and burglary, sentenced to death in 1990 and executed in 2005. Her death led Indiana to suspend furloughs and adopt victim notification.
lastSeen: March 4, 1989, her home in Mishawaka, IN

narrative: Lisa Bianco was killed on March 4, 1989, in Mishawaka, Indiana, by her former husband, Alan Matheney. According to the Associated Press account carried by NBC News, Matheney was at the time serving an eight-year prison sentence for a 1987 assault on Bianco and for confining their children, and had been released that day on an eight-hour furlough.

The couple had married in 1977 and divorced in 1985, according to the Wikipedia entry on Matheney, which says he was held at the Pendleton Correctional Facility. The South Bend Tribune reported that Bianco worked with battered women at a shelter in Elkhart County. The AP reported that she had asked to be told of any release, but was not informed of the furlough, and that Matheney's trip to Mishawaka violated the terms of his pass.

Prosecutors said Matheney drove to the South Bend area, broke into Bianco's house, chased her outside and beat her to death with an unloaded shotgun, the AP reported. WSBT reported that she told her daughters to call 911 before running from the house, and that she was attacked as she sought help at a neighbor's door. The couple's two daughters were in the home at the time.

Matheney was convicted of murder and burglary and was sentenced to death on May 11, 1990. His appeals continued for about 16 years. The Indiana Supreme Court rejected a request for a new trial in September 2005, and Governor Mitch Daniels denied a clemency request that had been based on claims of mental illness. Matheney was executed by lethal injection early on September 28, 2005.

The case had lasting policy consequences. Governor Evan Bayh suspended the state's prison furlough program after the killing; the AP reported that it was later reinstated with tighter restrictions. The state agreed to pay $900,000 to Bianco's estate and children. According to the South Bend Tribune and WSBT, Indiana created a system to notify victims when offenders are released, passed 1989 legislation allowing police to make arrests for misdemeanor battery they had not witnessed, and in 1996 adopted a constitutional amendment on victims' rights.

Bianco's mother, Millie Bianco, told WSBT in 2015 that she still received messages from women who said her daughter's case had protected them. St. Joseph County has since set up a domestic violence fatality review team and address confidentiality measures, the station reported.

name: Robert Ben Rhoades Victims
summary: Long-haul trucker Robert Ben Rhoades is serving life sentences for three murders. He pleaded guilty in Illinois in 1992 to killing 14-year-old Regina Walters of Pasadena, Texas, and in Texas in 2012 to the capital murders of Patricia Walsh and Douglas Zyskowski, a couple who accepted a ride in late 1989. He was arrested in Arizona in April 1990.

narrative: Robert Ben Rhoades, a long-haul truck driver based in Texas, has been convicted of three murders committed in 1989 and 1990. He is serving sentences of life without parole and is held in Illinois.

His arrest came in April 1990 in Arizona. According to an Illinois appellate court opinion, a state trooper who stopped to check on a tractor-trailer found a woman, unclothed and handcuffed, chained inside the sleeper compartment. The court's summary says a notebook belonging to Regina Walters was recovered from the truck. ABC13 reported that Rhoades was convicted in Arizona of aggravated assault, sexual assault and unlawful imprisonment.

Regina Kay Walters, 14, was last seen alive at her mother's apartment in Pasadena, Texas, on February 3, 1990, according to the court opinion. Her remains were found on September 29, 1990, in a barn along Interstate 70 in Illinois, and the evidence indicated she had been strangled with a wire ligature. Rhoades pleaded guilty to first-degree murder on September 11, 1992, and was sentenced to natural life in prison. Wikipedia's entry on Rhoades states that Walters had left home with a companion, Ricky Lee Jones, whose remains were later found in Texas; Rhoades has not been convicted in connection with Jones.

The other two victims were Patricia Walsh, 24, and her husband Douglas Scott Zyskowski, whose age is given as 28 in news reports. According to ABC News and ABC13, the newly married couple left Seattle in November 1989 intending to hitchhike to Georgia to do religious work, and accepted a ride from Rhoades in Texas. Zyskowski's body was found in January 1990 along Interstate 10 near Ozona, Texas, and identified in 1992. Walsh's remains were found by hunters in central Utah in October 1990 and were identified in 2003 through dental records.

In 2012 Rhoades pleaded guilty in West Texas to two counts of capital murder for the deaths of Walsh and Zyskowski. In exchange, prosecutors did not seek the death penalty; he received further life sentences and gave up his right to appeal, according to ABC13 and ABC News.

Authorities have said they suspect Rhoades of additional crimes. The Texas Observer reported that his trucking records showed regular travel through 22 states and that prosecutors suspected him of further killings, and ABC News quoted prosecutors as saying they did not know how many women he may have abducted. Estimates of the number of victims vary widely and none beyond the three convictions has been proven in court.

name: Gainesville Ripper Victims
summary: Danny Rolling murdered five college students over four days in Gainesville, Florida, in August 1990; four attended the University of Florida and one attended Santa Fe Community College. He pleaded guilty in 1994, was sentenced to death and was executed in 2006. The murders are widely cited as an inspiration for the film Scream, and the killings and posing of victims caused mass fear across the campus community.
lastSeen: August 24-27, 1990, Gainesville, FL

sources.title: Danny Rolling - Wikipedia
The Gainesville Student Murders - FFP Law
Rolling v. State (1997) - FindLaw
Rolling v. State (1997) - Justia (archived copy)
The Twisted Tale Of 'Gainesville Ripper' Killer Danny Rolling - Oxygen
Impacts of 1990 Gainesville murders remain strong - The Independent Florida Alligator

narrative: Over four days in late August 1990, five college students were murdered in Gainesville, Florida, in a series of killings that terrorized the University of Florida community as students returned for the fall semester. The killer, later dubbed the "Gainesville Ripper," broke into off-campus apartments at night, stabbing his victims and, in several cases, mutilating and posing the bodies. The five victims were University of Florida freshmen Sonja Larson, 18, and Christina Powell, 17, killed on August 24; Santa Fe Community College student Christa Hoyt, 18, killed on August 25; and University of Florida students Tracy Paules, 23, and Manuel "Manny" Taboada, 23, killed on August 27. The brutality of the crimes prompted many students to leave town, arm themselves, or sleep in groups amid a widespread panic.

In the early stage of the investigation, attention fell on Edward Lewis Humphrey, an 18-to-20-year-old University of Florida student with a documented history of mental illness. He was held in custody on an unrelated assault charge, and authorities publicly scrutinized him as a possible suspect. According to reporting and court records, a grand jury declined to indict Humphrey on the murders, citing insufficient evidence, and he was formally cleared after the actual killer was identified. Humphrey was never charged in the murders and later resumed his life; sources report he went on to graduate from college. He should not be associated with guilt in this case.

The murders were ultimately linked to Danny Harold Rolling, a drifter from Shreveport, Louisiana. Rolling had been arrested on September 7, 1990, for an armed robbery of a supermarket in Ocala, Florida, and was in custody on unrelated charges. Investigators connected him to the Gainesville crimes through forensic evidence, including blood-type and later DNA analysis matching material from the crime scenes, tools recovered from a wooded campsite he had used near Gainesville, and audio-tape recordings in which he alluded to the killings. A Crime Stoppers tip also helped focus attention on Rolling. Authorities determined he had committed the five Gainesville murders during a burglary and robbery spree, and he was also linked to a 1989 triple homicide in Shreveport.

On February 15, 1994, the day his trial was set to begin in Gainesville, Rolling unexpectedly pleaded guilty to all charges, including five counts of first-degree murder. Following a penalty phase, the jury recommended death for each murder by a vote of 12 to 0, and Judge Stan Morris imposed the death sentence in the spring of 1994. Rolling remained on Florida's death row for more than a decade. He was executed by lethal injection at Florida State Prison on October 25, 2006, at age 52, after the courts rejected his final appeals; he did not contest the execution.

The case left a lasting cultural and institutional mark. It inspired changes in campus safety practices and is widely cited as source material for screenwriter Kevin Williamson's 1996 horror film "Scream," directed by Wes Craven, which drew on the fear generated by a killer stalking a college town. With Rolling convicted by his own guilty plea and executed, the case is legally closed. It remains a defining event in the history of the University of Florida and Gainesville, and is regularly revisited in retrospective coverage of the murders and their impact on students, particularly college-aged women.

name: Paige Marie Renkoski
summary: Paige Renkoski, a 30-year-old substitute teacher from Okemos, Michigan, vanished on May 24, 1990. The car she was driving was found still running on the shoulder of westbound I-96 near Fowlerville, with her purse and shoes inside. A motorist reported seeing her beside a maroon minivan that afternoon. The Livingston County Sheriff's Office continues to investigate.
lastSeen: May 24, 1990, shoulder of westbound I-96 near Fowlerville, MI

sources.title: The Livingston Post - Cold case team continues to investigate disappearance of Paige Renkoski
NBC News Dateline - Paige Renkoski still missing from Michigan nearly 30 years after disappearing

WILX - Missing Paige: Family still searching for answers
Wikipedia - Disappearance of Paige Renkoski

narrative: Paige Marie Renkoski was 30 years old when she disappeared on May 24, 1990, in Livingston County, Michigan. News reports describe her as a substitute teacher from Okemos; NBC's Dateline reported that she was engaged, was working with young children and was studying early childhood development.

According to WILX and Dateline, she drove her mother to Detroit Metropolitan Airport that day and then went to see a friend in Canton. The Livingston County Sheriff's Office cold case team has said she was last seen leaving the friend's home at about 2:30 p.m. She was then expected to head back toward the Lansing area.

At about 3:30 p.m., a passing driver saw her standing on the shoulder of westbound Interstate 96 near the Fowlerville exit, according to Fox 2 Detroit and Dateline. Accounts of that sighting differ: some reports refer to one man and others to two men with her, beside a maroon or burgundy minivan.

That evening the silver 1986 Oldsmobile Calais she had been driving, which belonged to her mother, was found on the shoulder. The sheriff's office has said the engine was running with the keys in the ignition, that her shoes and purse were inside, and that there were no evident signs of a struggle. Reported times for the discovery range from about 6 p.m. to about 8 p.m. Dateline reported that fingerprints were recovered from the vehicle but have not been matched to anyone.

The case is handled by the Livingston County Sheriff's Office, whose cold case team said in 2020 that it remained under investigation. Fox 2 reported in 2023 that more than 1,000 tips had been received and that searches using cadaver dogs and ground-penetrating radar had not produced conclusive results. Wikipedia's entry on the case describes searches in Handy Township and Conway Township in 2011. No one has been charged, and no suspect has been officially named in the sources reviewed.

Crime Stoppers has offered a reward of up to $2,500 for information leading to her location, according to Fox 2. Her family has continued to seek answers; WILX reported in 2024 that her sister and niece returned to the site, and that a Michigan State University team has documented their efforts. Tips can be given to the sheriff's office.

WILX reports that Renkoski's family is still searching for answers.

name: Charles Albright Victims
summary: Charles Albright was convicted in December 1991 of murdering Shirley Williams, one of three women found shot in Dallas between December 1990 and March 1991 with their eyes removed. Charges over the deaths of Mary Lou Pratt and Susan Peterson were dropped for lack of evidence. Albright received a life sentence, maintained his innocence and died in prison custody in 2020.
lastSeen: N/A

sources.title: Oxygen - 'Eyeball Killer' Charles Albright
Texas True Crime Blog - Charles Albright
Radford University - Charles Albright case timeline
Wikipedia - Charles Albright

narrative: Between December 1990 and March 1991, three women were found shot dead in the Dallas area, and in each case the eyes had been removed. The killings led to the arrest of Charles Albright, a Dallas resident then in his late fifties, who was convicted of one of the murders.

The first victim, Mary Lou Pratt, was found on December 13, 1990, in southern Dallas. According to Oxygen and the Texas True Crime Blog, she had been shot in the back of the head. The second, Susan Peterson, 27, was found on February 10, 1991, a short distance from where Pratt had been left; she had also been shot. Sources give Pratt's age as 33 or 35.

The third victim, Shirley Williams, was found in March 1991 on a residential street near an elementary school. Sources reviewed give different dates for the discovery, either March 10 or March 19, and different ages. Oxygen reported that the tip of a craft-knife blade was found lodged near one of her eyes.

Albright was arrested on March 22, 1991. According to the accounts reviewed, investigators relied heavily on hair and fiber comparisons said to link him to the victims, and reported finding craft knives at his home. His trial began in December 1991, and later that month the jury found him guilty of the murder of Shirley Williams. He was sentenced to life in prison.

Charges relating to Pratt and Peterson did not proceed; Oxygen and Wikipedia state that they were dropped because of insufficient evidence. Wikipedia's entry also states that Albright had been charged in the 1988 death of another Dallas woman, Rhonda Bowie, and that this charge was likewise dropped. Albright was therefore never convicted in those cases, and they remain without a conviction.

The forensic evidence has since been questioned. Wikipedia's entry states that later DNA testing indicated that hairs presented at trial as consistent with Albright's came from a dog. Albright maintained that he was innocent throughout his imprisonment. He was held at a psychiatric prison unit in Lubbock, Texas, and died on August 22, 2020, at the age of 87, according to Wikipedia and the Texas True Crime Blog; Oxygen gives the date as August 10, 2020.

timeline.event: Mary Lou Pratt is found shot dead in southern Dallas.
Susan Peterson, 27, is found shot dead near the location where Pratt was found.
Shirley Williams is found dead on a street near an elementary school in Dallas.
Charles Albright is arrested.
Albright's trial begins in Dallas.
A jury convicts Albright of the murder of Shirley Williams; he is sentenced to life in prison. Other charges are later dropped.
Albright dies in Lubbock, Texas, at age 87, while in prison custody.

name: Danny Casolaro
summary: Freelance journalist Joseph Daniel "Danny" Casolaro, 44, was found dead on August 10, 1991, in the bathtub of Room 517 at the Sheraton hotel in Martinsburg, West Virginia, with cuts to his wrists. The medical examiner ruled the death a suicide, and a second review in 1992 reached the same finding. His family disputes the ruling, and research papers he was said to carry were not found.
lastSeen: August 10, 1991, Sheraton Hotel, Martinsburg, WV

sources.title: Wikipedia - Danny Casolaro
Unsolved Mysteries - The Mysterious Death of Dan Casolaro
Find a Grave - Joseph Daniel "Danny" Casolaro (1947-1991)

narrative: Joseph Daniel "Danny" Casolaro was a freelance writer from Fairfax, Virginia. He was born on June 16, 1947, and was 44 when he died. At the time, he was researching a story he called "The Octopus," which, according to accounts of his work, tied together the Inslaw software dispute, in which the company alleged that the Justice Department had misappropriated its Promis case-management program, with other political controversies of the 1980s.

On August 10, 1991, a housekeeper found Casolaro dead in the bathtub of Room 517 at the Sheraton hotel in Martinsburg, West Virginia. According to Wikipedia's summary of the case, he had 10 to 12 cuts to his wrists.

The medical examiner ruled the death a suicide caused by blood loss. Wikipedia's entry cites a short note asking for forgiveness that was found in the room, the absence of signs of forced entry or a struggle, and toxicology findings of alcohol, an antidepressant and acetaminophen. A first autopsy was carried out on August 14, 1991. A second examination by the state medical examiner's office in January 1992 again concluded that the death was a suicide.

Casolaro's family has not accepted that conclusion. His brother, Dr. Anthony Casolaro, told the television program Unsolved Mysteries that the body had been embalmed before the family gave permission, and pointed to bruising and damaged fingernails that he said were not explained. According to the accounts reviewed, relatives also said that Casolaro had received threatening telephone calls, that he had told them not to believe any report that he had died accidentally, and that he was notably uncomfortable around blood.
The family and the program also said that research papers Casolaro was believed to have had with him were not recovered. Official investigators did not find evidence of a homicide.

The death drew congressional attention because of the Inslaw connection. The House Judiciary Committee addressed the matter in its September 10, 1992, report on the Inslaw affair, House Report 102-857. Wikipedia's entry states that members of an FBI task force later questioned the suicide conclusion and recommended further inquiry, and that news organizations that examined the case did not find evidence of murder. In 2024 Netflix released a documentary series, "American Conspiracy: The Octopus Murders," that revisited his work. The official ruling of suicide remains in place.

timeline.event: Joseph Daniel Casolaro is born at Fort Meade, Maryland.

name: Latasha Harlins
summary: Latasha Harlins, 15, was shot in the back of the head by store owner Soon Ja Du at Empire Liquor Market in South Los Angeles on March 16, 1991, after a dispute over a bottle of orange juice. A jury convicted Du of voluntary manslaughter; Judge Joyce Karlin imposed probation, community service and a fine with no prison time. The sentence is widely cited as a factor in the 1992 riots.
lastSeen: March 16, 1991, Empire Liquor Market, Los Angeles, CA

sources.title: Wikipedia - Killing of Latasha Harlins
EBSCO Research Starters - Latasha Harlins murder

narrative: Latasha Harlins was a 15-year-old girl who was shot and killed on March 16, 1991, at Empire Liquor Market, a store at West 91st Street and South Figueroa Street in South Los Angeles. She was born on January 1, 1976. The shooting happened 13 days after the police beating of Rodney King and was recorded by the store's security camera.

According to the accounts reviewed, Harlins went into the store and picked up a bottle of orange juice priced at under two dollars. Soon Ja Du, who ran the store with her family, accused her of trying to steal it. Wikipedia's summary of the security footage says Harlins had money in her hand. Du took hold of the girl, and a physical struggle followed in which Harlins struck Du. Harlins put the juice on the counter and turned to go. Du then took a revolver from behind the counter and fired once, hitting Harlins in the back of the head. A review in the Los Angeles Review of Books notes that police found her holding two dollar bills.

Du was charged with murder. In 1991 a Los Angeles jury found her guilty of the lesser offense of voluntary manslaughter, which carried a maximum of 16 years in prison. In November 1991 Superior Court Judge Joyce Karlin suspended a ten-year prison term and placed Du on five years of probation, with 400 hours of community service, a $500 fine and an order to pay the Harlins family's funeral costs. Du served no prison time after sentencing.

The sentence was strongly criticized, including by the Los Angeles County District Attorney and by Black community leaders, according to Wikipedia's entry on Karlin. A state appeals court upheld the sentence on April 21, 1992. An effort to recall the judge in 1992 narrowly failed.

About a week after the appellate ruling, the acquittal of police officers in the Rodney King case was followed by several days of rioting in Los Angeles. Historians, including UCLA's Brenda Stevenson, who wrote a book on the case, regard the Harlins sentence as one of the events that set the stage for the unrest. Many Korean-owned businesses were damaged. Du's store was looted and burned and did not reopen.

In July 1992 a civil claim was settled for $300,000, paid to Harlins's estate for the benefit of her siblings, according to Wikipedia. Los Angeles has since recognized April 29 as Latasha Harlins Day, and in 2021 a mural honoring her was dedicated at the Algin Sutton Recreation Center.

name: Mark Himebaugh
summary: Eleven-year-old Mark Himebaugh disappeared on November 25, 1991, near his home on Sunray Road in Del Haven, Middle Township, New Jersey, after going to watch firefighters tackle a nearby brush fire. He was last seen at about 4 p.m. A search found one of his sneakers about 75 yards from his house. Middle Township police, county prosecutors and the FBI still investigate.
lastSeen: November 25, 1991, about 4:00 p.m., near his home on Sunray Road, Del Haven, NJ

sources.title: NCMEC - Have you seen this child? Mark Himebaugh
New Jersey State Police Missing Persons Unit - Mark Himebaugh
6abc - Mark Himebaugh case: Police using AI to find clues in 31-year-old case
WPG Talk Radio - 34 Years Ago Today, Mark Himebaugh Disappeared in Middle Twp., NJ

narrative: Mark Himebaugh was 11 years old when he went missing on November 25, 1991, in Del Haven, a community in Middle Township, Cape May County, New Jersey. According to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children, he disappeared at about 4:00 p.m. near his family's home.

6abc reported that a brush fire had broken out roughly a quarter of a mile from the house on Sunray Road that afternoon, and that Mark's mother allowed him to go and watch firefighters put it out. A local radio report on the 34th anniversary said that his mother had left to drive a neighbor home, that Mark had chosen to stay behind to see the fire, and that a park guard who saw him heading toward a playground at around 4 p.m. was the last person known to have seen him. He was reported missing at about 5 p.m., according to 6abc. The New Jersey State Police listing records that his mother last saw him at 3:15 p.m.

An extensive search followed. According to NCMEC, searchers found his left sneaker about 75 yards from his home, and no other physical evidence has come to light since. He was wearing a blue sweatshirt, a gray jacket, gray pants and white sneakers. The State Police listing describes him as about four feet tall and 85 pounds, with red hair and blue eyes; NCMEC notes that he had freckles.

The case is investigated by the Middle Township Police Department and the Cape May County Prosecutor's Office, with FBI involvement. No one has been charged in connection with the disappearance, and the sources reviewed do not identify any officially named suspect.

In May 2023, investigators announced that they were using an artificial intelligence tool in a pilot program to look for patterns in the accumulated case material, 6abc reported. Police Chief Chris Leusner said the department wanted to use every available resource and the newest technology to find Mark, and hoped the approach could serve as a model for other cold cases.

NCMEC has produced age-progressed images showing how Mark might look as an adult. As of the most recent coverage reviewed, in November 2025, he had not been found. Anyone with information is asked to contact the Cape May County Prosecutor's Office, the Middle Township Police Department or NCMEC.

name: I-70 Killer Victims
summary: Six store workers were shot dead at five small businesses near Interstate 70 in Indiana, Kansas and Missouri between April 8 and May 7, 1992. The killings were linked by ballistics and witness accounts to one gunman using a .22-caliber pistol. Five victims were women and one was a man. A multi-agency task force formed in 2021, but no one has been charged.
lastSeen: Various dates along I-70

sources.title: KSHB - 'Six people at five different scenes': Search for I-70 serial killer continues 32 years later
Men's Journal (via Yahoo News) - 34 Years Ago: The I-70 Killer Claimed His Sixth Victim
Men's Journal (via Yahoo News) - Investigators May Be Close to Solving 'I-70 Killer' Case
First Alert 4 (KMOV) - I-70 Killer coverage
Wikipedia - I-70 killer

narrative: Over 29 days in the spring of 1992, six people were shot dead while working in small shops close to Interstate 70 in three states. Police linked the crimes through ballistic testing, witness descriptions and the similar circumstances, and the unidentified gunman became known as the I-70 killer.

The first victim was Robin Fuldauer, 26, who was killed on April 8, 1992, at a Payless ShoeSource store in Indianapolis. Three days later, on April 11, Patricia Magers, 32, and Patricia Smith, 23, were shot at a bridal shop in Wichita, Kansas. On April 27, Michael McCown, 40, was killed at a ceramics store in Terre Haute, Indiana; he was the only man among the victims. Nancy Kitzmiller, 24, was killed on May 3 at a boot store in St. Charles, Missouri, and Sarah Blessing, 37, was killed on May 7 at a gift shop in Raytown, Missouri.

According to KSHB and other reports, the weapon was a .22-caliber pistol, and investigators have identified the Erma Werke ET22 as the likely model. The shops were generally staffed by one person at the time and little money was taken. Witnesses in Wichita and Raytown provided descriptions that were used for a composite sketch of a slim white man with light-colored hair.

Investigators have also looked at later shootings. Wikipedia's entry on the case describes three attacks on store workers in Texas in 1993 and 1994, two of them fatal, that were examined as possibly related, though ballistic tests indicated a different gun. One of those attacked, Vicki Webb, survived. The 2001 killing of a liquor store clerk in Terre Haute has also been reviewed for a possible link. None of these has been officially confirmed as the work of the same person.

In 2021 police from the affected cities formed a task force, led from St. Charles, and released age-progressed sketches. Investigators said in 2022 that they hoped newer DNA techniques, including touch DNA, might yield results. In April 2022 a St. Louis television station reported that detectives were examining whether Harry Edward Greenwell, who had been identified after his death as the so-called I-65 killer, could be connected; no such link has been announced.

No arrest has been made. In July 2026, Men's Journal reported that journalist Bob Cyphers, the author of a 2024 book on the case, said in a podcast that police had questioned a man they consider a suspect, who was not named and was not charged. That account has not been confirmed in an official statement in the sources reviewed, and the case remains unsolved.

name: Jeremy Guillory
summary: Six-year-old Jeremy Guillory was strangled on February 7, 1992, in a house near Iowa, Louisiana, where Ricky Langley rented a room. Langley confessed and was tried three times; after two convictions were overturned, a judge convicted him of second-degree murder in 2009 and imposed life without parole. Federal courts upheld that conviction in 2019, and the U.S. Supreme Court declined review in 2020.
lastSeen: February 7, 1992, at a neighbor's house near his home in Iowa, LA

sources.title: Louisiana Supreme Court - State v. Langley, No. 95-KA-1489 (opinion)
U.S. Supreme Court - Langley v. Prince, No. 19-6413, Brief in Opposition
U.S. Supreme Court - Docket No. 19-6413, Langley v. Prince

narrative: Jeremy Guillory, age six, was killed on February 7, 1992, near the town of Iowa in Calcasieu Parish, Louisiana. According to the facts set out by the Louisiana Supreme Court, Jeremy went to a neighboring house to look for two children he often played with. The family was away, and Ricky Joseph Langley, a tenant who rented a room there, let him in. Langley later told investigators that he strangled the boy and hid his body in a bedroom closet.

The court record states that Jeremy's mother, Lorilei Guillory, went to the house looking for her son and used the telephone there to report him missing, and that Langley told her he had not seen the child. Deputies, volunteer firefighters and neighbors searched the area through the weekend, and the FBI joined the case when he had not been found by Monday. A Louisiana parole agent then alerted police that Langley, who had a prior child molestation conviction and an outstanding Georgia parole violation warrant, was living in the area. He was arrested at the truck stop where he worked, admitted the killing, and led officers to the body, according to the opinion.

A Calcasieu Parish grand jury indicted Langley for first-degree murder on February 20, 1992, and he pleaded not guilty and not guilty by reason of insanity. After a change of venue to East Baton Rouge Parish, a jury convicted him on July 9, 1994, and he was formally sentenced to death on September 26, 1994. Court filings show that conviction was later set aside and the indictment quashed because of the way the grand jury foreperson had been selected.

At a second trial the jury did not convict Langley of first-degree murder and instead returned a verdict of second-degree murder. A state appeals court threw out that verdict in 2004 because of the trial judge's conduct, including absences from the courtroom, according to court filings and KPLC. The Louisiana Supreme Court ruled in 2007 that he could be retried only for second-degree murder. Jeremy's mother publicly opposed a death sentence for Langley and testified on that point at the retrial, KPLC reported.

Langley chose a bench trial the third time, and on December 10, 2009, Judge Robert Wyatt found him guilty of second-degree murder and imposed the mandatory sentence of life without parole, the American Press reported. Langley argued in federal court that the second jury's verdict meant the state could not again try to prove specific intent to kill. A three-judge panel of the U.S. Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals agreed in 2018, but the full court reheard the case and on June 6, 2019, upheld the denial of habeas relief.
The U.S. Supreme Court denied Langley's petition for review on April 20, 2020, according to the court's docket, leaving the 2009 conviction and life sentence in place.

name: Springfield Three
summary: Sherrill Levitt, her daughter Suzanne Streeter, and Suzanne's friend Stacy McCall all vanished from the Levitt home overnight. Their cars were still in the driveway, their purses inside. The porch light's glass globe was broken. Despite thousands of leads over 30 years, no trace of the three women has ever been found.
lastSeen: June 7, 1992, 1717 E. Delmar St., Springfield, MO

sources.title: Springfield Three - Wikipedia
Three Missing Women - City of Springfield, MO Official Website
The Springfield Three: 33 years and counting since the disappearance - KY3
Three Women Vanished. More Than 30 Years Later, No One Knows What Happened - Newsweek

narrative: On the night of June 6-7, 1992, three women vanished from a home in central Springfield, Missouri, in a case that has become known as "the Springfield Three." Suzanne "Suzie" Streeter, 19, and her friend Stacy McCall, 18, had graduated from Kickapoo High School that afternoon and spent the evening at graduation parties. Around 2 a.m. the two returned to the home Streeter shared with her mother, Sherrill Levitt, 47, a cosmetologist, at 1717 East Delmar Street. Levitt had last been heard from by a friend around 11:15 p.m. When friends stopped by the house the next morning, all three women were gone.

According to the Springfield Police Department and widely published accounts, the women left behind their cars, purses, keys, jewelry, cigarettes and nearly $900 in cash. There were no clear signs of a struggle or forced entry. The only notable physical anomaly reported at the scene was a shattered porch-light globe. A message left on the home's answering machine, which investigators considered potentially significant, was accidentally erased before police could preserve it. The scene was also compromised early on: reports indicate that a number of friends and relatives entered the house and tidied up before officers fully secured it, which police have said may have destroyed evidence.

The disappearance triggered one of the largest investigations in the region's history. The Springfield Police Department, aided by the FBI and the Missouri State Highway Patrol, has said it processed more than 5,000 tips and conducted numerous searches, yet no bodies, no confirmed sightings and no conclusive physical evidence have been found. A reward fund was established, and the case has been featured on programs such as "America's Most Wanted" and "48 Hours." Over the years several people have been publicly discussed as persons of interest, but no one has ever been charged.

The most widely reported person of interest is Robert Craig Cox, a convicted kidnapper and armed robber who was living in Springfield in 1992 and is serving a life sentence in Texas for a 1995 robbery. According to Wikipedia and news accounts, Cox told journalists in 1997 that he believed the three women were dead and that their bodies would never be found; investigators have publicly stated they do not regard his claims as credible, and he has never been charged in the case. His original 1992 alibi was reportedly later undercut when a girlfriend said she had been asked to corroborate it. Other individuals discussed in media coverage as persons of interest include Dustin Recla, a former boyfriend of Streeter, though he has never been charged. These individuals are described here only as publicly reported persons of interest; none has been convicted or charged in connection with the disappearances.

As of 2026, the Springfield Three case remains unsolved. Streeter and Levitt were legally declared dead in 1997, but the matter is still classified and investigated as a missing-persons case. Springfield police continue to describe the investigation as open and periodically renew appeals for information, while the families have marked each anniversary without answers. More than three decades on, what happened to Sherrill Levitt, Suzie Streeter and Stacy McCall is still unknown.

name: Holly Piirainen
summary: Ten-year-old Holly Piirainen disappeared on August 5, 1993, after leaving her grandparents' home in Sturbridge, Massachusetts, to see a neighbor's puppies. Hunters found her remains in Brimfield on October 23, 1993. No one has been charged. The Hampden District Attorney's Office is using forensic genetic genealogy to seek new leads.
lastSeen: August 5, 1993, near her grandparents' home by South Shore Road, Sturbridge, MA

sources.title: CBS Boston - 32 years after Holly Piirainen's murder, investigators turn to genealogy

Western Mass News - Closure of Springfield cold case sparks hope for other unsolved murders
Wikipedia - Murder of Holly Piirainen

narrative: Holly Piirainen was 10 years old when she disappeared on August 5, 1993, in Sturbridge, Massachusetts. According to Boston.com and CBS Boston, she had been staying at her grandparents' home and left late that morning, telling her father she was going to a neighbor's house to see a litter of puppies. She was last seen at about 11:45 a.m. near Allen and South Shore roads.

When Holly did not come back, her father went looking for her. Boston.com reported that about an hour later he found one of her sneakers near South Shore Road, and she was reported missing. A large search of the area followed, but she was not found.

On October 23, 1993, more than two months later, hunters came across skeletal remains in a wooded area off Five Bridge Road in Brimfield, a nearby town in Hampden County. The remains were identified as Holly's. According to CBS Boston, a white tank top printed with the word "Boston" in pink and purple letters was recovered near the remains; the Hampden District Attorney's Office released a photograph of the shirt to the public in 2023 in the hope that someone would recognize it.

No one has been charged in Holly's death. On January 3, 2012, then Hampden District Attorney Mark Mastroianni announced that forensic evidence found near the place where Holly's remains were recovered had been linked to David Pouliot, a Springfield man who died in 2003, according to Wikipedia's summary of that announcement. Pouliot was described as a person of interest; he was never charged, and officials have not said that he was responsible for the killing. Investigators have also considered whether the case is connected to the death of Molly Bish, who disappeared from Warren, Massachusetts, in 2000, but no link has been established publicly.

The investigation remains open under Hampden District Attorney Anthony Gulluni. In October 2025 his office announced that it was using forensic investigative genetic genealogy, in which DNA from crime scene evidence is compared with genealogy databases to find relatives of an unknown person. The office held a voluntary DNA collection event in Brimfield on November 9, 2025, asking local residents to contribute samples, and said that evidence from the original scene had been preserved and re-examined as technology improved.

In July 2026, after the same office announced that it had resolved an unrelated 1995 Springfield homicide through new DNA testing, Holly's family told Western Mass News that they were confident her case would also be solved. As of that report no arrest had been made. The district attorney's office maintains a tip line for the case at 413-426-3507.

name: Polly Klaas
summary: Twelve-year-old Polly Klaas was kidnapped at knifepoint from a slumber party at her Petaluma home and murdered. Richard Allen Davis was convicted and sentenced to death. Polly's case led directly to California's 'three strikes' law and influenced child safety legislation nationwide.
lastSeen: October 1, 1993, her home in Petaluma, CA

sources.title: Murder of Polly Klaas - Wikipedia
Richard Allen Davis - Wikipedia
How a Palm Print Broke Open the Polly Klaas Case - TIME

narrative: On the night of October 1, 1993, 12-year-old Polly Hannah Klaas was hosting a slumber party with two friends at her mother's home in Petaluma, California. At approximately 10:30 p.m., a man armed with a knife entered her bedroom, tied up her two friends, placed pillowcases over their heads, and told them to count to 1,000. He then carried Polly out of the house. Her mother and younger sister were asleep in another room. The two friends freed themselves and alerted Polly's mother, who called police. The abduction of a child from her own bedroom during a sleepover, with family nearby, shocked the nation.

The disappearance triggered one of the largest volunteer search efforts in the region's history. Over the following two months, roughly 4,000 people helped distribute flyers and comb the woods around Petaluma. The Polly Klaas Foundation was established to coordinate the search and support the family, and the case drew national media attention, including support from Petaluma native and actress Winona Ryder, who offered a reward. Despite the scale of the effort, weeks passed with no confirmed sightings of Polly or her abductor.

The investigation broke open through physical evidence and a chance encounter. On the night of the kidnapping, sheriff's deputies in nearby Sonoma Valley had briefly detained a man named Richard Allen Davis, a paroled repeat offender, whose car was stuck in a ditch off Pythian Road, but released him. Investigators later recovered a palm print from Polly's bedroom, and on December 2, 1993, criminalists matched it to Davis, who had been arrested on November 30 on an unrelated parole violation. On December 4, 1993, Davis confessed and led investigators to Polly's body, buried in a shallow grave off Highway 101 near Cloverdale. He had strangled her.

Davis, who had a long record including burglary, assault, and prior kidnappings and had been released from prison in June 1993, was tried in San Jose after a change of venue to Santa Clara County. On June 18, 1996, a jury convicted him of first-degree murder with four special circumstances: robbery, burglary, kidnapping, and an attempted lewd act on a child under 14. On August 5, 1996, the jury recommended death, and Judge Thomas Hastings formally imposed the death sentence on September 26, 1996. Davis has remained on California's death row since.

The murder of Polly Klaas became a defining catalyst for tougher sentencing laws. Public outrage over the fact that a career criminal on parole had abducted and killed a child helped drive the swift passage of California's "Three Strikes and You're Out" law, signed by Governor Pete Wilson on March 7, 1994, and later approved by voters as Proposition 184 in November 1994. The law mandated sentences of 25 years to life for a third serious or violent felony conviction. As of 2026, Richard Allen Davis remains incarcerated on death row at San Quentin; California has maintained a moratorium on executions, and courts have repeatedly rejected his efforts to overturn his death sentence.

name: Steve Branch, Michael Moore & Christopher Byers
summary: Three eight-year-old boys were murdered in West Memphis, Arkansas, in May 1993. Three teenagers — Damien Echols, Jason Baldwin, and Jessie Misskelley Jr. — were convicted in 1994 and released in 2011 after entering Alford pleas, under which their convictions stand while they maintain their innocence. DNA recovered from the crime scene has not been matched to any of the three men, no one else has ever been charged, and court-ordered advanced DNA testing of remaining evidence was under way in 2025-2026.
lastSeen: May 5, 1993, West Memphis, AR

narrative: On May 5, 1993, three eight-year-old boys, Steve Branch, Michael Moore, and Christopher Byers, went out to play in West Memphis, Arkansas, and did not return home. The following day, searchers found their bodies in a drainage ditch in a wooded area known as Robin Hood Hills. The children had been stripped, beaten, and bound with their own shoelaces. The brutality of the crime, committed against three second-grade Cub Scouts, shocked the community and drew intense local pressure to find those responsible.

In June 1993, police arrested three local teenagers: Jessie Misskelley Jr., Jason Baldwin, and Damien Echols. The case against them rested heavily on a statement Misskelley gave to police on June 3, 1993, after roughly twelve hours of questioning, of which only a portion was recorded. Misskelley, who was reported to have an IQ of about 72, confessed and implicated Echols and Baldwin, but he recanted soon afterward, and defense attorneys argued the statement was coerced and inconsistent with known facts about the crime. Prosecutors advanced a theory that the killings were part of a satanic ritual, a claim critics later cited as an example of the era's so-called 'satanic panic.'

The three were tried in early 1994. Misskelley was convicted in February 1994 of one count of first-degree murder and two counts of second-degree murder and sentenced to life plus 40 years. In March 1994, Echols and Baldwin were convicted of first-degree murder; Echols was sentenced to death and Baldwin to life imprisonment. All three maintained their innocence throughout. The convictions became the subject of the 'Paradise Lost' documentary trilogy by Joe Berlinger and Bruce Sinofsky, and later the film 'West of Memphis,' which drew celebrity support from figures including Peter Jackson, Eddie Vedder, Johnny Depp, and Natalie Maines, and helped fund new legal and forensic work.

Forensic testing reported in 2007 found that DNA recovered from the crime scene did not match any of the three convicted men. Defense filings pointed to other material, including a hair reported to be consistent with Terry Hobbs, stepfather of victim Steve Branch, though Hobbs has denied involvement and has never been charged. Authorities have not accepted these claims as establishing another perpetrator, and no one else has been charged in the case. Observers have cautioned that such forensic results are contested and do not, by themselves, resolve who committed the murders.

In November 2010, the Arkansas Supreme Court ordered a hearing on new evidence. On August 19, 2011, under a legal arrangement known as an Alford plea, Echols, Baldwin, and Misskelley pleaded guilty to reduced charges while continuing to assert their innocence; an Alford plea allows a defendant to concede that prosecutors have evidence sufficient for conviction without admitting the acts. Judge David Laser sentenced them to time served, about 18 years, and they were released the same day, with the state maintaining that the convictions stand. Because no other suspect has been prosecuted and the men continue to deny guilt, many regard the case as effectively unresolved. As of 2024, Echols was still seeking additional DNA testing of remaining evidence under Arkansas law.
