name: Crystal Ann Tymich
summary: Six-year-old Crystal Ann Tymich disappeared on June 30, 1994, while playing outside near her home on Brynhurst Avenue in South Los Angeles. According to the FBI, she was last seen picking peaches from a neighbor's tree between 2 and 5 p.m. Searches by the LAPD and FBI found no trace of her, and she remains missing.
lastSeen: June 30, 1994, 6000 block of Brynhurst Avenue, South Los Angeles, CA

narrative: Crystal Ann Tymich was six years old when she disappeared from her South Los Angeles neighborhood on June 30, 1994. According to the FBI's missing person poster, she had been playing near her residence with her three older brothers that afternoon and was last seen picking peaches from a neighbor's tree. She vanished at some point between 2 and 5 p.m.

The Polly Klaas Foundation and the case summary published by Solve the Case place the disappearance in the 6000 block of Brynhurst Avenue, in the Hyde Park area of what was then commonly called South Central Los Angeles. The Solve the Case summary states that her brothers rode away briefly on their bicycles and that Crystal was gone when they came back. The same summary says neighbors had seen her wander off earlier that day and had brought her back to her brothers.

Crystal was born on September 23, 1987, in Los Angeles. The FBI describes her as a white girl with blonde hair and hazel eyes who stood about four feet tall and weighed about 60 pounds at the time. She was wearing a pink T-shirt, shorts with a floral print, and tennis shoes with a picture of a mermaid on them.

The Los Angeles Police Department is the investigating agency, and the FBI's Los Angeles Field Office has assisted. According to the Solve the Case summary, the LAPD and FBI carried out extensive searches that included door-to-door canvassing of the neighborhood and searches from the air, none of which produced any sign of her. The summary also states that a reward of up to $10,000 was offered and was raised to $25,000 in 1996, and that in 2005 investigators acting on a tip searched a home near where she had lived and recovered only animal remains.

No arrest has been announced and no suspect has been publicly named by police in the sources reviewed. Crystal remains listed as missing by the FBI, which files her case under its kidnappings and missing persons listings, and by the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children. NCMEC has issued age-progressed images showing how she might have looked at 18 and at 29. She would be 39 years old in 2026.
Anyone with information is asked to contact the Los Angeles Police Department at (877) 275-5273, the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children at 1-800-843-5678, or the nearest FBI office.

name: Dr. John Bayard Britton
summary: Dr. John Britton, 69, and his volunteer escort James Barrett, 74, were shot dead outside the Ladies Center clinic in Pensacola, Florida, on July 29, 1994; Barrett's wife June was wounded. Paul Jennings Hill was convicted of two counts of first-degree murder, sentenced to death in December 1994, and executed on September 3, 2003.
lastSeen: July 29, 1994, Ladies Center clinic, Pensacola, FL

sources.title: Wikipedia - Paul Jennings Hill
Wikipedia - John Britton (doctor)
Death Penalty Information Center - Executions in 2003

narrative: Dr. John Bayard Britton, a 69-year-old physician, was shot and killed on the morning of July 29, 1994, as he arrived at the Ladies Center, a clinic in Pensacola, Florida, where he performed abortions. James Herman Barrett, 74, a retired U.S. Air Force lieutenant colonel who was escorting the doctor as a volunteer, was also killed. Barrett's wife, June Barrett, 68, was wounded.

According to Wikipedia's account of the case, the gunman approached as they arrived at the clinic, fired at close range with a 12-gauge pump-action shotgun, then laid the weapon on the ground and waited to be arrested. Britton, who was born in Boston in 1925, had begun working at Pensacola clinics after another physician, Dr. David Gunn, was shot to death outside a different Pensacola clinic in 1993 in an unrelated attack by a different man.

Paul Jennings Hill, then 40, was arrested at the scene. Hill had been ordained as a Presbyterian minister and was excommunicated in 1993 after television appearances in which he advocated what he called defensive action against abortion providers, according to Wikipedia. In Florida state court he was charged with two counts of first-degree murder, one count of attempted first-degree murder, and one count of shooting into an occupied vehicle. He chose to represent himself and pleaded not guilty. The trial judge refused to let him present a justification defense, in which he would have argued that the killings were necessary to prevent abortions.

A jury found Hill guilty on all counts in 1994, and on December 6, 1994, he was sentenced to death. Florida appellate courts, including the Florida Supreme Court in 1996, upheld the convictions and sentence, and the U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear the case in 1997. After those automatic appeals ended, Hill gave up his remaining appeals. In a statement before his execution he said he felt no remorse.

Hill was executed by lethal injection at Florida State Prison on September 3, 2003, at age 49. The Death Penalty Information Center's list of executions for that year records his execution in Florida on that date for the deaths of two victims. According to Wikipedia's article on Dr. Britton, Hill was the first person in the United States to be executed for murdering a doctor who performed abortions.

Hill spent almost nine years on death row. Florida Governor Jeb Bush signed the execution warrant in July 2003. The case is closed, with no outstanding charges or unresolved questions about who was responsible; it is included here as a record of the deaths of Dr. Britton and Mr. Barrett and the wounding of Mrs. Barrett.

name: Lamar Johnson (Exoneration)
summary: Markus Boyd was shot dead by two masked men on his St. Louis porch on October 30, 1994. Lamar Johnson was convicted in 1995 and served about 28 years before Judge David Mason vacated the conviction on February 14, 2023, finding clear and convincing evidence of innocence. A co-defendant pleaded guilty to a reduced charge, and another man testified he was one of the shooters.
lastSeen: October 30, 1994, St. Louis, MO

CBS News - Lamar Johnson's 28-year fight for freedom

narrative: Markus Boyd, 25, was shot and killed on the front porch of his home in St. Louis, Missouri, on October 30, 1994. According to CBS News, Boyd was sitting with a friend, Greg Elking, when two men wearing masks approached and opened fire. Boyd's first name appears as both Markus and Marcus in news coverage.

Police arrested Lamar Johnson a few days later, on November 3, 1994. Prosecutors alleged that Boyd was killed over a drug debt. Johnson maintained that he was elsewhere at the time of the shooting. He was tried in July 1995, convicted of murder, and sentenced to life in prison without parole. The case against him depended heavily on Elking's identification and on the testimony of a jail informant. A second man, Phillip Campbell, was also charged; CBS News reported that Campbell pleaded guilty to a reduced charge and received a seven-year sentence.

Doubts about the conviction grew over the following decades. According to CBS News, Campbell wrote letters as early as 1995 stating that Johnson had not been involved and naming James Howard as the other gunman, and Elking wrote to a clergyman in 2003 saying his identification had been false. It later emerged that Elking had received more than $4,000 in payments that were not disclosed to the defense at trial.

In 2019, the Conviction Integrity Unit of St. Louis Circuit Attorney Kim Gardner concluded that Johnson had been wrongly convicted and asked a court to set the verdict aside. St. Louis Public Radio reported that the Missouri Supreme Court ruled in 2021 that Gardner had no authority to bring such a motion, after which the legislature passed a law allowing prosecutors to do so. Gardner's office filed again under the new law, and the Missouri Attorney General's Office opposed the request.

Circuit Judge David Mason heard evidence beginning December 12, 2022. Elking recanted his identification under oath, and Howard, who is serving a life sentence in another case, testified that he and Campbell shot Boyd and that Johnson was not there. On February 14, 2023, Mason vacated the conviction, writing that the testimony amounted to clear and convincing evidence that Johnson was innocent. Johnson, then 50, was released the same day. The Attorney General's Office said it would take no further action.

On January 17, 2024, Johnson filed a federal civil rights lawsuit against the City of St. Louis and several former police officers, alleging that evidence was fabricated and that information favorable to him was withheld, St. Louis Public Radio reported. The sources reviewed do not report any new criminal charges in Boyd's death following Howard's testimony.

name: Melissa Witt
summary: Nineteen-year-old Melissa Witt was abducted from the parking lot of the Bowling World bowling alley in Fort Smith, Arkansas, on December 1, 1994. Hunters found her body on January 13, 1995, in the Ozark National Forest in Franklin County, about 50 miles away; she had been strangled. No one has been charged, and the investigation remains open.
lastSeen: December 1, 1994, Bowling World parking lot, Fort Smith, AR

sources.title: ABC News - Who killed Melissa Witt? 30 years later, the hunt continues
Fox News - Investigators hunt Melissa Witt's Arkansas killer 30 years after mysterious trail of blood

narrative: Melissa Witt, a 19-year-old college student from Fort Smith, Arkansas, disappeared on the evening of December 1, 1994. According to ABC News, she drove to the Bowling World bowling alley in Fort Smith intending to surprise her mother, who was bowling there in a league. The case website maintained by people working on the investigation says she went to the bowling alley at about 6:30 to 7 p.m., after class and work. She never made it inside.

Investigators concluded that she was attacked and abducted in the parking lot. ABC News and Fox News reported that blood and signs of a struggle were found in the lot and at her car, and that her keys were left behind. The case website also mentions an earring recovered at the scene. AY Magazine reported that a trail of blood led from the back of her car to a spot where another vehicle had been parked, and that her car sat in the lot for days.

On January 13, 1995, about six weeks after she vanished, two hunters found her body along a logging trail in the Ozark National Forest in Franklin County, roughly 50 miles from Fort Smith. She had been strangled. Investigators said her clothing, shoes and jewelry, including a Mickey Mouse watch, had been taken and have not been recovered.

No one has been charged. AY Magazine reported in 2021 that more than 330 people had been interviewed over the years. One person investigators have examined, according to ABC News and Fox News, is Charles Ray Vines, who was convicted in 2000 of murdering a woman in another Arkansas case. Those reports say a cigarette filter and other items associated with Vines were found in the forest area and that he had worked near the site. Vines died in September 2019 without being charged in Witt's death and without being interviewed about it a final time, and authorities have not declared him responsible.

The case has been the subject of sustained attention from the Fort Smith Police Department and the FBI, as well as from author LaDonna Humphrey, who co-directed the 2021 documentary "Uneven Ground: The Melissa Witt Story" and has written about the case. A Hulu docuseries, "At Witt's End: The Hunt for a Killer," was released in August 2024 and followed FBI agents and others working on the investigation. Investigators have said that DNA evidence exists in the case.
As of the most recent reports reviewed, from the 30th anniversary in late 2024, the killing remained unsolved. A tip line for the case is available at 1-800-440-1922.

narrative: Nicole Brown Simpson, 35, and Ronald Goldman, 25, were stabbed to death on the night of June 12, 1994, outside Brown's condominium at 875 South Bundy Drive in the Brentwood section of Los Angeles. According to Wikipedia's account, their bodies were discovered shortly after midnight on June 13. Goldman, a waiter and a friend of Brown's, had come to the home to return a pair of glasses that Brown's mother had left at the restaurant where he worked. The knife was never found.

Police attention turned to Brown's former husband, O.J. Simpson, the retired professional football player and actor. The couple had married in 1985 and divorced in 1992. On June 17, 1994, prosecutors charged Simpson with both murders. He did not surrender as arranged, and that evening police followed a white Ford Bronco carrying Simpson and driven by his friend A.C. Cowlings along Los Angeles freeways in a slow pursuit broadcast live on television. Simpson gave himself up at his Brentwood home. He pleaded not guilty on June 20 and was held without bail, and on July 7 a judge ruled that there was enough evidence for trial.

The trial in Los Angeles County Superior Court ran from January 24 to October 3, 1995. Prosecutors relied on blood, hair and fiber evidence, a pair of gloves, and shoe prints, according to History.com. The defense team, which included Johnnie Cochran and F. Lee Bailey, argued that evidence had been mishandled and that Simpson had been framed by police, focusing on Detective Mark Fuhrman. On October 3, 1995, after about four hours of deliberation, the jury found Simpson not guilty on both counts.

The victims' families then sued Simpson in civil court, where the standard of proof is lower. In February 1997 a jury in Santa Monica unanimously found him liable for Goldman's wrongful death and for battery against both victims. He was ordered to pay $33.5 million in compensatory and punitive damages. The families have recovered only a small part of that amount, according to Wikipedia and History.com.

In an unrelated case, Simpson was convicted on October 3, 2008, of armed robbery, kidnapping and other charges arising from a 2007 confrontation over sports memorabilia in a Las Vegas hotel room. He was sentenced to 33 years in prison, was granted parole in July 2017 and was released on October 1, 2017.

Simpson died of cancer in Las Vegas on April 10, 2024, at age 76. He always denied killing Brown and Goldman. Because he was acquitted and no one else has ever been charged, the murders remain without a criminal conviction. According to Wikipedia, no other suspect was identified by investigators.

summary: Seventeen-year-old Deanna Cremin was found strangled behind a senior housing complex on Jaques Street in Somerville, Massachusetts, on the morning of March 30, 1995, a short distance from her home. She had last been seen the night before while walking home from her boyfriend's house. No one has been charged, and a $70,000 reward remains on offer.

narrative: Deanna Cremin was a 17-year-old high school student in Somerville, Massachusetts, when she was killed in late March 1995. She had turned 17 only days earlier; according to Wikipedia she was born on March 26, 1978.

On the evening of March 29, 1995, Deanna spent time at her boyfriend's home watching television, Boston.com reported, after telling her mother by telephone that she loved her. Her boyfriend, then 18, told police that he walked her part of the way home and that they separated near the corner of Heath and Bond streets at about 10 p.m., a few tenths of a mile from her house. She did not arrive home.

At about 8 a.m. on March 30, two children on their way to school took a shortcut behind a senior housing complex on Jaques Street and found her body. According to the podcast Dark Downeast, which reviewed records of the case, the children knew her because she had been their babysitter. She was lying on her back near a fence, partly undressed, less than 500 feet from the intersection where she was reported to have been last seen and about a block from her home. The medical examiner determined that she had been strangled, and officials have said she may have been sexually assaulted.

No one has been charged. GBH News reported in 2013 that three men, including her boyfriend, had been described as persons of interest and that none had been charged. Boston.com reported in 2015 that the mayor of Somerville had spoken of three persons of interest, while police and the district attorney declined to confirm this, citing the open investigation. Being described as a person of interest is not an accusation, and none of the three has been named as a suspect by prosecutors.

The reward for information has grown over time, from $10,000 in 1995 to $20,000 in 2005, according to Wikipedia, and to $70,000 by the 20th anniversary. In 2005 the district attorney at the time, Martha Coakley, said new forensic techniques had been applied to evidence. In 2015 Middlesex District Attorney Marian Ryan said her office had assigned its chief of homicide and a State Police trooper to the case.

Deanna's family and friends hold a memorial Mass and walk every year. Around the 30th anniversary in March 2025, the Somerville City Council took up a resolution calling for renewed investigative effort in her case and another unsolved killing, and District Attorney Ryan was scheduled to address the council on April 10, 2025. Her office described the case as active, the Somerville Times reported. Tips can be given at (617) 544-7167.

name: Jodi Huisentruit
summary: Television news anchor Jodi Huisentruit disappeared on her way to work at KIMT-TV in Mason City, Iowa. Her car was found with signs of a struggle. Despite a 25+ year investigation and significant media attention, Jodi has never been found.

narrative: Jodi Sue Huisentruit was a 27-year-old morning news anchor for KIMT, the CBS affiliate in Mason City, Iowa, when she vanished in the early hours of June 27, 1995. A native of Long Prairie, Minnesota, and a 1990 graduate of St. Cloud State University, she had joined the station in 1994 and typically left for work before dawn to co-anchor the early broadcast. That morning she failed to arrive on time. At about 4:00 a.m., KIMT producer Amy Kuns telephoned Huisentruit's apartment; Huisentruit answered, said she had overslept, and indicated she was on her way. She never reached the station, and she has not been seen since.

Investigators who examined the parking lot of Huisentruit's apartment complex found evidence consistent with a struggle near her red Mazda Miata. According to police and widely published accounts, the scene included a bent car key, her high-heeled shoes, hair care items, earrings, and other personal belongings scattered on the ground. A partial palm print was reportedly recovered from her car. Several neighbors later said they heard a scream in the pre-dawn hours, and at least one reported seeing a white van in the vicinity. Authorities concluded the physical evidence pointed to an abduction rather than a voluntary departure.

The Mason City Police Department, later joined by the Iowa Division of Criminal Investigation and the FBI, conducted an extensive investigation that included more than 1,000 interviews over the years. The Huisentruit family also engaged private investigators. Over the decades several individuals have been publicly discussed in connection with the case, but no one has ever been arrested or charged. John Vansice, an acquaintance whom Huisentruit had visited the evening before she disappeared, was publicly identified as a person of interest; in 2017 authorities sought GPS data from two of his vehicles through a search warrant. Vansice, who was never charged and denied involvement, died in December 2024. Other names that have surfaced in media reports and documentaries — including Christopher Revak, a since-deceased suspected killer, and Brad Millerbernd — have likewise not been charged. These individuals are described here only as publicly reported persons of interest; none has been convicted of any crime related to the case.

The case has been kept in public view in part through the work of FindJodi, an effort launched in 2003 by Minnesota television journalists Josh Benson and Gary Peterson and later organized as a nonprofit clearinghouse for tips and information. Huisentruit's disappearance has also been featured on national programs such as America's Most Wanted and Unsolved Mysteries, and in 2025 was the subject of the Hulu documentary series Her Last Broadcast: The Abduction of Jodi Huisentruit. In May 2001, at her family's request, a Cerro Gordo County District Court judge declared Huisentruit legally dead after a court-appointed attorney found no evidence she had left voluntarily or was still alive.

As of 2026, Jodi Huisentruit's remains have never been found and the case remains unsolved and officially open, with Mason City police describing it as an active investigation. Renewed interest and new tips have prompted periodic searches, including efforts in Winsted, Minnesota, in 2024 and 2025, though authorities reported nothing of significance was recovered. A private reward for information leading to the recovery of her remains has been raised over time to as much as $100,000. Investigators continue to solicit tips through the Mason City Police Department and the Iowa DCI.

name: Oklahoma City Bombing Victims
summary: The bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah Federal Building killed 168 people and injured hundreds more. Timothy McVeigh and Terry Nichols were convicted; McVeigh was executed in 2001 and Nichols is serving life without parole. It remains the deadliest act of domestic terrorism in U.S. history and was the deadliest terrorist attack on U.S. soil until September 11, 2001. Questions about possible additional conspirators have persisted, but no further prosecutions have resulted.
lastSeen: April 19, 1995, Oklahoma City, OK

narrative: On the morning of April 19, 1995, at 9:02 a.m., a rented Ryder truck packed with roughly 4,800 pounds of ammonium nitrate fertilizer mixed with nitromethane and diesel fuel detonated outside the Alfred P. Murrah Federal Building in downtown Oklahoma City. The blast sheared away much of the building's north face, collapsed floors onto one another, and damaged or destroyed hundreds of surrounding structures. The attack killed 168 people, including 19 children, many of them in a day-care center on the second floor, and injured several hundred more. It was, at the time, the deadliest act of domestic terrorism in United States history and remains the deadliest carried out by American citizens.

The investigation moved with unusual speed. Within days, federal agents traced a vehicle axle bearing a serial number to the Ryder truck rented in Junction City, Kansas, and a composite sketch led to a motel registration linked to Timothy McVeigh, a 26-year-old Army veteran. McVeigh had already been arrested about 90 minutes after the bombing by an Oklahoma state trooper near Perry, Oklahoma, on unrelated charges of driving without a license plate and carrying a concealed weapon. He was identified and held as the bombing suspect just before his scheduled release. Investigators soon linked him to Terry Nichols, a former Army acquaintance, who surrendered to police in Herington, Kansas, on April 21, 1995.

Prosecutors described McVeigh as the principal planner and bomber, motivated by anti-government anger intensified by the 1993 federal siege at Waco, Texas, which had ended on the same April 19 date two years earlier. Nichols was accused of helping gather materials and assemble the bomb. A third associate, Michael Fortier, had advance knowledge of the plot and, with his wife Lori, became a key cooperating witness.

In federal court in Denver, McVeigh was convicted on June 2, 1997, of murder and conspiracy charges and was sentenced to death on June 13, 1997. He was executed by lethal injection at the U.S. Penitentiary in Terre Haute, Indiana, on June 11, 2001, the first federal prisoner put to death since 1963. Terry Nichols was convicted in federal court in December 1997 of conspiracy and involuntary manslaughter and sentenced to life in prison without parole; a later Oklahoma state trial in 2004 convicted him on 161 counts of first-degree murder, adding additional life sentences. Michael Fortier pleaded guilty to lesser charges, including failing to warn authorities of the plot, and received a 12-year sentence in exchange for his testimony; he was released in 2006 and entered the witness protection program. Lori Fortier received immunity for her cooperation.

The site of the Murrah Building was transformed into the Oklahoma City National Memorial, dedicated on April 19, 2000, five years after the attack. Its Field of Empty Chairs holds 168 chairs, one for each victim, arranged by the floor on which they died. The case is legally closed, with all identified conspirators convicted; McVeigh executed, Nichols serving life, and Fortier having completed his sentence. Questions about whether others may have been involved have persisted among some researchers, but no additional prosecutions have resulted.

name: Amber Hagerman
summary: Nine-year-old Amber Hagerman was abducted while riding her bicycle in the parking lot of an abandoned grocery store in Arlington, Texas. A witness saw a man pull her into a black pickup truck. Her body was found four days later in a creek behind an apartment complex, and no one has ever been charged. Her kidnapping directly inspired the creation of the AMBER Alert system, which has been credited with the recovery of more than 1,300 children.
lastSeen: January 13, 1996, Winn-Dixie parking lot, Arlington, TX

narrative: On the afternoon of January 13, 1996, nine-year-old Amber Rene Hagerman was abducted while riding her bicycle in Arlington, Texas. She had been riding with her younger brother in the parking lot of an abandoned grocery store near East Abram Street and Browning Drive. According to police, a witness saw a man get out of a black pickup truck, pull Amber from her bicycle, and force her into the vehicle as she kicked and screamed. Four days later, on January 17, 1996, her body was found near an apartment complex in north Arlington, roughly four to five miles from where she was taken. An autopsy determined she had died of severe laceration wounds to her neck.

No suspect has ever been publicly identified or charged, and the case remains classified as an unsolved homicide. Investigators have described the suspect, based on witness accounts, as a White or Hispanic man who was in his 20s or 30s at the time, under six feet tall, of medium build, with brown or black hair. The vehicle sought is a black 1980s or 1990s full-size, single-cab pickup truck with a short wheelbase. Because no one has been arrested, no named person of interest has been established as connected to the crime, and authorities have continued to appeal to the public for information.

Amber's murder prompted the creation of the AMBER Alert system (America's Missing: Broadcast Emergency Response), a coordinated public notification program for child abductions. Following her death, Dallas-area broadcasters and law enforcement developed the concept, and an early local alert framework emerged in the Dallas-Fort Worth area in 1996. The system gradually expanded nationally, gaining a congressional resolution encouraging adoption in 2000 and an endorsement from the Federal Communications Commission in 2002. In April 2003, President George W. Bush signed the PROTECT Act, which established federal coordination and national standards for AMBER Alerts. By 2005 all fifty U.S. states had operational programs, and the model was later adopted by numerous other countries. Officials have credited the system with the safe recovery of more than 1,000 children.

The investigation has remained active in the decades since. Arlington police have said they received thousands of tips over the years and have periodically renewed public appeals, including on the 25th anniversary in January 2021. At that time, officials announced plans to submit original evidence for advanced forensic testing in hopes of developing a more complete DNA profile of the perpetrator, an effort tied to the growing use of DNA technology and forensic genetic genealogy in cold cases. Police cautioned that they did not necessarily have a confirmed suspect DNA sample but were seeking to extract and enhance forensic evidence from the case.

As of the 30th anniversary in January 2026, the case is still unsolved. Arlington Police Assistant Chief Kevin Kolbye reiterated that detectives believe someone still holds knowledge of the crime and urged that person to come forward, and police said they remain in contact with crime labs about applying newer technology to the existing evidence. A reward of $10,000 offered by Oak Farms Dairy remains available for information leading to an arrest and conviction. Investigators note the suspect, if living, would now likely be in his 50s or 60s. The murder of Amber Hagerman continues to be one of the most prominent unsolved child homicides in the United States, both for its own unresolved status and for the nationwide alert system that bears her name.

Her remains have not been found.

narrative: Cayce Lynn McDaniel was 14 and about to begin her freshman year of high school when she disappeared from her home in Milan, a town in Gibson County, Tennessee. According to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children, she was last known to be at her residence on August 16, 1996. She was born on July 14, 1982, the Milan Mirror-Exchange reported.

That night she had attended a back-to-school party for young people at Double Springs Cumberland Presbyterian Church. WMC Action News 5 reported that an adult from the event dropped her off at home around midnight. When her family returned, the back door was standing open and she was gone. The station reported that the television in her bedroom was on, that the clothes she had worn that evening were laid out, and that a bowl of cookies and milk had been left on the floor. There were no signs of a struggle. A friend told the Mirror-Exchange that police believed she had changed for bed before she left the house.

Milan police and the FBI questioned many people in the following years without an arrest. In 2010 the police chief at the time said dozens of people had been interviewed and several given polygraph tests, and that Cayce was probably no longer alive.

In July 2018, Milan Police Chief Bobby Sellers publicly named Finis Ewin "Pete" Hill as a suspect. Hill was an acquaintance of the family, and Cayce knew him as "Uncle Pete," according to the Mirror-Exchange. He had earlier served a prison sentence for attempted kidnapping and aggravated assault in another case and was in federal custody in 2018 on a separate charge involving a minor. Sellers said Hill's alibi had not held up when investigators re-examined it. A Gibson County grand jury indicted Hill in October 2019 on two counts of first-degree murder and two counts of aggravated rape, and he pleaded not guilty.

On August 26, 2022, Hill, then 70, entered a best-interest plea to criminal responsibility for second-degree murder and abuse of a corpse. Under that type of plea a defendant accepts conviction and sentence without admitting the acts. He received a 15-year sentence to be served in full, followed by six years of supervised probation, and gave up his right to appeal; the other charges were dropped. District Attorney General Frederick Agee told the Mirror-Exchange that Hill did not admit to the killing but supplied corroborating details and information about where Cayce was believed to have been buried.

Agee said searches of a specific area had already been carried out and would continue, and that the agreement required Hill to keep cooperating. As of that report, and in the sources reviewed, Cayce's remains had not been recovered. She is still listed by NCMEC as missing.

name: JonBenét Ramsey
summary: Six-year-old JonBenét Ramsey was found dead in the basement of her family's Boulder home on December 26, 1996, hours after her mother reported finding a ransom note demanding $118,000. She had been struck on the head and strangled. Despite an extensive investigation in which police have followed up on more than 21,000 tips and interviewed over 1,000 people, no one has ever been charged and the case remains unsolved.

narrative: On the morning of December 26, 1996, six-year-old JonBenét Ramsey was reported missing from her family's home in Boulder, Colorado. Her mother, Patsy Ramsey, told police she found a two-and-a-half-page handwritten ransom note on a staircase demanding $118,000 — an amount reported to closely match a bonus her father, John Ramsey, had received. No child was taken. Several hours later, around 1:00 p.m., John Ramsey and a friend discovered the girl's body in a basement room of the house. According to the coroner, the autopsy attributed her death to "asphyxia by strangulation associated with craniocerebral trauma." The killing drew intense national media attention that has continued for decades.

The early investigation was widely criticized. Reporting and later official reviews noted that the crime scene was not immediately secured, that friends and family moved through the house, and that potential evidence was contaminated before forensic work was complete. Suspicion in the press and among some investigators initially focused on members of the Ramsey family, though none of them was ever charged with a crime. A Boulder County grand jury was convened on September 15, 1998, to examine the case. In 1999 the grand jury voted to indict John and Patsy Ramsey on charges related to child abuse resulting in death and being accessories to a crime, but District Attorney Alex Hunter declined to sign the indictment or prosecute, citing insufficient evidence. The existence and content of that grand jury vote were not made public until sealed documents were released on October 25, 2013.

On July 9, 2008, Boulder District Attorney Mary Lacy publicly cleared the Ramsey family. Citing newly applied "touch DNA" analysis of an unidentified male profile recovered from JonBenét's clothing, Lacy wrote in a letter to John Ramsey that the evidence "excludes" the family as suspects and stated, "to the extent that we may have contributed in any way to the public perception that you might have been involved in this crime, I am deeply sorry." The family members were therefore never charged and were publicly exonerated by the DA. Critics, including some forensic experts, later questioned how conclusive the DNA finding was, and in 2016 successor District Attorney Stan Garnett said Lacy's exoneration letter was not legally binding.

The case remains officially unsolved and is handled as an active homicide by the Boulder Police Department. The department says it convened a Cold Case Review Panel in December 2023 and reports having followed up on more than 21,000 tips and interviewed over 1,000 people across 19 states. In a statement dated November 27, 2024, Police Chief Steve Redfearn said, "The assertion that there is viable evidence and leads we are not pursuing — to include DNA testing — is completely false," adding that detectives continue to work with DNA experts and outside labs. John Ramsey has publicly urged police to pursue investigative genetic genealogy on the unidentified male DNA, saying he believes newer techniques could identify the killer. As of 2026, Boulder police continue to describe the case as active and ongoing, with periodic annual updates, and no arrest has been made.

narrative: Kristin Denise Smart, a 19-year-old freshman at California Polytechnic State University in San Luis Obispo, California, was last seen in the early morning hours of May 25, 1996, after attending an off-campus party. Found intoxicated on a neighbor's lawn, she began walking back toward campus in the company of several other students. One by one the others peeled off toward their own dorms until only fellow freshman Paul Flores remained with her. Flores said he left her near her residence hall, but Smart was never seen again. Because she was reported missing only after several days had passed, the trail was cold before a serious search began, a delay later blamed on a slow response by campus authorities.

Paul Flores emerged almost immediately as the prime suspect. He was seen with a black eye in the days after the disappearance, offered shifting explanations for it, and in a 1996 grand jury appearance and a later civil deposition repeatedly invoked his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination. Investigators searched multiple locations over the years, including properties tied to the Flores family, using cadaver dogs and ground-penetrating radar, but no body was recovered. Kristin Smart was legally declared dead in 2002. Despite persistent suspicion, prosecutors long felt they lacked enough physical evidence to bring charges, and the case languished for roughly two decades.

Renewed momentum came in 2019 when Chris Lambert, a local musician with no prior investigative background, launched the podcast "Your Own Backyard," which meticulously re-examined the case, interviewed witnesses, and pressed for answers. Downloaded millions of times, the series drew national attention, surfaced new witnesses, and helped reinvigorate the sheriff's investigation. On April 13, 2021, authorities arrested Paul Flores on a charge of murder and arrested his father, Ruben Flores, as an accessory after the fact, alleging that Ruben had helped conceal Kristin's body.

The two men were tried together but before separate juries in Monterey County, where the case had been moved because of extensive publicity. Prosecutors argued that Paul Flores killed Smart during an attempted rape in his dorm room and that her body had at one point been buried beneath the deck of Ruben Flores's Arroyo Grande home before being moved. On October 18, 2022, Paul Flores was convicted of first-degree murder. His father, Ruben Flores, was acquitted of the accessory charge the same day.

On March 10, 2023, Paul Flores was sentenced to 25 years to life in prison. Kristin Smart's remains have never been found, and searches connected to the case have continued in the years since. Her disappearance also prompted the Kristin Smart Campus Security Act, signed into California law in 1998, which requires public colleges to coordinate with local police on reporting serious crimes. Paul Flores has pursued appeals of his conviction.

name: Julianne Williams & Lollie Winans
summary: Julianne "Julie" Williams, 24, and Laura "Lollie" Winans, 26, were found dead at their campsite near Skyland Resort in Shenandoah National Park on June 1, 1996. In June 2024 the FBI announced that DNA testing had linked the killings to Walter "Leo" Jackson Sr., a convicted rapist from Ohio who died in prison in 2018. An earlier defendant, Darrell David Rice, had his charges dismissed.
lastSeen: May 24, 1996, Shenandoah National Park, VA

sources.title: CBS News - 1996 cold case killings of 2 campers at Shenandoah National Park solved, FBI says
ABC News - Suspect identified in women's 1996 double murder at national park
NBC4 Washington - Shenandoah hiker murder case solved after deaths of 2 women in 1996
WVTF - FBI: DNA evidence conclusively links Shenandoah National Park murders to convicted serial rapist
WTVR - Julie Williams and Laura Lollie Winans: Serial rapist is person responsible, FBI says

narrative: Julianne "Julie" Williams, 24, and Laura "Lollie" Winans, 26, were killed while on a backcountry camping trip in Shenandoah National Park, Virginia, in May 1996. According to ABC News, the two women had met through an organization that ran outdoor programs for women, and they entered the park on May 19, 1996, accompanied by a golden retriever.

CBS News reported that park personnel last saw the women alive on May 24, 1996. NBC Washington reported that Williams's father reported them missing on May 31 after they failed to return, and that rangers found their bodies the next day, June 1, at their campsite near Skyland Resort. According to news accounts of the FBI's findings, both women had been bound and gagged and their throats had been cut; CBS News reported that they had also been sexually assaulted.

The investigation produced one prosecution that did not go forward. Darrell David Rice, who had pleaded guilty in 1998 to the attempted abduction of a female cyclist in the same park, was charged with capital murder in the case in the early 2000s. According to WTVR and CBS News, the charges were dismissed after forensic testing of hair evidence excluded him, and ABC News reported that DNA pointed to an unidentified male. Rice was never convicted of any offense connected to the deaths of Williams and Winans.

In 2021 the FBI's Richmond field office assigned a new team to re-examine the file. According to reports of the FBI's announcement, a private laboratory extracted DNA from several items of crime-scene evidence, and the resulting profile was run through the national CODIS database. It matched Walter "Leo" Jackson Sr., a residential painter from the Cleveland, Ohio, area who, the FBI said, was an avid hiker and a frequent visitor to the park. A retained buccal swab confirmed the match, and officials put the odds of the DNA belonging to someone else at one in 2.6 trillion.

The FBI and the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Western District of Virginia announced the identification on June 20, 2024. Jackson had served several prison terms for kidnapping, rape and assault, and ABC News reported that he abducted and raped a woman in Ohio on June 5, 1996, days after the Shenandoah killings, and committed a similar attack about a month later. He died in an Ohio prison in March 2018 at age 70, so no charges can be brought and the evidence will not be tested at trial.

The deaths had long been discussed as a possible anti-gay hate crime because the victims were a couple. U.S. Attorney Christopher Kavanaugh said at the announcement that investigators had no evidence the attack was motivated by bias. WVTF reported that the FBI found no link between Jackson and Rice, or between Jackson and the Colonial Parkway murders.

Jackson dies in an Ohio prison.
FBI Richmond assigns a new investigative team to review the case and retest evidence.

name: Tupac Shakur
summary: Rapper Tupac Shakur was shot multiple times in a drive-by shooting in Las Vegas on September 7, 1996, after attending a boxing match, and died six days later at University Medical Center. The case went unsolved for 27 years until Duane "Keffe D" Davis was indicted and arrested in September 2023. On August 31, 2026, a Clark County jury convicted Davis of first-degree murder with use of a deadly weapon for orchestrating the shooting; sentencing was set for October 13, 2026, and Davis has said he will appeal.
lastSeen: September 7, 1996, MGM Grand Garden Arena, Las Vegas, NV

sources.title: Murder of Tupac Shakur — Wikipedia
Can the Tupac Shakur murder trial salvage any justice from a 27-year-old case? — NPR

narrative: On the night of September 7, 1996, rapper Tupac Shakur was shot in a drive-by attack on the edge of the Las Vegas Strip. Shakur, 25, had attended the Mike Tyson heavyweight bout at the MGM Grand earlier that evening with Death Row Records executive Marion "Suge" Knight. According to police accounts, hours before the shooting Shakur and members of his entourage were involved in a lobby altercation with a man later identified as Orlando "Baby Lane" Anderson, a member of the Compton-based South Side Crips. At about 11:15 p.m., as Shakur rode in a BMW driven by Knight and stopped at a red light near East Flamingo Road and Koval Lane in Paradise, Nevada, a white Cadillac pulled alongside and a gunman opened fire. Shakur was struck multiple times by rounds fired from a .40-caliber handgun. Knight was grazed.

Shakur was hospitalized at University Medical Center in critical condition and underwent surgery that included removal of his right lung. He died of his injuries six days later, on September 13, 1996, with authorities citing respiratory failure and cardiac arrest. His death, coming amid a widely publicized rivalry between East Coast and West Coast hip-hop figures, drew intense national attention. Despite that scrutiny, no one was charged for years, and the case remained officially unsolved for more than two and a half decades.

Over the years, investigators and journalists repeatedly pointed to Orlando Anderson as a suspect in the shooting. Anderson denied involvement and was never charged; he was killed in an unrelated gang shooting in Southern California in 1998. Attention also turned to Anderson's uncle, Duane "Keffe D" Davis, a self-described former gang figure who, in a 2018 memoir and in filmed interviews, publicly described being in the Cadillac and said he had supplied the gun used in the attack. Davis has said he was in the front passenger seat; accounts attributed to investigators allege Anderson was among those in the back of the vehicle. Davis's public statements would later become central to the prosecution.

On September 29, 2023 — roughly 27 years after the shooting — a Clark County grand jury indicted Davis on a charge of first-degree murder, and he was arrested. Prosecutors allege he orchestrated the drive-by and provided the firearm. Davis pleaded not guilty on November 2, 2023. Davis was convicted at trial: on August 31, 2026, a Clark County jury found him guilty of first-degree murder with use of a deadly weapon, and he has said he intends to appeal. His defense has argued that his prior accounts were fabricated or exaggerated for profit and has cited claimed immunity agreements from earlier interviews with law enforcement.

Through 2024 and 2025 the prosecution advanced slowly. A judge set bail at $750,000 in January 2024, but Davis remained in custody. His attorneys sought dismissal, arguing his earlier statements were protected by immunity; after a lower court upheld the charges, the defense pursued an appeal to the Nevada Supreme Court. Separately, in April 2025 Davis was convicted in an unrelated jailhouse altercation and later sentenced to a term in state prison. His murder trial, originally slated for 2024, was repeatedly postponed; as of late 2025 the trial was reset for August 10, 2026, before District Court Judge Carli Kierny. The trial began in August 2026, and on August 31, 2026, the jury convicted Davis of first-degree murder with use of a deadly weapon; he was ordered held without bail pending sentencing on October 13, 2026.

name: Amy Wroe Bechtel
summary: Amy Wroe Bechtel, a 24-year-old competitive runner, disappeared on July 24, 1997, in the mountains above Lander, Wyoming, where she is believed to have gone to check a race course. Her car was found on the Loop Road at Burnt Gulch. No trace of her has been found, no one has been charged, and she was declared legally dead in 2004. The Fremont County Sheriff's Office still takes tips.
lastSeen: July 24, 1997, Lander, WY; car found at Burnt Gulch on the Loop Road, Shoshone National Forest

sources.title: Cowboy State Daily - Police Believe Tip In Amy Wroe Bechtel's Disappearance Worth Looking Into
Cowboy State Daily - Disappearance Of Amy Wroe Bechtel Still Haunting After 26 Years
Wikipedia - Disappearance of Amy Wroe Bechtel

narrative: Amy Wroe Bechtel was 24 and had been married for about a year when she disappeared on July 24, 1997, near Lander, Wyoming. She was an accomplished distance runner, and according to Cowboy State Daily she was planning the route for a 10-kilometer race in the Shoshone National Forest. Her husband, Steve Bechtel, a rock climber, was climbing with a friend that day.

When she did not come home, a search began that night. Her white Toyota Tercel was found at about 1 a.m. on July 25 at Burnt Gulch on the Loop Road, roughly 15 miles from Lander in the Wind River Range, according to Wikipedia's summary of the case. Cowboy State Daily reported that her keys were on the passenger seat along with a to-do list, and that her wallet has never been recovered.

The search that followed was one of the largest in Wyoming. Cowboy State Daily reported that more than 300 trained searchers, National Guard units and helicopters with thermal imaging took part, and that after about eight days without results investigators concluded that foul play was likely. No physical evidence of what happened to her was found. In June 2003 a digital watch resembling one she owned was found near the Popo Agie River, but it could not be confirmed as hers.

Investigators initially focused on Steve Bechtel. According to published accounts, his climbing partner supported his account of being near Dubois that day, no physical evidence tied him to a crime, and he declined a polygraph test on the advice of his attorney. He has never been charged and has denied any involvement. He had his wife declared legally dead in 2004.

Later investigators turned their attention to Dale Wayne Eaton, who was convicted of the 1988 murder of Lisa Marie Kimmell. Fremont County Sheriff's Lt. John Zerga has said that Eaton's brother reported Eaton was camping in the Burnt Gulch area when Bechtel vanished. Eaton has refused to discuss the case and has not been charged in connection with it.

In October 2025, Cowboy State Daily reported that a Natrona County property owner who had once allowed Eaton to stay on her land told investigators she had found a gas receipt and newspaper clippings from around July 1997 in vehicles he left behind. Zerga told the outlet the tip was worth following up and that cadaver dogs could be brought to the property; no official search had been carried out at the time of that report. The case remains open and unsolved.

A watch resembling hers is found near the Popo Agie River; ownership cannot be confirmed.
She is declared legally dead.
Cowboy State Daily reports that the sheriff's office is reviewing a new tip concerning property where Dale Wayne Eaton once stayed.

name: Ennis Cosby
summary: Ennis Cosby, 27, the son of entertainer Bill Cosby, was shot dead on January 16, 1997, while changing a flat tire beside Interstate 405 in Los Angeles. Mikhail Markhasev was convicted of first-degree murder and attempted robbery in July 1998 and sentenced to life without parole. In 2001 he admitted his guilt in writing and dropped his appeal.
lastSeen: January 16, 1997, Skirball Center Drive off I-405 near Bel Air, Los Angeles, CA

sources.title: ABC News - Convicted Killer of Ennis Cosby Confesses
Hoodline - LA Appeals Court Dismisses Markhasev Appeal
History.com - Bill Cosby's son murdered along California interstate
Wikipedia - Murder of Ennis Cosby

narrative: Ennis William Cosby, the only son of entertainer Bill Cosby, was shot and killed in the early hours of January 16, 1997, in Los Angeles. He was 27 and, according to History.com, a graduate student in special education at Columbia University's Teachers College. He is widely reported to have been the inspiration for the character Theo Huxtable on his father's television series "The Cosby Show."

According to published accounts, Cosby had pulled off Interstate 405 at Skirball Center Drive, near Bel Air, at about 1 a.m. to change a flat tire. He was approached by a man who tried to rob him and was shot once in the head. Wikipedia's summary of the case notes that police received more than 800 tips in the weeks that followed.

Mikhail Markhasev, then 18, a Ukrainian-born resident of the Los Angeles area, was arrested in March 1997. The break reportedly came after an acquaintance of Markhasev contacted the National Enquirer, which had offered a $100,000 reward, and the information was passed to police.

Markhasev pleaded not guilty and was tried in Los Angeles County. On July 7, 1998, a jury convicted him of first-degree murder and attempted robbery. The following month he was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole, plus ten years. He was 19 at the time of sentencing.

Markhasev maintained his innocence through the trial, but that changed in February 2001. ABC News reported that he sent a handwritten letter to California Deputy Attorney General Kyle Brodie admitting that he was guilty, asking to withdraw his remaining appeal, and saying he wanted to apologize to the Cosby family. The development was announced by the state attorney general and the Los Angeles County district attorney, whose office described the abandonment of an appeal as very unusual.

The conviction and sentence have stood since. According to a March 2026 report by Hoodline, Markhasev filed a petition in November 2024 seeking resentencing, citing his education in prison, letters of support and a reentry plan. The trial court declined to act on the filing, and on March 18, 2026, a three-justice panel of California's 2nd District Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal from that decision. He remains imprisoned under the original sentence.

name: Gianni Versace
summary: Fashion designer Gianni Versace was shot on the steps of his Miami Beach mansion by spree killer Andrew Cunanan. Cunanan had already killed four others across the country before targeting Versace. He killed himself on a houseboat eight days after the Versace murder. The case was dramatized in 'The Assassination of Gianni Versace.'
lastSeen: July 15, 1997, his mansion steps at Ocean Drive, Miami Beach, FL

sources.title: Andrew Cunanan - Wikipedia
Fashion designer Gianni Versace murdered by Andrew Cunanan in killing spree | July 15, 1997 | HISTORY
Serial Killers, Part 6: Andrew Cunanan | Federal Bureau of Investigation
The Versace Murder: What Happened And Who Killed The Fashion Icon? | NBC 6 South Florida
The murder of fashion designer Gianni Versace 25 years later | CBS Miami

narrative: On the morning of July 15, 1997, the Italian fashion designer Giovanni Maria "Gianni" Versace, aged 50, was shot to death on the front steps of Casa Casuarina, his oceanfront mansion on Ocean Drive in Miami Beach, Florida. Versace had walked to a nearby cafe to buy magazines and was returning home at about 8:45 a.m. when a gunman approached and shot him twice in the head with a .40-caliber Taurus pistol. The attacker fled on foot and disappeared into a nearby parking garage. Versace was pronounced dead a short time later. The killing of one of the most celebrated figures in international fashion drew worldwide attention and shocked the design world.

Investigators quickly linked the shooting to Andrew Phillip Cunanan, a 27-year-old already sought in a multi-state manhunt. In the parking garage near the mansion, police found a red pickup truck connected to an earlier killing in New Jersey and tied to Cunanan. He had been placed on the FBI's Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list on June 12, 1997, weeks before Versace's death. Cunanan's motive was never established; police found no evidence that he and Versace had any prior relationship, though the two men reportedly may have crossed paths years earlier.

The Versace shooting was the final killing in a cross-country spree that had begun that spring. Cunanan's first known victim was Jeffrey Trail, a former U.S. Navy officer beaten to death in Minneapolis on April 27, 1997. Days later he killed David Madson, an architect, whose body was found near Rush Lake, Minnesota. He then traveled to Chicago and killed real-estate developer Lee Miglin in early May, and on May 9, 1997, he shot cemetery caretaker William Reese in Pennsville Township, New Jersey, stealing Reese's red pickup truck. Versace, killed on July 15, was his fifth and final victim.

A massive federal and local manhunt followed the Versace murder, one of the largest in the region's history. Cunanan evaded capture for eight days. On July 23, 1997, the caretaker of a houseboat about two miles north of Versace's mansion reported a gunshot; a police tactical team entered the vessel and found Cunanan dead from a single self-inflicted gunshot wound to the head, fired from the same weapon used in earlier killings. He left no confession or note explaining his actions.

Because Andrew Cunanan died by suicide before he could be arrested, he was never tried in court and never convicted of any of the five murders, including Versace's. Law enforcement formally identified him as the sole perpetrator based on physical evidence, ballistics, and witness accounts, and the cases were closed with his death. The murders were later dramatized in the 2018 anthology series "The Assassination of Gianni Versace: American Crime Story," renewing public interest, but the underlying question of Cunanan's motive remains unresolved.

Cunanan is found dead of a self-inflicted gunshot wound aboard a houseboat in Miami Beach, ending the manhunt before any arrest or trial.

name: Kristen Modafferi
summary: Kristen Modafferi, an 18-year-old North Carolina State University student spending the summer in the Bay Area, vanished on June 23, 1997, after finishing her shift at a coffee shop in San Francisco's Crocker Galleria. She was due to start a photography class at UC Berkeley the next day. She has never been found and no one has been charged. Oakland police keep the case open.
lastSeen: June 23, 1997, Crocker Galleria, Financial District, San Francisco, CA

sources.title: ABC7 News - The Kristen Modafferi Mystery: 20 years later, private investigators shed light on cold case
ABC7 News - The Kristen Modafferi Mystery: Persons of interest in 20-year-old cold case
CUE Center for Missing Persons - Kristen Modafferi
Wikipedia - Disappearance of Kristen Modafferi

narrative: Kristen Deborah Modafferi had turned 18 three weeks before she disappeared. She had just finished her first year as an industrial design student at North Carolina State University, and in June 1997 she travelled to the San Francisco Bay Area to take a summer photography course at the University of California, Berkeley. She rented a room in a house in Oakland and took jobs at Spinelli's coffee shop in the Crocker Galleria in San Francisco's Financial District and, on weekends, at the cafe of the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art.

On Monday, June 23, 1997, she worked the morning shift at Spinelli's, which ended at 3 p.m. According to the North Carolina missing-persons organization CUE Center, she had asked for directions to Baker Beach that day. At about 3:45 p.m. she was seen on the second level of the Galleria with a blonde woman who has never been identified, and ABC7 News reported that a bank camera recorded her withdrawing cash. She did not attend the first day of her class on June 24.

Her parents reported her missing to Oakland police a few days later, and the department has held the case since because she lived in that city. According to Wikipedia's summary, search dogs followed her scent along the route of the 38 Geary bus line toward Sutro Heights Park, but nothing belonging to her was recovered. A $50,000 reward was offered.

In July 1997 a man named Jon Onuma telephoned a local television station and claimed that Modafferi had been killed by two women. ABC7 News reported that he later admitted making the call, said he had never met her, and has never been charged with any crime; his then girlfriend has also denied any connection. ABC7 reported in 2017 that the FBI had cleared both and closed its file, while Oakland police still regarded them as persons of interest.

Private investigators working with the family returned to the Oakland house in 2015 and 2017. ABC7 reported that a cadaver dog alerted near the basement and that a forensic scientist detected chemical compounds associated with human decomposition between two houses. A subsequent police dig in the basement did not locate remains, according to published accounts.

The difficulty her parents faced in getting help for a missing 18-year-old, who was legally an adult, led to federal legislation. Kristen's Law, signed in 2000, funded organizations that assist in the search for missing adults; its funding lapsed in 2005. The case remains unsolved.

A cadaver dog working with private investigators alerts at the Oakland house where she had lived.
Further private forensic testing is reported near the house; a police dig in the basement finds no remains.

name: Michelle Moore-Bosko
summary: Michelle Moore-Bosko, 18, was raped and killed in her Norfolk, Virginia, apartment in July 1997. Omar Ballard, the only person whose DNA matched the scene, pleaded guilty in 2000. Four Navy sailors known as the Norfolk Four, who had confessed under police interrogation and were convicted, received conditional pardons in 2009 and absolute pardons in 2017, followed by an $8.4 million settlement.
lastSeen: July 1997, her apartment in Norfolk, VA

sources.title: Navy Times - Settlement reached in infamous Norfolk 4 case
PBS Frontline - The Confessions: Introduction
U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit - Wilson v. Flaherty, No. 11-6919 (opinion)
Wikipedia - Norfolk Four

narrative: Michelle Moore-Bosko was 18 and married to a Navy sailor when she was raped, stabbed and strangled in the couple's apartment in Norfolk, Virginia, in July 1997. According to Wikipedia's summary of the case, the crime took place on the night of July 7 to 8. The investigation that followed led to charges against eight men, although physical evidence pointed to only one.

Norfolk police first questioned Danial Williams, a sailor who lived in the same building. PBS Frontline reported that Williams confessed after about eleven hours of interrogation that included threats of the death penalty. When his DNA did not match evidence from the scene, detectives questioned his roommate, Joseph Dick Jr., and then Eric Wilson and Derek Tice. Each confessed and each later said the statement was false and had been given under pressure. Charges against three other men were eventually dropped.

None of the sailors' DNA matched the evidence. The only match was to Omar Ballard, who was already imprisoned for other violent offenses and who stated that he had acted alone. Ballard pleaded guilty to the rape and murder in March 2000 and remains in prison. Prosecutors nonetheless pursued the sailors on the theory that a group had taken part. Williams and Dick pleaded guilty and received life sentences, Tice was convicted at trial and sentenced to life, and Wilson was convicted of rape only and served eight and a half years before his release in 2005.

The convictions drew sustained criticism. Navy Times reported that dozens of former FBI agents and former prosecutors, along with the author John Grisham, supported the men's claims of innocence. In 2009 Virginia Governor Tim Kaine granted conditional pardons to Williams, Dick and Tice, freeing them but leaving the convictions on their records. Tice's conviction was vacated by a federal district court in 2009, a ruling the Fourth Circuit upheld in 2011. Wilson's federal challenge was dismissed on jurisdictional grounds in 2012 because he was no longer in custody, according to the Fourth Circuit's opinion.

The lead interrogator, Detective Robert Glenn Ford, was later convicted in federal court of extortion and lying to the FBI in unrelated matters. In 2016 a federal judge vacated the convictions of Williams and Dick, and in March 2017 Governor Terry McAuliffe granted all four men absolute pardons.

In December 2018 it was announced that the City of Norfolk would pay $4.9 million and the Commonwealth of Virginia $3.5 million to the four men, a combined $8.4 million. Ballard is the only person whose conviction for the killing of Michelle Moore-Bosko stands.

name: Peter Boy Kema

In 2017 his father, Peter Kema Sr., pleaded guilty to manslaughter and was sentenced to 20 years, and his mother, Jaylin Kema, also pleaded guilty to manslaughter. His remains have never been recovered.
lastSeen: Mid-1997, family home in Nanawale Estates, Puna district, Hawaii Island, HI

Hawaii News Now - The search for Peter Boy: A 20-year murder mystery, a family who never gave up
CBS News - Father of Hawaii boy missing for 2 decades is sentenced

narrative: Peter Kema Jr., known throughout Hawaii as Peter Boy, was born on May 1, 1991, and lived with his parents and siblings in Nanawale Estates on the island of Hawaii. He was 6 when he died. For nearly two decades his case was treated publicly as a disappearance, and his face appeared on posters across the state asking where he was.

According to Hawaii News Now, his siblings last saw him alive around June 1997, and his parents, Peter Kema Sr. and Jaylin Kema, did not file a missing-person report until about six months later. The Honolulu Star-Advertiser reported that the father told authorities in 1998 that he had left the boy with a family friend he called Auntie Rose Makuakane at Aala Park in Honolulu. No evidence that such a person existed was ever found.

Police reclassified the case as a homicide in 2000. In 2005 the state Department of Human Services released more than 2,000 pages of records, with redactions, documenting earlier abuse allegations involving the child, CBS News reported. The parents remained the focus of the investigation, but no charges were filed for years.

A grand jury indicted both parents on murder charges in 2016. Jaylin Kema pleaded guilty to manslaughter; CBS News reported that she was released after serving a year in custody. According to CBS News, one of the boy's sisters had told investigators that in the spring of 1997 she saw her mother trying to revive him and later saw him in a box. Prosecutors concluded that he died of septic shock from an arm wound that was never treated, an injury they attributed to abuse.

Peter Kema Sr. pleaded guilty in April 2017 to manslaughter and to hindering prosecution. Under the plea agreement he was required to show investigators where he had disposed of his son's body or to pass a polygraph examination about it. He took authorities to a remote stretch of the Puna coast and said he had put a box containing the remains into the ocean. Nothing was recovered, which prosecutors attributed to the passage of time and ocean conditions, and CBS News reported that he passed the polygraph.

He was sentenced to 20 years in prison for manslaughter, with a mandatory minimum of six years and eight months, and to a further five years for hindering prosecution, according to the Star-Advertiser. Peter Boy's remains have never been found.

name: The Notorious B.I.G. (Christopher Wallace)
summary: Rapper Christopher Wallace, known as The Notorious B.I.G., was killed in a drive-by shooting in Los Angeles shortly after leaving a Vibe magazine after-party at the Petersen Automotive Museum, held the night after the Soul Train Music Awards. He was killed just six months after Tupac Shakur. Despite a massive investigation and multiple civil lawsuits, no one has ever been charged with his murder.
lastSeen: March 9, 1997, Petersen Automotive Museum, Los Angeles, CA

sources.title: Murder of the Notorious B.I.G. - Wikipedia
FBI Releases Files in Notorious B.I.G. Murder - ABC News

narrative: Shortly after midnight on March 9, 1997, 24-year-old rapper Christopher Wallace, known professionally as The Notorious B.I.G. (and earlier as Biggie Smalls), was killed in a drive-by shooting in Los Angeles. Wallace had been attending an after-party hosted by Vibe magazine at the Petersen Automotive Museum, which was shut down early by the fire department because of overcrowding. As his GMC Suburban stopped at a red light near the corner of Wilshire Boulevard and South Fairfax Avenue, a dark Chevrolet Impala pulled alongside and a gunman opened fire. Wallace was struck by four of the shots and pronounced dead at 1:15 a.m. at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center. His second album, Life After Death, was released roughly two weeks later.

The killing came at the height of a widely reported rivalry between the East Coast and West Coast hip-hop scenes, often framed around New York's Bad Boy Entertainment, with which Wallace was associated, and Los Angeles-based Death Row Records, co-founded by Marion 'Suge' Knight. That rivalry had been intensified by the fatal shooting of West Coast rapper Tupac Shakur in Las Vegas in September 1996, a case that went unsolved for decades until Duane "Keffe D" Davis was convicted of the murder in August 2026. Many observers linked the two killings, and investigators explored whether Wallace's death was connected to Shakur's, though no such link has ever been established in court.

The Los Angeles Police Department and, later, the FBI investigated the case, but no one has ever been arrested, charged, or convicted in Wallace's death. Investigators recovered evidence including rare 9mm Gecko ammunition. The FBI's file, released in heavily redacted form under the Freedom of Information Act in 2011, indicated the bureau had examined the case before closing its inquiry in 2005. In 2012 the long-sealed county autopsy report was made public, detailing the gunshot wounds and noting no drugs or alcohol were found in Wallace's system.

Over the years several competing theories have been advanced, all of them contested and none proven. One line of investigation, reported by the Los Angeles Times, pointed to a member of Compton's Southside Crips acting for personal or financial motives. A 2002 book by Randall Sullivan, drawing on the work of former LAPD detective Russell Poole, alleged a conspiracy involving Suge Knight and corrupt LAPD officer David Mack, naming an associate as an alleged gunman; those claims were disputed and criticized as speculative, and the individuals named have denied involvement. Retired LAPD detective Greg Kading later alleged that Knight had arranged for a Mob Piru gang associate, Wardell 'Poochie' Fouse, to carry out the killing. All such accounts are allegations and theories only; none has resulted in charges, and the named individuals have not been found responsible in any court.

The Wallace family pursued civil litigation against the City of Los Angeles, alleging that rogue officers were involved. A 2005 wrongful-death trial ended in a mistrial after the court found evidence had not been properly disclosed, and the family was awarded attorneys' fees. A subsequent federal suit was dismissed on procedural grounds, and later refiled claims were also dismissed by 2010. The criminal case remains officially open but unsolved. Wallace's mother, Voletta Wallace, campaigned for answers for decades until her death in February 2025. More than a quarter-century after the shooting, the murder of The Notorious B.I.G. stands as one of Los Angeles's most prominent unresolved homicides.

name: James Byrd Jr.
summary: James Byrd Jr., a 49-year-old Black man, was chained by the ankles to a pickup truck and dragged about three miles to his death near Jasper, Texas, on June 7, 1998. Three white men were convicted of capital murder: Lawrence Russell Brewer was executed in 2011 and John William King in 2019, while Shawn Berry is serving life. Texas and federal hate crime laws bear Byrd's name.
lastSeen: June 7, 1998, Jasper, TX

sources.title: CBS News - John William King executed for dragging death of James Byrd Jr.
CBS News - White supremacist Lawrence Russell Brewer executed for dragging death

Wikipedia - Murder of James Byrd Jr.

narrative: James Byrd Jr. was born on May 2, 1949, and lived in Jasper, a town in East Texas. Relatives quoted by the Texas Tribune remembered him as a sociable man and a gifted musician who played piano and trumpet. He was 49 when he was killed in the early hours of June 7, 1998.

According to accounts of the trials, Byrd accepted a ride that night from Shawn Berry, who knew him from around town and was driving a pickup truck with two passengers, John William King and Lawrence Russell Brewer. CBS News reported that the attack took place at about 2:30 a.m. on a road outside Jasper. Byrd was chained by the ankles to the truck with a logging chain and dragged for roughly three miles along Huff Creek Road. Evidence presented in the case indicated that he was alive for a substantial part of that distance and died when his body struck a culvert. His remains were left along the same road, near a Black church and cemetery.

All three men were in custody by the end of the following day. The Texas Tribune reported that investigators recovered items along the road, including a cigarette lighter bearing Ku Klux Klan markings. The Texas Tribune described King and Brewer as avowed white supremacists.

The three were tried separately in 1999, and each was convicted of capital murder. King was tried first, in Jasper, and sentenced to death. Brewer's trial was moved to Bryan, about 150 miles away, and he also received a death sentence. Berry, tried in Jasper, was sentenced to life in prison; Wikipedia's summary of the case states that he becomes eligible for parole in 2038.

Brewer was executed by lethal injection at Huntsville on September 21, 2011. King was executed there on April 24, 2019, after the U.S. Supreme Court rejected his final appeal and the Texas Board of Pardons and Paroles declined to recommend clemency, CBS News reported. Byrd's sister Clara Taylor said afterward that King had shown no remorse.

The killing prompted changes in the law. In 2001 Texas Governor Rick Perry signed the James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Act, which increased penalties for offenses motivated by bias. On October 28, 2009, President Barack Obama signed the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act, which broadened federal hate crime law. Byrd's family also established a foundation devoted to racial healing, and some relatives, including his son Ross, later spoke publicly against the death penalty.

name: Hae Min Lee
summary: High school student Hae Min Lee was strangled and her body found in Leakin Park, Baltimore, in 1999. Her ex-boyfriend Adnan Syed was convicted of first-degree murder in 2000, and his case became the subject of the podcast Serial. His conviction was vacated in September 2022 and charges were dropped that October, but Maryland appellate courts reinstated the conviction in 2023-2024. In 2025 prosecutors withdrew their motion to vacate and a judge reduced his sentence to time served, so the conviction stands while Syed, who maintains his innocence, remains free.
lastSeen: January 13, 1999, Woodlawn High School, Baltimore, MD

narrative: Hae Min Lee, an 18-year-old senior at Woodlawn High School in Baltimore County, Maryland, disappeared on January 13, 1999. Her body was found nearly a month later, on February 9, 1999, buried in Leakin Park in Baltimore. She had been strangled. Investigators soon focused on her former boyfriend and fellow Woodlawn student, Adnan Syed, who was arrested on February 28, 1999, at age 17.

Syed's first trial ended in a mistrial in December 1999. At a second trial, a jury convicted him on February 25, 2000, of first-degree murder and related charges, largely on the testimony of an acquaintance, Jay Wilds, and disputed cellphone location records. He was sentenced to life in prison plus 30 years. The case drew little national attention until 2014, when the debut season of the NPR/'This American Life' podcast 'Serial' examined the investigation, the evidence, and Syed's defense in detail, reaching tens of millions of listeners and fueling years of debate over the reliability of his conviction.

The legal aftermath has swung repeatedly. A judge vacated the conviction in 2016 over ineffective-assistance-of-counsel claims, but Maryland's then-Court of Appeals reinstated it in a 4-3 decision on March 8, 2019. In September 2022, at the request of the Baltimore City State's Attorney's Office, Judge Melissa Phinn vacated Syed's conviction on September 19, 2022, citing possible Brady violations and undisclosed alternative suspects; he was released after roughly 23 years. Prosecutors dropped the remaining charges in October 2022.

That reversal did not hold. On March 28, 2023, the Appellate Court of Maryland reinstated the conviction on procedural grounds, ruling that the rights of Hae Min Lee's family had been violated because her brother, Young Lee, was not given adequate notice to attend the 2022 vacatur hearing in person. On August 30, 2024, the Supreme Court of Maryland affirmed that decision in a 4-3 ruling, holding that the victim's representative was entitled to reasonable notice and to attend and be heard in person, and ordering a new vacatur hearing before a different judge. The conviction remained legally reinstated in the interim, though Syed stayed free.

In early 2025 the posture shifted again. On February 25, 2025, Baltimore City State's Attorney Ivan Bates's office withdrew the pending motion to vacate the conviction, ending the effort to overturn it, while supporting a separate request to reduce Syed's sentence. On March 6, 2025, Circuit Court Judge Jennifer Schiffer granted that motion under Maryland's Juvenile Restoration Act, resentencing Syed to time served plus five years of supervised probation and finding he 'is not a danger to the public.' As of 2026, Adnan Syed's first-degree murder conviction for the killing of Hae Min Lee stands, and he remains free on the reduced sentence. Courts have not made any finding that he is innocent, and no other person has been charged; the case is best described as a standing conviction under continued public dispute.
