name: Yosemite Sightseer Murders
summary: Carole Sund, 42, her daughter Juli, 15, and family friend Silvina Pelosso, 16, were killed in February 1999 while staying at Cedar Lodge outside Yosemite National Park. Motel handyman Cary Stayner was convicted of the three murders in August 2002 and sentenced to death that December. He had earlier pleaded guilty in federal court to the July 1999 murder of naturalist Joie Armstrong.
lastSeen: February 15, 1999, Cedar Lodge, El Portal, near Yosemite National Park, CA

sources.title: SFGate / San Francisco Chronicle - Stayner guilty of 1st-degree murder
SFGate / San Francisco Chronicle - Yosemite killer sentenced to death
ABC News - Steven and Cary Stayner: A tale of two brothers, horror and heroism
Wikipedia - Cary Stayner

narrative: Carole Sund, 42, her 15-year-old daughter Juli and Silvina Pelosso, a 16-year-old family friend from Argentina, were visiting Yosemite National Park in February 1999. They were staying at Cedar Lodge, a motel outside the park, and were last known to be alive on February 15. Their disappearance set off a search that the FBI later described as the largest ever mounted in the Yosemite area, according to ABC News.

The burned remains of Carole Sund and Silvina Pelosso were found on March 18, 1999, in the trunk of their rental car. About a week later, Juli Sund's body was found at a separate location after investigators received an anonymous note with a map, according to Wikipedia's summary of the case. The San Francisco Chronicle later reported that Carole Sund and Pelosso had been strangled and that Juli Sund's throat had been cut.

The case remained open for months. On July 21, 1999, Joie Armstrong, 26, a naturalist who worked as a guide with the Yosemite Institute, was attacked near her cabin inside the park. Her decapitated body was found the next day. Attention turned to Cary Stayner, a maintenance worker at Cedar Lodge, and FBI agents arrested him on July 24 at the Laguna del Sol nudist resort, according to Wikipedia's summary. ABC News reported that he confessed to killing Armstrong and then to the murders of the three tourists.
Because Armstrong was killed on federal land, that case was prosecuted in federal court. Stayner pleaded guilty and was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole.

The state case was tried in Santa Clara County Superior Court in San Jose. Stayner pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity, and his lawyers argued that he suffered from long-standing mental illness. On August 26, 2002, a San Jose jury found him guilty of three counts of first-degree murder along with special circumstances that included kidnapping, sexual assault and burglary of the victims' motel room; the Chronicle reported that jurors rejected one special circumstance relating to robbery. The jury recommended death in October, and on December 12, 2002, Judge Thomas C. Hastings imposed that sentence after denying a defense motion for a new trial.

Stayner remains under a sentence of death. According to Wikipedia, citing a Courthouse News report, the California Supreme Court upheld the conviction and sentence in April 2026. California has not carried out an execution since 2006.

name: Asha Degree
summary: Nine-year-old Asha Degree left her family home in the early morning hours during a storm and was last seen walking along Highway 18. Her bookbag was found buried in a construction site 26 miles away over a year later. Despite extensive searches and investigations, Asha has never been found and the case remains open.
lastSeen: February 14, 2000, Highway 18 near Shelby, NC

Timeline of Asha Degree case: What happened since she went missing in 2000 — WBTV

narrative: Asha Jaquilla Degree, a nine-year-old from Shelby, North Carolina, disappeared during the early morning hours of February 14, 2000. According to investigators, she left her family's home sometime after midnight, carrying a packed bookbag, and walked south along rural North Carolina Highway 18 in heavy rain and wind. No reason for her leaving has ever been established. Two truck drivers reported seeing a girl matching her description walking along the highway roughly a mile from her home at around 4 a.m. When one motorist slowed and appeared to approach her, she reportedly ran into a wooded area beside the road. Her parents discovered her missing early that morning, and she has not been seen since.

The initial search drew hundreds of volunteers and law enforcement personnel. On February 15, 2000, investigators recovered items in a nearby shed — including candy wrappers, a pencil, a marker, and a hair bow — that her parents identified as belonging to Asha. A more significant find came in August 2001, when construction workers uncovered her bookbag buried at a site off Highway 18 in Burke County, roughly 25 to 30 miles north of Shelby. Investigators later disclosed that the bag contained two items that did not belong to Asha and that they could not explain: a New Kids on the Block concert T-shirt and a Dr. Seuss library book that had come from her elementary school but that she had not checked out. The bag and its contents were sent to the FBI laboratory in Quantico for analysis.

The FBI's Charlotte Field Office worked the case alongside the Cleveland County Sheriff's Office and the North Carolina State Bureau of Investigation for years. In 2016, investigators publicized a dark green early-1970s vehicle they believed Asha may have entered, and in 2017 an FBI team re-created the conditions of the disappearance to generate leads. Authorities have said hundreds of interviews were conducted over the years, and a standing reward was repeatedly increased to encourage tips.

Beginning in September 2024, the investigation entered a more active phase. On September 10–11, 2024, the FBI, SBI, and Cleveland County Sheriff's Office executed search warrants on multiple properties and towed an older-model vehicle; the warrants stated that authorities believe Asha was the victim of a homicide and that her body was concealed. Reporting on the unsealed warrants indicated that they named members of a Cleveland County family — identified in the documents as Roy Dedmon, Connie Dedmon, and their daughters AnnaLee Dedmon Ramirez, Lizzie Dedmon Foster, and Sarah Dedmon Caple. According to the warrants, two items from the backpack "returned evidentiary results," and a hair recovered from Asha's undershirt was reported to be consistent with a DNA profile associated with AnnaLee Dedmon Ramirez, who was 13 at the time Asha vanished. Additional warrants executed on February 13, 2025 sought cellphones and referenced text messages and a polygraph examination. The Dedmon family has denied any involvement, and authorities have not established a connection between the two families.

As of early 2026, no one has been arrested, charged, or convicted in connection with Asha Degree's disappearance, and the persons named in the search warrants have not been charged with any crime. The case remains an open, active investigation classified by authorities as a homicide. A reward of up to $100,000 was being offered for information leading to a conviction, and new billboards were posted in 2025 to solicit tips.

name: Molly Bish
summary: Molly Bish, 16, vanished on June 27, 2000, minutes after her mother dropped her off for her lifeguard shift at Comins Pond in Warren, Massachusetts. Her belongings were left at her post. Her remains were found on June 9, 2003, in woods in nearby Palmer. No one has been charged; in 2021 the Worcester County district attorney named a man who died in 2016 as a person of interest.
lastSeen: June 27, 2000, Comins Pond, Warren, MA

sources.title: Boston.com - Molly Bish case update from Worcester County District Attorney Joseph Early

narrative: Molly Anne Bish was 16 and working a summer job as a lifeguard at Comins Pond in Warren, Massachusetts, when she disappeared on the morning of June 27, 2000. She was born on August 2, 1983, the daughter of Magi and John Bish.

According to a CBS News account of the day, Magi Bish drove her daughter to the pond at about 10 a.m. and left around 10:20 after watching her walk toward the beach. At roughly 10:30 a woman arriving at the pond found a first-aid kit, a backpack, a towel, sandals and a water bottle at the lifeguard station, but no lifeguard. A town parks official alerted police about an hour later. Officers first considered that she might have left with friends or drowned before the case was treated as an abduction, and the Massachusetts State Police took over the investigation.

Magi Bish has said that on the previous morning she saw a man near the beach whose presence struck her as suspicious, and a composite sketch was circulated during the investigation. The search that followed has been described as the most extensive and expensive in the state's history.

In the fall of 2002 a hunter came across a blue swimsuit in the woods on Whiskey Hill in Palmer, about five miles from the Bish home. On June 9, 2003, searchers recovered Molly Bish's remains in the area. The condition of the remains did not allow a cause of death to be determined, but authorities have treated the case as a homicide.

Several men have been examined over the years, and none has been charged. In 2021, Worcester County District Attorney Joseph Early publicly identified Francis "Frank" Sumner Sr. as a person of interest, saying investigators had received information they considered credible. Sumner had been convicted in 1982 of aggravated rape and kidnapping and died in 2016. Boston.com reported that he resembled the man Magi Bish had described. He was never charged in the case and the allegation has not been tested in court.

In a June 2023 update, Early said investigators had identified a significant number of evidence items that could be re-examined using newer forensic methods and that the tip line remained active. Bish's parents founded the Molly Bish Foundation in 2004 to promote child safety. The case remains unsolved, and the district attorney's office continues to ask for information at 508-453-7575.

name: Valerie Mack
summary: Valerie Mack, 24, was last seen in 2000; partial remains were found that year in Manorville, Long Island, and more along Ocean Parkway in 2011. She was identified in May 2020. Rex Heuermann was charged with her murder in December 2024, pleaded guilty in April 2026 to killing Mack and six other women, and was sentenced on June 17, 2026, to life in prison without parole.
lastSeen: Spring or summer 2000, Port Republic, NJ area

narrative: Valerie Mack was 24 when she disappeared in 2000. According to Suffolk County police, she was living in Philadelphia, sometimes used the name Melissa Taylor, and was working as an escort. She was last seen in the spring or summer of that year in the area of Port Republic, New Jersey. She was the mother of a young son.

In November 2000, part of a woman's body was found in a wooded area off Halsey Manor Road in Manorville, in eastern Long Island. The remains could not be identified. More than ten years later, in April 2011, additional remains belonging to the same woman were found along Ocean Parkway near Gilgo Beach during the search that uncovered a series of bodies there. She was catalogued for years as Jane Doe No. 6.

On May 28, 2020, Suffolk County police announced that the woman was Valerie Mack. ABC7 New York reported that the identification was made with the FBI's help using DNA techniques. Then Police Commissioner Geraldine Hart said her family had spent two decades looking for answers.

Rex Heuermann, a Long Island architect, was arrested in 2023 and initially charged in the deaths of other women whose remains were found at Gilgo Beach. On December 17, 2024, prosecutors added a charge for the murder of Valerie Mack, the seventh killing attributed to him. NBC News reported that court filings cited a hair recovered with her remains that was linked by DNA to a member of Heuermann's household, along with a document on his computer that discussed removing identifying marks such as tattoos. Mack had a tattoo of her son's name on her leg. Heuermann pleaded not guilty at that time.

In April 2026 Heuermann changed his plea and admitted to the murders of seven women: Mack, Sandra Costilla, Jessica Taylor, Maureen Brainard-Barnes, Melissa Barthelemy, Megan Waterman and Amber Lynn Costello. According to the Associated Press, he also admitted to killing an eighth woman, Karen Vergata, a death for which he was not charged.

He was sentenced on June 17, 2026, to life in prison without the possibility of parole. The Associated Press reported that Mack's mother, JoAnn Mack, addressed him in court and spoke of the future her daughter had been denied. With the plea and sentence, the criminal case concerning Valerie Mack's death is concluded, a little more than 25 years after her remains were first found.

name: Bonny Lee Bakley
summary: Bonny Lee Bakley, 44, was shot on May 4, 2001, while sitting in a parked car near Vitello's restaurant in Studio City, Los Angeles. Her husband, actor Robert Blake, was acquitted of her murder in March 2005, and a civil jury later found him liable for her death. Blake died in 2023, and no one has been convicted of the killing.
lastSeen: May 4, 2001, in a parked car near Vitello's restaurant, Studio City, Los Angeles

NPR - Robert Blake, the actor acquitted in wife's killing, dies at 89

narrative: Bonny Lee Bakley was 44 years old when she was fatally shot on the evening of May 4, 2001, in the Studio City area of Los Angeles. According to accounts summarized by Biography and ABC News, she had eaten dinner with her husband, the actor Robert Blake, at Vitello's, an Italian restaurant he frequented, and was sitting in the passenger seat of his car on a nearby side street when she was shot. She died of her injuries.

Bakley was born on June 7, 1956, in New Jersey. Biography reports that she met Blake in 1999 and that the couple married in November 2000, after the birth of their daughter, Rose. The marriage was less than six months old at the time of the shooting, according to CBS News.

Blake told investigators that he had walked back to the restaurant to retrieve a handgun he had left behind and found his wife wounded when he returned to the car. That gun was not the murder weapon. CBS News reported that the weapon used in the killing was an old pistol recovered from a trash bin near the scene, and that it could not be traced to Blake. The same report noted that there were no eyewitnesses and that no blood or DNA evidence tied him to the shooting.

Blake was arrested on April 18, 2002, according to Biography, and charged with murder and with soliciting others to commit murder. He spent months in jail before trial. The prosecution relied heavily on two former stuntmen who testified that Blake had asked them to kill his wife; the defense challenged their credibility, citing histories of drug use. On March 16, 2005, a Los Angeles jury acquitted Blake of murder and of one solicitation count. Jurors deadlocked 11-1 in favor of acquittal on the second solicitation count, which the judge then dismissed.

Bakley's children pursued a wrongful-death suit. In November 2005 a civil jury, applying the lower standard of proof used in civil cases, found Blake liable for her death and awarded $30 million. An appeals court later cut the award in half, according to published accounts, and NPR reported that the judgment pushed Blake into bankruptcy. Blake consistently denied killing his wife.

Blake died of heart disease on March 9, 2023, at age 89, his family said. No other person has been charged in connection with Bakley's death, and the criminal case ended without a conviction. Published accounts continue to describe the killing as officially unsolved.

name: Chandra Levy
summary: Federal intern Chandra Levy disappeared from Washington, D.C., in 2001. Her remains were found in Rock Creek Park a year later. Her disappearance drew enormous attention due to her relationship with congressman Gary Condit, who was never charged or named a suspect. Ingmar Guandique was convicted in 2010, but he was granted a new trial in 2015 and prosecutors dropped all charges in 2016, leaving the case unsolved.
lastSeen: May 1, 2001, Washington D.C.

narrative: Chandra Ann Levy was a 24-year-old graduate student from Modesto, California, who had come to Washington, D.C., for an internship with the Federal Bureau of Prisons while completing a master's degree through the University of Southern California. Her internship eligibility had lapsed in the spring of 2001, and she was preparing to return home for her graduation. She was last known to have used her apartment computer on April 30, 2001, and was never seen again. When her family could not reach her, her parents contacted District of Columbia police, who opened a missing-person investigation on May 6, 2001. Over the following year, detectives conducted hundreds of interviews, pursued phone and internet records, and searched parts of Rock Creek Park without finding her.

The case drew intense and sustained national media coverage after it emerged that Levy had been in a romantic relationship with Gary Condit, a married U.S. congressman from her home district in California. Condit acknowledged a relationship but denied any involvement in her disappearance. It is important to state precisely: Condit was never charged with any crime, was never formally named as a suspect by police, and was eventually ruled out of involvement in the investigation. The scandal nonetheless damaged his political career, and he lost his Democratic primary in March 2002. Much of the 2001 coverage focused on the Condit angle rather than on evidence pointing to a specific perpetrator.

On May 22, 2002, a man walking his dog in a wooded section of Rock Creek Park discovered skeletal remains that were identified through dental records as Levy's. The medical examiner declared her death a homicide. Attention later turned to Ingmar Guandique, a Salvadoran immigrant who had been convicted of assaulting two other women in the same park around the time Levy vanished. Following a 2008 investigative series by The Washington Post that revived scrutiny of the case, police obtained an arrest warrant for Guandique in March 2009.

In November 2010 a jury convicted Guandique of first-degree murder, and in February 2011 he was sentenced to 60 years in prison. The conviction relied heavily on the testimony of Armando Morales, a former cellmate and convicted felon who said Guandique had confessed to him. That testimony became the case's central weakness. Defense lawyers challenged Morales's credibility, arguing he had misrepresented his history of cooperating with authorities and that prosecutors had withheld documents from the defense. In June 2015 a judge granted Guandique a new trial.

Rather than proceed with a retrial, federal prosecutors moved on July 28, 2016, to dismiss the charges, saying that in light of recent developments they could no longer prove the case beyond a reasonable doubt. Guandique was never retried; he was released into immigration custody and deported to El Salvador in 2017. Because the only conviction was vacated and dismissed, the murder of Chandra Levy is once again legally unsolved. As of 2026 no one stands convicted of her killing, and the case remains officially open.

name: Duran Bailey
summary: Duran Bailey, a homeless man, was found beaten, stabbed and mutilated beside a Las Vegas bank building on July 8, 2001. Kirstin Blaise Lobato, then 18, was convicted twice, but a judge vacated her convictions and all charges were dismissed in December 2017. A federal jury awarded her $34 million in 2024. No one else has been charged with the killing.
lastSeen: July 8, 2001, Las Vegas, NV

narrative: Duran Bailey, a homeless man living in Las Vegas, was found dead at about 10 p.m. on July 8, 2001, in a parking area next to a bank building. According to the Innocence Project, he had been severely beaten: his skull was fractured, teeth had been knocked out, his carotid artery had been cut and his penis had been severed. No one has been held responsible for his death, and the case is best known for the wrongful conviction that followed.

On July 20, 2001, Las Vegas police received a call from a resident of Panaca, a small Nevada town roughly three hours' drive away, reporting that 18-year-old Kirstin Blaise Lobato had spoken of cutting a man who attacked her. Detectives drove to Panaca and recorded a statement in which Lobato described fighting off an attempted rape in Las Vegas in May 2001, weeks before Bailey died. According to the Innocence Project, police treated that statement as a confession to Bailey's killing. No physical or forensic evidence connected her to the scene, and relatives and neighbors placed her in Panaca on July 8.

Lobato was convicted of first-degree murder in May 2002 and sentenced to 40 to 100 years. The Nevada Supreme Court reversed that conviction in 2004. At a second trial, a jury on October 6, 2006, convicted her of voluntary manslaughter and sexual penetration of a dead body, and she was sentenced to 13 to 45 years. She maintained her innocence throughout.

Years of post-conviction litigation followed. At a hearing in October 2017, forensic entomologists testified that the absence of blowfly eggs on Bailey's body indicated he died shortly before he was found, in the evening, a time when Lobato was documented to be in Panaca; a forensic pathologist supported that timing. On December 19, 2017, Clark County District Judge Stefany Miley granted a new trial. On December 29, 2017, the convictions were vacated and the charges dismissed at the request of the Clark County District Attorney's Office. Lobato was released on January 3, 2018, after nearly 16 years in custody.

In 2024 a Nevada state court issued Lobato a certificate of innocence. On December 12, 2024, a federal jury in Las Vegas found in her civil suit that detectives had fabricated evidence, and awarded $34 million in compensatory damages against the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department plus $10,000 in punitive damages against each of two former detectives, according to KSNV News 3 and her attorneys.
With Lobato exonerated, the killing of Duran Bailey has no identified perpetrator. None of the sources reviewed report any other arrest or charge in his death.

name: Henryk Siwiak
summary: Henryk Siwiak, a 46-year-old Polish immigrant, was shot at about 11:40 p.m. on September 11, 2001, in Bedford-Stuyvesant, Brooklyn, after getting lost on the way to a new job. With police resources committed to the World Trade Center attacks, the scene received limited attention. His death is the only homicide New York City recorded that day, and no arrest has been made.
lastSeen: September 11, 2001, near Albany Avenue and Decatur Street, Bedford-Stuyvesant, Brooklyn, NY

sources.title: ABC News - 'I asked him not to go anywhere that evening': One murder on 9/11 still unsolved in New York City

Hoodline - Henryk Siwiak Murder Unsolved 25 Years After 9/11 in Brooklyn

narrative: Henryk Siwiak was a 46-year-old Polish immigrant who had been in the United States for about eleven months when he was shot and killed in Brooklyn late on September 11, 2001. According to ABC News, he had arrived in October 2000 and was living in Queens near his sister, while his wife, Ewa, and their two children remained in Poland. He had previously worked for the Polish state railways and was taking construction and cleaning jobs in New York.

The construction site where Siwiak had been working in Lower Manhattan shut down after the attacks on the World Trade Center that morning. Needing income, he found overnight work cleaning floors at a Pathmark supermarket on Albany Avenue in Brooklyn and was due to start that night. ABC News reported that his wife, speaking to him by phone from Poland, had asked him not to go out that evening.

Siwiak did not know Brooklyn well. According to published accounts, he left the subway several miles from the supermarket and walked toward the low-numbered end of Albany Avenue, in Bedford-Stuyvesant, rather than the block where the store stood. At about 11:40 p.m. he was shot near Albany Avenue and Decatur Street. Wounded in the chest, he made his way to the stoop of a house on Decatur Street and rang the bell, but no one opened the door. He collapsed and died at the scene.

The investigation was constrained from the start. Former NYPD Chief of Detectives Robert Boyce told ABC News that the department could not respond as it normally would because resources were being sent to Lower Manhattan. According to accounts of the case, an evidence unit that ordinarily handles property crimes processed the scene, and far fewer detectives than usual were available to canvass the neighborhood. People nearby reported hearing gunshots, but no eyewitness came forward.

No motive has been established. Siwiak still had his wallet and cash. Retired detective Michael Prate, who led the case for years, has said he believes the shooting was most likely a robbery attempt that went wrong, possibly complicated by Siwiak's limited English. Investigators and Siwiak's sister have also raised the possibility that his camouflage-style clothing and accent led someone to associate him with the day's attacks. Police did not classify the killing as a hate crime.

Because the victims of the terrorist attacks are excluded from the city's crime statistics, Siwiak's death is the only homicide recorded in New York City for September 11, 2001. Reporting published for the 25th anniversary in September 2026 stated that no arrest has been made and that a $12,000 reward remains available through NYPD Crime Stoppers.

name: Jill-Lyn Euto
summary: Jill-Lyn Euto, 18, was stabbed to death in her sixth-floor apartment at 600 James Street in Syracuse, New York, on Super Bowl Sunday, January 28, 2001. Her mother found her the next day. Police have said they believe she knew her attacker and let the person in. No arrest has been made, and the Syracuse Police cold case unit still has the case.
lastSeen: January 28, 2001, her apartment at 600 James Street, Syracuse, NY

narrative: Jill-Lyn Euto was 18 years old when she was killed in her apartment in Syracuse, New York, on January 28, 2001. She lived alone on the sixth floor of an apartment building at 600 James Street, and, according to CNY Central, worked at a store in the Shoppingtown Mall and commuted by bus. Published accounts say she hoped to become a paramedic.

January 28 was Super Bowl Sunday, and Euto had planned to watch the game with her mother, Joanne Browning, and her sister, Jenna, at the family's home elsewhere in the city. She never arrived and did not answer phone calls. The next morning, after she also failed to turn up for work, her mother went to the apartment and found her dead.

Euto had been stabbed multiple times and had a cut to her neck. Investigators determined that the weapon was a knife taken from her own kitchen. Syracuse police detective Tom Murfitt said in 2016, according to Spectrum News, that neighbors had seen Euto enter her apartment alone. Detective Christopher DeJoseph told CNY Central in 2026 that investigators believe she knew her attacker and let that person into her home.

The investigation became one of the most extensive in the history of the Syracuse Police Department, and the case file is described as unusually large. Police have said over the years that several people have been looked at, but no one has been publicly named and no one has been charged. In January 2016, on the fifteenth anniversary, police announced that they had DNA evidence they hoped could help build a profile of a suspect. A decade later, DeJoseph said investigators had been unable to obtain a DNA profile from the knife, noting that many of the forensic tools available now did not exist in 2001.

Browning campaigned publicly for answers, appearing on national television programs and distributing fliers and billboards. She died in 2007 after an accidental fall. Euto's sister and other relatives have continued to speak publicly on anniversaries of the killing.

As of early 2026, twenty-five years after the murder, the case remained open and unsolved. Police have said that solving it is likely to depend on someone with direct knowledge of what happened coming forward, and have asked anyone with information to contact the Syracuse Police Department's cold case unit.

name: Kent Heitholt
summary: Columbia Daily Tribune sports editor Kent Heitholt, 48, was beaten and strangled in the newspaper's parking lot shortly after 2 a.m. on November 1, 2001. Charles Erickson pleaded guilty and was paroled in January 2023; he has since said his confession was coerced. Ryan Ferguson's 2005 conviction was vacated in November 2013 and he was not retried.
lastSeen: November 1, 2001, Columbia Daily Tribune parking lot, Columbia, MO

narrative: Kent Heitholt, the 48-year-old sports editor of the Columbia Daily Tribune, was killed in the newspaper's parking lot in Columbia, Missouri, in the early hours of November 1, 2001. He had left the building after work and was attacked near his car shortly after 2 a.m. He had been beaten and strangled. Two members of the building's cleaning staff saw two young men near the car, according to accounts of the case.

The investigation stalled for more than two years. Police then received a tip about Charles Erickson, who had been 17 at the time of the killing and had spent that night out with a high school friend, Ryan Ferguson. Erickson had no clear memory of the night and had told others he worried that he might have been involved. Questioned by Columbia police, he confessed and implicated Ferguson. Both were arrested in March 2004.

Erickson pleaded guilty in 2004 under an agreement that required him to testify against Ferguson, and he received a 25-year sentence. Ferguson, who has always maintained his innocence, was tried in 2005. A jury convicted him of second-degree murder and robbery, and he was sentenced to 40 years. According to KMIZ, no physical evidence connected either man to the crime; the prosecution rested mainly on Erickson's account and on a janitor's identification.

In 2012 both Erickson and the janitor, Jerry Trump, recanted their trial testimony. On November 5, 2013, the Missouri Court of Appeals for the Western District vacated Ferguson's conviction. He was released on November 12, 2013, and the Missouri attorney general's office chose not to retry him. Ferguson later brought a civil rights lawsuit, which ended in 2017 with an $11 million award, according to published accounts.

Erickson's conviction remains in place. He has said that his confession was coerced by police, the prosecutor and his own attorney, as he told reporters on his release, and he sought release through the courts and the parole board. After a parole hearing in November 2021 his release date was advanced, and he left the Boonville Correctional Center on parole on January 9, 2023, having served about 18 years of his sentence.

The case therefore stands in an unusual position: one man remains convicted on a guilty plea he now disputes, the other has been cleared and compensated, and no one else has been charged. None of the sources reviewed report any new suspect or arrest as of 2026.

name: Thomas C. Wales
summary: Assistant U.S. Attorney Thomas C. Wales, 49, was shot through a basement window of his Seattle home on the night of October 11, 2001, as he worked at his computer; he died the next day. Wales prosecuted white-collar crime and led the gun-safety group Washington CeaseFire. No one has been charged, and rewards totaling $2.5 million have been offered.
lastSeen: October 11, 2001, his home in the Queen Anne neighborhood of Seattle, WA

narrative: Thomas C. Wales was an Assistant United States Attorney in Seattle who had spent about eighteen years in the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Western District of Washington, where he concentrated on fraud and other white-collar cases. Outside work he was president of Washington CeaseFire, a gun-safety organization. He was 49 years old.

On the night of October 11, 2001, Wales was sitting at a computer in the basement office of his home in Seattle's Queen Anne neighborhood. According to The Seattle Times, someone entered the backyard and fired at least four shots through a basement window, striking him in the neck and torso. He died at a hospital the following day. Investigators have said the weapon was a Makarov pistol fitted with a replacement barrel, and the FBI has examined sales records for thousands of such barrels.

The FBI, the Seattle Police Department and federal prosecutors formed a task force that has remained in place for more than two decades. An FBI supervisor told KCPQ in 2021 that the file held more than 51,000 reports, making it one of the largest investigations the bureau has conducted. The Seattle Times has reported that the early inquiry was hindered by staffing shortages following the September 11 attacks.

No one has been charged with the killing. News reports state that investigators focused early on a commercial airline pilot whom Wales had prosecuted in a fraud case that was later dropped; the man has denied any involvement, his home was searched, and he has never been charged. In 2018 the FBI said publicly that evidence suggested the shooting may have been carried out by a hired gunman. Authorities also released a sketch of an unidentified man seen in the neighborhood before the shooting.

In 2019 a special prosecutor obtained an indictment of a Snohomish County woman for allegedly lying to a grand jury about what she knew of a person described in court papers as a possible participant. According to The Seattle Times, that case faltered and she pleaded guilty to a misdemeanor in August 2021. It did not result in any charge related to the murder itself.

On October 11, 2021, the twentieth anniversary, the Justice Department raised its reward to $2 million; together with roughly $500,000 offered by the National Association of Former United States Attorneys, the total reached $2.5 million. Oversight of the case was returned that day to the U.S. Attorney's Office in Seattle. No arrest has been reported since, and the motive remains unestablished.

name: Alexis Patterson
summary: Seven-year-old Alexis Patterson vanished on the morning of May 3, 2002, after her stepfather walked her toward Hi-Mount Community School in Milwaukee, a short distance from her home. She never reached her classroom. A 2016 DNA test on an Ohio woman ruled out a match, and a new age-progressed image was released in May 2026. She has never been found.
lastSeen: May 3, 2002, near Hi-Mount Community School, Milwaukee, WI

sources.title: FOX6 Milwaukee - Alexis Patterson missing case; new age-progressed photo released

narrative: Alexis Patterson was seven years old when she disappeared in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, on the morning of May 3, 2002. She attended Hi-Mount Community School, near 49th Street and Garfield Avenue, a short walk from her family's home.

That morning her stepfather, LaRon Bourgeois, walked her toward the school. According to his account, as reported by WTMJ and WITI, he watched her cross the street, where a crossing guard was on duty. Some students later said they had seen her outside the building, but teachers said she never came into class. Her mother, Ayanna Patterson, reported her missing that afternoon when she did not come home.

She was last seen wearing a red hooded jacket with gray stripes, a purple shirt, blue jeans and white Nike shoes. According to WITI, identifying features include a scar under her right eye and a bump on her left little finger.

Milwaukee police set up a mobile command post within a day, and neighbors joined in the search, according to local reports. The Journal Sentinel reported that within days the police chief at the time raised the possibility that she had run away after a disagreement at home over homework, a theory her family rejected. Detectives went on to follow hundreds of tips, some of which took them to other states. Police have said they have not ruled anyone out, and no one has ever been charged in connection with her disappearance.

Her case has often been discussed alongside that of Elizabeth Smart, who was abducted in Utah about a month later, in June 2002, and whose disappearance drew far more immediate national coverage. Commentators have cited the contrast in discussions of how race affects attention to missing children. Wisconsin had not yet adopted an Amber Alert system when Alexis vanished.

In 2016 a tip pointed to a woman living in Ohio who resembled an age-progressed image of Alexis. Milwaukee police arranged a DNA test and announced that the woman was not Alexis; her mother has publicly questioned that result. Bourgeois died in January 2021 of a suspected drug overdose, according to WTMJ. Alexis's relatives mark the anniversary each year, and in May 2026 the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children released a new image showing how she might look at 31. The Milwaukee Police Department continues to ask for information.

narrative: Between 2002 and 2004, three young women disappeared within a few miles of one another on the west side of Cleveland, Ohio. Michelle Knight, 21, vanished on August 23, 2002. Amanda Berry, 16, went missing on April 21, 2003, the day before her 17th birthday, after finishing a shift at a fast-food restaurant. Gina DeJesus, 14, disappeared on April 2, 2004, while walking home from middle school. Each had been lured into a car by Ariel Castro, a Cleveland school-bus driver and acquaintance of the DeJesus family, and taken to his house on Seymour Avenue, where he confined them.

For roughly a decade the women were held captive in the home, frequently restrained, and subjected to sustained physical and sexual abuse. Berry gave birth to a daughter during her captivity. The case drew little sustained public attention over the years, and to the outside world the three remained among Cleveland's long-term missing persons.

The captivity ended on May 6, 2013. When Castro left the house that afternoon without fully securing an interior door, Berry reached the front door with her young daughter, called out to passing neighbors, and pushed through a storm door with the help of neighbor Charles Ramsey and others. She reached a phone and told a 911 dispatcher, "I've been kidnapped and I've been missing for ten years, and I'm here, I'm free now." Police arrived within minutes, freed Knight and DeJesus from inside the house, and arrested Castro the same day.

Castro, then 52, was indicted on hundreds of counts. On July 26, 2013, he pleaded guilty to 937 charges, including multiple counts of kidnapping and rape and two counts of aggravated murder tied to forcibly ending one of Berry's pregnancies, as part of an agreement that removed the death penalty from consideration. On August 1, 2013, a Cuyahoga County judge sentenced him to life in prison without the possibility of parole plus 1,000 years. At the hearing Knight addressed Castro directly, telling him that the years he had taken "do not compare to the little time you will spend in prison." Roughly a month later, on September 3, 2013, Castro was found dead in his cell at the Correctional Reception Center in Orient, Ohio; the county coroner ruled the death a suicide by hanging.

In the years since, the three survivors have rebuilt their lives and become public advocates for missing persons. Knight, who later took the name Lily Rose Lee, published a memoir and has spoken widely about survival and recovery. Berry and DeJesus co-authored the book "Hope" and, with the Cleveland Family Center for Missing Children and Adults, have worked to support other families. Berry later joined a Cleveland television station highlighting missing-person cases. The Seymour Avenue house was demolished in August 2013. Castro's conviction stands as the resolution of the criminal case, and the survivors' continued advocacy remains the enduring public legacy.

name: Daniel Pearl
summary: Wall Street Journal reporter Daniel Pearl was kidnapped in Karachi, Pakistan, on January 23, 2002, and murdered. Ahmed Omar Saeed Sheikh was convicted and sentenced to death in Pakistan in 2002, but the Sindh High Court overturned his murder conviction in April 2020, leaving only a kidnapping conviction, and Pakistan's Supreme Court upheld that ruling in January 2021. Khalid Sheikh Mohammed has claimed he personally killed Pearl but has never been tried for it. The case highlighted dangers faced by journalists in conflict zones.
lastSeen: January 23, 2002, Karachi, Pakistan

narrative: Daniel Pearl was an American journalist and the South Asia bureau chief for The Wall Street Journal. In January 2002, while based in Karachi, Pakistan, he was reporting on militant networks, pursuing a story about alleged links between the British-born 'shoe bomber' Richard Reid and Islamist groups. On January 23, 2002, Pearl set out for what he believed would be an interview with a religious figure, Mubarak Ali Gilani, near Karachi's Metropole Hotel. He never returned. His captors soon circulated emails and photographs depicting him in captivity and issuing demands, and identifying him as an American and a Jew.

Pearl was killed by his captors, an act later dated to on or around February 1, 2002. On February 21, 2002, a video recording of his murder by beheading was released. His remains were recovered in May 2002 from a plot on the outskirts of Karachi. The killing drew worldwide condemnation and became one of the most prominent journalist murders of the post-9/11 era; his family later established the Daniel Pearl Foundation in his memory.

In July 2002, a Pakistani anti-terrorism court in Hyderabad convicted four men in connection with the case. British-born militant Ahmed Omar Saeed Sheikh, described by prosecutors as the principal organizer of the abduction, was sentenced to death. Three co-accused, Fahad Naseem, Salman Saqib and Sheikh Adil, received life sentences. Sheikh acknowledged a role in planning the kidnapping but denied carrying out the murder, and the convictions were subject to years of appeals.

The attribution of the killing itself grew more complicated over time. According to US government accounts, Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the alleged principal architect of the September 11 attacks who was captured in 2003, claimed during US custody that he had personally beheaded Pearl. The 9/11 Commission's 2004 report cited that claimed admission, and US officials said forensic 'vein-matching' analysis of the hand of the killer shown in the video pointed to Mohammed. Because that claim was made in the context of interrogations, including methods US officials later acknowledged as coercive, it has never been tested at an independent trial.

The Pakistani convictions were ultimately overturned. On April 2, 2020, the Sindh High Court set aside Sheikh's murder conviction and death sentence, reducing his liability to a lesser charge and treating his time already served as sufficient; the three co-accused were acquitted. Prosecutors and the Pearl family appealed. On January 28, 2021, Pakistan's Supreme Court, in a 2-1 decision, upheld the acquittals and ordered the men released, and dismissed the government's and family's appeals. US officials, including the White House, condemned the ruling. Despite the court orders, Pakistani authorities kept Sheikh in detention under provincial public-order measures rather than freeing him. The Pearl family called the outcome 'a complete travesty of justice.' As of publication, no one stands convicted in Pakistan of Pearl's murder, and the man once sentenced to death for it has been acquitted while remaining in state custody.

name: Danielle van Dam
summary: Seven-year-old Danielle van Dam was abducted from her Sabre Springs home on the night of February 1-2, 2002, and murdered by neighbor David Westerfield. Her body was found in a rural area east of San Diego on February 27, 2002, nearly four weeks later. Westerfield was convicted and sentenced to death; the California Supreme Court affirmed the sentence in 2019, and he remains under a death sentence in a California state prison.
lastSeen: February 1, 2002, family home in Sabre Springs, CA

narrative: Danielle van Dam was a 7-year-old girl who disappeared from her family's home in the Sabre Springs neighborhood of San Diego, California, during the overnight hours of February 1-2, 2002. Her parents had last seen her when she was put to bed on the evening of February 1. When the family discovered her missing the next morning, they reported her disappearance to police at about 9:39 a.m. on February 2. A sliding glass door and other openings in the home were later noted by investigators as possible points of entry, and the case quickly drew intense local and national attention.

In the days that followed, hundreds of volunteers joined organized searches across San Diego County, and law enforcement conducted an extensive investigation into the child's whereabouts. Suspicion focused on David Alan Westerfield, a self-employed design engineer who lived two doors from the van Dam family. Westerfield had been away in his motor home over the weekend of the disappearance, and investigators placed him under surveillance beginning February 4. Forensic examination of items connected to him produced physical evidence linking him to the girl, and he was arrested on February 22, 2002. Danielle's remains were found by searchers on February 27, 2002, in a remote area along Dehesa Road near Harbison Canyon, east of the city.

The trial of David Westerfield began June 4, 2002, in San Diego County Superior Court, with prosecutor Jeff Dusek leading the case. Prosecutors presented forensic evidence that included bloodstains matching Danielle's DNA profile found on Westerfield's jacket and inside his motor home, as well as her fingerprints in the motor home, hairs consistent with hers and with the family dog, and fiber evidence. A DNA analyst testified that the probability of the blood matching someone other than Danielle exceeded one in a billion. The prosecution also introduced evidence of child pornography found in Westerfield's possession. The defense challenged the timeline and forensic entomology estimates of when the body was left, arguing the insect evidence pointed to a period when Westerfield was already under police surveillance.

On August 21, 2002, after a trial lasting roughly two months, a jury found Westerfield guilty of first-degree murder and kidnapping, and of possession of child pornography, and found true a special-circumstance allegation that the murder occurred during a kidnapping. On September 16, 2002, the same jury recommended the death penalty. In January 2003, Superior Court Judge William Mudd formally sentenced Westerfield to death.

Westerfield's conviction and death sentence were subject to automatic appeal in California. On February 25, 2019, the California Supreme Court unanimously affirmed both his conviction and his death sentence in People v. Westerfield. Westerfield has remained on death row. California has maintained a moratorium on executions since Governor Gavin Newsom ordered one in 2019, meaning no execution date has been set. As of the most recent reporting, Westerfield remains incarcerated in the California state prison system as a condemned inmate.

name: Elizabeth Smart
summary: Fourteen-year-old Elizabeth Smart was abducted from her Salt Lake City bedroom by Brian David Mitchell and his wife. She was held captive for nine months, often in plain sight. She was rescued after being recognized in public. Mitchell was convicted and sentenced to life in prison in 2011.
lastSeen: June 5, 2002, family home in Salt Lake City, UT

narrative: In the early hours of June 5, 2002, 14-year-old Elizabeth Smart was abducted at knifepoint from the bedroom she shared with her younger sister in her family's home in Salt Lake City, Utah. Her nine-year-old sister, Mary Katherine, witnessed the abduction but pretended to be asleep out of fear. She would later recall the intruder's voice, an observation that proved central to identifying the man responsible. The case drew intense national attention and became one of the most closely followed missing-child investigations in the United States.

The abductor was Brian David Mitchell, a self-styled itinerant street preacher who had briefly done handyman work at the Smart home the previous year. Mitchell held Smart captive with the help of his wife, Wanda Barzee. For roughly nine months the pair kept her at a makeshift camp in the hills above Salt Lake City and later moved with her to San Diego County, California. During the captivity Smart was tethered, threatened, and repeatedly sexually assaulted by Mitchell.

On March 12, 2003, Smart was recovered alive in Sandy, Utah, less than 20 miles from her home, after passersby who had seen news coverage recognized Mitchell and Barzee walking with a disguised girl and alerted police. Mitchell and Barzee were taken into custody. Smart was reunited with her family, and the case shifted to a lengthy set of legal proceedings complicated by extended disputes over Mitchell's competency to stand trial.

Wanda Barzee pleaded guilty in November 2009 to federal charges of kidnapping and unlawful transportation of a minor, and she also entered a plea in the related state case. She was sentenced to 15 years, the maximum under her state conviction. Brian David Mitchell was found guilty by a federal jury on December 10, 2010, of kidnapping and unlawful transportation of a minor across state lines, and on May 25, 2011, he was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole. He is held in federal custody. Barzee was released on September 19, 2018, after credit for time served advanced her release date; she remained subject to supervised release and sex-offender registration.

In the years after her recovery, Elizabeth Smart became a prominent advocate for missing persons and survivors of sexual assault and abduction. She founded the Elizabeth Smart Foundation, worked as a commentator and author, and campaigned for legislation and education aimed at preventing child abduction and supporting survivors. As of 2026, Mitchell remains imprisoned for life, Barzee is out of custody under supervision, and Smart continues her public advocacy work.

name: Samantha Runnion
summary: Five-year-old Samantha Runnion was abducted from outside her Orange County apartment complex and murdered. Her mother Erin Runnion became a prominent child safety advocate, founding the Joyful Child Foundation. Alejandro Avila was convicted and sentenced to death in 2005.
lastSeen: July 15, 2002, outside her apartment in Stanton, CA

narrative: On the early evening of July 15, 2002, five-year-old Samantha Runnion was playing with a friend near a condominium complex in Stanton, California, when a man driving a green car approached the two girls at about 6:30 p.m. He asked whether they had seen a lost puppy, and when Samantha responded, he seized her, threw her screaming and struggling into his car, and drove away. Her friend, who was also five, witnessed the abduction and later gave investigators a detailed description of the man and the vehicle. The following day, July 16, a hiker discovered Samantha's nude body along the Killen Trail off the Ortega Highway near Lake Elsinore in the Cleveland National Forest, roughly 50 miles from her home. An autopsy determined she had been sexually assaulted and died of asphyxiation.

The Orange County investigation moved with unusual speed. Drawing on the young witness's account, authorities produced and widely circulated a composite sketch of the suspect within hours, and Sheriff Michael Carona publicly appealed for help and warned the killer that he would be caught. The rapid distribution of the sketch, combined with tips from the public, quickly focused attention on Alejandro Avila, a 27-year-old former factory worker from Lake Elsinore. Avila had been tried in Orange County for molesting two young girls, the daughter and niece of a former girlfriend, but a jury had acquitted him in early 2001. He was arrested on July 19, 2002, three days after Samantha's body was found.

Avila was charged with kidnapping, murder with special circumstances, and two counts of committing lewd and lascivious acts on a child under 14. At his trial, which was moved to Orange County Superior Court, prosecutors presented DNA evidence recovered from beneath Samantha's fingernails that matched Avila, as well as the victim's DNA found inside his car, shoe prints consistent with Fila sneakers he had purchased, tire impressions, and cell phone and financial records placing him in the relevant areas. The jury also heard evidence of prior molestation and of child pornography accessed on a computer. After deliberating less than nine hours over two days, the jury convicted Avila on all counts on April 28, 2005. On May 16, 2005, the same jury recommended a death sentence, and the court formally imposed the death penalty on July 22, 2005.

The case had a lasting influence on child-safety awareness in California. In its wake, then-Governor Gray Davis expanded the use of electronic freeway signs to broadcast child-abduction alerts statewide, reinforcing the emerging AMBER Alert system. Samantha's mother, Erin Runnion, founded The Joyful Child Foundation, which develops education and community programs aimed at preventing crimes against children. More than 4,000 people attended Samantha's funeral. Avila's conviction and death sentence were upheld on direct appeal by the California Supreme Court on June 30, 2014, which rejected his challenges to the venue, the admission of prior-crimes evidence, and other rulings. Avila remains on California's death row; no execution has been carried out because of a statewide moratorium on executions in effect since 2019.

The recorded status of the case is a conviction: Alejandro Avila was tried, convicted, and sentenced to death for the kidnapping, sexual assault, and murder of Samantha Runnion, and that conviction has been affirmed on appeal.

narrative: John Gilbride was a 34-year-old baggage supervisor for US Airways at Philadelphia's airport who lived in the Ryan's Run apartment complex in Maple Shade, Burlington County, New Jersey. He was found shot to death in his car in the complex's parking lot at 12:08 a.m. on September 27, 2002. According to The Philadelphia Inquirer, a gunman had fired multiple rounds through the driver's-side window of his Ford Crown Victoria, hitting him in the head and chest. The engine was still running.

Gilbride had once belonged to MOVE, the Philadelphia-based group, and had been married to Alberta Africa, a leading member. He left her in 1998 and filed for divorce, and the two then fought over access to their young son for roughly four years. In the weeks before his death, a Philadelphia Family Court judge granted him unsupervised visits. The Inquirer reported that the first such visit was set for the day after he was killed.

The dispute had grown tense. According to the Inquirer's reporting, in the two weeks before the shooting MOVE members fortified their house in West Philadelphia, held a demonstration in South Jersey, made accusations against Gilbride, and posted an online alert about the custody case. Gilbride's father, Jack Gilbride, has said his son believed his life was in danger, and he has long stated that he holds the organization responsible.

MOVE members have denied any involvement. The group's statements, as reported by the Inquirer, have included claims that Gilbride was killed by the government, or that he was not dead at all and was in hiding. A Philadelphia police official once suggested that gambling debts might have been behind the killing. None of these explanations has been substantiated by investigators.

The Burlington County Prosecutor's Office has never named a suspect or made an arrest. Then-Prosecutor Robert Bernardi told the Inquirer in the years after the killing that the timing of the homicide in relation to the custody proceedings remained a question for investigators, without asserting a connection. In 2009 and 2014 the office said the investigation was open but had no new developments.

In August 2021, amid renewed public attention to MOVE after former members spoke out about life inside the group, Burlington County Prosecutor Scott Coffina told the Inquirer that his office remained committed to the case and hoped that witnesses would come forward. No charges have been reported since, and the homicide remains unsolved.

name: Laci Peterson
summary: Laci Peterson was eight months pregnant when she disappeared on Christmas Eve 2002. Her husband Scott Peterson reported her missing and became the prime suspect. Laci's remains and those of her unborn son Conner washed ashore in April 2003. Scott Peterson was convicted of first-degree murder in 2004 and sentenced to death in 2005; the California Supreme Court overturned the death sentence in 2020, and in December 2021 he was resentenced to life without parole. His convictions stand.

narrative: Laci Peterson, a 27-year-old substitute teacher who was roughly eight months pregnant with her first child, was reported missing from her home in Modesto, California, on the evening of December 24, 2002. Her husband, Scott Peterson, told police he had left that morning to go fishing at the Berkeley Marina on San Francisco Bay, some 90 miles away, and returned to find their home empty and their dog wandering the neighborhood with its leash attached. Laci's disappearance on Christmas Eve drew immediate national attention, and the couple's family, friends, and thousands of volunteers mounted an extensive search across Modesto and the surrounding region in the weeks that followed.

As the search continued, investigators grew suspicious of Scott Peterson, in part because his stated fishing location coincided with the area of the bay that became central to the case, and in part because he was found to have been having an extramarital affair with a woman named Amber Frey, who came forward publicly in January 2003. On April 13, 2003, the remains of a male fetus washed ashore on a tidal flat along San Francisco Bay, and the next day a woman's partial remains were found nearby along the Point Isabel shoreline in Richmond. DNA testing confirmed the bodies were those of Laci and the couple's unborn son, whom the family had named Conner. Scott Peterson was arrested on April 18, 2003, near La Jolla and was charged with two counts of murder.

Peterson's trial, moved to Redwood City in San Mateo County because of pretrial publicity, began in June 2004. Prosecutors presented a largely circumstantial case, arguing that Peterson had killed his wife and disposed of her body in the bay near where he claimed to have been fishing. On November 12, 2004, a jury convicted him of first-degree murder in the death of Laci and second-degree murder in the death of Conner. The same jury recommended death, and on March 16, 2005, Peterson was formally sentenced to death and later sent to San Quentin State Prison's death row.

In August 2020, the California Supreme Court overturned Peterson's death sentence, ruling that the trial court had improperly dismissed prospective jurors who expressed opposition to capital punishment during jury selection. The court left his underlying murder convictions intact. A separate review of claims that a juror had committed misconduct did not result in a new trial. In December 2020 the court declined to reconsider the conviction, and in 2021 Peterson was resentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole. He was later transferred to Mule Creek State Prison in Ione, California.

Beginning in early 2024, the Los Angeles Innocence Project took up Peterson's case and sought post-conviction discovery and new DNA testing, arguing on his behalf that physical evidence could point to another perpetrator. A judge granted limited relief, ordering new DNA testing on a piece of duct tape associated with the case while denying broader testing requests. The organization later pursued a habeas corpus petition alleging wrongful conviction based on what it characterized as false evidence. In an order issued in April 2026, a San Mateo County Superior Court judge denied that petition, finding the claims procedurally barred or without merit, and Peterson's attorneys said they would appeal to a higher court. The claims of innocence are advanced by Peterson's defense and have not been endorsed by the courts; as of 2026, his murder convictions stand and he remains incarcerated serving life without parole.

narrative: Rachel Louise Cooke was a 19-year-old college freshman when she disappeared from Georgetown, Texas, north of Austin, on January 10, 2002. She was studying at San Diego Mesa College in California and had come home for the winter break, staying on after the New Year to attend a family wedding, according to KTBC.

Authorities believe she left her parents' house on Navajo Trail, in the North Lake subdivision, at about 9:30 that morning to go running. KTBC reported that a neighbor later saw her roughly 200 yards from the house, apparently walking to cool down at the end of her run. She was not seen again. She had been wearing gray running clothes, a green sports bra and Asics running shoes, and was carrying a yellow Walkman with headphones.

The Williamson County Sheriff's Office describes her as about 5 feet 3 inches tall and 115 pounds, with blonde hair, and with two heart-shaped cherry tattoos on her left foot. Investigators have said they suspect foul play, noting that she had no known reason to leave. Searches and years of investigation have not located her.

Several leads involving vehicles have been examined. According to KTBC, investigators located a white Trans Am that had been of interest but found no evidence linking it to the case, and FBI forensic specialists later examined a vehicle recovered in the Dallas area. Neither produced charges. The sheriff's office has said it has worked through more than 2,000 tips and ruled out numerous people.

A cold case unit took up the file in later years. On January 10, 2020, the eighteenth anniversary, the sheriff's office released new digital sketches of persons of interest, developed with the FBI and a forensic artist after the original witnesses were interviewed again. In January 2021 the office said it was seeking a person who lived in the Georgetown area in 2002, knew Cooke, and was involved in the cattle or horse business, and who investigators think may have talked about the disappearance to an acquaintance. No name was released.

The sheriff's office and the FBI jointly offer a reward of up to $100,000 for information leading to Cooke's location. Reports marking later anniversaries describe the investigation as active. No one has been arrested, and Cooke's whereabouts remain unknown.

name: Sara Ann Lewis Trusty
summary: Sara Trusty, 23, was last seen riding her bicycle near Algoa Baptist Church in Algoa, Galveston County, Texas, on July 12, 2002. About two weeks later, fishermen found her body on the Texas City Dike. Her death was ruled a homicide. The Galveston County Sheriff's Office has asked for information, and no arrest has been reported.
lastSeen: July 12, 2002, riding her bicycle near Algoa Baptist Church, Algoa, TX

sources.title: The Galveston County Daily News - Unsolved deaths, disappearances in the county
CBS News - Can you help solve these cases?
Wikipedia - Texas Killing Fields
Find a Grave - Sara Ann Lewis Trusty (1978-2002)

narrative: Sara Ann Lewis Trusty was 23 years old when she disappeared in Galveston County, Texas, in the summer of 2002. Some news reports spell her first name Sarah. Little biographical detail about her has been published in the sources available.

According to The Galveston County Daily News, Trusty was last seen on July 12, 2002, riding her bicycle near Algoa Baptist Church in Algoa, a small unincorporated community in the mainland part of the county. CBS News, in a feature on unsolved cases from the region, likewise reported that she was last seen riding her bike in Algoa on that date. Other published summaries of the case place the sighting late in the evening and state that her bicycle was later found at the church, but those details could not be confirmed in news reports.

Fifteen days later, two fishermen found her body on the Texas City Dike, the long levee that extends into Galveston Bay from Texas City. The Daily News reported that the body was decomposed, that her death was ruled a homicide, and that doctors determined she had been dead for more than a week when she was found. The sources reviewed do not state a cause of death.

The Galveston County Sheriff's Office is the agency identified with the investigation, and CBS News published its telephone number for tips on the case. No suspect has been publicly identified in any source reviewed, and no arrest has been reported.

Trusty's death is frequently listed among the cases grouped under the label 'Texas Killing Fields,' a term used for the deaths and disappearances of more than thirty girls and women along the Interstate 45 corridor between Houston and Galveston since the 1970s. The label refers to a geographic pattern and a period of time. It does not mean that the cases are linked to one another or to a single offender, and no official finding connects Trusty's death to any other case.

A 2006 Daily News survey of unresolved deaths and disappearances in Galveston County included Trusty's case, and later compilations continue to list it as unsolved. Public information about the investigation is limited, and no recent official update was found. Anyone with information has been asked to contact the Galveston County Sheriff's Office.

Trusty is last seen riding her bicycle near Algoa Baptist Church in Algoa, Texas.

name: Shawn Hornbeck
summary: Eleven-year-old Shawn Hornbeck was abducted on October 6, 2002, while riding his bike near Richwoods, Missouri, and was found alive on January 12, 2007, in the St. Louis-area apartment of Michael Devlin. Police located him while searching for Ben Ownby, 13, taken four days earlier. Devlin pleaded guilty in state and federal courts in October 2007 and received multiple life sentences.
lastSeen: October 6, 2002, riding his bicycle near his home in Richwoods, MO

sources.title: NBC News - Kidnapper pleads guilty to dozens of charges
Alcatraz East Crime Museum - Shawn Hornbeck
Wikipedia - Michael J. Devlin

narrative: Shawn Hornbeck was 11 years old when he disappeared on October 6, 2002, while riding his bicycle near his home in Richwoods, a rural community in Washington County, Missouri. According to an account published by the Alcatraz East Crime Museum, he was on his way to a friend's house when a man struck his bike with a pickup truck and took him. NBC News later reported that prosecutors said the boy had been taken at gunpoint.

For more than four years there was no public trace of him. According to the accounts given in court and summarized by NBC News, he was living in the St. Louis-area apartment of Michael J. Devlin, where he was repeatedly abused and threatened.

The case broke open because of a second abduction. On January 8, 2007, 13-year-old Ben Ownby was abducted in Franklin County. A schoolmate saw a white pickup truck leaving the area and described it to police. Investigators traced a truck matching that description to Devlin, and on January 12, 2007, officers found both Ben Ownby and Shawn Hornbeck alive in his apartment. Shawn was then 15.

Devlin was charged in several jurisdictions. A federal grand jury indicted him on March 1, 2007, on counts of producing child pornography and transporting a minor across state lines, according to Wikipedia's summary of the case. In October 2007 he resolved all of the cases with guilty pleas over three days. NBC News reported that he received a life sentence in Franklin County on October 8 for the Ownby kidnapping, three life sentences plus 60 years in Washington County on October 9 for the crimes against Shawn Hornbeck, and 18 consecutive life sentences in St. Louis County after pleading guilty to 71 counts, including two of kidnapping and 69 of forcible sodomy. He pleaded guilty to the six federal counts the following day and was later sentenced to an additional 170 years in federal court.

Published totals for the number of life terms differ from source to source, depending on how concurrent and consecutive sentences are counted, but every account agrees that Devlin has no realistic prospect of release. According to Wikipedia, he was moved to Crossroads Correctional Center in Cameron, Missouri, in January 2008, and survived a stabbing by another inmate there in April 2011.

Because Shawn Hornbeck was recovered alive and the person responsible admitted guilt in court, the case is considered resolved. It is often cited in discussions of long-term missing children because he was found so long after he vanished, and only because of a witness's description of a vehicle in an unrelated abduction.

Ben Ownby, 13, is abducted in Franklin County; a schoolmate reports seeing a white pickup truck.

Devlin pleads guilty in Franklin County and is sentenced to life in prison for the Ownby kidnapping.
Devlin pleads guilty in Washington County and St. Louis County, receiving three life sentences plus 60 years and 18 consecutive life sentences.
Devlin pleads guilty to all six federal counts.
Devlin is sentenced in federal court to 170 years.
Devlin is stabbed by another inmate at Crossroads Correctional Center and survives.

name: Blue Ridge Savings Bank Murders
summary: Three people were shot dead during a robbery of the Blue Ridge Savings Bank in Greer, South Carolina, on May 16, 2003: teller Sylvia Holtzclaw and customers James "Eb" Barnes and his wife Margaret "Maggie" Barnes. Police found them in a back room minutes after an alarm was triggered. Cash and the security tape were taken. No one has been charged.
lastSeen: May 16, 2003, Blue Ridge Savings Bank, Greer, SC

sources.title: Yahoo News - 20 years after triple homicide at SC bank, police haven't given up
Unsolved Mysteries - Three Dead at Blue Ridge Bank
Trace Evidence - Blue Ridge Savings Bank Triple Homicide
Wikipedia - Blue Ridge Savings Bank murders

narrative: Early on the afternoon of May 16, 2003, an alarm was triggered at the Blue Ridge Savings Bank in Greer, South Carolina. According to reporting published on the twentieth anniversary of the case, the alert came from a cash drawer at about 1:28 p.m. When police reached the building minutes later, they found three people shot to death in a utility room at the back of the bank.

The victims were Sylvia Holtzclaw, the teller on duty, and two customers, James Elbert "Eb" Barnes and his wife Margaret "Maggie" Barnes. Holtzclaw was a lifelong Greer resident and the mother of two sons. Eb Barnes was a physics professor at the University of South Carolina Upstate who was close to retirement, and Maggie Barnes, his wife of 38 years, worked for the National Beta Club in Spartanburg. Wikipedia's entry on the case gives their ages as 56, 61 and 58.

Investigators determined that all three were killed with a .40-caliber Glock handgun. Cash was taken from the teller drawer, though the anniversary reporting describes the amount as small and says no marked bills were among it. The Unsolved Mysteries summary of the case notes that the VHS tape from the bank's security recorder was also missing, leaving police without any images from inside the building. There was little physical evidence and no sign of a struggle.

The main lead came from cameras at nearby gas stations, which recorded a red car on the road in front of the bank, followed by the Barneses' truck. The red car, thought to be possibly an Oldsmobile Alero, was seen again leaving the area around the time of the shootings. Police have said they would like to identify its driver.

Over the years investigators examined several people without being able to tie anyone to the crime. The most widely reported involved a man who shot himself during a traffic stop in Georgia; he had been driving a stolen rental car taken from Columbia. According to the anniversary reporting, investigators found no evidence that he had been in Greer, and he was never confirmed as being involved. Wikipedia's entry says other individuals were also looked at and none was conclusively linked; no one has been named by police as responsible.

Greer police and the FBI have pursued hundreds of leads, and the case remains open. Greer Police Chief Matt Hamby told reporters in 2023 that solving it would be a highlight of his career. Sylvia Holtzclaw's son, David Holtzclaw, has worked to keep attention on the case, and tips are directed to the Greer Police Department and Greenville Crime Stoppers.

timeline.event: Investigators recover gas station video showing a red car near the bank around the time of the killings.
About 1:28 p.m., an alarm from a cash drawer at the Blue Ridge Savings Bank in Greer alerts police to a robbery.
Responding officers find Sylvia Holtzclaw, Eb Barnes and Maggie Barnes shot dead in a back utility room; cash and the security tape are missing.
A man driving a stolen red rental car kills himself during a traffic stop in Georgia; investigators examine him but do not confirm any link to the Greer case.
Twenty years on, Greer police say the case remains open and unsolved after hundreds of leads.

name: Dru Sjodin
summary: University of North Dakota student Dru Sjodin was abducted from a mall parking lot in Grand Forks by registered sex offender Alfonso Rodriguez Jr. Her body was found near Crookston, Minnesota, in April 2004. Because the kidnapping crossed state lines, Rodriguez was tried federally, convicted in 2006 and sentenced to death in 2007. The death sentence was vacated in 2021, and in May 2023 he was resentenced to life in prison without parole.
lastSeen: November 22, 2003, Columbia Mall parking lot, Grand Forks, ND

sources.title: Murder of Dru Sjodin - Wikipedia
About Dru | Dru Sjodin National Sex Offender Public Website (U.S. DOJ)
Two decades later, Dru Sjodin case still resonates in Grand Forks and across the nation - Grand Forks Herald
Rodriguez moved to Florida prison after death sentence in Sjodin killing overturned - Bismarck Tribune (archived copy)
Death penalty dropped in Dru Sjodin abduction, murder case - FOX 9 Minneapolis-St. Paul

narrative: Dru Katrina Sjodin was a 22-year-old University of North Dakota student from Pequot Lakes, Minnesota, working her way through college with several jobs. On November 22, 2003, she finished a shift at a Victoria's Secret store and was abducted from the parking lot of Columbia Mall in Grand Forks, North Dakota, in the late afternoon. She was on her cell phone with her boyfriend when the call abruptly ended, and she never returned to her car. Her disappearance triggered a massive, weeks-long search across the Grand Forks region and drew national attention.

Investigators soon focused on Alfonso Rodriguez Jr., a Crookston, Minnesota man who had been released from a Minnesota prison on May 1, 2003, roughly six months earlier, after serving 23 years for offenses including rape, aggravated assault, and kidnapping. He had been classified as a Level 3 (high-risk) sex offender. Rodriguez was arrested on December 1, 2003. Physical evidence, including a knife sheath and blood recovered from his car, linked him to Sjodin. Despite an extensive search, her body was not found during the winter. On April 17, 2004, her remains were discovered in a ravine near Crookston, showing evidence of assault and stabbing.

Because the abduction crossed state lines, the case was prosecuted federally under the Federal Kidnapping Act. On August 30, 2006, a federal jury in Fargo convicted Rodriguez of kidnapping resulting in death. In the penalty phase, the jury recommended capital punishment, and on February 8, 2007, U.S. District Judge Ralph R. Erickson formally sentenced Rodriguez to death, marking one of the few federal death sentences imposed in a state that had abolished capital punishment.

The murder spurred federal legislation. On July 27, 2006, President George W. Bush signed the Adam Walsh Child Protection and Safety Act, which incorporated a provision known as Dru's Law. It established and named the Dru Sjodin National Sex Offender Public Website (NSOPW), a U.S. Department of Justice-operated tool that lets the public search for registered sex offenders across state, tribal, and territorial jurisdictions.

In September 2021, Judge Erickson, by then serving on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit, vacated the death sentence in a habeas proceeding. He found that Rodriguez's constitutional rights had been violated by misleading and inaccurate testimony from a medical examiner and by his trial lawyers' failure to adequately present mental-health evidence and the possibility of an insanity defense. Prosecutors initially sought to reinstate the death penalty but ultimately announced on March 14, 2023, that they would no longer pursue it. On May 18, 2023, Rodriguez was resentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole. He remains incarcerated in federal custody.
