name: Teekah Lewis
summary: Two-year-old Teekah Lewis vanished from the arcade of a Tacoma, Washington, bowling alley while her family bowled nearby in January 1999. Despite more than 700 tips and descriptions of a man and a car seen that night, no suspect has ever been identified and the case is unsolved.
lastSeen: January 23, 1999, in the arcade of New Frontier Lanes bowling alley in Tacoma, Washington, around 10:30 p.m.

sources.title: Taken from a Bowling Alley: The Teekah Lewis Mystery - NCMEC
Where is Teekah Lewis? 2-year-old vanished from Tacoma bowling alley 25 years ago - KOMO News
Where is Teekah Lewis? 2-year-old vanished from Tacoma bowling alley 24 years ago - KOMO News
Teekah Lewis's Disappearance from Tacoma, Washington - NBC News Dateline
Yahoo News (The News Tribune) - Recent search at Tacoma home was part of Teekah Lewis investigation, police say

narrative: Teekah Lewis was a two-year-old girl from Tacoma, Washington. On the night of January 23, 1999, she was at the New Frontier Lanes bowling alley on Center Street with her mother, Theresa, and other family members. As the adults bowled, Teekah played in the alley's arcade area nearby. When her mother finished a turn and looked over, the little girl was gone. It was around 10:30 p.m., and no one had seen her leave or be taken. In an instant, a routine family night out became the start of a mystery that would stretch across decades.

Staff shut the bowling alley down and police began checking vehicles leaving the parking lot, but Teekah had vanished. Over the course of the investigation, Tacoma police received more than 700 tips, yet no primary suspect was ever identified, and neither Teekah nor the clothing she was wearing was ever found. Detectives have said it remains possible she is still alive and simply does not know she was abducted as a toddler, a possibility that has kept the case classified as an open abduction rather than a presumed death.

Two pieces of information have anchored the investigation for years. Witnesses described a man seen near Teekah in the arcade that night: a white male, roughly 30 to 40 years old and about five feet eleven inches tall, with a husky build, brown wavy or curly hair, a thick mustache, and pockmarks on his face, wearing blue jeans and a blue checkered flannel shirt. Investigators also focused on a vehicle seen speeding out of the parking lot around the time she vanished, described as a maroon or dark-colored late-1980s or early-1990s Pontiac Grand Am with tinted windows and a spoiler. Despite widespread circulation of these descriptions, neither the man nor the car has ever been conclusively identified.

In the years since, the case has drawn periodic renewed attention. Detectives revisited the person-of-interest lead in 2020, and the Tacoma Police Department has continued to release age-progression images showing what Teekah might look like as an adult. At least one person later came forward claiming to be Teekah, prompting the department to investigate, but the case remains unsolved. Her mother has never stopped searching, holding candlelight vigils and pressing for answers more than two decades after her daughter disappeared. The National Center for Missing & Exploited Children continues to feature Teekah's case, and her disappearance stands as one of the Pacific Northwest's most painful unsolved child abductions, a two-year-old who slipped away from a crowded arcade and was never seen again.

name: Joseph Augustus Zarelli
summary: A young boy's battered, naked body was found in a cardboard box in Fox Chase, Philadelphia. Known for decades as 'America's Unknown Child,' he was finally identified in 2022 as Joseph Augustus Zarelli through DNA genealogy. His killer has never been identified.
lastSeen: Unknown

sources.title: Boy in the Box (Philadelphia) - Wikipedia
America's Unknown Child identified after 65 years - NBC News
CBS News Philadelphia - Police reveal identity of 'The Boy in the Box': Joseph Augustus Zarelli
PhillyVoice - Philly's cold-case homicide victim, the 'Boy in the Box,' identified as Joseph Augustus Zarelli, police say

narrative: On February 25, 1957, a young college student discovered the nude, battered body of a small boy wrapped in a plaid flannel blanket inside a large cardboard box in a wooded area of Fox Chase, northeast Philadelphia. The child, estimated to be between four and six years old, had been severely beaten, and his body showed signs of long-term malnourishment. His hair appeared to have been recently and crudely cut, with clippings still clinging to his skin. Despite an enormous investigation, no one came forward to identify him.

The Philadelphia Police Department launched one of the largest investigations in the city's history. Officers distributed flyers across the region showing a photograph of the boy, posed as if sleeping to appear less disturbing, but no leads materialized. The JCPenney box he was found in was traced to a nearby store, but that lead also went cold. The boy was buried in a potter's field in 1957 and later moved to a named grave in Ivy Hill Cemetery in 1998, marked 'America's Unknown Child.'

For over six decades, the case haunted investigators and the public alike. Multiple theories emerged, including that the boy had been a foster child or had been sold by his birth parents, but none could be confirmed. Advances in forensic genealogy finally led to a breakthrough in 2019 when DNA was extracted from the boy's remains after he was exhumed.

In December 2022, the Philadelphia Police Department announced that the boy had been identified as Joseph Augustus Zarelli through investigative genetic genealogy. Born on January 13, 1953, he was the son of a Philadelphia-area family. Despite the identification, his killer has never been charged, and the circumstances of his death remain under investigation, making it one of the longest-running open homicide cases in American history.

name: Sodder Children
summary: Five of the ten Sodder children disappeared during a Christmas Eve house fire in Fayetteville, West Virginia. No remains were found in the ashes. The family believed the children were kidnapped, and the case has never been resolved.
lastSeen: December 24, 1945, Fayetteville, West Virginia

sources.title: Sodder children disappearance - Wikipedia
The Children Who Went Up In Smoke - Smithsonian Magazine

narrative: On Christmas Eve 1945, a fire engulfed the home of George and Jennie Sodder in Fayetteville, West Virginia. The couple and four of their ten children escaped, but five children—Maurice (14), Martha (12), Louis (9), Jennie (8), and Betty (5)—were trapped upstairs. George Sodder attempted to re-enter the house but was unable to reach them. The fire department, an all-volunteer force, did not arrive until approximately 8:00 a.m., by which time the house had burned to the ground.

What made this case extraordinary was the absence of any human remains in the ashes. When the debris was searched, no bones, teeth, or other evidence of the five children was found. A fire hot enough to destroy bone completely would have also destroyed the household appliances that survived, leading the Sodders to believe their children had not perished in the fire at all but had been kidnapped. Several witnesses reported seeing the children in a passing car that night, and others noted suspicious circumstances: the phone lines had been cut, a ladder was moved away from the house, and the fire appeared to have started from outside.

George and Jennie Sodder spent decades searching for their children, erecting a billboard along Route 16 that remained in place until 1989. In 1968, Jennie received a photograph in the mail, purportedly of her son Louis as an adult, but the lead was never confirmed. A private investigator hired by the family in the 1950s also disappeared without providing any final report.

Despite numerous theories—including arson, kidnapping by organized crime figures upset at George Sodder's anti-Mussolini views, or that the children were sold—no definitive answer has ever been established. George Sodder died in 1969 and Jennie in 1989, both without knowing what happened to their five missing children.

timeline.event: Fire destroys the Sodder family home; five children go missing.
Fire department searches the rubble; no human remains are found.

name: Hinterkaifeck Farm Victims
summary: Six people, including two children, were beaten to death with a mattock at the isolated Hinterkaifeck farmstead near Waidhofen, Bavaria, on the night of March 31, 1922. The bodies were found four days later; the livestock had been tended in the meantime. About a hundred suspects were investigated, the files were closed in 1955, and no one was ever convicted.
lastSeen: March 31, 1922, Hinterkaifeck farm, near Waidhofen, Bavaria

sources.title: Süddeutsche Zeitung - Mysteriöser Mord 1922: Geheimnis um eine siebte Leiche
Augsburger Allgemeine - Kriminalgeschichte: Hinterkaifeck oder der Reiz des Ungewissen
OVB Heimatzeitungen - Hinterkaifeck: Wilde Theorien um den Täter
Wikipedia (German) - Hinterkaifeck
Wikipedia - Hinterkaifeck murders

narrative: Hinterkaifeck was a solitary farmstead between the hamlets of Gröbern and Laag, near Waidhofen in Upper Bavaria, roughly 70 kilometres north of Munich. In March 1922 it was home to the retired farmer Andreas Gruber and his wife Cäzilia, their widowed daughter Viktoria Gabriel, 35, who owned the farm, and her children Cäzilia, 7, and Josef, 2. Viktoria's husband had been killed in France in 1914 while serving as a soldier. A new maid, Maria Baumgartner, arrived on the afternoon of Friday, March 31, 1922.

According to Wikipedia's account of the investigation files, Andreas Gruber had told neighbours in the preceding weeks about unexplained events: a newspaper nobody nearby subscribed to, tracks in the snow leading to the farm, a missing house key, a forced padlock and footsteps in the attic. He did not ask neighbours or police for help.

All six residents were killed that night or in the early hours of April 1. As the Süddeutsche Zeitung summarises it, the couple, their daughter and granddaughter died in the barn area, and the maid and the two-year-old boy were killed inside the house. The weapon was a mattock belonging to the farm. It is not known why the first four victims went to the barn. The post-mortem examination found that the seven-year-old had survived for some time after the attack.

Over the following days a coffee salesman, the postman and a mechanic each called at the farm and found nobody. On April 4, 1922, neighbour Lorenz Schlittenbauer entered the buildings with Michael Pöll and Jakob Sigl and found the bodies, most of them covered. Investigators noted that the cattle had been fed and milked, and that bread and meat had been consumed, indicating that someone had stayed at or returned to the farm after the killings.

The court physician Johann Baptist Aumüller carried out the autopsies at the farm. The victims' skulls were removed for examination and were later destroyed in Augsburg during a Second World War air raid. The victims were buried at Waidhofen cemetery on April 8, 1922, where a memorial stone stands. The farm was demolished in 1923.

Police looked at about a hundred suspects, and several people were arrested over the years, but nothing was proven against anyone. Schlittenbauer, who had had a relationship with Viktoria Gabriel, was widely suspected locally; the Süddeutsche Zeitung reports that police could never prove anything against him and that he denied involvement until his death in 1941. The files were closed in 1955, although final interviews took place as late as 1986. In 2007 a group of students at the police college in Fürstenfeldbruck re-examined the files. The Augsburger Allgemeine quoted the project leader as saying that guilt could no longer be proven because no crime-scene evidence survives. The students did not publish the name of the person they considered most likely responsible.

name: Jack the Ripper Victims
summary: At least five women were murdered and mutilated in the Whitechapel district of London in 1888. The killer, who was never identified, taunted police with letters signed 'Jack the Ripper.' The case became the world's most famous unsolved serial murder investigation.
lastSeen: Various locations in Whitechapel, London

sources.title: Jack the Ripper - Wikipedia
Jack the Ripper | Biography, Victims, Letters, Suspects, & Facts | Britannica

narrative: Between August 31 and November 9, 1888, at least five women were brutally murdered in the impoverished Whitechapel district of London's East End. The canonical five victims—Mary Ann Nichols, Annie Chapman, Elizabeth Stride, Catherine Eddowes, and Mary Jane Kelly—were all killed by throat-slashing, and most exhibited escalating mutilations that suggested the killer possessed some anatomical knowledge. The murders terrorized Victorian London and spawned one of the largest police investigations of the era.

The Metropolitan Police, led by detectives Frederick Abberline, Henry Moore, and Walter Andrews, interviewed thousands of witnesses and investigated hundreds of suspects. The investigation was complicated by the poverty and transient nature of Whitechapel's population, the lack of forensic science, and intense media pressure. Letters received by police and newspapers, most famously the 'Dear Boss' letter and the 'From Hell' letter (which was accompanied by half a preserved human kidney), may or may not have been from the actual killer.

The identity of Jack the Ripper has been the subject of more than a century of speculation, with suspects ranging from local tradesmen and doctors to members of the royal family. Among the most frequently cited suspects are Montague John Druitt, a barrister who drowned shortly after the last murder; Aaron Kosminski, a Polish immigrant; Michael Ostrog, a Russian con man; and Prince Albert Victor, Duke of Clarence. DNA analysis conducted in the 2010s produced inconclusive results, and no suspect has ever been definitively linked to the crimes.

The case essentially defined the concept of the serial killer in the public imagination and continues to generate books, films, walking tours, and academic studies. The Whitechapel murders file was officially closed in 1892, but the case has never been solved. It remains the most famous unsolved serial murder case in history.

name: Beaumont Children
summary: Three siblings—Jane (9), Arnna (7), and Grant Beaumont (4)—vanished from Glenelg Beach in Adelaide, Australia on Australia Day 1966. Despite being one of Australia's largest investigations, no trace of the children has ever been found.
lastSeen: January 26, 1966, Glenelg Beach, Adelaide, South Australia

sources.title: Disappearance of the Beaumont children - Wikipedia
Australia's Most Infamous Cold Case - ABC News

narrative: On Australia Day, January 26, 1966, siblings Jane (9), Arnna (7), and Grant Beaumont (4) left their home in the Adelaide suburb of Somerton Park to catch a bus to Glenelg Beach, a popular seaside destination about five minutes away. Their mother Nancy expected them home by noon on the 12:15 bus, but they never returned. It was a trip the children had made before without incident.

Witnesses at the beach reported seeing the three children playing with a tall, thin, blond-haired man in his mid-thirties. The children appeared comfortable with him, and some witnesses said the man had been seen with them on previous occasions. The children were last seen leaving the beach around noon with this man. When they failed to return home, their father Jim drove to the beach to search but found no trace of them.

The investigation that followed was the largest in Australian history at that time. Thousands of people were interviewed, hundreds of leads were pursued, and the case attracted international attention. Several suspects were investigated over the decades, most notably convicted child killer Bevan Spencer von Einem, whose crimes in the 1970s and 1980s bore similarities to the Beaumont case. Despite multiple excavations of suspected burial sites—including a factory site in 2018—no remains have ever been found.

The disappearance fundamentally changed Australian culture, ending an era of relative innocence in which children were routinely allowed to travel unsupervised. The case prompted significant changes to child safety awareness across the country. Nancy Beaumont died in September 2019 and Jim Beaumont died in April 2023, both in Adelaide, without ever learning what happened to their children.

name: Madeleine McCann
summary: Three-year-old Madeleine McCann disappeared on May 3, 2007, from a holiday apartment in Praia da Luz, Portugal, while her parents dined at a nearby restaurant. German prosecutors said in June 2020 that they suspect Christian Brückner of her murder, and Portugal made him a formal suspect in 2022. He denies involvement and has not been charged. Madeleine has never been found.
lastSeen: May 3, 2007, Apartment 5A, Ocean Club, Praia da Luz, Portugal

narrative: Madeleine Beth McCann, a British girl born on May 12, 2003, disappeared on the evening of May 3, 2007, from a ground-floor holiday apartment in Praia da Luz, in the Algarve region of Portugal. She was a few days short of her fourth birthday. According to Wikipedia's account of the case, her parents, Kate and Gerry McCann, had left Madeleine and her two-year-old twin siblings asleep while they ate with friends at a restaurant about 55 metres away, and she was found to be missing at about 10 p.m. The twins were unharmed.

The first Portuguese inquiry gave formal suspect (arguido) status to a local resident, Robert Murat, on May 15, 2007, and to Madeleine's parents on September 7, 2007. According to Wikipedia, all three had that status lifted on July 21, 2008, when the Portuguese case was archived. The Guardian has reported that the McCanns were cleared. The Metropolitan Police opened its own review, Operation Grange, in May 2011, and the Portuguese investigation was reopened in October 2013.

In June 2020, Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office and prosecutors in Braunschweig announced that they were investigating a German man then aged 43 on suspicion of Madeleine's murder, Deutsche Welle reported. A spokesman for the prosecutors, Hans Christian Wolters, said they were working on the assumption that she was dead, while British police continued to treat the case as a missing-person inquiry. The man, later widely named as Christian Brückner, had lived in the Algarve between 1995 and 2007 and was in prison for unrelated offences.

On April 21, 2022, Portuguese prosecutors announced that a man had been made an arguido at the request of the German authorities; The Guardian identified him as Brückner and noted that he had not been arrested or charged. Searches followed at the Arade dam, about 30 miles from Praia da Luz, in May 2023, and across scrubland and derelict buildings near Praia da Luz in early June 2025. The Independent reported that the 2025 search ended with limited findings.

Brückner has denied any involvement in the disappearance. According to Wikipedia, a court in Braunschweig acquitted him on October 8, 2024, of five unrelated sexual offences alleged to have been committed in Portugal. He completed a seven-year sentence for the rape of a 72-year-old woman in the Algarve and was released from prison in Germany on September 17, 2025. ABC News (Australia) reported that he was required to wear an electronic tag, report to probation services and surrender his passport, and that his lawyer said charges would already have been brought if the evidence were sufficient.

No one has been charged in connection with Madeleine McCann's disappearance, and she has not been found. No charge or other resolution was identified in the sources reviewed for this record as of September 2026.

name: Sandra Rivett
summary: Sandra Rivett, 29, nanny to the children of Lord and Lady Lucan, was killed in the basement of the family home at 46 Lower Belgrave Street, London, on November 7, 1974. A 1975 inquest jury named Lord Lucan as her killer, but he vanished that night and was never tried. A court declared him dead in 1999 and a death certificate was issued in 2016; police say the case remains open.
lastSeen: November 7, 1974, 46 Lower Belgrave Street, Belgravia, London

sources.title: BBC News - Lord Lucan: Murdered nanny's son searches for missing killer
BBC News - Lord Lucan death certificate granted
BBC News - Lady Lucan, widow of Lord Lucan, found dead in London
Wikipedia - John Bingham, 7th Earl of Lucan

narrative: Sandra Rivett was working as nanny to the three children of the Earl and Countess of Lucan when she was killed on the evening of November 7, 1974, at 46 Lower Belgrave Street in Belgravia, London. According to Wikipedia's account, which draws on books about the case, she was born on September 16, 1945, and died of head injuries inflicted with a blunt instrument. A former Metropolitan Police detective sergeant told the BBC that he found her body in a sack in the basement.

Lady Lucan was attacked in the house the same night. The BBC reports that she was badly beaten but got away and raised the alarm at a nearby pub. She identified her estranged husband, Richard John Bingham, the 7th Earl of Lucan, as her attacker, and said he had admitted killing the nanny. The couple had separated in 1972 and Lucan had lost a custody case over the children.

Lucan drove that night to the home of friends in East Sussex in a borrowed Ford Corsair. The car was later found abandoned in Newhaven with bloodstains inside; Wikipedia dates the discovery to November 10. In letters to friends he wrote that he had interrupted a fight at the house and acknowledged that the circumstantial evidence against him was strong, the BBC reported. He has not been reliably seen since, and a warrant for his arrest was issued days after the killing.

In June 1975 an inquest jury returned a verdict naming Lord Lucan as the person who murdered Sandra Rivett. He was never arrested or tried, so the inquest finding has never been tested in a criminal court. His son, George Bingham, has said he believes his father died soon after the events, and has publicly left open the question of guilt.

The High Court declared Lucan dead for probate purposes in 1999. On February 3, 2016, following an application by his son under the Presumption of Death Act, a High Court judge ruled that he was presumed dead and a death certificate was issued, allowing the title to pass. Lady Lucan was found dead at her London home in September 2017; police did not treat her death as suspicious.

Rivett's son, Neil Berriman, who was adopted as a baby and learned of his birth mother's identity as an adult, has spent years investigating the case. His search was the subject of a three-part BBC series, Lucan, first broadcast in November 2024. Numerous reported sightings of Lucan over the decades, in countries including Australia, South Africa and India, have never been verified. A Metropolitan Police spokesperson told the BBC in 2024 that the investigation into Sandra Rivett's death remains open and that any significant new information would be considered.

name: Somerton Man
summary: An unidentified man was found dead on Somerton Beach in Adelaide, Australia with a scrap of paper reading 'Tamám Shud' (meaning 'ended' in Persian) hidden in his pocket. Identified in 2022 as Carl 'Charles' Webb, his cause of death remains unknown.
lastSeen: December 1, 1948, Somerton Park Beach, Adelaide

sources.title: Tamam Shud case - Wikipedia
Somerton Man identified as Carl Webb - ABC News Australia
Wikipedia - Somerton Man

narrative: On the morning of December 1, 1948, the body of a well-dressed, physically fit man was found propped against a seawall on Somerton Park Beach in Adelaide, South Australia. The man carried no identification, and all labels had been removed from his clothing. An unsmoked cigarette rested on his collar as though it had fallen from his mouth. An autopsy found no clear cause of death, though the pathologist noted signs consistent with poisoning.

Investigation revealed a small piece of paper hidden in a concealed pocket in the man's trousers. The paper bore the printed words 'Tamám Shud,' meaning 'ended' or 'finished' in Persian—the final words of the Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam. The book from which the scrap had been torn was later found in the back seat of a car parked near the beach. On the back of the book, investigators found faint penciled letters that appeared to be a code, along with a phone number linked to a local nurse named Jessica Thomson, who denied knowing the man.

The case became one of Australia's most enduring mysteries, generating theories ranging from Cold War espionage to a spurned lover's suicide. The coded letters were never deciphered. Despite fingerprints, dental records, and photographs being circulated internationally, no country claimed the man. He was buried in Adelaide's West Terrace Cemetery in 1949 under the name 'The Unknown Man.'

In July 2022, Professor Derek Abbott of the University of Adelaide announced that DNA analysis and genealogical research had identified the man as Carl 'Charles' Webb, a 43-year-old electrical engineer and instrument maker born in Melbourne in 1905. Despite this breakthrough identification, the manner and cause of his death remain undetermined, and the meaning of the code has never been explained.

timeline.event: The body of an unidentified man is found on Somerton Park Beach, Adelaide.
A suitcase belonging to the man is found at Adelaide Railway Station.
The 'Tamám Shud' scrap and the Rubaiyat with coded letters are discovered.
The man is buried at West Terrace Cemetery as 'The Unknown Man.'
The body is exhumed for DNA testing.
The man is identified as Carl 'Charles' Webb through DNA genealogy.

name: Betsy Aardsma
summary: Graduate student Betsy Aardsma was stabbed to death in the stacks of Penn State's Pattee Library on the day after Thanksgiving 1969. Despite a massive investigation, her killer was never identified.
lastSeen: November 28, 1969, Pattee Library, Penn State University

sources.title: Murder of Betsy Aardsma - Wikipedia

narrative: On Friday, November 28, 1969—the day after Thanksgiving—22-year-old Betsy Ruth Aardsma, a first-year English graduate student at Penn State University, entered the Pattee Library's core stacks area on the ground floor around 4:45 p.m. to conduct research. Minutes later, she collapsed between rows of bookshelves. Two male students nearby heard a brief commotion and a man's voice say something like 'somebody better help that girl,' but assumed she had fainted.

When help arrived, no wound was immediately visible. It was only at the hospital that doctors discovered a single, precise stab wound to the left breast that had pierced her pulmonary artery. The killer had used a thin blade, possibly a hunting or paring knife, and the wound was so small it was initially hidden by Betsy's red dress. She was pronounced dead at Centre Community Hospital.

The investigation revealed that despite being in a busy university library, almost no one noticed anything unusual. A man was seen running from the stacks, and two students reported a brief encounter with a nervous individual near the crime scene, but descriptions were vague and inconsistent. The library's layout—a maze of dimly lit shelving rows with limited sightlines—provided ideal cover for the attack.

Penn State Police and the Pennsylvania State Police investigated extensively, interviewing hundreds of people and examining Betsy's personal life for potential motives. She was by all accounts a well-liked, studious young woman with no known enemies. Investigators later focused on a suspect named Richard Haefner, a Penn State graduate student who had known Aardsma and had a history of sexual offenses, but he was never charged before his death in 2002. The case remains officially open and unsolved.

timeline.event: Betsy Aardsma is stabbed to death in the stacks of Penn State's Pattee Library.
She is pronounced dead at Centre Community Hospital; a single stab wound is discovered.

name: Mary Pinchot Meyer
summary: Mary Pinchot Meyer, a Washington socialite and former mistress of President John F. Kennedy, was shot to death while walking along the C&O Canal towpath in Georgetown. Raymond Crump Jr. was acquitted, and the case has never been solved.
lastSeen: October 12, 1964, C&O Canal towpath, Georgetown, Washington D.C.

sources.title: Mary Pinchot Meyer - Wikipedia

narrative: On October 12, 1964, Mary Pinchot Meyer, a 43-year-old painter, socialite, and ex-wife of CIA officer Cord Meyer, was shot twice—once in the head and once in the back—while walking along the Chesapeake & Ohio Canal towpath in Georgetown, Washington, D.C. A mechanic working nearby heard screams and gunshots and saw a man standing over a woman's body. He called police, and within minutes, Raymond Crump Jr., a 25-year-old local laborer, was found nearby, wet and disheveled.

Crump was charged with the murder, but at trial in July 1965, his attorney Dovey Johnson Roundtree systematically dismantled the prosecution's case. No murder weapon was ever found, the eyewitness's identification was shaky, and Crump did not match the physical description given by other witnesses. The jury acquitted him after deliberating for less than twelve hours.

The case took on deeper significance when it emerged that Meyer had been having an affair with President Kennedy in the two years before his assassination. Her diary, which reportedly described their relationship and her experiments with psychedelic drugs, was sought by CIA counterintelligence chief James Jesus Angleton, who was found at her art studio attempting to retrieve it the night of her death. CIA involvement in the case—or at least intense interest—fueled decades of conspiracy theories.

Despite numerous investigations, books, and documentaries, no one has ever been definitively identified as Mary Meyer's killer. Some researchers believe it was a random attack, while others point to possible connections to the CIA, the Kennedy assassination, or the Cold War intelligence community. The case remains one of Washington's most intriguing unsolved murders.

timeline.event: Mary Pinchot Meyer is shot twice and killed on the C&O Canal towpath in Georgetown.
Raymond Crump Jr. is arrested near the scene.
CIA's James Angleton attempts to retrieve Meyer's diary from her studio.
Crump is acquitted; no one else is ever charged.

name: Joan Risch
summary: Joan Risch vanished from her Lincoln, Massachusetts home, leaving behind a trail of blood and signs of a violent struggle. She had recently checked out several library books about disappearances. She has never been found.
lastSeen: October 24, 1961, Lincoln, Massachusetts

sources.title: Disappearance of Joan Risch - Wikipedia
Joan Risch Disappearance - Charley Project
The Mysterious Disappearance of Joan Risch - New England Historical Society

narrative: On October 24, 1961, 31-year-old Joan Risch, a housewife and mother of two, vanished from her home on Old Bedford Road in Lincoln, Massachusetts. Her husband Martin was away on a business trip, and her two children—a four-year-old daughter and a two-year-old son—were at home. When a neighbor checked on the Risch home in the afternoon, she found the children alone and a trail of blood leading from the kitchen through the garage to the driveway.

The kitchen floor was smeared with a significant quantity of blood—investigators estimated half a gallon—and there were signs of a struggle. The telephone had been pulled from the wall. A wastebasket containing bloodstained paper towels and Joan's bloodstained clothing was found in the kitchen. Several witnesses reported seeing a woman matching Joan's description walking along Route 2 near her home that afternoon, apparently disoriented and with blood on her clothing, but she was not approached.

The investigation revealed an intriguing detail: in the weeks before her disappearance, Joan had borrowed at least 25 library books about murders and disappearances, including titles about people who had vanished and assumed new identities. This led to theories that she had staged her own disappearance, but the large amount of blood found argued against a voluntary departure. Other theories included foul play by an unknown assailant, an accident followed by disorientation, or a connection to Joan's mysterious past—she had been adopted and raised in affluent circumstances.

Despite extensive searches of the surrounding woods, ponds, and wells, no trace of Joan Risch has ever been found. No body, no weapon, and no conclusive evidence of what happened to her. The case has been featured on numerous true crime programs but remains unsolved more than six decades later.

timeline.event: Joan Risch disappears from her Lincoln, Massachusetts home; blood is found throughout the kitchen.
Witnesses report seeing a bloodied, disoriented woman walking along Route 2.

name: Arlis Perry
summary: Arlis Perry, 19, was found murdered inside Stanford Memorial Church on October 13, 1974. In 2018 the Santa Clara County Sheriff's Office said DNA from her clothing matched Stephen Blake Crawford, the former campus security guard who had reported finding her body. Crawford, 72, shot himself on June 28, 2018 as detectives arrived to serve a search warrant; he was never charged or tried.
lastSeen: October 12, 1974, at about 11:30 p.m., Stanford Memorial Church, Stanford, California

sources.title: Palo Alto Online - Sheriff: Grisly 1974 Stanford murder solved
Palo Alto Online - Sheriff: Suicide note, serial killer book jacket at murder suspect's home
ABC News - Suspect in 44-year-old killing shoots himself to death as police close in
ABC7 News - Suspect in 1974 Stanford murder case contemplated suicide before
Stanford Magazine - 50 Years After the Stanford Murders, Three of Four Families Have Answers
Wikipedia - Murder of Arlis Perry

narrative: Arlis Perry was 19 and recently married when she was killed inside Stanford Memorial Church on the Stanford University campus in October 1974. According to Palo Alto Online, she had moved to Stanford from Bismarck, North Dakota, in August 1974 with her husband, Bruce Perry, a Stanford sophomore, and was working at a local law firm.

On the evening of October 12, 1974, the couple had a minor argument while walking on campus, and Arlis Perry went on alone to Memorial Church to pray, arriving at about 11 p.m., Palo Alto Online reported. Other visitors saw her there when security guard Stephen Crawford came in to say the building would soon close. Crawford told police he locked the church at about 11:45 p.m. and checked it again at 2 a.m. without seeing her. When she did not come home, her husband called Stanford police at about 3 a.m.

At about 5:40 a.m. on October 13, Crawford reported that he had found her body in the east transept, near the altar. According to news accounts, she had been stabbed in the head with an ice pick, showed injuries consistent with attempted strangulation, was unclothed from the waist down and had been sexually assaulted with a candle. The arrangement of the scene led to years of public speculation about a ritual motive, which investigators never substantiated.

Sheriff Laurie Smith said Bruce Perry, who voluntarily gave a DNA sample, was cleared, and that Crawford remained a person of interest for decades without enough evidence for an arrest. Stanford Magazine reported that a turning point came when investigators realised that trousers stored as the victim's had actually belonged to her husband; when her own clothing was analysed in 2016, DNA on it matched Crawford. The sheriff's office said his reference sample had been obtained from an item he discarded.

On the morning of June 28, 2018, sheriff's detectives went to Crawford's apartment on Camden Avenue in San Jose to serve a search warrant. According to San Jose police and the sheriff, detectives saw Crawford, 72, holding a handgun, withdrew, and then heard a single shot; he was pronounced dead at the scene of a self-inflicted wound, and no officer fired a weapon. Inside, detectives found the dust jacket of a book that discusses the Perry murder and a note dated 2016 that did not mention the killing.

Smith said investigators considered the case closed and were not looking for anyone else, while acknowledging the motive would remain unknown. Because Crawford died before any charge was filed, the evidence against him was never tested in court.

Arlis Perry goes alone to Stanford Memorial Church at about 11 p.m.; guard Stephen Crawford says he locked the church around 11:45 p.m.

An item of Perry's clothing is submitted for DNA testing; the result matches Crawford, according to investigators.

Sheriff Laurie Smith says investigators consider the case closed and describes items found in the apartment.

name: Mickey & Trudy Thompson
summary: Racing legend Mickey Thompson and his wife Trudy were ambushed and shot in their driveway by two hooded gunmen. Former business partner Michael Goodwin was convicted in 2007 after 19 years. The actual shooters were never identified.
lastSeen: March 16, 1988, Bradbury, California

sources.title: Murder of Mickey Thompson - Wikipedia
Wikipedia - Mickey Thompson

narrative: On the morning of March 16, 1988, legendary auto racing promoter and land-speed record holder Marion 'Mickey' Thompson, 59, and his wife Collene 'Trudy' Thompson, 40, were ambushed in the driveway of their home in the exclusive gated community of Bradbury, California, in the San Gabriel Valley foothills. As Mickey backed his truck out of the garage at approximately 5:30 a.m. to go jogging, two hooded gunmen on bicycles appeared, shot him, then chased Trudy as she fled across the yard and killed her as well.

Suspicion quickly focused on Michael Frank Goodwin, a former business partner of Thompson's who had lost millions in a failed stadium racing venture. Thompson and Goodwin had been embroiled in a bitter civil lawsuit, and Thompson had won a $793,000 judgment against Goodwin shortly before the murders. Goodwin, however, had an alibi—he was in another state at the time of the killings—and the actual triggermen were never identified.

The case languished for nearly two decades due to insufficient evidence to bring charges. The break came when cold case investigators with the Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department reinvestigated and found new witnesses. In 2001, Goodwin was arrested and charged with two counts of murder for hire. His trial in 2007 resulted in a conviction, and he was sentenced to two consecutive life terms without the possibility of parole.

Despite Goodwin's conviction as the mastermind, the two hooded shooters have never been identified. The murder weapons were never recovered, and the mystery of who actually pulled the triggers remains unsolved. Mickey Thompson, who in 1960 became the first American to exceed 400 mph on land at the Bonneville Salt Flats, was inducted into numerous motorsports halls of fame posthumously.

timeline.event: Mickey and Trudy Thompson are shot and killed by two hooded gunmen in their driveway.
Suspicion falls on former business partner Michael Goodwin.

name: Jam Master Jay
summary: Jason Mizell, known as Jam Master Jay of Run-DMC, was shot in the head at his recording studio in Queens on October 30, 2002. Ronald Washington and Karl Jordan Jr. were indicted in 2020 and found guilty by a federal jury in February 2024, but in December 2025 the trial judge overturned Jordan's conviction for insufficient evidence while upholding Washington's. A third defendant, Jay Bryant, pleaded guilty to a firearm-related murder charge in April 2026.
lastSeen: October 30, 2002, 24/7 Recording Studio, Jamaica, Queens, New York

sources.title: Murder of Jam Master Jay - Wikipedia
NBC News - Judge overturns murder conviction in the killing of rap legend Jam Master Jay

narrative: On the evening of October 30, 2002, Jason William Mizell, known worldwide as Jam Master Jay—the DJ and co-founding member of the pioneering hip-hop group Run-DMC—was shot once in the head at his 24/7 Recording Studio on Merrick Boulevard in the Jamaica neighborhood of Queens, New York. He was 37 years old. A friend in the studio, Uriel Rincon, was also shot in the leg. Despite the shooting occurring in a room with several people present, witnesses were initially uncooperative with investigators.

The murder sent shockwaves through the music industry. Run-DMC had been one of the most influential groups in hip-hop history, helping bring the genre into mainstream culture with songs like 'Walk This Way' and 'It's Tricky.' Mizell was widely regarded as a beloved figure in Queens and the hip-hop community, making the murder particularly shocking. The case quickly went cold as the 'no snitching' code prevalent in the neighborhood stifled witness cooperation.

For 18 years, the case remained one of New York City's most high-profile unsolved murders. The breakthrough came in August 2020, when federal prosecutors indicted Ronald Washington and Karl Jordan Jr. The charges alleged that the murder was connected to a failed drug deal involving kilogram quantities of cocaine. Mizell had allegedly agreed to distribute cocaine but then cut Jordan out of the deal, leading to the deadly confrontation.

Ronald Washington and Karl Jordan Jr. both pleaded not guilty and were convicted by a federal jury in Brooklyn on February 27, 2024. On December 19, 2025, U.S. District Judge LaShann DeArcy Hall overturned Jordan's conviction, finding the evidence of a drug-related motive insufficient, and upheld Washington's conviction. Washington's conviction, and a later guilty plea by a third defendant, brought a measure of resolution to one of hip-hop's most notorious cold cases, though many in the community expressed surprise at the alleged drug-dealing motive, which contrasted with Jam Master Jay's public image as a mentor and community figure.

timeline.event: Jam Master Jay is shot and killed at his recording studio in Jamaica, Queens.
Police investigation begins but witnesses are uncooperative.

name: Mary, Bobby & Brittney Fisher
summary: Mary Fisher and her children Brittney and Bobby were found dead after their Scottsdale, Arizona home exploded on April 10, 2001. Her husband, Robert William Fisher, is charged with three counts of first-degree murder and arson but has never been found or tried. The FBI kept him on its Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list from June 2002 to November 2021, and he remains wanted.
lastSeen: April 10, 2001, Scottsdale, Arizona

sources.title: FOX 10 Phoenix - FBI removes Robert Fisher from Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list
FOX 10 Phoenix - 20 years later: Search continues for Robert Fisher
ABC15 Arizona - Is one of FBI's most wanted, Robert Fisher, dead or living a secret life? Lead detective shares his theory
Wikipedia - Robert William Fisher
Robert Fisher - FBI Most Wanted
Robert Fisher case - Arizona Republic

narrative: On the morning of April 10, 2001, an explosion and fire destroyed the Fisher family's house in Scottsdale, Arizona. Inside, responders found the bodies of Mary Fisher and her two children, Brittney and Bobby. According to FOX 10 Phoenix, all three had their throats cut and Mary Fisher had also been shot in the head. Investigators concluded that a natural gas line in the house had been disconnected to cause the blast.

Mary Fisher's husband, Robert William Fisher, then about 40, was not in the house and could not be found. ABC15 reported that the last confirmed sighting of him came the evening before the explosion, when a surveillance camera recorded him withdrawing $280 from an ATM. Police allege that he killed his family and set up the explosion; FOX 10 reported that investigators believe the motive was connected to his wife's intention to divorce him. Fisher has not been tried, and these remain allegations.

The family's SUV was found abandoned in the Tonto National Forest near Young, Arizona, roughly 90 to 100 miles from Scottsdale. Wikipedia's account dates the discovery to April 20, 2001; news reports describe it as days to two weeks after the explosion. The family dog was found with the vehicle. More than 100 officers searched the surrounding mountainous terrain, FOX 10 reported, and the search was called off after several days without any trace of Fisher, who was described as an experienced outdoorsman and hunter.

Fisher was charged in Arizona with three counts of first-degree murder and one count of arson, and a federal warrant was issued for unlawful flight to avoid prosecution. On June 29, 2002, the FBI added him to its Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list. A reward of up to $100,000 was offered for information leading to his arrest.

On November 3, 2021, the FBI removed Fisher from the Ten Most Wanted list. According to FOX 10, the bureau said that nearly 20 years of extensive publicity had not led to his location or capture. The removal did not change his legal status: the charges and warrants remain in place and he is still a wanted fugitive.

In coverage marking 25 years since the killings, ABC15 reported that Scottsdale police still treat the case as active and receive one to two tips a week. Detective John Heinzelman, the third lead investigator on the case, told the station he thinks it likely that Fisher died by suicide in the forest, given that there has been no confirmed sighting since 2001, while acknowledging that Fisher may instead have fled and taken on a new identity. No remains have been identified as his.

name: Mary Ellen Deener
summary: Mary Ellen Deener, 14, was murdered in Mansfield, Ohio, on November 14, 1965, while walking to a laundromat. Lester Eubanks was convicted in May 1966 and sentenced to death, later commuted to life. He walked away from a furlough at a Columbus shopping center on December 7, 1973, and remains a fugitive on the U.S. Marshals 15 Most Wanted list.
lastSeen: November 14, 1965, walking to a laundromat in Mansfield, Ohio

sources.title: Richland Source - Have you seen Lester Eubanks? U.S. Marshals Office offers new images
Spectrum News 1 - Search heats up for escaped killer 60 years after Ohio teen's murder
NBC News - Most wanted fugitive who escaped in 1973 now sought in Los Angeles
Wikipedia - Lester Eubanks

narrative: Mary Ellen Deener was 14 years old when she was killed in Mansfield, Ohio, on November 14, 1965. According to the U.S. Marshals Service account reported by Richland Source and Spectrum News, she had been walking to a laundromat to help with her family's washing. Wikipedia's summary of the case states that she was attacked during an attempted sexual assault, shot, and then struck on the head.

Lester Eubanks, then 22, was arrested the following day, according to Wikipedia. Richland Source reports that he was convicted on May 25, 1966, of murder committed during the perpetration of rape and was sentenced to death two days later. His sentence was commuted to life imprisonment in 1972, after the U.S. Supreme Court ruling that invalidated death sentences then in force.

On December 7, 1973, Eubanks was among inmates taken on an honor furlough to a shopping center in Columbus to do Christmas shopping. He was allowed to move around unsupervised and did not return. NBC News reported that investigators believe he later lived in the Los Angeles area under the name Victor Young, in communities including Gardena, Long Beach, North Hollywood and South Los Angeles, and that he may have worked as a janitor at a hospital in Lynwood around the late 1980s or early 1990s.

The U.S. Marshals Service cold case unit in northern Ohio took over the search in 2016, according to Richland Source. On December 7, 2018, the forty-fifth anniversary of the escape, Eubanks was added to the agency's 15 Most Wanted Fugitives list. A reward of up to $50,000 is offered for information leading to him. The case was featured in the Netflix series Unsolved Mysteries in October 2020, which NBC News said generated new leads, including photographs pointing to the Los Angeles area.

On May 27, 2025, the Marshals released updated age-progression images showing how Eubanks might look in his eighties. In November 2025, around the sixtieth anniversary of the killing, Spectrum News reported that the Cuyahoga County Medical Examiner's Office had retested clothing connected to the 1965 case and recovered Eubanks's DNA, a development U.S. Marshal Peter Elliott described as significant for confirming his identity if he is located. A deputy marshal told the outlet he believed someone had been in recent contact with the fugitive.
No report of Eubanks's capture or death was found as of September 2026. He would be 82 years old. The Marshals ask anyone with information to call 1-866-4-WANTED.

name: Robert Keith Palomares
summary: Armored car guard Robert Keith Palomares, 24, was shot and killed during a robbery outside a movie theater in Phoenix on November 29, 2004. Jason Derek Brown was charged with murder and armed robbery but has never been arrested or tried. The FBI kept him on its Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list from December 2007 until September 2022, and the warrants remain active.
lastSeen: November 29, 2004, outside an AMC movie theater in the Ahwatukee area of Phoenix, Arizona

sources.title: Arizona's Family - Man accused of killing armored car guard in Phoenix removed from FBI's 10 Most Wanted Fugitives list
Yahoo News / Arizona Republic - Why Arizona fugitive Jason Derek Brown was removed from FBI 10 Most Wanted list
Phoenix Magazine - Arizona's Most Wanted
Wikipedia - Jason Derek Brown
Jason Derek Brown - FBI Most Wanted
Jason Brown case - AZ Central
America's Most Wanted - Jason Brown

narrative: Robert Keith Palomares, 24, was working as an armored car guard on the morning of November 29, 2004, when he was shot outside an AMC movie theater in the Ahwatukee area of Phoenix, Arizona. According to the Arizona Republic's reporting, carried by Yahoo News, he was shot several times in the head, and the gunman took a money bag holding about $56,000 before leaving the scene on a mountain bike. Phoenix Magazine reported that the money was the theater's receipts.

Investigators focused on Jason Derek Brown within days. According to Phoenix Magazine, fingerprints recovered from the bicycle, which had been left behind, were matched to prints on file in Utah, where Brown had recently bought a .45-caliber Glock pistol and ammunition from a firearms instructor. The magazine also reported that witnesses had described a man resembling Brown watching the area from a silver BMW, and that he had checked into a hotel near the theater several days before the shooting.

According to Wikipedia's summary of the case, an Arizona warrant charging Brown with first-degree murder and armed robbery was issued on December 4, 2004, and a federal warrant for unlawful flight to avoid prosecution followed on December 6. Brown has not been arrested, and the charges have never been tested in court. He is an accused person, not a convicted one.

News accounts say Brown drove the BMW to California and later switched to a Cadillac Escalade. That vehicle was found at Portland International Airport in January 2005, according to Phoenix Magazine. On December 8, 2007, the FBI added him to its Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list as the 489th person named to it. Phoenix Magazine reported that the reward was doubled to $200,000 in March 2013. Reported sightings in Utah, Idaho and overseas were never confirmed.

The FBI removed Brown from the Ten Most Wanted list on September 7, 2022. An FBI spokeswoman quoted by the Arizona Republic said that years of investigation and publicity had not established where he was, and that keeping him on the list was not expected to produce information leading to his capture. Arizona's Family (KTVK/KPHO) reported that the bureau had received more than 10,000 tips and quoted retired agent Lance Leising as saying that none had produced a corroborated sighting. Leising also said he believed Brown would have been found if he were alive, while acknowledging there is no proof of that.
The FBI said the investigation remains active and the warrants are still in force. As of September 2026 no arrest has been reported, and no one has been tried for the killing of Robert Palomares.

name: Bradford Bishop Family
summary: Annette Bishop, 37, her mother-in-law Lobelia, 68, and sons William, 14, Brenton, 10, and Geoffrey, 5, were beaten to death at their Bethesda home on March 1, 1976. Their burned bodies were found the next day in Tyrrell County, North Carolina. William Bradford Bishop Jr., a State Department officer, was indicted on five counts of murder but has never been found or tried.
lastSeen: March 1, 1976, Bethesda, Maryland

sources.title: Montgomery County Police - FBI Announces Placement of Bradford Bishop on Ten Most Wanted List
CBS News - William Bradford Bishop Jr., former State Department diplomat, added to FBI's most wanted
NBC Washington - How William Bradford Bishop Was Added to the FBI's Ten Most Wanted List
Ghosts of DC - Bishop Family Murders: A 1976 Bethesda Manhunt
Wikipedia - Bradford Bishop

narrative: Five members of the Bishop family were killed at their home in Bethesda, Maryland, on the night of March 1, 1976. According to a Montgomery County Police release issued with the FBI in 2014, the victims were Lobelia Bishop, 68; her daughter-in-law Annette Bishop, 37; and Annette's sons William, 14, Brenton, 10, and Geoffrey, 5. Police said the family had been beaten to death.

The following day a forest service worker in Tyrrell County, North Carolina, near the town of Columbia, found five bodies in a shallow grave in a wooded area where a fire had been set. Wikipedia's account, drawing on contemporary reporting, says the remains were confirmed as the Bishop family through dental records. The site was roughly a six-hour drive from Bethesda, CBS News reported.

Investigators focused on William Bradford Bishop Jr., then 39, Annette's husband and a Foreign Service officer at the State Department. CBS News reported that he is alleged to have bought a small metal mallet at a Sears store before the killings, and that he spoke several languages and had long experience living abroad. On March 18, 1976, the family's maroon 1974 Chevrolet station wagon was located at the Elkmont campground in Great Smoky Mountains National Park in Tennessee; police said it contained bloody items and an ax. A Montgomery County grand jury indicted Bishop on five counts of murder that month. He has not been seen by authorities since, and the family dog was also never found.

Bishop has never been arrested or tried, and the allegations against him remain unproven in court. Wikipedia lists reported sightings in Sweden in 1978, Italy in 1979 and Switzerland in 1994, none of which was confirmed.

On April 10, 2014, the FBI added Bishop to its Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list, with a reward of up to 100,000 dollars and an age-progressed bust showing how he might look decades later. NBC Washington reported that, at 77, he was the oldest person ever added to the list. He was taken off the list on June 27, 2018; according to later accounts the FBI wanted the place for another fugitive, while the warrants and an Interpol notice stayed in force.

In 2021 a North Carolina woman who had been adopted as an infant learned through consumer DNA testing that Bishop was her biological father, a relationship reported to have been confirmed against a DNA profile held by the FBI. No arrest or confirmed trace of Bishop has been reported since. He was born in August 1936 and would now be 90 if alive; he remains wanted.

A Montgomery County grand jury indicts William Bradford Bishop Jr. on five counts of murder.

The FBI removes Bishop from the Ten Most Wanted list; he remains a wanted fugitive.

name: Isdal Woman
summary: A partially burned female body was found in Isdalen Valley near Bergen, Norway surrounded by sleeping pills, bottles of liquor, and evidence of a deliberately concealed identity. Despite international investigation, her identity and cause of death remain unknown.
lastSeen: November 29, 1970, Isdalen Valley, Bergen, Norway

sources.title: Isdal Woman - Wikipedia
Death in Ice Valley - BBC/NRK Podcast
The Isdal Woman: Norway's Most Famous Cold Case - NRK

narrative: On November 29, 1970, a university professor and his two daughters discovered a partially burned female body in the remote Isdalen Valley near Bergen, Norway. The woman's body was surrounded by an arrangement of objects: an empty bottle of liquor, a collection of sleeping pills, and the remains of a fire. Her face was badly burned, and her fingerprints had been sanded off. All labels had been removed from her clothing.

At nearby Bergen Railway Station, investigators found two suitcases linked to the woman. The contents deepened the mystery: multiple wigs, various pairs of non-prescription glasses, antimicrobial cream, currency from several European countries, and a diary listing coded entries showing she had traveled extensively through Europe under at least eight different aliases with fake passports. Hotel records showed she had checked in under different names and nationalities across Norway, Germany, Belgium, and other countries.

The investigation revealed the woman had been seen at hotels in Bergen and Stavanger in the days before her death. Hotel staff described her as elegant and reserved, speaking German and broken English. She had requested rooms not overlooking the street—possibly to avoid observation. Forensic analysis suggested she had not died where she was found but had been moved, and the fire appeared to have been set to destroy evidence.

Despite cooperation between Norwegian police and Interpol, the woman was never identified. Theories have centered on Cold War espionage—she bore hallmarks of an intelligence operative—while others suggest she was fleeing from something or someone. In 2017, Norwegian police and the BBC launched a joint investigation using modern forensic techniques, including isotope analysis of her teeth, which suggested she grew up in the Nuremberg area of Germany. As of 2024, the Isdal Woman remains unidentified.

timeline.event: A partially burned female body is found in Isdalen Valley near Bergen.
Two suitcases with coded diary entries and multiple identities are found at Bergen Railway Station.
International investigation begins; Interpol is contacted.
The woman is buried in a zinc coffin in Bergen; she is never identified.

name: Kelly (El Dorado Jane Doe)
summary: A young woman using several aliases was killed in a room at the Whitehall Motel in El Dorado, Arkansas on July 10, 1991. Her ex-boyfriend James McAlphin was convicted in her death, but her true identity remained unknown for more than 30 years. In May 2022 genetic genealogy identified her; only her first name, Kelly, was released, with her surname withheld for family privacy.
lastSeen: July 10, 1991, Whitehall Motel, El Dorado, Arkansas

sources.title: El Dorado Jane Doe - Wikipedia
NamUs case
Defrosting Cold Cases - Identified: El Dorado Jane Doe
Wikipedia - Kelly (murder victim)

narrative: On May 4, 1991, the body of a young woman was found in Room 37 of the Whitehall Motor Lodge (now the Pines Motel) on North West Avenue in El Dorado, Arkansas. She had been shot once behind the right ear. The room had been paid for in cash, and the woman had checked in under a false name. She carried no identification, and her fingerprints matched no records in any database.

The woman was described as approximately 20 to 30 years old, about 5'4" tall, with brown hair. She appeared well-groomed and was wearing nice clothing. Investigators found few clues: a small amount of cash, cigarettes, and toiletries. The room yielded no physical evidence pointing to a killer. Some investigators believed her death may have been a suicide, while others suspected foul play due to the unusual angle of the gunshot.

For over three decades, the case remained one of the most frustrating in Arkansas. Facial reconstructions were created and distributed, and the case was featured on various true crime platforms, but no one came forward to identify her. The DNA Doe Project eventually took on the case, using genetic genealogy techniques to trace family connections.

In October 2022, authorities announced the woman had been identified as Mercedes Yvette Edmond, 25, from the Dallas-Fort Worth area of Texas. The identification was confirmed through DNA genealogy and family verification. While her identity was finally established, the circumstances of her death—and how she came to be alone in a motel room 300 miles from home—remain under investigation.

timeline.event: A woman is found shot dead in a motel room in El Dorado, Arkansas.
Investigation reveals no identification; she is designated El Dorado Jane Doe.
DNA Doe Project takes on the case using genetic genealogy.

name: Sharon Lee Gallegos
summary: The remains of a young girl were found near Congress, Arizona in 1960. Known as 'Little Miss Nobody' for over 60 years, she was identified in 2022 as Sharon Lee Gallegos, a child who had been abducted from New Mexico.
lastSeen: July 21, 1960, Alamogordo, New Mexico (abduction)

sources.title: Little Miss Nobody - Wikipedia
Wikipedia - Little Miss Nobody case

narrative: On July 31, 1960, the partially skeletonized remains of a young girl were found in the desert near Congress, Arizona, a small mining community about 80 miles northwest of Phoenix. The child appeared to have been between three and six years old. She was wearing a white cotton nightgown and had been left in a shallow depression in the desert. The cause of death could not be determined due to the condition of the remains.

The discovery made national headlines, and the unidentified child was given the name 'Little Miss Nobody' by the media. The community of Congress rallied around the case, raising money for a proper burial. She was laid to rest in the Yavapai Cemetery in Prescott, Arizona with a headstone reading 'Little Miss Nobody' and a plea for information. Despite widespread publicity, no one came forward to identify her.

Over the decades, investigators periodically revisited the case as forensic technology advanced. The National Center for Missing & Exploited Children created facial reconstructions, and DNA was eventually extracted from the remains. Through genetic genealogy, investigators were able to trace family connections.

In March 2022, Yavapai County authorities announced that Little Miss Nobody had been identified as Sharon Lee Gallegos, who had been abducted on July 21, 1960, from the front yard of her grandmother's home in Alamogordo, New Mexico. She had been snatched by a couple in a green car. The identification confirmed that Sharon had been transported across state lines and killed. Her killers have never been identified.

timeline.event: Sharon Lee Gallegos is abducted from her grandmother's yard in Alamogordo, New Mexico.
Remains of a young girl are found in the desert near Congress, Arizona.
She is buried as 'Little Miss Nobody' in Prescott, Arizona.

name: Bible John Victims
summary: Three young women were strangled after leaving the Barrowland Ballroom in Glasgow between 1968 and 1969. The suspect, nicknamed 'Bible John' for quoting scripture, was never identified despite being Scotland's most famous serial murder case.
lastSeen: Various dates 1968-1969, Barrowland Ballroom, Glasgow

sources.title: Bible John - Wikipedia

narrative: Between February 1968 and October 1969, three young women were murdered in Glasgow, Scotland after attending Thursday night dances at the Barrowland Ballroom on Gallowgate. Patricia Docker (25) was found strangled on February 23, 1968. Jemima McDonald (32) was found in a derelict building on August 16, 1969. Helen Puttock (29) was found strangled in her own backyard on October 31, 1969. All three women were menstruating at the time of their deaths, a detail that would prove significant.

The crucial witness was Jean Langford, Helen Puttock's sister, who had shared a taxi with Helen and the suspect after the dance on the night Helen was killed. Jean described a tall, slim, well-dressed man with reddish-brown hair who quoted extensively from the Bible and expressed strong views about adultery and promiscuity. He gave his name as 'John.' This description earned him the nickname 'Bible John' in the press.

The Glasgow police investigation was one of the largest in Scottish history. Over 50,000 statements were taken, thousands of men were interviewed, and Jean Williams worked with police on numerous identification attempts. A detailed composite sketch was circulated widely. Despite the extensive effort, Bible John was never identified.

In the 1990s and 2000s, police reinvestigated using DNA technology and briefly focused on John Irvine McInnes, a distant relative of one of the victims who had committed suicide in 1980. His body was exhumed in 1996 for DNA comparison; the initial results were inconclusive, and later testing excluded McInnes as the source of the crime-scene DNA. The investigation was scaled back but has never been officially closed. Bible John remains Scotland's most notorious unidentified serial killer.

timeline.event: Patricia Docker is found strangled after attending the Barrowland Ballroom.
Jemima McDonald is found murdered in a derelict building.
Helen Puttock is murdered; her sister Jean provides a detailed description of the suspect.
Suspect John McInnes is exhumed for DNA testing; results are inconclusive.

name: Suzy Lamplugh
summary: Estate agent Suzy Lamplugh, 25, vanished on July 28, 1986 after leaving her Fulham office to show a property on Shorrolds Road to a client recorded as 'Mr Kipper'. She has never been found and was declared dead in 1993. Police named convicted murderer John Cannan as their prime suspect in 2002; he was never charged, denied involvement and died in prison in November 2024. No one has been convicted.
lastSeen: July 28, 1986, Shorrolds Road, Fulham, London

sources.title: BBC News - Unsolved Suzy Lamplugh case 'haunts' detectives
BBC News - Suzy Lamplugh murder suspect dies in prison
BBC News - Suzy Lamplugh suspect refused treatment in prison
BBC News - Suzy Lamplugh case still open after suspect dies
The Guardian - Met finds no evidence in Suzy Lamplugh case after digging up garden
The Independent - Suzy Lamplugh 'declared dead' by her family (28 July 1993)
The Negotiator - Police launch final Suzy Lamplugh appeal on 40th anniversary
Wikipedia - Disappearance of Suzy Lamplugh

narrative: Susannah 'Suzy' Lamplugh was a 25-year-old estate agent working in Fulham, west London. On the afternoon of July 28, 1986 she left her office to show a client a property on Shorrolds Road. According to the BBC, her diary recorded the appointment under the name 'Mr Kipper'. She did not come back, and the client has never been traced. Her white Ford Fiesta was found abandoned elsewhere in Fulham later that day; Wikipedia's account, drawn from police appeals at the time, places it on Stevenage Road, about a mile from the property.

The disappearance led to one of the largest missing person inquiries in the United Kingdom, the BBC reports, but no trace of her was found. Seven years later, on July 27-28, 1993, her father signed the papers for a legal presumption of death, as The Independent reported at the time. Some later reports give 1994 as the year. Within months of her disappearance her parents, Paul and Diana Lamplugh, had founded the Suzy Lamplugh Trust, a personal safety charity that now also runs the National Stalking Helpline.

Attention later turned to John Cannan, who was jailed for life in 1989 for the abduction and murder of Shirley Banks in Bristol and for other sexual offences. According to The Guardian, the Metropolitan Police named him in 2002 as the prime suspect in Lamplugh's presumed murder and questioned him several times. The BBC reports that a file was sent to prosecutors in 2002 but that there was never enough evidence to charge him, and that no forensic evidence has linked him to her. Cannan always denied any involvement.

Several searches for a body have been made, at sites in Worcestershire and Somerset and, in late 2018, at a house in Sutton Coldfield that had belonged to Cannan's mother. The Guardian reported that the two-week excavation there ended on November 12, 2018 without any evidence being recovered.

Cannan died at HMP Full Sutton on November 6, 2024, aged 70. An inquest found that he died of natural causes, according to the BBC. The Metropolitan Police said afterwards that the investigation remained open.

On the 40th anniversary, in July 2026, the Met issued what was described as a final appeal for witnesses. The senior investigating officer, Detective Chief Inspector Teresa Foster, told the BBC she thought Lamplugh may have been targeted by a stalker who lured her to a false appointment. The trade publication The Negotiator reported that officers planned to follow up about 30 potential witness leads over the following year. If nothing comes of them, the inquiry will move to an inactive phase in 2027, in which new information is still assessed but the case is no longer actively worked.

timeline.event: Suzy Lamplugh leaves her Fulham office to meet a client recorded as 'Mr Kipper' on Shorrolds Road and is not seen again; her car is found abandoned in Fulham.
Her parents establish the Suzy Lamplugh Trust (date per Wikipedia).
John Cannan is jailed for life for the abduction and murder of Shirley Banks.
On the seventh anniversary, her father signs the papers for a legal presumption of death.
The Metropolitan Police name Cannan as prime suspect; prosecutors find insufficient evidence to charge him.
Police end a two-week search of a house in Sutton Coldfield once owned by Cannan's mother; nothing is found.
The Parole Board refuses to release Cannan.
Cannan dies at HMP Full Sutton, never charged over Lamplugh's disappearance.
On the 40th anniversary the Met makes a final appeal and says the inquiry will become inactive in a year if new leads produce nothing.

name: Jill Dando
summary: BBC presenter Jill Dando, 37, was shot once in the head outside her home in Fulham, London, on April 26, 1999. Barry George was convicted of her murder in 2001, but the Court of Appeal quashed the conviction in 2007 and a jury acquitted him at a retrial in 2008. No one else has been charged, and the Metropolitan Police inquiry remains open.
lastSeen: April 26, 1999, outside her home at 29 Gowan Avenue, Fulham, London

sources.title: LBC - Met Police to re-examine CCTV in Jill Dando murder case 27 years on
Yahoo News UK - Who killed Jill Dando? Timeline of events since BBC presenter was shot
RTE - George denied compensation for wrongful conviction
Yahoo Entertainment - 'Who Killed Jill Dando?' features Barry George
Wikipedia - Murder of Jill Dando
Wikipedia - Barry George

narrative: Jill Dando was one of the BBC's best-known presenters and had co-hosted the programme Crimewatch since 1995. At about 11:32 on the morning of April 26, 1999, she was shot once in the head at close range on the doorstep of her house in Gowan Avenue, Fulham, in west London. She was 37. According to LBC, she was pronounced dead at Charing Cross Hospital at 1:03 pm.

A neighbour heard her scream but did not hear a shot, and saw a white man of about six feet, aged around 40, walking away from the house, according to a timeline published by Yahoo News UK. The Metropolitan Police inquiry, Operation Oxborough, interviewed around 2,500 people. Wikipedia's account says the weapon was a 9mm Short calibre pistol and that no gun was recovered.

On May 25, 2000, police arrested Barry George, who lived nearby. He was charged with murder and tried at the Old Bailey, where a jury convicted him on July 2, 2001, by a majority of ten to one. The prosecution case included a single particle of firearm discharge residue found in a coat pocket. His defence suggested that the killing could have been connected to Dando's appearance in an appeal for Kosovan refugees. A first appeal was dismissed in 2002.

After a referral by the Criminal Cases Review Commission, the Court of Appeal quashed the conviction on November 15, 2007, finding it unsafe because of the way the residue evidence had been presented. George was tried again and was found not guilty on August 1, 2008, having spent about eight years in prison. He is legally innocent of the murder. In January 2013 the High Court rejected his claim for compensation, RTE reported, and he separately received damages from newspaper publishers over their coverage of him.

No one else has been charged. Theories discussed publicly over the years include a contract killing and a link to Serbia, but none has been established in court. The case was revisited in a 2023 Netflix documentary series, and Yahoo News UK reported that lawyers had urged police to examine a possible link to a man convicted in Serbia.

In September 2026, LBC reported that Metropolitan Police detectives would re-examine CCTV footage from Putney Bridge station showing an unidentified man, recorded roughly 20 minutes after the shooting about a mile away, using newer enhancement technology. The force said this was part of continuing inquiries and should not be read as a significant line of inquiry or as a new investigation.

Barry George is arrested; he is charged with murder days later.

The Court of Appeal dismisses George's first appeal.
The Court of Appeal quashes the conviction as unsafe and orders a retrial.
George is acquitted at the retrial.
