narrative: Hannah Graham was an 18-year-old second-year student at the University of Virginia. Her family had moved from England to the United States, and she graduated from West Potomac High School in Fairfax County in 2013. According to NBC4 Washington, she had dinner with friends on Friday, September 12, 2014, went to two off-campus parties, left the second one alone, and later sent a friend a text message saying she was lost.

Surveillance video from the early hours of September 13 showed her walking unsteadily, and at times running, past a pub and a gas station and onto Charlottesville's Downtown Mall. Footage also showed her with a man who put his arm around her. Police identified him as Jesse Leroy Matthew Jr., 32, a former taxi driver who worked as a patient technician at the University of Virginia Medical Center. Police said they had no reason to believe the two had met before.

ABC News reported that Matthew went to the Charlottesville police station with relatives but left before being questioned and drove away at speed. He was charged first with reckless driving and then with abduction with intent to defile. On September 24, 2014, Galveston County deputies arrested him on a beach on the Bolivar Peninsula in Texas, and he was returned to Virginia.

Searchers found human remains at about noon on October 18, 2014, on an abandoned property off Old Lynchburg Road in Albemarle County, roughly eight miles from where Graham was last seen. Albemarle County police announced on October 24 that the medical examiner had identified them as hers. Matthew was later charged with first-degree murder, and in May 2015 prosecutors added a capital murder charge, citing new forensic evidence.

According to NBC4 Washington, DNA obtained during the Graham investigation linked Matthew to a September 2005 attack on a 26-year-old woman in the City of Fairfax, a case that had earlier been linked by DNA to the death of Virginia Tech student Morgan Harrington, who disappeared in Charlottesville in October 2009. In the Fairfax case he entered an Alford plea in June 2015, which is not an admission of guilt, and was sentenced in October 2015 to three life terms.

On March 2, 2016, Matthew pleaded guilty to first-degree murder and abduction with intent to defile in the deaths of both Graham and Harrington. The court imposed four consecutive life sentences, and under the agreement he waived parole, appeal and geriatric release. Prosecutors withdrew the capital murder charge. Both families said they supported the agreement.

timeline.event: Hannah Graham has dinner with friends and attends two off-campus parties in Charlottesville.
She is last seen on surveillance video in the early morning on the Downtown Mall, accompanied by a man later identified as Jesse Matthew Jr.
Matthew, charged with abduction with intent to defile, is arrested on a beach in Galveston County, Texas.
Searchers find human remains on an abandoned property off Old Lynchburg Road in Albemarle County.
Police announce that the remains have been identified as Hannah Graham.
Prosecutors add a capital murder charge against Matthew in the Graham case.
Matthew enters an Alford plea in the 2005 Fairfax attack.
Matthew is sentenced to three life terms in the Fairfax case.
Matthew pleads guilty to the murders and abductions of Hannah Graham and Morgan Harrington and receives four consecutive life sentences.

name: Susan Walsh
summary: Freelance journalist Susan Walsh disappeared from her Nutley, New Jersey apartment while investigating the Russian mafia's involvement in strip clubs. She had expressed fear for her life. She was never found.
lastSeen: July 16, 1996, Nutley, New Jersey

sources.title: Disappearance of Susan Walsh - Wikipedia
Susan Walsh - Charley Project

narrative: Susan Walsh, a 36-year-old freelance journalist and former exotic dancer, vanished from her apartment in Nutley, New Jersey on July 16, 1996. Walsh had been working on investigative pieces about the Russian mafia's involvement in the strip club industry for the Village Voice and other publications. She had told friends and colleagues that she feared for her safety because of her reporting.

On the day she disappeared, Walsh was seen by her estranged husband and their young son. She left her apartment on foot, telling her husband she would return shortly. She never came back. Her car, purse, and personal belongings remained at the apartment. There were no signs of a struggle, and no witnesses reported seeing her after she left.

The investigation explored multiple theories. Walsh had been receiving threats related to her journalism work, and her reporting on Russian organized crime made her a potential target. She also had a history of drug use and had worked as a dancer, leading some to theorize she may have returned to that world. Others suggested she might have voluntarily disappeared to escape her troubled life.

Despite extensive investigation by Nutley police and attention from media outlets, Susan Walsh was never found. No body, no financial activity, no credible sightings. The case remains open and is considered one of New Jersey's most perplexing missing person cases.

timeline.event: Susan Walsh leaves her Nutley apartment on foot and vanishes.
Her estranged husband reports her missing.
Investigation reveals her work on Russian mafia stories.

name: Robert Wone
summary: Attorney Robert Wone, 32, was found stabbed to death on August 2, 2006 in the guest room of a friend's townhouse on Swann Street in Washington, D.C. No one has been charged with his murder. The three residents were acquitted in June 2010 of obstruction, conspiracy and evidence-tampering charges, and a wrongful-death suit brought by Wone's widow was settled in August 2011.
lastSeen: August 2, 2006, Swann Street NW, Washington, D.C.

sources.title: Metro Weekly - Not guilty verdict in Wone trial
DCist - Three Wone Defendants Found Not Guilty On Charges
Washington Blade - Settlement reached in Robert Wone civil case
NBC Washington - Civil Suit Settled in Robert Wone Death
Washington Blade - Wone case defendants: Where are they now?
ABA Journal - Prosecutor Seeks More Charges in Case of Murdered D.C. Area Attorney
Oxygen - The Mysterious Circumstances Of Robert Wone's Death
Watermark Out News - Gay men linked to 2006 Wone murder failing to make lawsuit settlement payment

narrative: Robert Wone, a 32-year-old lawyer, was found with fatal stab wounds on the night of August 2, 2006 in a townhouse on Swann Street NW, near Dupont Circle in Washington, D.C. According to Metro Weekly and NBC Washington, the house belonged to Joseph Price, a college friend of Wone and a local attorney, who lived there with his partner Victor Zaborsky and with Dylan Ward. Wone was staying in the second-floor guest room. Wikipedia's summary of the case, citing contemporary press reports, says he had recently become general counsel at Radio Free Asia and lived in Oakton, Virginia, with his wife Katherine.

The three residents told police that an unknown intruder had entered the house and stabbed Wone while they were in their rooms. Investigators disputed that account. According to reporting by Oxygen and the Washington Blade, Wone had three stab wounds to the chest and abdomen, no defensive injuries, and needle puncture marks on his body; the medical examiner concluded he was alive but incapacitated when stabbed. Police alleged in court filings that he had been immobilized and sexually assaulted, although the Wikipedia article notes that toxicology testing did not detect a drug. The ABA Journal reported that prosecutors believed there had been a delay between the discovery of Wone and the call to 911.

No one was charged with the killing itself. In late 2008 Price, Zaborsky and Ward were charged with obstruction of justice, and conspiracy charges followed; Price also faced an evidence-tampering count. The men chose a bench trial in D.C. Superior Court. On June 29, 2010, Judge Lynn Leibovitz found all three not guilty on every count. According to DCist and the Washington Blade, the judge said she did not believe an intruder was responsible, but that prosecutors had not proven obstruction, conspiracy or tampering beyond a reasonable doubt.

Wone's widow filed a $20 million wrongful-death suit in 2008. On August 3, 2011, her lawyers announced an out-of-court settlement on confidential terms, with payments directed to the Robert E. Wone Memorial Trust for scholarships and free legal services. The settlement involved no court finding of liability. The Washington Blade reported that, during discovery, each of the three men had declined to answer questions, citing the Fifth Amendment.

The Blade reported in 2016 that the three men had left Washington and that two had changed their surnames. A documentary series, Who Killed Robert Wone?, was released on Peacock in 2023. In 2026, according to Watermark Out News, Katherine Wone filed complaints in D.C. Superior Court alleging that Price and Zaborsky had fallen behind on installment payments owed under the settlement, with a scheduling conference set for September 22, 2026.
The homicide remains unsolved. No person has been charged with or convicted of killing Robert Wone, and the three former residents of the house were acquitted of all charges brought against them.

timeline.event: Robert Wone is found stabbed in the guest room of a Swann Street NW townhouse; a 911 call is placed late that night and he is pronounced dead shortly afterwards.
Dylan Ward is charged with obstruction of justice; Joseph Price and Victor Zaborsky are charged the following month.
Wone's widow, Katherine Wone, files a $20 million wrongful-death lawsuit against the three men.
Prosecutors seek additional charges, including conspiracy and evidence tampering.
Midway through the bench trial, Ward and Zaborsky are acquitted of evidence tampering.
Judge Lynn Leibovitz finds Price, Zaborsky and Ward not guilty of all remaining charges.
Settlement of the wrongful-death suit is announced; terms are confidential and payments go to the Robert E. Wone Memorial Trust.
The documentary series Who Killed Robert Wone? is released on Peacock.
Katherine Wone files complaints in D.C. Superior Court alleging Price and Zaborsky defaulted on settlement installments.

name: Terri Lynn Hollis
summary: Eleven-year-old Terri Lynn Hollis disappeared while riding her bicycle in Torrance, California on Thanksgiving Day 1972 and was found dead the next day in Ventura County. She had been sexually assaulted and strangled. In September 2019, Torrance police announced that genetic genealogy and DNA from exhumed remains identified Jake Edward Brown, who died in 2003, as the killer.
lastSeen: November 23, 1972, riding her bicycle in Torrance, California

sources.title: Spectrum News 1 - Cold Case Solved in Kidnap, Murder of 11-Year-Old Torrance Girl
ABC7 Los Angeles - Torrance police identify the suspect in killing of 11-year-old
The Press Democrat (AP) - Southern California cold case solved through DNA, genealogy
Police1 (AP) - Calif. cold case solved through DNA, genealogy
Oxygen - Police Say Jake Edward Brown Killed 11-Year-Old Terri Lynn Hollis In 1972
Wikipedia - Parabon NanoLabs (Terri Lynn Hollis entry)

narrative: Terri Lynn Hollis was 11 years old when she went missing from Torrance, California, on Thanksgiving Day, November 23, 1972. According to Spectrum News 1 and Oxygen, she had gone out for a bicycle ride and did not come home.

Her body was found the following day, November 24, 1972, in Ventura County. The Associated Press reported that fishermen discovered her on a cliff below Pacific Coast Highway in the Oxnard area, and that she was wearing only a T-shirt; ABC7 Los Angeles described the location as the cliffs at Point Mugu. Police said she had been sexually assaulted and strangled.

The case stayed open for close to 47 years. According to the Associated Press, investigators carried out roughly 2,000 interviews over the decades and later ran searches on the DNA evidence preserved from the crime, without finding a match.

In 2018, Torrance police turned to Parabon NanoLabs, a Virginia company that performs genetic genealogy analysis. The Associated Press reported that the company compared the crime-scene DNA profile against publicly available genealogy databases and found a relative of the unknown man, which allowed detectives to narrow their inquiry to Jake Edward Brown. Spectrum News 1 reported that Brown had also used the name Thomas Tracy Burum.

Brown had died in Arizona in 2003 and was buried there. Investigators exhumed his remains, and according to Spectrum News 1 a Florida laboratory, DNA Labs International, obtained DNA from the bones. ABC7 reported that police described the result as a match to the evidence collected from Terri, with odds of roughly one in 20 septillion of a coincidental match. ABC7 and the Associated Press reported that Brown had arrests for narcotics, robbery and two rapes that occurred after the 1972 killing.

Torrance Police Chief Eve Irvine announced the finding at a news conference on September 11, 2019, and said the case was solved. Because Brown died 16 years before he was identified, he was never charged or tried, and the conclusion rests on the police investigation and DNA comparison rather than a court verdict. Terri's brother, Randy Hollis, spoke at the announcement and said he wished their parents had lived to see the day. Police said they were examining whether Brown could be connected to other unsolved crimes.

timeline.event: Terri Lynn Hollis, 11, disappears on Thanksgiving Day after going for a bicycle ride in Torrance.
Fishermen find her body on a cliff below Pacific Coast Highway in Ventura County; she had been sexually assaulted and strangled.
Jake Edward Brown dies in Arizona.
Parabon NanoLabs performs genetic genealogy analysis on the crime-scene DNA and finds a relative of the source in a public database.
Brown's remains are exhumed in Arizona and DNA from his bones is matched to the evidence.
Torrance Police Chief Eve Irvine announces that Brown has been identified as the killer and that the case is solved.

name: Sherri Rasmussen
summary: Hospital nursing supervisor Sherri Rasmussen was beaten and shot in her home. The case went cold for 23 years until DNA from a bite wound matched LAPD detective Stephanie Lazarus, who had been Sherri's husband's ex-girlfriend. Lazarus was convicted in 2012.
lastSeen: February 24, 1986, Van Nuys, Los Angeles, California

sources.title: Murder of Sherri Rasmussen - Wikipedia

narrative: On February 24, 1986, Sherri Rasmussen, a 29-year-old hospital nursing supervisor, was found beaten and shot to death in the condominium she shared with her husband John Ruetten in Van Nuys, Los Angeles. The scene was staged to look like a burglary, with items strewn about and a stereo stacked by the door. Sherri had been beaten severely, bitten on the arm, and shot three times with a .38 caliber revolver.

The investigation initially focused on two men seen near the home, and the case was classified as a burglary-homicide. However, Sherri's father repeatedly told detectives that an LAPD officer named Stephanie Lazarus—Ruetten's ex-girlfriend—had been harassing Sherri before the murder and had even confronted her at the hospital. These leads were not aggressively pursued, and the case went cold.

In 2004, cold case detective Jim Nuttall reopened the file and noticed the bite mark evidence had never been tested for DNA. When the DNA was finally analyzed, it matched a female profile in the California DNA database: LAPD detective Stephanie Lazarus, who had been on the force for over 20 years by that time. Investigators secretly obtained a fresh DNA sample from a cup Lazarus discarded and confirmed the match.

Lazarus was arrested in June 2009 in a carefully orchestrated confrontation at Parker Center. The dramatic arrest of an active-duty LAPD detective shocked the department. At trial in 2012, Lazarus was convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to 27 years to life. The case became a landmark example of how DNA evidence can solve decades-old crimes and exposed troubling questions about whether Lazarus's position as an LAPD officer had shielded her from earlier investigation.

timeline.event: Sherri Rasmussen is found beaten and shot in her Van Nuys home.
Case classified as burglary-homicide; goes cold.
Cold case detective reopens file; orders DNA testing of bite mark.
LAPD detective Stephanie Lazarus is arrested for the murder.
Lazarus is convicted of first-degree murder; sentenced to 27 years to life.

name: Dorothy Forstein
summary: Dorothy Forstein, the wife of Philadelphia magistrate Jules Forstein, disappeared from her home on the night of October 18, 1949. Her young daughter said she saw a man in a brown cap carry her unconscious mother out of the house. Police found no forced entry, no fingerprints and nothing stolen. Forstein had survived a severe beating at home in 1945. She was never found.
lastSeen: October 18, 1949, at her home in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania

sources.title: Wikipedia - Disappearance of Dorothy Forstein
Strange Outdoors - The strange disappearance of Dorothy Forstein
Strange Company - The Strange Disappearance of Dorothy Forstein
Missing Persons Commentary - Dorothy Forstein, Missing Since 1949

narrative: Dorothy Forstein, born Dorothy Cooper in 1909, lived in Philadelphia with her husband, Jules Forstein, a city magistrate, and their children. Most of what is known about her case comes from newspaper coverage in October 1949 and from later retellings, notably Jay Robert Nash's book Among the Missing, which Wikipedia cites as a principal source.

Several years before she vanished, Forstein was attacked at home. Later accounts, including one that cites a Camden Courier-Post report of January 26, 1945, date the assault to late January 1945. According to those accounts she was left with a concussion, a broken nose and jaw and a fractured shoulder, and could not identify the person who struck her. Nothing was taken from the house, and no one was charged.

On the evening of October 18, 1949, Jules Forstein was out, and according to Wikipedia he telephoned his wife to say he would be home late. When he returned, Dorothy was gone and two of the children, Marcy and Edward, were together in a bedroom in distress. Marcy, who later accounts say was nine, told her father that a noise had woken her and that she had seen a middle-aged man in a brown peaked cap carrying her mother over his shoulder. She said the man told her to go back to sleep and that her mother was all right.

Wikipedia, citing the Milwaukee Journal of October 24, 1949, says police found no fingerprints and no sign of forced entry, and that nothing had been stolen. Investigators at first doubted the child's story but came to accept it after she was interviewed by a psychiatrist. Their initial theory was that someone with a grudge connected to the magistrate's work had targeted his wife, in view of the earlier assault.

The search was extended across the country. According to an Associated Press report in the Reading Eagle of October 26, 1949, cited by Wikipedia, Captain James Kelly of the Philadelphia detective bureau sent about 10,000 notices describing Forstein to police departments and institutions, and hospitals, hotels, morgues and convalescent homes were asked to check for unidentified women.

No trace of Dorothy Forstein was found, and no suspect was ever publicly identified. Later accounts state that Jules Forstein died in the mid-1950s and that she was subsequently declared legally dead; these details come from secondary sources and their exact dates differ between accounts. The disappearance remains unexplained.

timeline.event: Dorothy Cooper is born (per Wikipedia).
Forstein is severely beaten by an unidentified attacker at her Philadelphia home; nothing is stolen.
Forstein disappears from her home at night; her daughter reports seeing a man carry her out.
Newspapers including the Milwaukee Journal and Chicago Tribune report the disappearance and fears of an abduction.
The Associated Press reports a nationwide search, with some 10,000 notices sent out by Philadelphia detectives.
By this time Jules Forstein has died; later accounts say Dorothy was declared legally dead seven years after she vanished.

name: Diane Augat
summary: Diane Augat, 40, walked away from a home in Pasco County, Florida, on April 10, 1998 and has not been found. Days later the severed tip of one of her fingers was discovered beside U.S. 19 in Hudson and matched to her by fingerprint. Her mother also received a brief answering-machine message in which she called for help. The Pasco County Sheriff's Office still lists the case as open.
lastSeen: April 10, 1998, leaving a residence in Pasco County, Florida (Hudson/Odessa area); reported sighting on U.S. 19 in Hudson on April 11

sources.title: The Charley Project - Diane Louise Augat (archived copy)
Patch - Search For Pasco Woman Continues 19 Years Later
Crime Junkie Podcast - MISSING: Diane Louise Augat (episode page and source list)

narrative: Diane Louise Augat was 40 years old when she disappeared from Pasco County, on Florida's Gulf coast north of Tampa. According to the Charley Project, she was last seen leaving a residence at about 11 a.m. on April 10, 1998. Sources differ on the address: the Charley Project gives Chesapeake Drive in Odessa, while Pasco County detectives quoted by Patch in 2017 said she left a home on Cobblestone Drive in Hudson. Her mother reported her missing the following day.

The Charley Project states that Augat had been diagnosed with bipolar disorder in the late 1980s, had been released from a mental health facility a few weeks earlier, and did not have her medication with her when she left. A witness reported seeing her walking north along U.S. 19 near New York Avenue in Hudson on April 11.

On April 13, according to the Charley Project, a call reached her mother's answering machine while no one was home. In the recording Augat asked for help and asked to be let out, and the call ended after what sounded like someone trying to take the phone from her. Caller ID showed the name of a business in the Odessa area; when her mother rang the number back, nobody answered.

On April 15, 1998, the severed tip of Augat's right middle finger was found on the roadside along U.S. 19 in Hudson, in the same area as the reported sighting. Fingerprint analysis confirmed it was hers, Pasco detectives told Patch. About two weeks after she was reported missing, a bag holding her neatly folded clothing was found in the outdoor freezer of a convenience store in Odessa. In 2000, a day after a local newspaper story on the case, a plastic bag labeled "Diane" and containing cosmetics and toothpaste was found at another convenience store in Pasco County; the Charley Project notes investigators could not confirm the items were hers.

No one has been charged in connection with her disappearance. The Charley Project reports that authorities believe foul play is likely. Cold-case detectives at the Pasco County Sheriff's Office renewed their appeal for information in 2017, and Crime Stoppers of Tampa Bay offered a reward of up to $3,000, according to Patch. Augat has not been located and the case remains unsolved.

timeline.event: Diane Louise Augat is born.
A bag of her folded clothing is found in a convenience store's outdoor freezer in Odessa.
Augat leaves a residence in Pasco County, Florida, at about 11 a.m. and does not return.
Her mother reports her missing; a witness reports seeing her walking north on U.S. 19 in Hudson.
A call from Augat asking for help is recorded on her mother's answering machine, according to the Charley Project.
The severed tip of her right middle finger is found beside U.S. 19 in Hudson and later matched by fingerprint.
A plastic bag labeled "Diane" containing toiletries is found at a Pasco County convenience store; investigators cannot confirm it is hers.
Patch reports that Pasco County cold-case detectives are seeking new leads and that a reward is offered.

name: Springfield Jane Doe
summary: The nude body of a young woman was found wrapped in a shower curtain in a ditch in Springfield Township, Pennsylvania. Despite distinctive physical features and evidence of pregnancy, she has never been identified.
lastSeen: Unknown
narrative: On February 7, 1976, the nude body of a young woman was found in a ditch along a rural road in Springfield Township, Mercer County, Pennsylvania. She was wrapped in a floral shower curtain and had been dead for several days. The woman appeared to be between 17 and 25 years old, approximately 5'2" tall, and had been approximately six months pregnant at the time of her death.

Autopsy determined she had been strangled. She had brown hair and brown eyes, and her teeth showed some dental work. Despite extensive efforts to identify her through dental records, fingerprints, and public appeals, no match was ever found. The case was featured in local and regional media, but no one came forward to identify her.

Over the decades, investigators have pursued numerous leads and compared her description to missing persons reports from across the country. Forensic artist reconstructions were created and widely distributed. DNA was eventually extracted from the remains and submitted to genealogy databases.

The Springfield Jane Doe case remains one of Pennsylvania's oldest unidentified person cases. Her killer has never been identified, and the mystery of who she was—and who killed her and her unborn child—continues to haunt investigators.

timeline.event: Body of unidentified woman found in a ditch in Springfield Township, Pennsylvania.
Autopsy determines cause of death as strangulation; she was six months pregnant.
Extensive but unsuccessful efforts to identify her begin.

name: Janet Lee Lucas (formerly "Christy Crystal Creek")
summary: Skeletal remains of a woman with two gunshot wounds to the skull were found by a bear hunter in the Crystal Creek drainage near Missoula, Montana, in September 1985. Known for decades as "Christy Crystal Creek," she was identified in May 2021 through forensic genetic genealogy as Janet Lee Lucas, 23, of Spokane, Washington. No one was ever charged with her death.
lastSeen: Summer 1983, Sandpoint, Idaho

sources.title: DNASolves (Othram) - Christy Crystal Creek / Janet L. Lucas
Helena Independent Record - In search of Christy's true identity (archived)
Wikipedia - Wayne Nance

narrative: In September 1985, a hunter tracking a bear came across scattered human bones on a hillside in the Crystal Creek drainage east of Missoula, Montana. According to the forensic laboratory Othram and the Helena Independent Record, the remains were those of a small woman, about five feet tall and roughly 100 pounds, with brown wavy hair. Her skull had two close-range .32 calibre bullet wounds. The Missoula County Sheriff's Office opened the matter as case number 8509102.

With no name to attach to her, investigators called the woman "Christy Crystal Creek." The site was one drainage over from Deer Creek, where the body of another unidentified young woman, nicknamed "Debbie Deer Creek," had been found on December 24, 1984. That woman was identified in 2006 as Marcella Bachmann, a 16-year-old from Vancouver, Washington, through DNA work at the University of North Texas, the Independent Record reported.

Identification of the Crystal Creek remains proved much harder. A 2006 Independent Record article described the work of Sydney Bacon, a University of Montana forensic anthropology graduate who studied the skeleton for her master's thesis. Bacon noted extensive and distinctive dental work, including fillings in most teeth and two root canals, and said the care appeared to have stopped about a year before death. Repeated checks against dental records in national databases produced no match. Early estimates put the woman's age at 18 to 21, and examiners thought she might have had both Caucasian and Asian ancestry; both assessments later turned out to be inaccurate.

According to Othram, the case was entered in NamUs as UP10760. With funding from the Montana Department of Justice's Sexual Assault Kit Initiative, the sheriff's cold case unit sent skeletal material to Othram, which produced a DNA profile suitable for genealogy. Investigators, including Special Deputies Susan Lane and Diana Parker, researched family trees of DNA relatives and confirmed the result by testing a relative. In May 2021 the woman was identified as Janet Lee Lucas, 23, of Spokane, Washington, who had last been seen in Sandpoint, Idaho, in the summer of 1983.

No one has been charged in Lucas's death. Investigators have long regarded Wayne Nance, an East Missoula man, as the suspected killer, according to the Independent Record and Othram. Nance was shot dead in 1986 by a homeowner during an attack on a couple in their house, and he was never tried for or convicted of any killing. The link to Lucas is a suspicion held by investigators and has not been proven in court.
How and when Lucas came to Montana is not known, according to Wikipedia's summary of the case.

timeline.event: Janet Lee Lucas, 23, of Spokane, Washington, is last seen in Sandpoint, Idaho, during the summer.
The body of another unidentified young woman, later identified as Marcella Bachmann, is found in the nearby Deer Creek drainage.
A bear hunter finds skeletal remains with two gunshot wounds to the skull in the Crystal Creek drainage near Missoula.
Wayne Nance, later regarded by investigators as the suspected killer, is shot dead by a homeowner during a home invasion.
Bachmann is identified through DNA; attention turns to identifying the Crystal Creek remains, studied by forensic anthropologist Sydney Bacon.
The Missoula County Sheriff's Office and Othram announce that the remains are those of Janet Lee Lucas, identified through forensic genetic genealogy.

name: Paula Jean Welden
summary: Bennington College sophomore Paula Welden went for a hike on the Long Trail near Bennington, Vermont and was never seen again. Her disappearance was the most prominent in a series called the 'Bennington Triangle' disappearances and led to the creation of the Vermont State Police.
lastSeen: December 1, 1946, Long Trail, near Bennington, Vermont

sources.title: Disappearance of Paula Jean Welden - Wikipedia
Paula Welden - Charley Project

narrative: On the afternoon of Sunday, December 1, 1946, 18-year-old Paula Jean Welden, a sophomore at Bennington College in southwestern Vermont, told her roommate she was going for a walk. She was last seen on the Long Trail near Route 9, heading toward Glastenbury Mountain. A couple hiking the trail saw her round a bend in the path ahead of them, and when they reached the same spot moments later, she had vanished.

Despite immediate and extensive search efforts—eventually involving hundreds of volunteers, state police, FBI, and even the Army—no trace of Paula was found. No clothing, no footprints leading off the trail, no evidence of an accident or foul play. The search was hampered by approaching winter weather and the dense, rugged terrain of the Green Mountains.

Paula was described as a bright, attractive young woman who had seemed somewhat preoccupied in the days before her disappearance. Her father, an engineer in Stamford, Connecticut, was critical of the Vermont authorities' response, which he considered inadequate and poorly coordinated. His criticism, combined with public pressure, led directly to the creation of the Vermont State Police in 1947.

Paula Welden's disappearance was later grouped with several other unsolved vanishings in the Bennington area between 1945 and 1950, a pattern that author Joseph Citro dubbed the 'Bennington Triangle.' These included the disappearances of Middie Rivers (1945), James Tedford (1949), Paul Jepson (1950), and Frieda Langer (1950, the only one found—months later, though the cause of death could not be determined). No connection between the cases was ever established, and Paula's fate remains unknown.

timeline.event: Paula Welden goes for a hike on the Long Trail and vanishes.
Search parties begin combing the trail and surrounding wilderness.
FBI joins the investigation at the family's request.
Vermont State Police is created partly in response to the case.

name: Charlie Brewer
summary: Charlie Brewer disappeared after attending a party in Raleigh, North Carolina. His car was found days later parked at the Raleigh-Durham Airport. Despite extensive investigation, he was never found.
lastSeen: December 4, 1999, Raleigh, North Carolina
narrative: On the night of December 4, 1999, 26-year-old Charlie Brewer attended a holiday party at an apartment complex in Raleigh, North Carolina. He had been drinking and was reportedly in good spirits. He was last seen leaving the party late that night. He did not return to his own apartment.

Several days later, Charlie's car was found parked at the Raleigh-Durham International Airport. However, there was no record of Charlie purchasing a plane ticket or boarding any flight. The car's location raised the possibility that someone else had driven it there to create a false trail.

The investigation explored multiple theories, including voluntary disappearance, suicide, and foul play. Charlie's bank accounts were never accessed, and he made no contact with family or friends. Searches of areas near the party location and the airport yielded nothing.

Charlie Brewer's family has continued to seek answers, keeping his case in the public eye through social media and local news coverage. The Raleigh Police Department maintains the case as an open missing person investigation.

timeline.event: Charlie Brewer attends a party in Raleigh and disappears.
His car is found at Raleigh-Durham Airport with no travel record.
Raleigh police begin formal missing person investigation.

name: Steven Damman
summary: Two-year-old Steven Damman was taken from his stroller outside a Long Island bakery on Halloween 1955. His mother had left him briefly with his baby sister. Despite FBI involvement and national attention, Steven was never found.
lastSeen: October 31, 1955, East Meadow, Long Island, New York

sources.title: Disappearance of Steven Damman - Wikipedia

narrative: On the afternoon of October 31, 1955—Halloween—Marilyn Damman left her two-year-old son Steven and seven-month-old daughter Pamela in a stroller outside a bakery on Hempstead Turnpike in East Meadow, Long Island, New York while she went inside to make a purchase. When she returned minutes later, Steven was gone. Pamela was still in the stroller, unharmed.

The abduction made national headlines and prompted an intensive search. The FBI joined the investigation due to the possibility of kidnapping. Hundreds of tips poured in, and sightings were reported across the country, but none led to Steven. The case became one of the most publicized child abductions of the 1950s.

In 2009, the FBI examined the case again after John Barnes of Kalkaska, Michigan came forward believing he might be Steven Damman. DNA testing, however, conclusively ruled him out. The investigation continued to pursue other leads without success.

Steven Damman's disappearance occurred during an era of relative innocence when leaving children unattended briefly was common. The case helped change attitudes about child safety and contributed to growing awareness of the danger of child abduction. Marilyn Damman spent the rest of her life hoping for Steven's return and died in 2019 without ever learning his fate.

timeline.event: Steven Damman is taken from a stroller outside a bakery in East Meadow, Long Island.
FBI joins the investigation; national search begins.
FBI DNA testing rules out Michigan man John Barnes as Steven Damman.

name: Deysi Garcia
summary: Deysi Garcia, a 28-year-old Honduran immigrant, vanished from San Francisco's Mission District. She was last seen leaving her workplace. Despite community efforts, she has never been found.
lastSeen: October 20, 2010, Mission District, San Francisco, California
narrative: On October 20, 2010, 28-year-old Deysi Garcia left her workplace in San Francisco's Mission District and vanished. She was a Honduran immigrant who worked in the food service industry and lived in the city. She had spoken to family members that day and gave no indication of plans to leave or any concerns for her safety.

When Deysi failed to return home, her family and community raised the alarm. The Mission District, a vibrant and densely populated neighborhood, was canvassed by police and volunteers. Flyers were distributed in both English and Spanish throughout the area. Her case gained attention from immigrant advocacy groups who highlighted the vulnerability of undocumented workers.

Investigators explored theories including foul play, voluntary disappearance, and the possibility that immigration concerns might have prevented witnesses from coming forward. Deysi's bank accounts showed no activity after her disappearance, and her phone went silent.

Deysi Garcia's case is representative of the many missing person cases involving immigrants in large American cities, where language barriers, immigration status fears, and limited family connections can make investigations more difficult. Her case remains open with the San Francisco Police Department.

timeline.event: Deysi Garcia is last seen leaving her workplace in the Mission District.
She is reported missing by family members.
Community distributes flyers; SFPD investigates.

name: Emma Fillipoff
summary: Emma Fillipoff, 26, was last seen on the evening of November 28, 2012, barefoot outside the Empress Hotel in Victoria, British Columbia. Police officers called to the scene spoke with her at length and let her continue on her way; she was reported missing hours later. Victoria police say hundreds of tips have produced no confirmed sighting, and the case remains open.
lastSeen: November 28, 2012, outside the Empress Hotel, Victoria, British Columbia

sources.title: CTV News Vancouver Island (archived) - New Emma Fillipoff photos released on 9-year anniversary of her disappearance
Vice - A Young Woman Was Last Seen by Police, Then Never Again
Victoria Buzz - Emma Fillipoff disappeared 3 years ago, man of interest still unidentified
CTV News Ottawa - Mother of Perth, Ont. woman who disappeared in B.C. 10 years ago hopes new sketch helps find daughter
Wikipedia - Disappearance of Emma Fillipoff

narrative: Emma Fillipoff grew up in Perth, Ontario, and moved to Victoria, British Columbia, in the fall of 2011. According to Victoria Buzz, she went west to pursue art, poetry and photography while supporting herself with restaurant work. By November 2012 she was staying at the Sandy Merriman House women's shelter, Vice reported.

Her mother, Shelley Fillipoff, booked a flight to Victoria after a distressed phone call from Emma on November 27, 2012, according to Vice. Wikipedia's account, drawing on local reporting, says that on November 28 Emma bought a prepaid mobile phone and a prepaid card at a convenience store, and that evening got into a taxi bound for the airport but got out again shortly afterwards; these details rest on Wikipedia alone.

At about 7 p.m. that evening, a man who found her barefoot near the Empress Hotel called police, Vice reported. Victoria police later said they had received calls about a woman behaving oddly in front of the hotel. Officers spoke with her for more than 40 minutes and, according to the department, were satisfied as to her well-being before she continued on her way. Her mother arrived at the shelter later that night, and Emma was reported missing within hours. She has not been seen or heard from since.

Police searched her red Mazda MPV van, which Wikipedia says was parked at the Chateau Victoria hotel garage. Inside were her passport, laptop, camera, journals and other belongings, according to Vice.

In May 2014, security cameras at a clothing store in Vancouver's Gastown district recorded a man carrying one of the reward posters her mother had distributed. The store owner said the man claimed Emma was his girlfriend and wanted to be left alone, Victoria Buzz reported. Police were unable to identify him. According to Wikipedia, a witness account led to a search of an area near Esquimalt in December 2018, which found nothing, and an updated sketch was released around the tenth anniversary in 2022.

On the ninth anniversary in November 2021, Victoria police released additional photographs of Emma and said that an extensive investigation had not determined what happened to her. The department said it had received hundreds of tips but had confirmed no sightings, CTV News reported. The case was the subject of an episode of CBC's The Fifth Estate and has been covered by several podcasts. Anyone with information is asked to call Victoria police at 250-995-7654.

name: Heidi Allen
summary: Eighteen-year-old Heidi Allen disappeared from the D&W Convenience Store in New Haven, New York, where she was working alone on Easter Sunday, April 3, 1994. Gary Thibodeau was convicted of kidnapping her in 1995 and died in prison in 2018 maintaining his innocence; his brother Richard was tried separately and found not guilty. Heidi has never been found.
lastSeen: April 3, 1994, D&W Convenience Store, New Haven, New York

sources.title: WRVO Public Media - Gary Thibodeau, convicted of kidnapping Heidi Allen in 1994, dead at 63
WRVO Public Media - Gary Thibodeau loses state appeal for new trial in Heidi Allen case
WRVO Public Media - Renewed Heidi Allen search opens door for convicted kidnapper to have case overturned
WRVO Public Media - Gary Thibodeau to get another chance to appeal his conviction in Heidi Allen case
CNY Central - Marking 30 years since Heidi Marie Allen's mysterious disappearance from Oswego County
CNY Central - Richard Thibodeau, brother of man convicted in 1994 kidnapping of Heidi Allen, passes away

Wikipedia - Murder conviction without a body (Heidi Allen entry)

narrative: Heidi Marie Allen, 18, worked at the D&W Convenience Store at the junction of State Routes 104 and 104B in New Haven, a town in Oswego County, New York. According to CNY Central, she opened the store alone at about 5:45 a.m. on Easter Sunday, April 3, 1994. At about 7:55 a.m. the store was reported to be unattended. She was last seen wearing a gray Syracuse University sweatshirt and white sneakers.

WRVO reported that hundreds of volunteers, police officers and military personnel searched for her, without result. Some months later, brothers Gary and Richard Thibodeau were arrested and charged with kidnapping. They were tried separately. Gary Thibodeau was convicted in June 1995 and sentenced to 25 years to life. Richard Thibodeau was found not guilty that September.

Gary Thibodeau maintained his innocence throughout his imprisonment. In 2014 his federal public defender, Lisa Peebles, filed a motion to vacate the conviction, citing what she described as newly discovered evidence that three other men were responsible, and arguing that material had been withheld from the defence at trial, including information that Allen had acted as a drug informant. Around the same time investigators searched the site of a collapsed cabin in the town of Mexico, New York. Oswego County District Attorney Greg Oakes said no evidence had been found to suggest a wrongful conviction. None of the three men named by the defence was charged in the case.

After more than a year of hearings, an Oswego County judge denied the request for a new trial in 2016, finding the new evidence not credible enough. The appellate division agreed to hear an appeal, and the case reached the New York Court of Appeals. On June 14, 2018, that court ruled 4-3 against a new trial; the majority described the new evidence as uncorroborated hearsay, while the dissent called the original trial evidence not overwhelming.

Gary Thibodeau died on August 12, 2018, at Coxsackie Correctional Facility, aged 63, after a chronic lung illness. His lawyer said a planned federal appeal would not go ahead. Richard Thibodeau died in early January 2024, aged 77.

Heidi Allen has never been found. CNY Central reported that the Oswego County Sheriff's Office has kept her missing person case open and continues to ask for information. Her family marked the 30th anniversary of her disappearance in April 2024 with a vigil at the New Haven Fire Department, where the first vigil had been held in 1994.

name: Lisanne Froon & Kris Kremers
summary: Two Dutch tourists disappeared while hiking near Boquete, Panama. Their backpack was found weeks later with phones, camera, and disturbing nighttime photos. Skeletal remains were found months later. Whether they died from misadventure or foul play is unknown.
lastSeen: April 1, 2014, Pianista trail, Boquete, Panama

sources.title: Deaths of Kris Kremers and Lisanne Froon - Wikipedia
Lost in the Jungle - Daily Beast

narrative: On April 1, 2014, Kris Kremers (21) and Lisanne Froon (22), two Dutch women volunteering in Boquete, Panama, set out for a day hike on the popular Pianista trail near the continental divide. Photos from Lisanne's camera show them reaching the summit of the trail around 1:00 p.m. and then continuing beyond the marked path into more remote terrain. They were never seen alive again.

Phone records show that at 4:39 p.m. that day, Kris's phone made an emergency call to 112 (the European emergency number) and then to 911 (the Panamanian number). Lisanne's phone made a similar call shortly after. None of the calls connected—the area had extremely limited cell coverage. Over the following days, more emergency calls were attempted from both phones, but none went through. The phones' batteries were gradually depleted, with Kris's phone dying on April 5 and Lisanne's being periodically turned on until April 11.

Ten weeks later, Lisanne's backpack was found on a riverbank by a local woman. Inside were the phones, Lisanne's camera, cash, and their passports—none of which had been taken. The camera contained 90 photos taken in darkness between 1:00 and 4:00 a.m. on April 8, showing jungle vegetation, rocks, and what appeared to be scraps of material. Some interpreted these as distress signals; others as attempts to use the flash as a light source.

Skeletal remains of both women were found over subsequent months along the same river system. Some bones showed signs of bleaching inconsistent with the timeline, and a foot was found inside a boot still laced up, raising questions. The official Panamanian conclusion was that the women became lost and died of exposure, starvation, or a fall. Dutch investigators were unable to rule out foul play. The case has generated intense online debate about whether their deaths were accidental or criminal.

timeline.event: Kris Kremers and Lisanne Froon set out for a hike on the Pianista trail.

name: José & Kitty Menéndez
summary: José and Kitty Menéndez were shot dead in their Beverly Hills home on August 20, 1989, by their sons Lyle and Erik, who were convicted of first-degree murder in 1996 and sentenced to life without parole. In May 2025 a judge resentenced them to 50 years to life. Both were denied parole in August 2025; a new hearing is tentatively set for March 2027.
lastSeen: August 20, 1989, at their home in Beverly Hills, California

sources.title: ABC News - Menendez brothers granted early parole suitability hearing for March 2027
ABC News - Erik Menendez denied parole, Lyle Menendez to learn his fate on Friday
NBC Los Angeles - Live updates: Lyle Menendez denied parole
The Guardian - California judge resentences Menendez brothers to be eligible for parole
ABC News - Menendez brothers latest: LA district attorney recommends resentencing
Wikipedia - Lyle and Erik Menendez

narrative: José Menéndez, 45, an entertainment executive, and his wife Mary Louise, known as Kitty, 47, were shot to death at their home in Beverly Hills, California, on August 20, 1989. According to ABC News, their sons Lyle, then 21, and Erik, then 18, carried out the killings with shotguns bought a few days earlier. Wikipedia's account of the case gives the parents' ages and states that both were shot multiple times.

The brothers were not arrested for several months. Wikipedia dates Lyle's arrest to March 8, 1990, and says Erik surrendered three days later after returning from a tennis tournament abroad. At their first trial, which began in 1993, the brothers admitted the shootings but said they had acted in fear after years of sexual, physical and emotional abuse by their father. Prosecutors argued the motive was the family's wealth. Separate juries for each brother could not agree, and mistrials were declared in January 1994.

At a second trial that began in 1995, the judge excluded much of the abuse evidence, ABC News reported. In March 1996 both brothers were convicted of first-degree murder, and each received two consecutive sentences of life without the possibility of parole. Their appeals over the following years were unsuccessful.

Interest in the case revived in the 2020s. On October 24, 2024, Los Angeles County District Attorney George Gascón recommended resentencing. ABC News reported that the material under review included a letter Erik is said to have written to a cousin months before the killings describing abuse, and an allegation by a former member of the band Menudo that José Menéndez had abused him. Gascón's successor, Nathan Hochman, opposed resentencing, saying the brothers had not taken full responsibility, and his office twice tried to withdraw the request, according to The Guardian.

On May 13, 2025, Judge Michael Jesic reduced the sentences to 50 years to life, which made the brothers eligible for parole under California's youthful offender law because they were under 26 at the time of the crime. The judge said that the decision on release was not his to make but that they had earned the chance to seek it.

The Board of Parole Hearings denied parole to Erik on August 21, 2025, and to Lyle on August 22, each for three years. ABC News reported that the panel cited prison rule violations, including the use of contraband cellphones, and found a continuing risk to public safety. In September 2026 ABC News reported that both brothers had been granted an earlier parole suitability hearing, tentatively set for March 2027 rather than August 2028. Both remain in prison. Clemency from the governor remains a separate possible route.

name: Maëlys de Araujo
summary: Eight-year-old Maëlys de Araujo disappeared from a wedding party in Pont-de-Beauvoisin, in the French Alps, in the early hours of August 27, 2017. Wedding guest Nordahl Lelandais, a former soldier, led investigators to her remains in February 2018. On February 18, 2022, a court in Grenoble sentenced him to life in prison, with a 22-year minimum, for her abduction and murder.
lastSeen: August 27, 2017, at a wedding party in Pont-de-Beauvoisin, Isère, France

sources.title: France 24 - Former French soldier sentenced to life in prison for abduction, murder of 8-year-old
France 24 - Remains found of girl who disappeared at French wedding
France 24 - Girl 'got into my car', says French wedding kidnap suspect
The Local France - The story of the missing 9-year-old French girl and the suspect who still denies everything
KSAT / Associated Press - French court finds former soldier guilty of child's murder
Wikipedia - Murder of Maëlys de Araujo

narrative: Maëlys de Araujo went missing in the early hours of Sunday, August 27, 2017, while attending a wedding party with her family at a community hall in Pont-de-Beauvoisin, a town near Chambéry in south-eastern France. Most contemporary news reports gave her age as nine; Wikipedia gives her date of birth as November 5, 2008, which would make her eight at the time.

According to France 24, the search that followed lasted about a week and involved police, rescue teams, divers and cavers. Sniffer dogs followed the child's scent but lost it in the venue's car park. Investigators questioned the wedding guests, and attention turned to Nordahl Lelandais, a 34-year-old local man and former soldier who had been at the party.

France 24 reported in early September 2017 that Lelandais was placed under formal investigation for kidnapping and illegal confinement after traces of the girl's DNA were found on the dashboard of his car, which he had cleaned the day after the wedding. He told investigators that the girl and another child had briefly got into the car to see whether his dogs were there and had then gone back to the hall. The Local reported that he was additionally charged with murder on November 30, 2017, and that investigators relied on enhanced CCTV images showing a small figure in a white dress in the passenger seat of his car as it left the venue, and on records showing his phone had been switched to airplane mode for 39 minutes around the time she vanished. He continued to deny involvement.

On February 14, 2018, according to France 24, Lelandais asked to be questioned by the investigating judges after traces of the child's blood were found in the boot of his car. He admitted killing her, saying it had been unintentional, and led investigators to a snow-covered ravine where her skull and other remains were recovered. He did not explain at that time how she had died.

In a separate case, Lelandais was sentenced in May 2021 to 20 years in prison for the killing of Arthur Noyer, a 23-year-old army corporal who disappeared in April 2017 after hitchhiking near Chambéry, France 24 reported.

His trial for the abduction and murder of Maëlys was held before the Isère assize court in Grenoble and lasted about three weeks. The Associated Press reported that he admitted in court to taking the girl in his car and striking her several times, while maintaining that he had not meant to kill her. On February 18, 2022, the court found him guilty and sentenced him to life imprisonment with a minimum of 22 years to be served. According to the Associated Press, he was also found guilty of sexually assaulting two young cousins, aged four and six. France 24 reported that prosecutors reopened several other unsolved disappearances in the region but that no evidence had linked him to them.

name: Yuba County Five
summary: Five young men from the Yuba City area disappeared after attending a basketball game in Chico in February 1978. Their car was found abandoned on a remote mountain road in Plumas National Forest. That June, Ted Weiher was found dead in a Forest Service trailer about 19 miles from the car and the remains of three others were found in the surrounding forest; Gary Mathias was never found.
lastSeen: February 24, 1978, Oroville, California

sources.title: Yuba County Five - Wikipedia

narrative: On the evening of February 24, 1978, five young men from Yuba City, California—Jack Madruga (30), Bill Sterling (29), Ted Weiher (32), Jack Huett (24), and Gary Mathias (25)—drove together to watch a college basketball game at California State University, Chico. They were all described as intellectually disabled or living with mental health conditions, and they were close friends who played on a Special Olympics basketball team. They were in good spirits and planned to return home that night.

The men never returned. Their Mercury Montego was found days later, abandoned on a remote dirt road near Oroville, approximately 70 miles from the basketball game—in the opposite direction from their home in Yuba City. The car was in working condition with gas in the tank, parked on a snowy mountain road at an elevation of approximately 4,000 feet. There was no logical reason for the men to have driven to this remote location.

The search for the five men was hampered by heavy snow. In June 1978, as the snow melted, the bodies of Ted Weiher, Jack Madruga, Bill Sterling, and Jack Huett were found. Madruga and Sterling were found about 11 miles from the car, apparently having died of hypothermia. Weiher was found inside a Forest Service trailer about 19 miles from the car, and Huett's remains were found about two miles from the trailer, along with evidence that someone had survived in the trailer for an extended period—up to 13 weeks. The trailer contained canned food, matches, and heavy clothing, but the food was barely touched. Weiher had been wrapped in bedsheets and had lost significant weight.

Gary Mathias, the fifth man—and the only one with outdoor survival experience as an Army veteran—was never found. His shoes were discovered in the trailer, but no other trace of him has surfaced. The central mystery remains: why did the men drive to this remote location, and why didn't they use the ample supplies in the trailer to survive? The case has been called 'America's Dyatlov Pass' for its parallels to the Russian mystery.

name: Suzanne Bombardier
summary: Suzanne Bombardier, 14, was abducted in June 1980 while babysitting at her sister's home in Antioch, California; a fisherman found her body in the San Joaquin River days later. She had been raped and stabbed. After a DNA match, Mitchell Lynn Bacom was arrested on December 11, 2017. A jury convicted him of first-degree murder on March 15, 2022, and he was sentenced to life without parole.
lastSeen: June 21, 1980, her sister's home in Antioch, California

sources.title: Contra Costa County District Attorney - Mitchell Bacom Murder Conviction
CBS News Bay Area - Antioch Man Convicted In 1980 Cold Case Rape, Murder of 14-Year-Old
ABC7 News - Antioch police say DNA tech helped solve city's oldest open cold case

Wikipedia - Murder of Suzanne Bombardier

narrative: Suzanne Arlene Bombardier was a 14-year-old junior high school student in Antioch, California. On the night of June 21, 1980, she was babysitting her young nieces at the home of her older sister, Stephanie Mullen, in Antioch. According to Wikipedia's summary of local reporting, her sister came home at about 4 a.m. and found that Suzanne was gone. ABC7 News reported that the home was on Hudson Court.

Several days later a fisherman found her body in the San Joaquin River east of the Antioch Bridge. Wikipedia gives the date as June 27, 1980. According to the Contra Costa County District Attorney's Office, she had been sexually assaulted and had died from a single stab wound to the chest. The case was investigated by the Antioch Police Department and became the city's oldest open homicide.

No one was charged for 37 years. According to Newsweek, the investigation was reopened in 2015 at the urging of two retired detectives, and biological evidence was sent to a forensic laboratory so that a DNA profile could be developed. In early 2017 the FBI's Combined DNA Index System produced a tentative match, which further testing confirmed. On December 11, 2017, Antioch police arrested Mitchell Lynn Bacom, then 63, an Antioch resident who had been acquainted with the Bombardier family.

The District Attorney's Office has said that Bacom had been a suspect early in the original investigation, because he had earlier convictions for rape and other felonies and was on parole when Suzanne was killed. Newsweek reported that he was also convicted of further offences in the early 1980s and, in 2002, of failing to register as a sex offender.

Bacom stood trial in Contra Costa County. On March 15, 2022, a jury found him guilty of first-degree murder, and found true the special circumstances that the killing took place during a burglary, a kidnapping and a rape. That verdict carries a mandatory sentence of life in prison without the possibility of parole, which, according to Oxygen, was imposed on June 27, 2022, with Suzanne's sister addressing the court. No later appeal ruling was found in the sources consulted.

name: Blair Adams
summary: Canadian construction worker Blair Adams was found murdered in a Knoxville, Tennessee parking lot after a bizarre cross-country flight from his home in Surrey, British Columbia. His erratic behavior before death and the strange circumstances remain unexplained.
lastSeen: July 11, 1996, Knoxville, Tennessee

sources.title: Murder of Blair Adams - Wikipedia
Blair Adams - Unsolved Mysteries

narrative: In early July 1996, 31-year-old Blair Adams, a construction worker living in Surrey, British Columbia, began behaving erratically. He quit his job, withdrew his life savings of $6,000 Canadian dollars, and told friends and family he believed someone was trying to kill him, though he could not or would not identify who. He attempted to cross into the United States at the border but was turned back because of his agitated state.

Adams then flew from Vancouver to Frankfurt, Germany, but immediately turned around and flew back. He crossed the US border at a different checkpoint, bought a round-trip ticket from Seattle to Washington, D.C., then rented a car in D.C. and drove south. His rental car broke down in Knoxville, Tennessee. He was seen at various locations in Knoxville, including a gas station and a hotel where he appeared confused and frightened.

On July 11, 1996, Adams's body was found in the parking lot of a Knoxville construction site. He had been struck by a violent blow that ruptured his stomach and had a head wound; he died of sepsis from the abdominal injury. His pants were pulled down, and money and valuables were scattered around his body. Despite having been carrying thousands of dollars in multiple currencies, gold, and platinum, nothing appeared to have been stolen.

The Knox County Sheriff's Office investigated extensively but could find no connection between Adams and anyone in Tennessee. No DNA or fingerprints at the scene matched anyone in databases. The bizarre journey—from Canada to Germany and back, then across the United States—combined with his paranoid behavior and the seemingly motiveless murder, make this one of the most perplexing unsolved cases in American true crime. The case has been featured on Unsolved Mysteries and remains open.

name: Johnny Gosch
summary: Twelve-year-old Johnny Gosch disappeared while delivering the Sunday Des Moines Register in West Des Moines, Iowa, on September 5, 1982; his wagon of papers was found two blocks from home. No one has been arrested and he has never been located. His case prompted a 1984 Iowa law requiring an immediate police response to missing-child reports, and he was among the first children pictured on milk cartons.
lastSeen: September 5, 1982, on his newspaper route near 42nd Street and Marcourt Lane, West Des Moines, Iowa

sources.title: National Center for Missing & Exploited Children - 40 years later, still a mystery: Where is Johnny Gosch?
Iowa Cold Cases - Johnny Gosch
The Charley Project - John David Gosch (archived copy)
Wikipedia - Disappearance of Johnny Gosch

narrative: John David "Johnny" Gosch, born November 12, 1969, was a 12-year-old newspaper carrier for the Des Moines Register in West Des Moines, Iowa. According to the Charley Project, his father normally went with him on his Sunday route, but on September 5, 1982, Johnny got up at about 5:45 a.m. and left without waking him, taking the family's dachshund, Gretchen.

Witnesses told authorities that Johnny was seen near 42nd Street and Marcourt Lane speaking with a man in a two-tone blue Ford Fairmont who appeared to be asking for directions, the Charley Project reports. Iowa Cold Cases, citing other carriers who were present, adds that a man was later seen following the boy on foot. Around 7 a.m. customers began phoning the Gosch home to say their papers had not arrived. The dog came home alone, and Johnny's wagon, still loaded with newspapers, was found two blocks from the house.

The National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC) says police at first suspected an abduction, then considered that he might have run away when he could not be found; he is now presumed to have been abducted, and the Charley Project classifies the case as a non-family abduction. His mother, Noreen Gosch, publicly criticised the early police response. According to Wikipedia's summary of contemporary reporting, Iowa's governor signed the "Johnny Gosch Bill" in July 1984, requiring police to act immediately on reports of missing children, and other states passed similar laws. That year his photograph appeared on milk cartons alongside that of Eugene Martin, a 13-year-old Des Moines carrier who vanished on August 12, 1984. NCMEC notes that a third boy, Marc Allen, 13, disappeared in Des Moines in 1986. No link between the cases has been established.

Noreen Gosch has said that her son, by then an adult, came to her apartment with an unidentified man one night in March 1997 and stayed for more than an hour. NCMEC notes that Johnny's father doubts the visit took place and that law enforcement has never confirmed it.

In 2006 she reported finding photographs at her door showing bound and gagged boys, one of whom she believed was Johnny. According to the Charley Project, a Florida officer said he had investigated the same pictures in the 1970s, before Johnny disappeared, and Iowa police suggested the delivery may have been a cruel prank.
No arrest has ever been made. NCMEC reported in 2022 that West Des Moines police still hold the case evidence and continue to receive tips each year. The case remains open and unsolved.

Noreen Gosch says her adult son visited her apartment at night; the account has never been confirmed by law enforcement.
Noreen Gosch reports photographs of bound boys left at her door; police doubt they show her son.

name: Diane Elsroth
summary: Diane Elsroth died after taking a cyanide-laced Tylenol capsule in Yonkers, New York—a copycat of the 1982 Chicago Tylenol murders. This second poisoning incident led Johnson & Johnson to permanently switch from capsules to caplets. No one was ever charged.
lastSeen: February 8, 1986, Yonkers, New York

sources.title: 1986 Tylenol poisoning - Wikipedia
Wikipedia - Chicago Tylenol murders (1986 copycat section)

narrative: On February 8, 1986, 23-year-old Diane Elsroth took two Extra-Strength Tylenol capsules at the home of her boyfriend in Yonkers, New York. She collapsed almost immediately and was rushed to the hospital, where she died. Toxicology tests revealed she had ingested capsules laced with potassium cyanide—echoing the terrifying Chicago Tylenol murders of 1982.

The discovery triggered immediate action. Johnson & Johnson, the parent company of Tylenol, pulled all capsule products from shelves nationwide and announced it would permanently discontinue the sale of over-the-counter capsule medications, switching entirely to solid caplets that were far more difficult to tamper with. The FDA tested thousands of bottles from the region and found a second contaminated bottle at a store in Bronxville, New York.

The investigation by the FBI, FDA, and Westchester County authorities was extensive. Unlike the 1982 Chicago poisonings, where the contamination appeared widespread, the 1986 incident seemed more targeted—only two contaminated bottles were found, both in Westchester County. Investigators examined whether the tampering occurred at the retail level or during distribution.

Despite years of investigation, no one was ever charged in the 1986 Tylenol poisoning. The case, like the 1982 Chicago murders, demonstrated the vulnerability of consumer products to tampering and led to permanent changes in pharmaceutical packaging across the industry. Diane Elsroth's death remains an unsolved homicide.

timeline.event: Diane Elsroth dies after taking cyanide-laced Tylenol in Yonkers.
A second contaminated bottle is found in Bronxville, New York.
Johnson & Johnson permanently discontinues all capsule medications.
FDA mandates tamper-evident packaging for all OTC drugs.

name: Gary and Linda Haas
summary: Gary and Linda Haas, both 61, of Tecumseh, Oklahoma, were carjacked at an Interstate 40 rest area in Quay County, New Mexico, on August 2, 2010, and shot dead in their travel trailer, which was then burned. Escaped Arizona inmate John McCluskey was convicted in 2013 and sentenced to life plus 235 years. Tracy Province received life and Casslyn Welch 40 years after plea agreements.
lastSeen: August 2, 2010, Interstate 40 rest area, Quay County, New Mexico

sources.title: US Attorney's Office, District of New Mexico (via FBI Albuquerque, archived) - Arizona Fugitives Charged with Causing the Deaths of Oklahoma Couple
FBI (archived) - Sentence in 2010 Murder of Oklahoma Couple
Albuquerque Journal (archived) - McCluskey: Life plus 235 years
KFOR (archived) - Man convicted of murdering Oklahoma couple in New Mexico dies in prison
Wikipedia - 2010 Arizona prison escape

narrative: Gary and Linda Haas, both 61 and recently retired, left their home in Tecumseh, Oklahoma, in early August 2010 for Pagosa Springs, Colorado, where, according to the US Attorney's Office for the District of New Mexico, they had spent the previous 11 summers with family and friends. They were towing a camping trailer behind their pickup truck. On August 2, 2010, they stopped at a rest area off Interstate 40 in Quay County, New Mexico.

Three days earlier, on July 30, inmates John Charles McCluskey and Tracy Allen Province had escaped from an Arizona state prison with help from Casslyn Mae Welch. A third inmate who escaped with them was separated from the group and caught two days later. According to an FBI account of the case, the three had been travelling in a small stolen sedan and stopped at the rest area intending to take a camper or trailer.

Federal prosecutors said the three carjacked the Haases at gunpoint and had them drive to a location between Tucumcari and Santa Rosa, where McCluskey shot both of them inside the trailer. The group then towed the trailer to a remote part of Guadalupe County, unhitched it and set it on fire with the bodies inside. They left the couple's truck at a shopping center in Albuquerque.

New Mexico State Police and the Guadalupe County Sheriff found the burned trailer and the couple's remains on August 4, 2010, and the truck was located in Albuquerque later that day. The FBI said that although the truck had been wiped down, fingerprint and DNA evidence identified the three. Province was arrested in Wyoming on August 9, and McCluskey and Welch were arrested at a campground in Arizona on August 19 after a US Forest Service employee alerted authorities. The FBI said the handgun used in the killings was recovered there and that McCluskey was wearing a cap belonging to Gary Haas.

Federal arrest warrants on carjacking and firearms charges were announced on August 23, 2010. According to Wikipedia's account, Province and Welch reached plea agreements and testified against McCluskey, whose trial began with jury selection in July 2013 and ended in a guilty verdict on October 7, 2013. The jury did not reach the unanimous decision required for a death sentence.

On June 2, 2014, Province was sentenced to life in prison and Welch to 40 years. The following day, US District Judge Judith Herrera sentenced McCluskey to life plus 235 years on the 20 counts of conviction, the Albuquerque Journal reported. Relatives of the couple spoke at the hearing. McCluskey died in March 2017, aged 52, at a federal prison near Florence, Colorado, according to KFOR.

Gary and Linda Haas are carjacked at an Interstate 40 rest area in Quay County, New Mexico, and shot dead in their trailer.

McCluskey and Welch are arrested at a campground in Arizona.

A federal jury convicts McCluskey; it later fails to agree on a death sentence.
Province is sentenced to life in prison and Welch to 40 years.
McCluskey is sentenced to life plus 235 years.
McCluskey dies in federal prison near Florence, Colorado, aged 52.

name: Christopher Wilder Victims
summary: Investigators attribute the abduction of at least twelve young women and girls, eight of whom died, to Christopher Wilder during a cross-country series of crimes between February 26 and April 13, 1984. Wilder, an Australian-born Florida businessman, died of a gunshot wound during a struggle with New Hampshire state troopers and was never tried. Rosario Gonzalez and Elizabeth Kenyon have never been found.
lastSeen: Various locations across the United States, February 26 to April 13, 1984

sources.title: UPI Archives - Murder suspect Christopher Wilder dead as police move in to arrest
ABC News - Survivors of serial killer Christopher Wilder speak out for first time
History.com - Serial killer Christopher Wilder dies by suicide
Wikipedia - Christopher Wilder

narrative: Christopher Bernard Wilder was born in Sydney, Australia, in 1945 and moved to the United States in 1969, settling in Boynton Beach, Florida, where he worked in construction and real estate and raced sports cars. According to Wikipedia's account of his background, he had faced sexual offence charges in both countries before 1984. He was never tried for the killings described here, because he died before he could be arrested; the attribution of these crimes to him comes from investigators and from the accounts of survivors.

The series began on February 26, 1984, when 20-year-old Rosario Gonzalez disappeared from the Miami Grand Prix, where she had been working. Elizabeth Kenyon, 23, of Coral Gables, vanished in early March; sources give the date as March 5 or March 8. Neither woman has been found. ABC News reported that Wilder often approached young women at shopping centres with offers of modelling work.

As described by Wikipedia, Theresa Ferguson, 21, disappeared from Merritt Island, Florida, on March 18 and was found dead days later. Linda Grober, 19, was abducted in Tallahassee on March 20 and escaped from a motel. Terry Walden, 23, was abducted in Beaumont, Texas, on March 23 and found dead on March 26. Suzanne Logan, 21, disappeared in Oklahoma City on March 25 and her body was found in Kansas. Sheryl Bonaventura, 18, was taken from Grand Junction, Colorado, on March 29, and Michelle Korfman, 17, from Las Vegas on April 1; the bodies of both were found in May.

On April 4, 16-year-old Tina Marie Risico was abducted from a shopping centre in Torrance, California, and held for nine days, according to ABC News. UPI reported at the time that authorities regarded her as a victim rather than an accomplice. Dawnette Wilt, 16, was abducted in Indiana on April 10, stabbed and left in New York State, where she survived. Beth Dodge, 33, was shot dead near Victor, New York. Risico was released alive.

UPI reported that Wilder had been added to the FBI's Ten Most Wanted list the week before his death. On April 13, 1984, two New Hampshire state troopers acting on an FBI alert confronted him at a service station in Colebrook, about 12 miles from the Canadian border. According to state police statements carried by UPI, two shots were fired from Wilder's gun during the struggle; one wounded a trooper, who survived, and the other killed Wilder.

Because Wilder died, no court ever ruled on the cases. Wikipedia notes that police in Australia and the United States have considered him a possible suspect in several other unsolved cases, none of which has been proven. The families of Gonzalez and Kenyon have never recovered their remains.

Theresa Ferguson, 21, disappears from Merritt Island, Florida; her body is found days later.

Sheryl Bonaventura, 18, disappears from Grand Junction, Colorado.
Michelle Korfman, 17, disappears in Las Vegas.
Tina Marie Risico, 16, is abducted in Torrance, California; she is held for nine days and survives.
Dawnette Wilt, 16, is abducted in Indiana; she is later stabbed and left in New York State but survives.
Wilder dies of a gunshot wound during a struggle with New Hampshire state troopers in Colebrook; a trooper is wounded.

name: Michael Dunahee
summary: Four-year-old Michael Dunahee disappeared from the playground of Blanshard Elementary School in Victoria, British Columbia, on March 24, 1991, while his family was close by for a flag football game. The search became one of the largest missing-child investigations in Canada, and Victoria police say they have received more than 10,000 tips. He has never been found and the case remains open.
lastSeen: March 24, 1991, Blanshard Elementary School playground, Victoria, British Columbia

sources.title: RCMP Canada's Missing - Michael Wayne Dunahee (case 2011002299)
CBC News - Victoria police release age-enhanced sketch of Michael Dunahee, 30 years after he disappeared
Victoria News - Michael Dunahee's disappearance still baffles Victoria after 35 years
CTV News - Michael Dunahee: 35 years since he went missing in Victoria
MichaelDunahee.ca - Michael Dunahee
Wikipedia - Disappearance of Michael Dunahee

narrative: Michael Wayne Dunahee was four years old when he went missing in Victoria, British Columbia, on Sunday, March 24, 1991. According to the RCMP's Canada's Missing database, he was at the Blanshard Elementary School playground with his parents and his younger sister. Victoria News and CBC News report that the family had gone there for a flag football game, and that the area was busy with players, families and spectators.

According to Wikipedia's account, which cites Canadian news coverage, his mother Crystal was taking part in the football and his father Bruce was nearby when Michael asked to go to the playground, a short distance away. He disappeared at about 12:30 p.m. CBC News reported that he vanished only a short distance from his family. No witness to the disappearance itself has been identified.

The RCMP listing describes Michael as about three feet tall and 51 pounds, with short blond hair, blue eyes and freckles beginning to show on his nose. He was wearing a blue hooded jacket with red lining and cuffs, a Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles T-shirt, multicoloured rugby pants and blue canvas sneakers.

CBC News reported that hundreds of volunteers and officers from several police agencies carried out an extensive search. The Victoria Police Department, which leads the investigation, has treated the case as a suspected abduction, according to Wikipedia. On the 30th anniversary in March 2021, a police spokesperson told CBC News that more than 10,000 tips had been received. On the same day the department released an age-enhanced forensic sketch showing how Michael might look at 34, prepared by a police forensic artist working with the family, and opened an online tip portal.

Several men thought to resemble Michael have been investigated over the years. Wikipedia, citing news reports, records that DNA testing ruled out men in British Columbia in 2006, 2011 and 2013. These details rest on that secondary summary and should be treated with some caution.

Michael's family has continued to campaign publicly. An annual Keep the Hope Alive walk and run is held in Esquimalt each March and raises money for Child Find BC; Victoria News reported that the 35th event took place on March 29, 2026. Around the 35th anniversary, Greater Victoria Crime Stoppers and police renewed their appeal for information, and CTV News reported that the case remains unsolved. The RCMP lists the Victoria police file number as 91-10349.

Michael Dunahee, 4, disappears from the Blanshard Elementary School playground in Victoria at about 12:30 p.m.
