The US Supreme Court, in Silkwood v. Kerr-McGee Corp., restores the jury's verdict after an appeals court had reduced it.
Kerr-McGee and the estate announce a $1.38 million settlement with no admission of liability.

name: Skelton Brothers
summary: Brothers Andrew (9), Alexander (7) and Tanner (5) Skelton disappeared while staying with their father in Morenci, Michigan over Thanksgiving 2010 and have never been found. Their father, John Skelton, pleaded no contest to unlawful imprisonment in 2011 and was sentenced to 10 to 15 years. A court declared the boys dead in March 2025, and in November 2025 Skelton was charged with three counts of open murder and tampering with evidence; he has not been convicted of those charges and the case is pending.
lastSeen: November 26, 2010, Morenci, Michigan

sources.title: Disappearance of the Skelton brothers - Wikipedia
ClickOnDetroit (WDIV) - Preliminary exam underway for John Skelton, accused of murdering 3 young sons

narrative: Over the Thanksgiving holiday in 2010, nine-year-old Andrew, seven-year-old Alexander, and five-year-old Tanner Skelton were staying with their father, John Skelton, at his home in Morenci, Michigan, a small town near the Ohio border. John and the boys' mother, Tanya Zuvers, were going through a contentious divorce, and John had the boys for the holiday as part of a custody arrangement. He was supposed to return them to their mother on November 26.

When John Skelton did not return the boys, Tanya called police. Officers went to Skelton's home and found him in the garage, having attempted suicide by hanging. He was hospitalized but survived. When questioned, Skelton gave contradictory accounts. He initially said the boys were with a woman named Joann Taylor, but no such person could be found. He later claimed he had given the boys to an underground group called 'United Foster Outreach' that would protect them from their mother. No such organization exists.

An extensive search was conducted throughout Lenawee County, Michigan and across the border into Ohio. Dogs, divers, aerial searches, and hundreds of volunteers covered wide areas. Some of the boys' clothing was found in a wooded area near a river, and evidence suggested Skelton had visited the area. However, the boys themselves were never found.

John Skelton pleaded no contest to unlawful imprisonment in July 2011 and was sentenced to 10-15 years in prison. He has consistently refused to reveal the boys' location. He has been periodically questioned by investigators but has not provided useful information. The FBI and Michigan State Police continue to investigate, and the boys' mother has made regular public appeals for information. The Skelton brothers would be in their teens and twenties today.

timeline.event: John Skelton fails to return his three sons to their mother.
Skelton is found having attempted suicide; claims boys are with a caretaker.
Massive search begins; boys' clothing found near a river.
John Skelton is convicted of unlawful imprisonment.
A Lenawee County court declares Andrew, Alexander and Tanner Skelton legally dead.

John Skelton is charged with three counts of open murder and three counts of tampering with evidence, shortly before his scheduled release from prison; a preliminary examination is held in August-September 2026.

name: Megan Kanka
summary: Seven-year-old Megan Kanka was sexually assaulted and murdered on July 29, 1994, by Jesse Timmendequas, a neighbor in Hamilton Township, New Jersey, who had two prior convictions for sex offenses against children. He was convicted in 1997 and is serving life without parole. The case led to Megan's Law, which requires sex offender registration and community notification.
lastSeen: July 29, 1994, Hamilton Township, New Jersey

sources.title: FindLaw - State v. Timmendequas (N.J. Supreme Court, 1999)
CNN - 'Megan's Law' killer escapes death under N.J. execution ban
Time - 'Megan's Law' Killer Found Guilty
CBS New York - Court: Jesse Timmendequas, Man Convicted Of Killing Megan Kanka, Can Continue Appeal
New Jersey State Police - Megan's Law
Encyclopedia.com - Jesse Timmendequas Trial: 1997
Wikipedia - Murder of Megan Kanka

narrative: Megan Nicole Kanka was seven years old when she disappeared from her neighborhood in Hamilton Township, Mercer County, New Jersey, on the evening of July 29, 1994. According to the New Jersey Supreme Court's 1999 opinion in State v. Timmendequas, she was last seen at about 6:30 p.m. and had gone to a house across the street, where a neighbor, Jesse Timmendequas, had a puppy.

Timmendequas, then 33, shared the house with two other men, Brian Jenin and Joseph Cifelli. Court records and news reports state that all three had previous convictions for sex offenses and that Timmendequas had met them while in custody. According to Wikipedia's summary of the record, he had been convicted in 1979 and again in 1981 of offenses against young girls and had served about six years at the Adult Diagnostic and Treatment Center in Avenel. Megan's family said they had not known about the men's histories.

According to the court opinion, Timmendequas was questioned by police and confessed on July 30, 1994, telling officers that the child's body was in Mercer County Park and leading them to it. Prosecutors said he had lured her into the house with the offer of seeing the puppy, sexually assaulted her and strangled her. He was charged with capital murder, felony murder, kidnapping and four counts of aggravated sexual assault.

The trial was held in Trenton before Judge Andrew J. Smithson, with a jury drawn from Hunterdon County because of pretrial publicity, according to the court opinion. Time reported that the jury found him guilty on all counts on May 30, 1997. On June 20, 1997, the same jury returned a verdict of death, as reported by CNN and the Washington Post. The New Jersey Supreme Court affirmed the conviction and the sentence on August 11, 1999.

New Jersey abolished capital punishment in December 2007. CNN reported that Governor Jon Corzine commuted the sentences of the eight men on the state's death row, including Timmendequas, to life imprisonment without parole, and signed the abolition law on December 17, 2007. In June 2011, CBS New York reported that an appeals court allowed him to continue pursuing a claim that his trial lawyers were ineffective, while leaving his sentence in place. No source consulted indicates that his conviction has been disturbed.

Megan's parents, Maureen and Richard Kanka, campaigned for communities to be told when convicted sex offenders move in. According to the New Jersey State Police, the state's registration and community notification laws were signed on October 31, 1994, about three months after the murder. President Bill Clinton signed a federal Megan's Law on May 17, 1996, amending the Jacob Wetterling Act so that states were required to release information about registered sex offenders to the public.

timeline.event: Megan Kanka, 7, disappears from her Hamilton Township neighborhood at about 6:30 p.m.
Neighbor Jesse Timmendequas confesses to police and leads them to her body in Mercer County Park.
Governor Christine Todd Whitman signs New Jersey's sex offender registration and community notification laws, known as Megan's Law.
President Bill Clinton signs the federal Megan's Law.
A jury finds Timmendequas guilty of murder, kidnapping and aggravated sexual assault.
The jury returns a death verdict in the penalty phase.
The New Jersey Supreme Court affirms the conviction and death sentence.
New Jersey abolishes the death penalty; Timmendequas's sentence becomes life imprisonment without parole.
An appeals court allows Timmendequas to pursue an ineffective-counsel claim while upholding his sentence.

name: Mollie Tibbetts
summary: University of Iowa student Mollie Tibbetts, 20, disappeared while out for an evening run in Brooklyn, Iowa, on July 18, 2018. Her body was found in a Poweshiek County cornfield on August 21, 2018. Cristhian Bahena Rivera was convicted of first-degree murder in May 2021 and sentenced to life in prison without parole; the Iowa Court of Appeals affirmed the conviction in 2023.
lastSeen: July 18, 2018, at about 7:30 p.m., Brooklyn, Iowa

sources.title: NBC News - Cristhian Bahena Rivera convicted of first-degree murder in slaying of Iowa college student Mollie Tibbetts
ABC News - Guilty verdict in murder of Iowa student Mollie Tibbetts
ABC News - The disappearance of University of Iowa student Mollie Tibbetts: A timeline
CBS News - Mollie Tibbetts found dead
Iowa Judicial Branch - Case No. 21-1202: State of Iowa v. Cristhian Bahena Rivera (Court of Appeals opinion)
Wikipedia - Murder of Mollie Tibbetts

narrative: Mollie Cecilia Tibbetts, 20, was a University of Iowa student spending the summer of 2018 in Brooklyn, a small town in Poweshiek County, Iowa. According to an ABC News timeline, she was staying at the home of her boyfriend, Dalton Jack, and looking after his dogs while he was away working in Dubuque. At about 7:30 p.m. on July 18, 2018, she went out for a run wearing running clothes and carrying her phone and a Fitbit. She did not return.

Her family reported her missing on July 19 after she failed to arrive at work. ABC News and CBS News reported that investigators reviewed surveillance video from the town and data from her fitness tracker, followed hundreds of leads, and ruled out a reported sighting in Missouri. A reward fund for her safe return grew to more than $385,000, according to CBS News.

Investigators identified Cristhian Bahena Rivera, then 24, a farm worker from Mexico who was living in the area, after surveillance video showed a black Chevrolet Malibu repeatedly passing through the area where Tibbetts was running, ABC News reported. He was interviewed by police and, in the early hours of August 21, 2018, led officers to a cornfield in rural Poweshiek County, where her body lay covered with corn leaves. According to Wikipedia's summary of the state medical examiner's findings, she died of multiple sharp force injuries. He was charged with first-degree murder and pleaded not guilty.

The trial was moved from Poweshiek County and held in Davenport in May 2021 before Judge Joel Yates, after a delay caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. Prosecutors relied on the surveillance video, on DNA consistent with Tibbetts found in the trunk of the car, and on statements Bahena Rivera made to police, ABC News reported. He testified that two masked, armed men had forced him to take part and that they, not he, killed her. On May 28, 2021, the jury found him guilty of first-degree murder after about seven hours of deliberation, according to NBC News.

Sentencing was postponed while the court considered defence motions for a new trial based on claimed new evidence; the motions were denied. On August 30, 2021, he was sentenced to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole, the mandatory sentence in Iowa. On October 11, 2023, the Iowa Court of Appeals affirmed the conviction, rejecting arguments that his statements to police should have been suppressed and that he was entitled to a new trial.

The case received national attention, in part because of public debate about the defendant's immigration status. News reports at the time noted that members of Tibbetts's family asked that her death not be used for political purposes.

timeline.event: Mollie Tibbetts goes for a run in Brooklyn, Iowa, at about 7:30 p.m. and does not return.
Her family reports her missing after she does not show up for work.
The family holds a press conference; the reward fund continues to grow.
Cristhian Bahena Rivera leads investigators to her body in a Poweshiek County cornfield; he is arrested and charged with first-degree murder.
Bahena Rivera pleads not guilty.
Trial begins in Davenport after a change of venue and pandemic delays.
The jury finds Bahena Rivera guilty of first-degree murder.
He is sentenced to life in prison without parole after motions for a new trial are denied.
The Iowa Court of Appeals affirms the conviction.

name: Lori Erica Ruff
summary: A Texas woman known as Lori Erica Ruff died by suicide on Christmas Eve, leaving behind evidence she had been living under a stolen identity for decades. Her true identity—Kimberly McLean of Pennsylvania—was not discovered until 2016 through DNA genealogy.
lastSeen: December 24, 2010, Longview, Texas

sources.title: Lori Erica Ruff - Wikipedia
Lori Ruff identified - NBC News

narrative: On Christmas Eve 2010, a 42-year-old woman known as Lori Erica Ruff shot and killed herself in the driveway of her in-laws' home in Longview, Texas. She had recently separated from her husband, Blake Ruff, and was in a custody dispute over their young daughter. After her death, her in-laws found a lockbox containing documents that revealed her identity was fabricated.

The lockbox contained a birth certificate for a deceased Idaho girl named Becky Sue Turner, who had died in a house fire as a toddler in 1971. Lori had apparently used this deceased child's identity to obtain a new Social Security card and then legally changed her name to 'Lori Erica Kennedy' before marrying Blake Ruff. She had created an entirely new person, complete with a GED, college attendance, and a social history—all under a false identity.

Lori had been secretive and controlling throughout her marriage, refusing to discuss her past and cutting off contact with anyone from before her marriage. She told various conflicting stories about her childhood and family. Her in-laws described her as increasingly paranoid and emotionally unstable. After her death, investigators tried for years to determine who she really was, but her fingerprints and DNA were not in any law enforcement database.

In 2016, genetic genealogy researchers used DNA from Lori's remains to identify her as Kimberly McLean, born in 1968 in the Philadelphia area. She had run away from her family as a teenager in the late 1980s and reinvented herself completely. Her biological family in Pennsylvania was located and confirmed the identification. The case became a landmark example of genetic genealogy's power to solve identity mysteries.

timeline.event: Woman known as Lori Erica Ruff dies by suicide in Longview, Texas.
In-laws discover lockbox with evidence of stolen identity.
Investigation reveals identity was built on a deceased child's records.
Genetic genealogy identifies her as Kimberly McLean of Pennsylvania.

name: William Tyrrell
summary: Three-year-old William Tyrrell disappeared from his foster grandmother's home on Benaroon Drive in Kendall, New South Wales, on the morning of September 12, 2014, while wearing a Spider-Man suit. Large searches, a $1 million reward announced in 2016 and a long-running coronial inquest have not established what happened. No trace of him has been found and no one has been charged over his disappearance.
lastSeen: September 12, 2014, Benaroon Drive, Kendall, New South Wales, Australia

sources.title: 7NEWS - Major development in investigation into the disappearance of William Tyrrell
Sydney Morning Herald - Woman confronts foster mother outside William Tyrrell inquest
AAP - Tyrrell foster mother admits assaulting child
Wikipedia - Disappearance of William Tyrrell

narrative: William Tyrrell, born June 26, 2011, was three years old when he went missing on September 12, 2014. He was visiting his foster grandmother's house on Benaroon Drive in Kendall, on the Mid North Coast of New South Wales, with his foster family. According to 7NEWS and Wikipedia's summary of police statements, he had been playing outside with his sister in a Spider-Man suit and is believed to have disappeared between about 10:00 and 10:25 a.m. He was reported missing shortly before 11 a.m.

The initial search lasted nine days and involved police, the State Emergency Service, the Rural Fire Service and hundreds of volunteers, 7NEWS reported. Strike Force Rosann was set up on September 16, 2014. For roughly seven years investigators worked mainly on the theory that William had been abducted. On September 12, 2016, the second anniversary, the NSW government announced a $1 million reward, which Wikipedia describes as the largest offered in the state for a missing person and payable for William's recovery. 7NEWS reported that more than 700 persons of interest were identified over the years.

Some of those early lines of inquiry were later discredited. A tradesman who had been publicly scrutinised was confirmed to have been elsewhere that morning, and according to Wikipedia he was awarded A$1.48 million in December 2022 after suing NSW Police over his treatment.

In November 2021 police announced new searches around Kendall and said they were now looking for remains. It was reported at the time that the foster mother was being treated as a person of interest. In April 2022 she was charged with giving false or misleading information to the NSW Crime Commission; she was found not guilty in November 2022. On June 27, 2023, it was reported that police had sent a brief to the Director of Public Prosecutions recommending she be charged with perverting the course of justice and interfering with a corpse. No such charges have been laid. Through her lawyer, she has said she had nothing to do with William's disappearance, 7NEWS reported.

A coronial inquest that opened in 2019 resumed at Lidcombe in November 2024 before Deputy State Coroner Harriet Grahame. The Sydney Morning Herald reported that the court was told of the police theory that William died in an accidental fall from a balcony and that his body was then moved, a theory the foster mother has always firmly denied. Expert witnesses gave evidence about the 2021 searches, which found nothing connected to William.

As far as could be established for this entry, the coroner's findings had not been published by September 2026. William has never been found, his fate is unknown, and nobody has been charged in connection with his disappearance.

timeline.event: William Tyrrell is born.
William disappears from his foster grandmother's home on Benaroon Drive, Kendall, between about 10:00 and 10:25 a.m.; a nine-day search begins.
NSW Police establish Strike Force Rosann.
The NSW government announces a $1 million reward.
A coronial inquest into the disappearance begins.
Police announce renewed searches around Kendall and say they are looking for remains.
The foster mother is found not guilty of giving false or misleading information to the NSW Crime Commission.
A man once treated as a person of interest is awarded A$1.48 million in his claim against NSW Police (per Wikipedia).
Reports say police have recommended to the Director of Public Prosecutions that the foster mother be charged; no charges follow.
The inquest resumes at the Coroner's Court in Lidcombe and hears the police theory, which the foster mother denies.

name: Jack the Stripper Victims
summary: Six women, all sex workers, were found murdered in or near the Thames in west London between 1964 and 1965. The killer, dubbed 'Jack the Stripper' by the media, was never identified despite a massive police investigation led by Detective Chief Superintendent John du Rose.
lastSeen: Various locations in west London, 1964-1965

sources.title: Jack the Stripper - Wikipedia

narrative: Between February 1964 and February 1965, six women were found dead in or near the River Thames in the Hammersmith and surrounding areas of west London. All were sex workers, and all had been asphyxiated—several showed evidence of having teeth forcibly removed. The victims were Hannah Tailford, Irene Lockwood, Helen Barthelemy, Mary Fleming, Margaret McGowan, and Bridie O'Hara. Their nude or partially clothed bodies were found at various locations along the river.

The murders became known as the 'Hammersmith nude murders' and the killer was dubbed 'Jack the Stripper' by the press, drawing a deliberate parallel to Jack the Ripper. Detective Chief Superintendent John du Rose of Scotland Yard was assigned to lead the investigation—one of the largest police operations in London at that time.

A key forensic lead was microscopic paint particles found on several of the victims' bodies, suggesting they had been stored in or near an industrial paint spraying facility before being dumped. Du Rose's investigation narrowed the search to premises near the Heron Trading Estate in Acton, where a transformer provided warm air that could explain the bodies' condition. The investigation identified a number of suspects in the area.

Du Rose later stated publicly that the killer was among his final shortlist of suspects, and that the man had committed suicide before he could be arrested. However, he never publicly named the individual, and his claim has been disputed by other investigators. Several suspects have been proposed over the decades, including a security guard, a boxer, and a disgraced Metropolitan Police officer. The case remains officially unsolved, and the identity of Jack the Stripper has never been conclusively established.

timeline.event: Hannah Tailford's body is found in the Thames near Hammersmith.
Helen Barthelemy found with paint particles on her body.
Mary Fleming found; investigation intensifies.
Margaret McGowan found; media dubs killer 'Jack the Stripper.'
Bridie O'Hara found; last confirmed victim.
DCS du Rose claims prime suspect committed suicide.

name: Sofia Silva, Kristin Lisk & Kati Lisk
summary: Sofia Silva, 16, vanished from the front steps of her Spotsylvania County, Virginia home on September 9, 1996, and sisters Kristin, 15, and Kati Lisk, 12, were taken from their front yard on May 1, 1997. All three were found dead. In August 2002 authorities announced that hair, fiber and print evidence tied the killings to Richard Marc Evonitz, who had shot himself in Florida that June, and closed the cases.
lastSeen: September 9, 1996 (Silva) / May 1, 1997 (Lisk sisters), outside their homes in Spotsylvania County, Virginia

sources.title: The Washington Post (archived) - 3 Slain Girls' Cases Closed
The Free Lance-Star (archived) - Discovering deadly secrets
Wikipedia - Richard Evonitz

narrative: Sofia Silva, a 16-year-old junior at Courtland High School, was last seen on the afternoon of September 9, 1996, when she took her homework and a can of soda out to the front steps of her family's home in Spotsylvania County, Virginia. According to The Washington Post, she disappeared with no sign of a struggle. Her body was found about five weeks later in water in neighboring King George County.

On May 1, 1997, Ron Lisk came home from work to find his daughters Kristin, 15, and Kati, 12, missing and Kristin's book bag lying on the front lawn, the Post reported. Kristin was a freshman at Spotsylvania High School. A large search followed, and five days later the sisters' bodies were found in the South Anna River, about 40 miles away.

A task force of local, state and federal investigators worked the cases for five years. The Post reported that it followed more than 12,000 tips, that more than 10,000 forensic examinations were carried out on hairs, fibers and tire impressions, and that DNA from the scene was compared with about 1.2 million database samples without identifying anyone.

The break came from South Carolina. On June 24, 2002, a 15-year-old girl was abducted at gunpoint from the yard of a friend's house in the Columbia area and held in an apartment, according to police accounts reported by the Post. She freed herself the next morning while her captor slept and led police to Richard Marc Evonitz, 38. A worker at the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children noticed that Evonitz had lived in Spotsylvania at the time of the Silva and Lisk abductions and alerted the task force. Evonitz fled, and on June 27, 2002, he shot himself as police surrounded him in Sarasota, Florida, according to Wikipedia's summary of contemporary reports.

At a news conference on August 13, 2002, reported by The Washington Post, Spotsylvania County Sheriff Ronald Knight and members of the task force said the evidence showed that Evonitz had abducted and killed all three girls. Hair consistent with his was found on each of the bodies, and blue acrylic fibers from a pair of fur-covered handcuffs he owned were recovered from all three. Fibers from the carpet of a house where he had lived in the Fredericksburg area and from the trunk of his Ford Taurus also matched. Examiners found a palm print and fingerprints matching Kristin Lisk's inside the trunk of his car, five years after the abduction. Detectives also learned that he had taken time off work on the days of both abductions.

Evonitz was never charged or tried, because he died before he was identified as a suspect in the Virginia cases; the conclusion that he was responsible is the official finding announced by the task force. Sheriff Knight said at the time that nothing linked him specifically to any other unsolved murder, although the FBI said it was continuing to reconstruct his movements. The Free Lance-Star reported in 2004 that investigators were still examining possible connections to other crimes.

Silva's body is found in King George County, about five weeks after she vanished.

name: Sarah and Jacob Hoggle
summary: Two-year-old Sarah and three-year-old Jacob Hoggle were last seen with their mother, Catherine Hoggle, in Montgomery County, Maryland, in September 2014 and have never been found. Murder charges against Catherine Hoggle, who was repeatedly found incompetent to stand trial, were dismissed in 2022. After her release from a psychiatric hospital in July 2025 she was reindicted on two counts of first-degree murder; she has since been found competent, intends to plead not criminally responsible, and her trial is scheduled for October 2027.
lastSeen: September 8, 2014, Clarksburg, Maryland

sources.title: WTOP - Catherine Hoggle, reindicted with murder of her 2 kids, deemed flight risk during first court appearance
CBS News Baltimore - Mental evaluation ordered for Catherine Hoggle

narrative: On September 8, 2014, three-year-old Jacob and two-year-old Sarah Hoggle were last seen with their mother, Catherine Hoggle, in the Clarksburg area of Montgomery County, Maryland. Their father, Troy Turner, became alarmed when Catherine returned home without the children and gave inconsistent accounts of their whereabouts.

Catherine initially told Troy she had left the children with a friend, but the friend said she had not seen them. Police were called, and Catherine was taken into custody. She made various conflicting statements about where the children were, at times saying they were with other people and at other times claiming not to remember.

Catherine Hoggle was diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia and was repeatedly found incompetent to stand trial. For years, the legal proceedings were delayed as courts grappled with her mental state. She was held at a state psychiatric facility while attempts were made to restore her competency. Maryland law at the time limited how long an incompetent defendant could be held, creating a possibility she could go free without ever revealing the children's location.

Extensive searches of areas where Catherine was known to have been—including parks, wooded areas, and bodies of water in Montgomery County—yielded no results. The children's bodies have never been found. In 2020, Maryland passed legislation (dubbed 'Jacob and Sarah's Law') extending the period an incompetent defendant can be held in serious cases. Catherine Hoggle remained in psychiatric custody until July 2025; the original murder charges were dismissed in 2022, and she was reindicted on two counts of first-degree murder in August 2025. The fate of Sarah and Jacob Hoggle remains unknown.

Catherine returns home without the children; gives conflicting accounts.

name: Debra Jan Baker
summary: Debra Jan Baker was found stabbed to death in her Cheyenne, Wyoming apartment. Her six-month-old daughter was found unharmed in a crib nearby. Despite DNA evidence from the scene, her killer has never been identified.
lastSeen: April 8, 1986, Cheyenne, Wyoming
narrative: On April 8, 1986, 32-year-old Debra Jan Baker was found stabbed to death in her apartment in Cheyenne, Wyoming. Her six-month-old daughter was found unharmed in a crib in the same apartment. The discovery was made by a concerned acquaintance who had been unable to reach Debra.

The crime scene yielded biological evidence that was preserved for future testing. As DNA technology advanced, the evidence was analyzed and a male profile was obtained. However, the profile has not matched anyone in law enforcement databases, including CODIS.

The Cheyenne Police Department investigated the case extensively, interviewing associates and exploring possible motives. Debra's personal life was examined, but no clear suspect emerged. The case was periodically reviewed as part of cold case initiatives.

Debra Jan Baker's murder remains one of Cheyenne's most prominent unsolved cases. The preserved DNA evidence offers the possibility that advances in genetic genealogy could one day identify her killer.

timeline.event: Debra Jan Baker is found stabbed to death in her Cheyenne apartment.
Cheyenne police begin investigation; her infant daughter is unharmed.
DNA from the scene is analyzed; no match found.

name: Austin Yogurt Shop Victims
summary: Four girls aged 13 to 17 were shot and an I Can't Believe It's Yogurt! shop was set on fire in Austin, Texas, on December 6, 1991. Two men convicted in 2001 and 2002 had their convictions overturned and charges dismissed in 2009. In September 2025 Austin police said DNA and ballistic evidence identified Robert Eugene Brashers, who died in 1999, and in February 2026 a judge declared the four accused men innocent.
lastSeen: December 6, 1991, I Can't Believe It's Yogurt! shop, Austin, Texas

sources.title: Texas Public Radio - New details: How Austin Police identified yogurt shop murders suspect
CBS News - Bullet casing in drain at Texas yogurt shop links serial killer to the infamous murders, says original investigator
CBS News - The Yogurt Shop Murders: Key moments in the Austin, Texas, investigation
KFVS - Texas court officially exonerates men once accused of Yogurt Shop Murders
KERA News - Austin yogurt shop murders: exonerated suspects reach $35 million settlement
Wikipedia - 1991 Austin yogurt shop murders
AOL/People - Who Committed the Yogurt Shop Murders? Here's How Robert Eugene Brashers Was Finally Caught

narrative: On the night of December 6, 1991, four girls were killed inside an I Can't Believe It's Yogurt! shop near Northcross Mall in Austin, Texas. According to Texas Public Radio and CBS News, Eliza Thomas and Jennifer Harbison, both 17, were closing the shop, where they worked, and were joined by Jennifer's sister Sarah Harbison, 15, and Sarah's friend Amy Ayers, 13. The girls were bound, gagged and shot, and the building was set on fire, which destroyed much of the evidence. Police have said at least one victim was sexually assaulted.

The Austin Police Department formed a dedicated task force, and federal agencies assisted, but the case went cold. In 1999 a new team of investigators re-examined it and four men who had been teenagers in 1991 were arrested: Robert Springsteen, Michael Scott, Maurice Pierce and Forrest Welborn. CBS News reported that investigators obtained confessions from Springsteen and Scott, which both men later recanted, saying they had been coerced. A grand jury did not indict Welborn, and the charges against Pierce were dismissed in 2003 after he had spent years in the Travis County jail, according to Texas Public Radio.

Springsteen was convicted in 2001 and Scott in 2002. Both convictions were later thrown out by the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals. While prosecutors prepared to retry the men, Y-STR testing produced a partial male DNA profile that matched none of the four. The charges against Springsteen and Scott were dismissed in 2009 after the two had spent close to ten years in custody, CBS News reported. Pierce was shot and killed by an Austin police officer in 2010, according to KERA News.

In late September 2025, Austin police announced that they had identified Robert Eugene Brashers as the person responsible. Brashers, who died by suicide in January 1999 during a standoff with police in Missouri, had already been linked by DNA to murders in South Carolina and Missouri. At a news conference on September 29, 2025, detective Dan Jackson explained that a .380 shell casing recovered from a floor drain in the shop was resubmitted to a national ballistics database in June 2025 and produced a link to another cold case, and that retesting of Amy Ayers' fingernail clippings in September 2025 found DNA matching Brashers. Because Brashers is dead, no one can be prosecuted; Travis County District Attorney José Garza said the evidence pointed to the guilt of one man and the innocence of four.

On February 19, 2026, Travis County Judge Dayna Blazey declared Scott, Springsteen, Welborn and the late Maurice Pierce innocent and dismissed the charges against each of them with prejudice, KFVS reported. In May 2026 the City of Austin agreed to a $35 million settlement with the three surviving men and Pierce's family, and, according to KERA News, the police department agreed to ban unsupervised interrogations of underage suspects.

Relatives of the victims spoke publicly after the identification. Barbara Wilson, the mother of Jennifer and Sarah Harbison, said the families had never wanted anyone punished for something they did not do, Texas Public Radio reported.

name: Jaycee Dugard
summary: Jaycee Dugard, 11, was abducted on June 10, 1991, while walking to a school bus stop near South Lake Tahoe, California. She was held for 18 years at the Antioch home of Phillip and Nancy Garrido and was found alive in August 2009. Both pleaded guilty in April 2011; Phillip Garrido was sentenced to 431 years to life and Nancy Garrido to 36 years to life.
lastSeen: June 10, 1991, walking to a school bus stop near her home in the South Lake Tahoe area, California

sources.title: NBC News - Dugard details ordeal; kidnappers sentenced
KABC - Phillip, Nancy Garrido plead guilty to Jaycee Dugard kidnapping
ABC News - Parole Agents Should Have Found Jaycee Dugard, Report Says
Yahoo / People - Jaycee Dugard on Phillip Garrido's Eligibility for Parole
Wikipedia - Kidnapping of Jaycee Dugard

narrative: Jaycee Lee Dugard was 11 years old when she was abducted on the morning of June 10, 1991, while walking from her home to a school bus stop in the South Lake Tahoe area of California. Wikipedia's account, drawing on court records and news coverage, places the abduction in Meyers, just south of the city, and says her stepfather saw her being pulled into a car and tried to follow. At the 2011 sentencing, the judge said Phillip Garrido had used a stun device on her during the abduction, NBC News reported.

She was taken to the Garridos' home in an unincorporated area near Antioch, in Contra Costa County. According to NBC News, she was kept first in a backyard shed and later in tents behind the house. During her captivity she gave birth to two daughters fathered by Phillip Garrido. Wikipedia gives their birth dates as August 1994 and November 1997, when Dugard was 14 and 17.

Phillip Garrido was on parole throughout. He had been convicted in the 1970s of kidnapping and raping a woman, served about 11 years in prison and was paroled in 1988, according to a People report carried by Yahoo. California took over his supervision from federal authorities in 1999. A November 2009 report by the California Office of the Inspector General, described by ABC News, found that the corrections department had failed to supervise him properly and had missed repeated chances to discover the people living behind his house.

The case broke open in late August 2009. According to ABC News, Garrido appeared on the University of California, Berkeley campus with the two girls, and campus police employees who checked his background learned he was a registered sex offender and alerted his parole office. When he came to a parole office meeting on August 26, 2009, accompanied by his wife, Dugard and the children, Dugard's identity was established and the Garridos were arrested.

On April 28, 2011, both defendants pleaded guilty in El Dorado County Superior Court. KABC reported that Phillip Garrido admitted 14 counts, including kidnapping and rape, and that Nancy Garrido admitted kidnapping and a rape-related charge. On June 2, 2011, Judge Douglas Phimister sentenced Phillip Garrido to 431 years to life and Nancy Garrido to 36 years to life; both waived their right to appeal, according to NBC News. Dugard did not attend, and her mother read a statement on her behalf.

California paid Dugard a $20 million settlement over the failures in parole supervision. According to Wikipedia, a separate suit against the federal government was rejected by the Ninth Circuit in 2016. Dugard published memoirs in 2011 and 2016 and founded the JAYC Foundation.

Phillip Garrido is sentenced to 431 years to life and Nancy Garrido to 36 years to life.
Dugard's memoir A Stolen Life is published.
The Ninth Circuit rejects Dugard's civil claims against the federal government, according to Wikipedia.

name: Nique Leili
summary: Dominique "Nique" Leili, 44, was last seen at her home near Lawrenceville, Georgia, in the early hours of July 9, 2011. Volunteer searchers found her body hidden under vegetation at the entrance to her neighborhood on July 16. Her husband, Matthew Leili, was charged in 2015, convicted of malice murder on February 5, 2016, and sentenced to life without parole. Georgia's Supreme Court affirmed in 2019.
lastSeen: Early morning of July 9, 2011, at her home in unincorporated Lawrenceville, Gwinnett County, Georgia

sources.title: FindLaw - Leili v. State (Supreme Court of Georgia, 2019)
FOX 5 Atlanta - Gwinnett County man found guilty of murdering wife
ABC News - How This Georgia Man Almost Got Away With His Wife's Murder
Atlanta Journal-Constitution - Family petitions for custody of slain woman's kids

narrative: Dominique "Nique" Leili, 44, lived with her husband, Matthew Leili, and their two younger daughters in a subdivision in unincorporated Lawrenceville, Gwinnett County, Georgia. According to the Georgia Supreme Court's summary of the trial evidence, she was last seen in the early morning hours of July 9, 2011, after the couple had returned from dinner and a movie. The Atlanta Journal-Constitution reported in July 2011 that she had called 911 on June 28 of that year and told the dispatcher that her husband would not let her leave the house.

The court's opinion states that her husband did not report her disappearance. Her father tried to reach her by telephone on Monday, July 11, learned that she was gone, and filed a missing-person report with police. The Journal-Constitution reported that Matthew Leili filed for divorce on July 13, asking for sole custody of the children. Some news accounts, including an ABC News report, say he was the one who reported her missing; the appellate opinion attributes the report to her father.

On Saturday, July 16, 2011, relatives and friends organized a volunteer search. According to the court opinion, two members of the search party found her unclothed body face down beneath a mound of loose dirt and vegetation near the front of the neighborhood. The autopsy found no obvious cause of death. The medical examiner described injuries consistent with strangulation and considered the death highly suspicious for homicidal violence, but concealment and decomposition prevented a definitive finding. ABC News reported that the cause of death was officially undetermined and that toxicology results indicating GHB were part of the prosecution's theory.

Police seized computers and home surveillance equipment early in the investigation, but no arrest followed at the time. FOX 5 Atlanta reported that a later re-examination of that equipment led Gwinnett County police to announce murder and eavesdropping charges in March 2015; ABC News gives the arrest date as March 5, 2015. A grand jury indicted Matthew Leili in May 2015 on malice murder, two counts of felony murder, two counts of aggravated assault and three counts of unlawful eavesdropping and surveillance.

The trial ran from January 25 to February 5, 2016. The jury found him guilty of malice murder, one count of felony murder, one count of aggravated assault and all three eavesdropping counts, and acquitted him on the remaining two counts. He was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole, plus three consecutive five-year terms on the eavesdropping counts.

His motion for a new trial was denied on August 31, 2018. On appeal he argued that evidence should have been suppressed, that testimony from his former wife about other acts was wrongly admitted, and that his trial lawyers were ineffective. On October 21, 2019, the Supreme Court of Georgia found no reversible error and affirmed the convictions.

She is last seen at home in the early morning hours after an evening out with her husband.

A grand jury indicts him on malice murder, felony murder, aggravated assault and unlawful eavesdropping counts.
Trial begins in Gwinnett County.
The jury convicts him of malice murder and five other counts; he is sentenced to life in prison without parole.
The trial court denies his motion for a new trial.
The Supreme Court of Georgia affirms the convictions in Leili v. State.

name: Darlene Hulse
summary: Darlene Hulse, 28, was attacked by a stranger who came to the door of her rural home near Argos, Indiana, on the morning of August 17, 1984, while her three young daughters were inside. She was taken from the house, and her body was found the next day in woods about six miles away; she died of blunt force trauma. No one has been charged.
lastSeen: August 17, 1984, her home near Argos, Marshall County, Indiana

sources.title: WNDU - Michiana Unsolved: The Murder of Darlene Hulse
The Deck Investigates - Episode 1: Take a Bath
The Deck Investigates - Episode 2: A Stranger's Wrath
The Deck Investigates - Episode 18: Our Lingering Obsession

narrative: Darlene Hulse, 28, was at home with her three daughters on the morning of Friday, August 17, 1984. The family lived on a rural road off Old U.S. 31 near Argos, in Marshall County, Indiana, and her husband was at work. According to WNDU's 2023 report on the case, a man knocked on the door at about 9:30 a.m., forced his way in and tried to bind her with tape.

Two of the girls saw the attack begin. WNDU reported that one of them tried to telephone for help before the intruder pulled the phone away, and that the two then ran to their grandmother's house nearby. The youngest child, aged one, was left in the house. According to the investigative podcast The Deck Investigates, which interviewed all three daughters, the man struck Hulse with a poker from the family's wood stove. When police arrived she was gone, and a trail of blood led from the living room to the driveway where a vehicle had been parked.
Her body was found the following day in woods about six miles from the house. WNDU reported that the cause of death was blunt force trauma and that a fireplace poker was missing from the home.

The children and other witnesses gave descriptions of the man and his car. As reported by WNDU, he was thought to be in his early twenties, clean-shaven, with neatly combed blond hair and a long face, and was wearing corduroys and a striped T-shirt. The car was described as an older, rusted four-door sedan from the 1970s, green or bluish-green in colour; it was never found. WNDU reported that several men were looked at in 1984, including people in Texas and Alabama as well as local residents, and that all were ruled out. The investigation slowed after the first year.

Indiana State Police hold the evidence in the case, more than four dozen items according to WNDU, including clothing from which a partial male DNA profile has been recovered. In the 2023 report, Marshall County Prosecutor Nelson Chipman said those still working on the case remained confident that a breakthrough was close. The Deck Investigates devoted its first season to the case in 2023, and in October 2023 it reported that Hulse's family had started a petition asking for further DNA testing and comparison. No arrest has been announced and no one has been charged.

timeline.event: Investigators examine and rule out several men, including individuals in Texas and Alabama, according to WNDU.
At about 9:30 a.m., a man forces his way into Darlene Hulse's home near Argos and attacks her; two of her daughters run to their grandmother's house for help. Hulse is taken from the home.
Hulse's body is found in woods about six miles from her home; the cause of death is blunt force trauma.

WNDU reports that a partial male DNA profile has been recovered from Hulse's clothing and that the Marshall County prosecutor remains hopeful of a breakthrough.
The Deck Investigates reports that Hulse's family has launched a petition seeking further DNA testing and comparison.

name: Corrie McKeague
summary: RAF gunner Corrie McKeague, 23, vanished after a night out in Bury St Edmunds, Suffolk, on September 24, 2016. CCTV showed him entering an area containing commercial waste bins, and a months-long landfill search found no remains. In March 2022 an inquest jury concluded that he died of compression asphyxia after climbing into a bin that was emptied into a bin lorry; his body has never been found.
lastSeen: September 24, 2016, Bury St Edmunds, Suffolk, England

sources.title: Disappearance of Corrie McKeague - Wikipedia
Yahoo News/BBC - Corrie Mckeague's mum: 'We did all we could to find him'

narrative: In the early morning hours of September 24, 2016, Corrie McKeague, a 23-year-old RAF gunner based at RAF Honington, went missing after a night out with friends in Bury St Edmunds, Suffolk, England. CCTV footage showed him walking alone through the town center at approximately 3:25 a.m. and entering an area behind a Greggs bakery known as the 'horseshoe' area, which contained large commercial rubbish bins. He was not seen on any camera leaving the area.

Police initially conducted a missing person investigation, searching the town and surrounding areas. The inquiry eventually focused on a garbage collection truck that serviced the bins in the horseshoe area. Records showed the truck had picked up a load significantly heavier than usual that morning—approximately 100 kg heavier—consistent with the weight of a person.

The garbage truck's load was deposited at the Milton landfill in Cambridgeshire. An extensive search of the landfill was conducted over 20 weeks, sifting through thousands of tons of waste. Despite this extraordinary effort, Corrie's remains were not found. The landfill search cost over £1 million.

Suffolk Police concluded that the most likely explanation was that Corrie had climbed into a bin—possibly to sleep, as he was intoxicated—and was collected by the garbage truck and taken to the landfill. His mother, Nicola Urquhart, has publicly questioned this conclusion, pointing to the failure to find remains and other inconsistencies. In March 2022 an inquest jury reached the same conclusion, and Suffolk Police consider the investigation complete unless new credible information emerges.

timeline.event: Corrie McKeague is last seen on CCTV entering the horseshoe area.
A garbage truck collects an unusually heavy load from the area.
20-week search of Milton landfill begins; no remains found.
Police conclude Corrie likely entered a bin; case remains open.
An inquest jury concludes that McKeague died of compression asphyxia after climbing into a commercial waste bin that was emptied into a bin lorry.

name: Aniah Blanchard
summary: Nineteen-year-old Aniah Blanchard, stepdaughter of UFC fighter Walt Harris, disappeared from Auburn, Alabama, in October 2019. Her remains were found a month later in Macon County. Ibraheem Yazeed was convicted of murder and felony murder in March 2026 and sentenced in May 2026 to life in prison. Her case led to 'Aniah's Law' in Alabama.
lastSeen: October 23, 2019, Auburn, Alabama

sources.title: Murder of Aniah Blanchard - Wikipedia
Yahoo News - Ibraheem Yazeed sentenced to life in prison for 2019 murder of Aniah Blanchard

narrative: On October 23, 2019, 19-year-old Aniah Haley Blanchard was last seen at a convenience store in Auburn, Alabama. Her abandoned car was found two days later in a Montgomery apartment complex parking lot with blood evidence inside. Aniah was a Southern Union State Community College student and the stepdaughter of UFC heavyweight fighter Walt Harris.

An intensive search and investigation led police to Ibraheem Yazeed, a 30-year-old man with a lengthy criminal history including charges of kidnapping and robbery. Yazeed had been captured on surveillance footage at the convenience store where Aniah was last seen. He was arrested on November 7.

Aniah's remains were found on November 25 in a wooded area in Macon County, approximately 25 miles from Auburn. The medical examiner determined she had died from a gunshot wound. Yazeed was charged with capital murder. The case drew national attention partly due to Walt Harris's public profile in the UFC.

After years of delays, Yazeed was convicted in March 2026 of murder and felony murder, rather than capital murder, and was sentenced in May 2026 to life in prison. Aniah's case exposed a gap in Alabama law: Yazeed had been free on bond at the time of her murder despite facing charges for kidnapping and attempted murder in another case. In response, Alabama voters approved 'Aniah's Law' in 2022, amending the state constitution to allow judges to deny bail in certain violent felony cases.

Her car is found abandoned with blood evidence inside.
Ibraheem Yazeed is arrested.
Aniah's remains are found in Macon County.

name: Summer Wells
summary: Five-year-old Summer Wells was reported missing on June 15, 2021 from her family's home on Ben Hill Road in the Beech Creek community of Hawkins County, Tennessee. A statewide AMBER Alert issued the next day is still active. Large ground searches and more than 2,000 tips have not located her, and no arrests have been made. The Tennessee Bureau of Investigation says the case remains active.
lastSeen: June 15, 2021, Ben Hill Road, Beech Creek community, Hawkins County, Tennessee

sources.title: Tennessee Bureau of Investigation Newsroom - AMBER Alert: Summer Wells
WSMV - What happened to Summer Wells? Case remains unsolved 5 years after TN girl's disappearance
WVLT - Family, sheriff release statements on fifth anniversary of Summer Wells disappearance
WVLT - TBI agents, detectives follow up on lead in Summer Wells case
WCYB - Summer Wells now missing from Hawkins County home for 5 years, TBI releases video
NewsChannel 9 - Timeline: AMBER Alert search for missing Tennessee 5-year-old Summer Wells

narrative: Summer Moon-Utah Wells was five years old when she was reported missing at about 6:30 p.m. on June 15, 2021 from her family's home on Ben Hill Road, in the Beech Creek community near Rogersville in Hawkins County, Tennessee. According to the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation (TBI), she has blonde hair and blue eyes, stood about three feet tall and weighed around 40 pounds. She was last seen wearing grey pants and a pink shirt and may have been barefoot. WSMV reports that she was last seen heading towards the basement of the house, which has a door leading outside.

The TBI issued an Endangered Child Alert the same evening and upgraded it to a statewide AMBER Alert on June 16. The search that followed was one of the largest of its kind in the state. According to the TBI, three large-scale ground searches covered roughly 3,000 acres and drew on more than 100 local, state and federal agencies, with additional searches of waterways and from the air. The family's house and land, including the basement and crawl space, were searched several times. A timeline published by NewsChannel 9 states that the FBI's child abduction response team was brought in on June 21 and that the ground operation was scaled back to specialized teams on June 27, 2021.

On June 26, 2021 the TBI asked for help in identifying a possible witness: the driver of a maroon or red 1998-2000 Toyota Tacoma with a ladder rack and white buckets, which a witness reported seeing near Beech Creek Road and Ben Hill Road on June 14 or 15. The TBI has said the driver was never identified. The bureau has also said that it has found no evidence that Summer was abducted, while stressing that every possibility is still being examined.

The number of tips grew from about 870 in early July 2021 to more than 2,000 by June 2022. The TBI has said that most of them concerned rumor and speculation and that investigators have few clues about what happened. No one has been named as a suspect or charged in connection with the disappearance. WSMV reports that Summer's three brothers were removed from the home by the state's children's services department in July 2021, and that her father, Don Wells, pleaded guilty in February 2022 to an unrelated driving-under-the-influence charge.

The investigation is led by the TBI with the Hawkins County Sheriff's Office and the FBI. A new age-progression image was released in August 2025. In November 2025, according to WVLT, agents and detectives followed up a lead on Van Hill Road in Greeneville, about ten miles from the family home; the TBI did not say what, if anything, was found. On the fifth anniversary, June 15, 2026, the TBI released a video appeal and said the investigation remained active with no new developments to announce publicly. The AMBER Alert remains in effect.

name: Maddie Clifton
summary: Eight-year-old Maddie Clifton disappeared in Jacksonville, Florida, on November 3, 1998. A week later her body was found hidden in the waterbed frame of her 14-year-old neighbor, Joshua Phillips, by his mother. Phillips was tried as an adult, convicted of first-degree murder in 1999, and resentenced to life in 2017 with a review after 25 years. He withdrew his review application in May 2026.
lastSeen: November 3, 1998, near her home in Jacksonville, Florida

sources.title: CBS News - Life In Prison For Teen Killer
News4Jax - Joshua Phillips withdraws bid for sentence review, cites need for professional counseling
News4Jax - Judge to review life sentence of man who killed 8-year-old girl in 1998
News4Jax - Nearly 30 years after Maddie Clifton's murder, her killer is preparing to ask for freedom
News4Jax - Wednesday marks 23 years since murder of Maddie Clifton
Wikipedia - Josh Phillips (murderer)

narrative: Madelyn "Maddie" Clifton was eight years old when she disappeared from her neighborhood in Jacksonville, Florida, on November 3, 1998. According to WJXT News4Jax, police, relatives and members of the community searched for her for about a week. CBS News reported that one of the people who took part in the neighborhood search was Joshua Phillips, a 14-year-old who lived near the Clifton family.

On November 10, 1998, seven days after Maddie was last seen, Phillips's mother, Melissa Phillips, found the girl's body beneath the plywood that supported her son's waterbed, according to CBS News. She reported the discovery to police, and Joshua Phillips was arrested the same day. CBS News reported that an autopsy found Maddie had been struck on the head and stabbed at least nine times in the chest and twice in the neck.

Phillips was prosecuted as an adult. CBS News reported that the trial was moved from Jacksonville to Polk County. According to that report, Phillips said he had accidentally hit Maddie with a baseball, panicked, and then killed her to stop her screaming. The defense argued for a manslaughter conviction, but the jury found him guilty of first-degree murder in July 1999. In August 1999, at age 15, he was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole.

In 2012 the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in Miller v. Alabama that mandatory life-without-parole sentences for juveniles are unconstitutional, which made Phillips eligible for a new sentencing hearing. According to News4Jax, Circuit Judge Waddell Wallace III heard the matter in 2017 and in November of that year again imposed a life sentence, describing the crime as one of the rare and unusual cases that justify life in prison for a juvenile offender. Under Florida law the new sentence carries a judicial review after 25 years. Wikipedia's summary of the appellate record states that a Florida appeals court upheld the sentence in December 2019 and that the Florida Supreme Court declined to take the case in June 2020.

News4Jax reported that in May 2025 Phillips, then 41, filed a formal application for the sentence review and was moved to the Duval County jail. Hearings were held during 2025, including one on October 21, and Maddie's family publicly opposed any reduction; her sister Jessie Clifton told the station that Maddie never received a second chance.

On May 6, 2026, Phillips filed a notice withdrawing his application, News4Jax reported. According to the filing, after reading the report of a state expert he concluded that he needed professional counseling about the crime and other issues before returning to court. The filing noted that the sentencing court keeps jurisdiction for the length of his sentence, so he may apply again. He remains in prison serving a life sentence.

name: Fort Worth Missing Trio
summary: Mary Rachel Trlica, 17, Lisa Renee Wilson, 14, and Julie Ann Moseley, 9, disappeared on December 23, 1974, after going Christmas shopping at Seminary South Shopping Center in Fort Worth, Texas. Rachel's car was found in the mall parking lot, and a letter signed with her name reached her husband the next day. None of the three has been found and no one has been charged.
lastSeen: December 23, 1974, Seminary South Shopping Center, Fort Worth, Texas

sources.title: NCMEC - Missing poster: Mary Rachel Trlica
NBC 5 Dallas-Fort Worth - Fort Worth cold case families feel 'forgotten'
FOX 7 Austin - 3 Fort Worth girls still missing 50 years later
FOX 7 Austin - Fort Worth missing trio: Family of Julie Moseley shares their story
Wikipedia - Fort Worth missing trio

narrative: Mary Rachel Trlica, 17, Lisa Renee Wilson, 14, and Julie Ann Moseley, 9, have been missing since December 23, 1974. According to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC), the three were last seen at Seminary South Shopping Center in Fort Worth, Texas. Rachel, who used her middle name, was a married high school student; according to Wikipedia's summary of the case, she had been married to Tommy Trlica for about six months and was driving a 1972 Oldsmobile 98.

FOX 7 Austin, which interviewed Julie's brother Terry Moseley in 2025, reported that the girls set out to shop for Christmas, visiting an Army/Navy store and then the mall. Wikipedia's account, which draws largely on Fort Worth Star-Telegram reporting, says Julie asked to go along at the last minute and that Renee wanted to be home by about 4 p.m. for a party. They did not return. The car was found that evening in a parking lot at the mall, and the same account says gifts the girls had bought were inside.

The following day a letter arrived at the Trlica home. It was signed with Rachel's name and said, in substance, that the girls had needed to get away, were going to Houston, and would be back in about a week. NBC 5 Dallas-Fort Worth reported that the families regarded the note as suspicious because Rachel's name was misspelled in the signature. According to Wikipedia, handwriting examinations, including one by the FBI, were inconclusive. The families have consistently rejected the idea that the girls ran away; Terry Moseley told FOX 7 that no one in the families believed the letter.

Wikipedia's account describes numerous leads over the following years, none of which produced a result: a private investigator hired by the families organized searches in 1975, and skeletal remains found in Brazoria County in 1976 and 1981 were compared with the girls' records and excluded. The same account says Fort Worth police assigned the case to a homicide detective in January 2001, and that two cars raised from Benbrook Lake in 2018 yielded nothing connected to the case. These details rest on Wikipedia and were not confirmed independently.

In November 2024, NBC 5 reported that the families wanted the letter tested to determine who wrote or handled it. Fort Worth Police Chief Neil Noakes told the station that the department would review cold cases for evidence that could be submitted for additional testing. NCMEC marked the 50th anniversary of the disappearance, and FOX 7 reported in January 2025 that the organization continues to publish age-progressed images of the three.
No one has been charged, and no public source reviewed identifies a suspect. Anyone with information is asked to call the Fort Worth Police Department at 817-335-4222 or NCMEC at 1-800-843-5678.

name: Cornelia Crilley
summary: Cornelia Crilley, a 23-year-old TWA flight attendant, was found strangled in her apartment on Manhattan's Upper East Side in June 1971. The case stayed unsolved for about 40 years until a Manhattan grand jury indicted Rodney Alcala, already on death row in California, in 2011. He pleaded guilty in December 2012 to murdering Crilley and Ellen Hover and was sentenced to 25 years to life.
lastSeen: June 12, 1971, Upper East Side, Manhattan, New York City

sources.title: CBS News (48 Hours) - Rodney Alcala: The Killing Game
HuffPost / AP - Rodney Alcala, California Killer Sentenced To Death, Admits To Killing Two New York City Women (archived)
New York Post - Manhattan DA indict cold-case 'killer' Rodney Alcala (archived)
Wikipedia - Rodney Alcala

narrative: Cornelia Crilley was 23 and worked as a flight attendant for Trans World Airlines when she was killed in her apartment on the Upper East Side of Manhattan in June 1971. Wikipedia gives the date as June 12, 1971, and the address as 427 East 83rd Street. According to CBS News and the New York Post, she had been sexually assaulted and strangled with a nylon stocking, and there was a bite mark on her body.

The New York Police Department investigated at the time but did not identify a suspect, and the case went cold. CBS News reported that a letter found beneath her body carried a fingerprint that remained unmatched for many years.

Rodney Alcala, a photographer, was arrested in California in July 1979 and, after two convictions that were overturned on appeal, was found guilty in 2010 of murdering four women and a 12-year-old girl in Southern California between 1977 and 1979. He was sentenced to death. He became widely known as the "Dating Game Killer" because he had appeared as a contestant on the television show in 1978. According to Wikipedia, Alcala had lived in New York in 1971 under the name John Berger and enrolled at New York University after fleeing a California arrest warrant.

NYPD Chief of Detectives Phil Pulaski told the New York Post that the investigation gained momentum around 2003 because of changes in technology. Court papers cited by the Associated Press, as published by HuffPost, say a New York detective interviewed Alcala in California in 2005. CBS News reported that the fingerprint on the letter was eventually matched to Alcala through the FBI database and that the bite mark was compared with an impression of his teeth. The Manhattan District Attorney's cold case unit reopened the file, and officials said more than 100 witnesses were interviewed.

In January 2011, District Attorney Cyrus Vance Jr. announced that a Manhattan grand jury had indicted Alcala for the murders of Crilley and of Ellen Hover, 23, who disappeared from Manhattan in 1977 and whose remains were found in Westchester County the following year. Alcala was brought to New York in 2012 and first pleaded not guilty. On December 14, 2012, he changed his plea to guilty on both counts, telling the judge he wanted to return to California to work on the appeal of his death sentence.

According to Wikipedia, he was sentenced on January 7, 2013, to 25 years to life, to run concurrently with his other sentences. Alcala died of natural causes on July 24, 2021, aged 77, while still under sentence of death in California.

name: Dee Dee Blanchard
summary: Dee Dee Blanchard was murdered by her daughter Gypsy Rose's boyfriend after years of medical child abuse (Munchausen syndrome by proxy). Gypsy had been forced to feign illness and disability her entire life. The case exposed one of the most extreme instances of Munchausen by proxy ever documented.
lastSeen: June 10, 2015, Springfield, Missouri

sources.title: Murder of Dee Dee Blanchard - Wikipedia
Gypsy Rose Blanchard case - BuzzFeed News
ABC News - Gypsy Rose Blanchard released from prison after serving time for mom's murder
ABC News - How a young woman forced to use a wheelchair ended up in prison for her mother's murder

KY3 - Greene County judge deciding motion in Nicholas Godejohn's attempt for new trial

narrative: For Gypsy Rose Blanchard's entire life, her mother Clauddine 'Dee Dee' Blanchard had subjected her to severe medical child abuse known as Munchausen syndrome by proxy (factitious disorder imposed on another). Dee Dee claimed Gypsy suffered from leukemia, muscular dystrophy, epilepsy, and brain damage, among other conditions. Gypsy was confined to a wheelchair, had her head shaved, was fed through a feeding tube, and took numerous medications—none of which she needed.

Dee Dee and Gypsy received free housing from Habitat for Humanity (as Hurricane Katrina victims), free trips from Make-A-Wish Foundation, and considerable charitable donations. Dee Dee controlled every aspect of Gypsy's life, including her age—Gypsy was actually several years older than her mother claimed. Medical professionals who questioned Dee Dee's claims were swiftly cut off.

As Gypsy grew older and gained internet access, she began to understand the extent of her mother's deception. She formed an online relationship with Nicholas Godejohn, a 26-year-old man from Wisconsin. Together they planned Dee Dee's murder. In June 2015, Godejohn traveled to their Springfield, Missouri home and stabbed Dee Dee to death while Gypsy hid in the bathroom; her body was discovered on June 14.

The case captivated the public when it was uncovered, raising complex questions about victimhood and justice. Gypsy, who had been a victim of extreme abuse her entire life, was also a participant in planning her mother's murder. She pleaded guilty to second-degree murder and was sentenced to 10 years in prison. She was released in December 2023. Godejohn was convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to life in prison. The case was adapted into the Hulu series 'The Act' and multiple documentaries.

Facebook post by Gypsy's account reads 'That bitch is dead'; police discover body.

name: Nipsey Hussle
summary: Grammy-nominated rapper and community activist Nipsey Hussle was shot and killed outside his Marathon Clothing store in the Hyde Park neighborhood of Los Angeles. Eric Holder Jr. was convicted of first-degree murder in 2022.
lastSeen: March 31, 2019, Marathon Clothing store, Hyde Park, Los Angeles
narrative: On March 31, 2019, Ermias Joseph Asghedom, known professionally as Nipsey Hussle, a 33-year-old Grammy-nominated rapper and beloved community activist, was shot and killed in the parking lot of his Marathon Clothing store on Slauson Avenue in the Hyde Park neighborhood of South Los Angeles. He was shot multiple times, including in the head, and was pronounced dead at a hospital.

Nipsey Hussle was far more than a rapper to his community. He had invested heavily in the Crenshaw neighborhood where he grew up, opening businesses, creating jobs, and working to reduce gang violence. He owned the shopping plaza where his store was located and was developing plans for affordable housing. He had been scheduled to meet with LAPD officials to discuss strategies for reducing gang violence the day after his murder.

The shooter was identified as Eric Ronald Holder Jr., 29, a man from the same neighborhood who had been at the Marathon store that day. Holder and Nipsey had a brief conversation before Holder left and returned minutes later with a handgun, shooting Nipsey multiple times and then kicking him in the head. The motive appeared to be personal—reportedly related to a conversation about Holder being a snitch—rather than gang-related, though both men had gang associations.

Holder fled the scene but was arrested two days later. He was charged with murder and two counts of attempted murder for injuring bystanders. In July 2022, a jury convicted Holder of first-degree murder. He was sentenced to 60 years to life in prison. Nipsey Hussle's death sparked an outpouring of grief in Los Angeles and beyond, and his legacy as a community leader and entrepreneur has only grown since his passing.

name: Daniel Morcombe
summary: Thirteen-year-old Daniel Morcombe disappeared while waiting for a bus at Woombye on Queensland's Sunshine Coast on December 7, 2003. After an undercover police operation, Brett Peter Cowan was arrested in August 2011 and Daniel's remains were found in bushland near the Glass House Mountains. Cowan was convicted of murder in March 2014 and sentenced to life imprisonment.
lastSeen: December 7, 2003, Kiel Mountain Road underpass, Woombye, Queensland

sources.title: Murder of Daniel Morcombe - Wikipedia
Cowan conviction - ABC News

narrative: On December 7, 2003, thirteen-year-old Daniel James Morcombe was waiting at a bus stop beneath the Kiel Mountain Road overpass on the Sunshine Coast, Queensland, Australia. He was heading to a shopping centre to buy Christmas presents. When a bus passed without stopping due to running late, Daniel was left waiting for the next one. He was never seen again.

Daniel's disappearance sparked one of Queensland's largest missing person investigations. Despite extensive searches, public appeals, and the establishment of a dedicated task force, no trace of Daniel was found for years. His parents, Bruce and Denise Morcombe, became prominent advocates for child safety, founding the Daniel Morcombe Foundation.

In 2011, a covert police operation targeting convicted child sex offender Brett Peter Cowan led to a breakthrough. Undercover officers posing as members of a criminal organization befriended Cowan, who eventually confessed to abducting, sexually assaulting, and murdering Daniel. He led officers to Daniel's remains in bushland near the Glass House Mountains.

Cowan was arrested in August 2011 and stood trial in 2014. He was found guilty of murder, indecent treatment of a child, and interfering with a corpse, and was sentenced to life imprisonment with a non-parole period of 20 years. The case led to significant reforms in child protection legislation in Queensland.

name: Sarah Everard
summary: Sarah Everard, 33, was kidnapped, raped and murdered by serving Metropolitan Police officer Wayne Couzens while walking home in south London on March 3, 2021. Couzens pleaded guilty and on September 30, 2021 received a whole-life sentence.
lastSeen: March 3, 2021, Clapham Common, London

sources.title: Murder of Sarah Everard - Wikipedia
Everard vigil - The Guardian

narrative: On the evening of March 3, 2021, 33-year-old Sarah Everard left a friend's house in Clapham, south London, to walk home to Brixton Hill, a journey of about 50 minutes. She was seen on CCTV walking along the A205 Poynders Road near Clapham Common at approximately 9:30 p.m. She never arrived home.

Sarah's boyfriend reported her missing the following day when she failed to arrive at work. A major investigation was launched, and CCTV footage revealed that Sarah had been stopped near Clapham Common by a man who had used his Metropolitan Police warrant card and handcuffs to carry out a fake arrest, claiming she had violated COVID-19 lockdown restrictions.

The man was identified as Wayne Couzens, a serving Metropolitan Police diplomatic protection officer. He had hired a rental car for the abduction. Phone and CCTV evidence traced Couzens' movements as he drove Sarah to Kent, where he raped and strangled her. He burned her body in a refrigerator in an area of woodland near Ashford, Kent, where her remains were discovered on March 10.

Couzens was arrested on March 9 and charged with kidnap and murder. He pleaded guilty to both charges and on September 30, 2021, was sentenced to a whole-life order, meaning he will never be released from prison. The case provoked widespread outrage, vigils, and protests across the UK, sparking a national conversation about women's safety and leading to significant scrutiny of the Metropolitan Police's vetting procedures and culture.

Wayne Couzens, a serving police officer, is arrested.

name: Jenny Lin
summary: Fourteen-year-old Jenny Lin was stabbed to death in her family's home in Castro Valley, California, on May 27, 1994; her father found her in a bathroom when he returned from work. The Alameda County Sheriff's Office says an intruder entered through a window. No one has been charged, and a $200,000 reward funded by her family and friends remains on offer.
lastSeen: May 27, 1994, her home in Castro Valley, California

sources.title: ABC7 News (via Yahoo News) - Jenny Lin's family searching for answers 32 years after murder
ABC7 News - New technology may lead to breakthrough in 1994 murder of Castro Valley teen Jenny Lin, sheriff says
Pleasanton Weekly - Reward doubled in cold-case murder of Jenny Lin in Castro Valley
San Francisco Chronicle / SFGATE - How man convicted in Oregon became suspect in girl's killing
Hoodline - Alameda County Sheriff's Office marks anniversary of Jenny Lin's murder

narrative: Jennifer "Jenny" Lin was an eighth-grade student in Castro Valley, an unincorporated community in Alameda County, California. Her father, John Lin, has described her as a well-liked, straight-A student, and the Alameda County Sheriff's Office remembers her as a skilled musician and honor roll student.

On May 27, 1994, she was at home after school. According to the Pleasanton Weekly, she was stabbed to death between 5:15 p.m. and 6:45 p.m. ABC7 News, citing the sheriff's office, reported that the killer entered the house through a window and waited for her. Her father found her body in a bathroom when he came home from work. No motive was apparent, and investigators have long believed the killer had little or no prior contact with her, the San Francisco Chronicle reported.

The family set up a $100,000 reward shortly after the killing and founded the Jenny Lin Foundation, incorporated in 1994, which promotes child safety and youth music education. The foundation runs a free summer music camp that ends with an annual tribute concert.

In May 2006 the sheriff's department publicly named Sebastian Shaw, a man serving three life sentences in Oregon for murders committed in Portland, as its suspect. The Chronicle reported that he had been one of more than 50 people examined early in the inquiry, that he had been found in August 1994 in a car stolen in nearby San Ramon, and that he had not been arrested or charged in the Lin case. He never was. Shaw died in prison in October 2021, and in June 2022 Sheriff Greg Ahern told ABC7 that Shaw had once been considered the prime suspect but was later ruled out.

In April 2022 the family and friends doubled the reward to $200,000. Two months later, at the annual vigil, Ahern said all the evidence had been re-examined with newer DNA technology capable of extracting additional cells, that this had produced new leads, and that investigators had possibilities they would not disclose. The sheriff's office said on the anniversary in 2025 that the evidence is resubmitted to crime laboratories as technology develops.

The case remained unsolved in July 2026, when ABC7 reported on the foundation's concert and the family's continuing appeal. Anyone with information can contact the Alameda County Sheriff's Office Cold Case Homicide Unit at (510) 667-3661 or its anonymous tip line at (510) 667-3622.
