name: Lina Sardar Khil
summary: Lina Sardar Khil, 3, disappeared on December 20, 2021, from the playground of the Villas Del Cabo apartment complex in San Antonio, Texas, where her family, who had come from Afghanistan, was living. An AMBER Alert and searches by police and the FBI produced no trace of her. A 2024 search prompted by a tip found nothing, and the case remains unsolved.
lastSeen: December 20, 2021, playground at the Villas Del Cabo apartments, San Antonio, Texas

sources.title: KSAT - Timeline: 3 years since Lina Khil's disappearance on San Antonio's Northwest Side
National Center for Missing and Exploited Children - National spotlight on missing Texas girl Lina Sardar Khil
FOX 7 Austin - Missing in Texas: Lina Sardar Khil
KSAT - Lina Khil topic page
Wikipedia - Disappearance of Lina Khil

narrative: Lina Sardar Khil was three years old when she disappeared from the playground of the Villas Del Cabo apartment complex on the northwest side of San Antonio, Texas, on December 20, 2021. According to a KSAT timeline of the case, she was last seen between 5 and 6 p.m. and was reported missing at 7:15 p.m. She was wearing a black jacket, a red dress and black shoes. FOX 7 Austin reported that her mother said she had stepped away briefly and that Lina was gone when she came back.

Lina's family had come to the United States from Afghanistan. Wikipedia's summary of the case, citing local reporting, states that her father had worked with the U.S. Army and that the family arrived on a special visa. An AMBER Alert was issued, according to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children, and San Antonio police and the FBI carried out an extensive search of the area without locating her.

On the first anniversary, December 20, 2022, San Antonio police released surveillance video showing Lina at the playground shortly before she vanished. KSAT quoted the lead detective as saying that at some point in the footage she walks out of the camera's view. The Islamic Center of San Antonio raised a reward of $250,000 for information, KSAT reported; Wikipedia states that the total later rose to $280,000.

An age-progression sketch was released around her fifth birthday in February 2023. On April 20, 2023, her father, Riaz Sardar Khil, took a polygraph examination at the FBI's San Antonio office, which KSAT described as an effort to clear his name. No one has been named as a suspect or charged in connection with the disappearance.

On February 14, 2024, a tip led police to search a wooded area near Interstate 10 and Wurzbach Road, not far from the apartment complex, using drones and ground-penetrating radar. Two days later police said the tip was not credible. KSAT reported that the family subsequently asked for new investigators to be assigned. In March 2024 the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children released an image showing how Lina might look at age six.

KSAT's coverage shows that in October 2025 the family announced plans to hire a private investigator, and that relatives and supporters gathered in December 2025 to mark four years since she vanished. No arrest, recovery or other resolution was found as of September 2026. Anyone with information is asked to contact the San Antonio Police Department's missing persons unit at 210-207-7273 or the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children at 1-800-843-5678.

name: Amina and Sarah Said
summary: Sisters Amina Said, 18, and Sarah Said, 17, were found shot to death in a taxi outside a hotel in Irving, Texas, on January 1, 2008. Their father, Yaser Said, was a fugitive for more than 12 years before his arrest in Justin, Texas, in August 2020. A Dallas County jury convicted him of capital murder on August 9, 2022, and he received life in prison without parole.
lastSeen: January 1, 2008, Irving, Texas

sources.title: NBC 5 Dallas-Fort Worth - Yaser Said Convicted of Capital Murder in Deaths of Teen Daughters
ABC News - Yaser Said found guilty of capital murder in 2008 shootings of daughters
CBS News Texas - Yaser Said found guilty of capital murder in deaths of his two daughters
NBC 5 Dallas-Fort Worth - Brother of Yaser Said Sentenced to 12 Years for Concealing Murder Suspect
Wikipedia - Yaser Abdel Said

narrative: Amina Said, 18, and her sister Sarah Said, 17, were found shot to death in a taxi parked outside a hotel in Irving, Texas, on New Year's Day 2008. CBS News Texas reported that both were students at Lewisville High School. According to NBC 5 Dallas-Fort Worth, Amina had been shot twice and Sarah nine times, and Sarah made a 911 call in which she said her father had shot her and that she was dying.

The taxi was one driven by their father, Yaser Said, an Egyptian-born cab driver who, according to CBS News Texas, had immigrated to the United States in 1983 and become a citizen. ABC News reported that in the days before the shooting Amina had written to a teacher that she feared her father would kill them, that the sisters and their mother had left for Oklahoma on December 25, 2007, and that they had returned to the Dallas area on December 31.

Said was not found after the shooting. According to Wikipedia's account, the FBI added him to its Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list on December 4, 2014; NBC 5 reported that he spent six years on the list. He was arrested on August 26, 2020, in Justin, Texas, more than 12 years after the killings.

Two relatives were prosecuted in federal court for helping him hide. NBC 5 reported that his son, Islam Said, pleaded guilty and was sentenced on April 27, 2021, to 10 years in federal prison, and that his brother, Yassein Said, was convicted by a jury in February 2021 and sentenced on June 4, 2021, to 12 years. Both cases involved charges of conspiracy to conceal a person from arrest, concealing a person from arrest, and conspiracy to obstruct an official proceeding.

Yaser Said's capital murder trial took place in Dallas County in August 2022. Prosecutors argued that he was preoccupied with controlling his daughters and killed them because they were dating and seeking independence, and they described the deaths as so-called honor killings. Said testified and denied killing his daughters, saying he had left the taxi and gone into nearby woods because he believed someone was following them. His lawyers argued that the investigation had been weak and had focused on him because he is Muslim.

On August 9, 2022, after about three hours of deliberation, the jury found him guilty of capital murder. Because prosecutors had not sought the death penalty, Judge Chika Anyiam imposed the automatic sentence of life in prison without the possibility of parole. A Texas court of appeals opinion in Yaser Abdel Said v. State, dated December 21, 2023, is listed on CourtListener; search results describe it as affirming the conviction.

name: Karlie Gusé
summary: Sixteen-year-old Karlie Lain Gusé disappeared from her family's home in Chalfant, Mono County, California, early on October 13, 2018, after a night of paranoia that followed smoking marijuana at a party. Neighbors reported seeing a girl matching her description walking toward U.S. Highway 6. Extensive searches found nothing, and the Mono County Sheriff's Office and FBI still treat the case as open.
lastSeen: October 13, 2018, White Mountain Estates, Chalfant, California, walking toward U.S. Highway 6

sources.title: Las Vegas Review-Journal - Missing teen's case leads from California to Nevada
Sierra Wave - MCSO: No new information on Karlie Guse
Sierra Wave - MCSO: No new information Karlie Lain Gusé
KRNV News 4 - Still no sign of missing Mono County teen three months after the 16-year-old disappeared

narrative: Karlie Lain Gusé was 16 when she disappeared from Chalfant, a small high-desert community in Mono County, California, about 11 miles north of Bishop. The Mono County Sheriff's Office said she was last seen in the early morning of Saturday, October 13, 2018, in the White Mountain Estates neighborhood, on Ponderosa Street near White Mountain Estate Road, walking toward U.S. Highway 6.

According to a Las Vegas Review-Journal account, Karlie told her stepmother, Melissa Gusé, on the evening of October 12 that she planned to attend a football game at her high school in Bishop. She instead went to a house party, where she smoked marijuana with her boyfriend and another teenager. She became frightened and called her stepmother, who picked her up and took her home. The newspaper reported that Melissa Gusé spent the night trying to calm the teenager, who moved between lucidity and paranoia, and recorded about eight minutes of their conversation.

Melissa Gusé woke on the morning of October 13 to find Karlie gone. Her cellphone had been left on the kitchen counter. Melissa and Karlie's father, Zachary Gusé, searched the neighborhood and then called 911, the Review-Journal reported. The Sheriff's Office said Karlie left without personal belongings or a phone and might be disoriented; a later release said she was possibly wearing a white T-shirt and gray sweatpants.

Three witnesses told investigators they saw someone matching Karlie's description that morning. Two neighbors described a tall, slender girl walking past around daybreak holding a piece of paper, heading toward the highway. A third, unnamed witness reported a girl standing in the sagebrush near Highway 6, the same area where tracking dogs lost her scent, according to the Review-Journal.

The Sheriff's Office said it used helicopters, scent dogs, search and rescue teams and off-road vehicles to search the neighborhood and surrounding desert, interviewed family and friends, and examined her social media and electronic devices. On October 31, 2018, it said there was no evidence of an abduction or any other crime but that all possibilities were being considered. The FBI and the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children assisted. The Review-Journal reported that cellphone data corroborated the accounts given by her father, stepmother and the two teenagers from the party, and that a search of the home and of Karlie's devices produced no incriminating evidence.

In October 2023 the Review-Journal reported that the Sheriff's Office had received a call in March 2021 from a witness who claimed to have seen Karlie at a party in Tonopah, Nevada, roughly 100 miles away, and that investigators had located a vehicle that may have been used to pick her up beside Highway 6. Sheriff Ingrid Braun confirmed that the lead was being actively investigated with the FBI. No arrest has been announced and Karlie has not been found.

name: Katelin Akens
summary: Katelin Akens, 19, vanished on December 5, 2015, after being dropped at her former stepfather's home in Partlow, Spotsylvania County, Virginia, for a ride toward a flight to Arizona. Her suitcase was found two days later beside River Road. She has not been found and no one is charged in her disappearance. Her former stepfather was arrested in April 2026 on child sex-offense charges and has pleaded not guilty.
lastSeen: December 5, 2015, at her former stepfather's home in Partlow, Spotsylvania County, Virginia

sources.title: WTOP - New charges against Virginia stepfather in missing woman, child sex abuse case
WTOP - Former stepfather had 'motive to kill' teenager last seen in Spotsylvania County in 2015, prosecutors say
Fredericksburg Free Press - 'Primary suspect' in Akens' disappearance not cooperating with authorities, police say
Fredericksburg Free Press - Spotsylvania detectives, state police arrest stepfather of missing area woman
NBC4 Washington - Former stepfather of missing woman charged with sex offenses
WTVR CBS 6 - Katelin Akens: Stepfather James Branton arrested 10 years after disappearance

narrative: Katelin Akens was 19 when she disappeared on December 5, 2015. She had grown up in Spotsylvania County, Virginia, was living in Arizona and had been visiting family, according to NBC Washington. She was due to fly home from Reagan National Airport that day.

According to WTOP and the Fredericksburg Free Press, her mother dropped her off at the home of her former stepfather, James Branton, in Partlow, in Spotsylvania County, because he had agreed to give her a ride. The plan was for him to take her to the Springfield mall in northern Virginia, where she would catch a Metro train to the airport. The Spotsylvania County Sheriff's Office said her plane ticket was never used. Two days later her suitcase was found along River Road in Spotsylvania County with most of its contents missing. NBC Washington reported that Branton told investigators he had dropped her off at the mall, but that no evidence confirming this was found.

The case remained a missing-person investigation for more than ten years. On April 10, 2026, Spotsylvania detectives and Virginia State Police arrested Branton on charges including aggravated sexual battery, custodial indecent liberties and child cruelty. WTOP reported that the charges concern alleged abuse of Akens and her younger sister between 2006 and 2011, when the girls and their mother lived with him. The sheriff's office named Akens as one of the alleged victims. Branton pleaded not guilty and was denied bond.

Branton has not been charged in connection with the disappearance. At the April bond hearing, Commonwealth's Attorney Ryan Mehaffey told the court that newly obtained evidence showed a potential motive to kill Akens; WTOP noted it was the first time prosecutors had said in court that they believe she is dead, and that investigators had not disclosed evidence of her death. Defense attorney John Spencer said his client had cooperated, had been cleared by Child Protective Services years earlier, and that the allegation was a stretch. Lt. Col. Delbert Myrick of the sheriff's office told the Free Press that Branton was the primary suspect, though possibly not the only one.

Investigators from the sheriff's office, state police, the FBI and the Virginia Department of Emergency Management searched three properties linked to Branton in April 2026 using excavators and ground-penetrating radar. Akens was not found, the Free Press reported.

In September 2026, WTOP reported that a Spotsylvania County grand jury had indicted Branton on 13 additional counts of possession of child sexual abuse material, and that his trial on the abuse charges, earlier set for July and then September, was expected to move to December. The sheriff's office says the investigation into the disappearance remains open and active.

A grand jury indicts Branton on 13 counts of possession of child sexual abuse material; his trial on the abuse charges is expected to be rescheduled for December.

name: Flora Fire Victims
summary: Four sisters aged 5 to 11 - Keyana Davis, Keyara Phillips, Kerriele McDonald and Kionnie Welch - died in a house fire in Flora, Indiana, on November 21, 2016. Indiana State Police say the fire was intentionally set. Their mother and two police officers were injured. No one has been arrested, and the FBI joined state police in a renewed appeal for information in July 2025.
lastSeen: November 21, 2016, 103 East Columbia Street, Flora, Indiana

sources.title: Indiana State Police - Flora Arson
Carroll County Comet - Investigators renew efforts in 2016 fatal Flora fire
WNDU - Outside review confirms Flora fire that killed 4 was arson
WISH-TV - A chase for answers: Questions remain after Flora fire kills 4 girls
WRTV - One year later: No arrest in deadly Flora fire that claimed the lives of four young sisters
Bing results - WTHR headlines (article itself blocked)

narrative: In the early hours of November 21, 2016, fire broke out in a rented two-story home at 103 East Columbia Street in Flora, a small town in Carroll County, Indiana. According to the Indiana State Police, four sisters died: Keyana Davis, 11, Keyara Phillips, 9, Kerriele McDonald, 7, and Kionnie Welch, 5. Their mother, Gaylin Rose, and two police officers who responded to the scene suffered injuries that the agency described as not life-threatening. WISH-TV reported that the first 911 call came at 3:35 a.m. and that the girls died from asphyxiation and inhalation of carbon monoxide and soot.

The cause of the fire was not settled at once. According to WRTV and WISH-TV, the state fire marshal's office first listed the cause as undetermined. On January 28, 2017, WRTV reported, the finding was changed to an intentionally set fire after investigators said accelerants had been detected. The Carroll County Comet reported that the criminal case was opened in February 2017. The Indiana State Police lead the investigation, with help from the Carroll County Sheriff's Department, the Flora Police Department and fire investigators from the Indiana Department of Homeland Security.

The investigation drew criticism in its first year. WRTV reported that investigators later revised their account of the accelerant evidence, saying it had been found in one location rather than several, and that the state fire investigator who worked on the case resigned in June 2017. The same report said the Flora fire chief resigned in November 2017 and that the Indiana NAACP became involved in October 2017, raising concerns about how the case was being handled. State police denied that detectives had mishandled the investigation, according to an Associated Press report carried by WNDU.

An outside review was then ordered. WNDU reported that the Indianapolis Fire Department began examining the case in early December 2017 and concluded on January 25, 2018, that the fire was arson, in agreement with the state's finding. State Police Superintendent Doug Carter said the criminal investigation would continue.

No suspect has been publicly named and no one has been charged. The house was demolished in October 2023, according to the Carroll County Comet. In July 2025, the newspaper reported, FBI agents and state police returned to Flora to talk with residents, and a joint statement from the two agencies asked anyone who saw, heard or was told anything about the fire to come forward, including people who had already been interviewed. A state police spokesman declined to say what prompted the renewed effort.

The Indiana State Police continue to list the case as an open criminal investigation and offer a reward of up to $5,000 for information leading to an arrest and conviction. Tips can be submitted to the FBI at tips.fbi.gov or 1-800-CALL-FBI.

State fire investigator assigned to the case resigns, according to WRTV.
Indiana NAACP becomes involved, citing concerns about the investigation, according to WRTV.
Flora fire chief resigns, according to WRTV.
Indianapolis Fire Department completes an outside review that agrees the fire was arson.
The house is demolished.
FBI agents and Indiana State Police return to Flora to seek information from residents; no arrests have been made.

name: Claremont Serial Murders
summary: Three women vanished from the upscale suburb of Claremont in Perth, Australia between 1996-1997. Telstra technician Bradley Edwards was convicted of two murders in 2020.
lastSeen: Various dates, Claremont, Perth, Western Australia

sources.title: Claremont serial killings - Wikipedia

narrative: Between 1996 and 1997, three young women disappeared after nights out in Claremont, an affluent suburb of Perth, Western Australia. Sarah Spiers (18) vanished on January 27, 1996; Jane Rimmer (23) on June 9, 1996; and Ciara Glennon (27) on March 14, 1997. The bodies of Rimmer and Glennon were found in bushland; Spiers has never been found.

The investigation became the longest and most expensive in Western Australian history. It spanned over two decades and involved new forensic techniques including DNA analysis of fibers found on the victims.
In 2016, Bradley Robert Edwards, a Telstra technician, was arrested. DNA evidence linked him to the crimes, specifically fibers from his Telstra-issued work car found on Ciara Glennon's body.

In 2020, Edwards was convicted of the murders of Rimmer and Glennon and acquitted of Spiers' murder due to insufficient evidence (her body has never been found). He was sentenced to life with a minimum of 40 years.

name: Saronno Hospital Patient Deaths (Leonardo Cazzaniga case)
summary: Leonardo Cazzaniga, a former deputy head of the emergency department at Saronno Hospital in Lombardy, Italy, was convicted of killing patients with overdoses of morphine, anaesthetics and sedatives. He was sentenced to life in January 2020. Italy's Court of Cassation upheld convictions for ten killings in 2022 and a further one, the death of Domenico Brasca on August 18, 2014, in 2024.
lastSeen: August 18, 2014, Saronno Hospital, Saronno, Lombardy, Italy (death of Domenico Brasca, the last killing for which Cazzaniga was convicted)

narrative: Leonardo Cazzaniga was deputy head of the emergency department at the hospital in Saronno, a town in Lombardy, northern Italy. Italian courts have found that he killed patients there by giving them large intravenous doses of morphine, anaesthetics and sedatives in quick succession. According to the news agency AGI, the practice was known among staff as the 'Cazzaniga protocol' and was applied to elderly patients with multiple illnesses.

AGI reported that the inquiry began in 2014, when an emergency department nurse, Clelia Leto, went to the Carabinieri. The investigation, called 'Angeli e Demoni' and led by the prosecutor's office in Busto Arsizio, resulted in the arrest in late November 2016 of Cazzaniga and of Laura Taroni, a nurse at the hospital with whom he was in a relationship. The initial accusations concerned four patients and Taroni's husband, Massimo Guerra, who died on June 30, 2013. Investigators later examined about fifty sets of medical records.

Cazzaniga was tried on fifteen counts of murder: twelve patients and three members of Taroni's family. On January 27, 2020, the Court of Assizes in Busto Arsizio sentenced him to life imprisonment with three years of daytime isolation, Il Fatto Quotidiano reported. He was convicted on twelve counts and acquitted on three, including the death of patient Domenico Brasca. Four doctors who had sat on an internal hospital commission that reviewed his conduct were given sentences of two years and six months for aiding and abetting. His defence argued that he had been providing palliative sedation to relieve suffering and had no intention to kill, and he told the court he was innocent.

On April 13, 2021, the Court of Assizes of Appeal in Milan upheld the life sentence, confirming ten murder convictions and acquitting him of three, according to ANSA. The same court ruled that the case against the four commission doctors was time-barred. VareseNews reported that the Court of Cassation upheld the life sentence in 2022, making final his convictions for the deaths of eight patients and two of Taroni's relatives, and sent one remaining count back for a further appeal hearing.

That count concerned Domenico Brasca, a man in his eighties from Rovello Porro who died on August 18, 2014. Cazzaniga was convicted of his murder at the new appeal hearing in Milan on June 27, 2023, and the Court of Cassation rejected the defence's appeal in March 2024, VareseNews reported.
Taroni was tried separately under a fast-track procedure. According to Il Fatto Quotidiano, she was sentenced to 30 years for her part in the deaths of her husband and her mother.

name: Michael & Alex Smith
summary: Michael Smith, 3, and his brother Alex, 14 months, drowned on October 25, 1994 when their mother, Susan Smith, let her car roll into John D. Long Lake near Union, South Carolina, with the boys strapped inside. She first claimed a Black man had carjacked her, then confessed nine days later. She was convicted of two counts of murder in July 1995, is serving life, and was denied parole in November 2024.
lastSeen: October 25, 1994, John D. Long Lake, Union, South Carolina

narrative: Michael Daniel Smith, aged three, and Alexander Tyler Smith, aged 14 months, died on October 25, 1994 in John D. Long Lake near Union, South Carolina. Their mother, Susan Smith, told police that evening that a Black man had taken her car at gunpoint and driven away with both boys still in the back seat. According to CBS News, she kept to that account for nine days while a widely publicized search took place and she made public appeals for the children's return.

On November 3, 1994, ABC News reports, investigators confronted Smith and she confessed. She said she had let her car, a Mazda Protégé according to Wikipedia, roll down a boat ramp into the lake with the two boys fastened into their car seats. CBS News reports that the investigation later established the car took about six minutes to go under. The man she had described did not exist, and the false report was widely criticized for the suspicion it had directed at Black residents of the area.

Smith was tried in 1995. Prosecutors, led by Tommy Pope, sought the death penalty. According to CBS News, their case was that she killed her sons because she believed they stood in the way of a relationship with the son of a wealthy local business owner, who had ended the affair. Wikipedia's account says that he had written to her that he did not want children, and that her lawyers, David Bruck and Judy Clarke, argued that she suffered from depression and a dependent personality disorder.

Fox News reports that the jury convicted Smith of two counts of murder on July 22, 1995. The jurors declined to impose a death sentence and she received life in prison. Under the South Carolina law in force at the time, she became eligible to apply for parole after serving 30 years. She is held at Leath Correctional Institution in Greenwood.

Smith's first parole hearing was held on November 20, 2024, when she appeared by video link. The boys' father, David Smith, and the trial prosecutor both asked the board to refuse release. The board voted unanimously to deny parole, citing the nature and seriousness of the crime and her record of offenses in prison, which according to ABC News includes sexual contact with corrections officers and drug possession. Fox News reports that in October 2025 she was found to have broken prison rules by communicating with a documentary filmmaker. She may reapply every two years, and her next hearing has been reported as scheduled for November 19, 2026.

name: Yates Children
summary: Five children of the Yates family, aged six months to seven years, were drowned by their mother, Andrea Yates, at their home in the Clear Lake area of Houston on June 20, 2001. Her 2002 capital murder conviction was overturned on appeal in 2005, and a second jury found her not guilty by reason of insanity on July 26, 2006. She was committed to a Texas state hospital.
lastSeen: June 20, 2001, family home in Clear Lake, Houston, Texas

sources.title: CNN - Andrea Yates Fast Facts

narrative: On June 20, 2001, the five children of Andrea and Russell Yates were drowned in the bathtub of the family home in Clear Lake, in the Houston area. The Houston Chronicle reported that the children were Noah, 7, John, 5, Paul, 3, Luke, 2, and Mary, 6 months, and that their mother called police and led officers to them.

Andrea Yates, a former nurse, had a documented history of serious mental illness. According to a CNN chronology of the case, she was admitted to a psychiatric unit in June 1999 after an overdose and diagnosed with a major depressive disorder, was treated again the following month after a suicide attempt, and was admitted twice to a treatment facility in the spring of 2001. CNN reports that her prescription for the antipsychotic drug Haldol was discontinued by her psychiatrist on June 4, 2001, a little over two weeks before the deaths.

Yates was indicted on July 30, 2001, on two counts of capital murder and pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity. On March 12, 2002, a Harris County jury convicted her on charges covering the deaths of Noah, John and Mary; CNN notes she was not tried for the deaths of Paul and Luke. The jury rejected the death penalty and she was sentenced to life in prison.

On January 6, 2005, the Texas First Court of Appeals reversed the conviction. NBC News reported that the ruling turned on testimony by the prosecution's psychiatric expert, Park Dietz, who had told jurors about an episode of the television drama "Law & Order" involving a mother who drowned her children and was found insane. No such episode existed. The court said the record did not show that Dietz had intentionally lied, but that the false testimony could have affected the jury's judgment.

At a second trial in Houston, a jury deliberated for more than 12 hours over three days and on July 26, 2006, found Yates not guilty by reason of insanity, according to the Houston Chronicle. She was ordered to a state mental hospital. CNN reports that she was moved in January 2007 from North Texas State Hospital's Vernon campus to Kerrville State Hospital.

Yates has remained at Kerrville since. Today.com reported in 2022, citing her longtime attorney George Parnham, that she is entitled to an annual review of her commitment and has waived it each year. A fund established in 2002 in memory of the children supports education about postpartum depression and psychosis.

name: Teresa Sievers
summary: Dr. Teresa Sievers, 46, was beaten to death with hammers in her Bonita Springs, Florida home on June 28, 2015. Her husband, Mark Sievers, was convicted of first-degree murder in December 2019 and sentenced to death. Curtis Wayne Wright Jr. pleaded guilty to second-degree murder and received 25 years; Jimmy Ray Rodgers was convicted of second-degree murder and sentenced to life.

narrative: Dr. Teresa Sievers, a 46-year-old physician who ran a medical practice in Bonita Springs, Florida, was killed in her home on the night of June 28, 2015. According to the facts set out by the Florida Supreme Court, she had left a family vacation in Connecticut and travelled home alone, while her husband, Mark Sievers, and their two daughters stayed behind at her mother's home. She pulled into the garage shortly before 11:25 p.m., took her luggage and walked into the house, where two men were waiting.

The court's opinion states that Curtis Wayne Wright Jr. and Jimmy Ray Rodgers, both from Missouri, struck her in the head with hammers until she died. The Lee County medical examiner testified that she died of blunt head trauma. The next morning, after she failed to arrive at work, Mark Sievers asked a family friend, Dr. Mark Petrites, to check on her; he found her on the kitchen floor.

According to the opinion, the first break came about two weeks later, when an informant in Illinois came forward and Wright, a longtime friend of Mark Sievers, emerged as a suspect. Searches in Missouri produced a GPS unit and phone evidence linking Wright to Rodgers, and Rodgers' girlfriend led detectives to items bought at a Lee County Walmart on the day of the killing and to discarded coveralls. Wright initially denied involvement, then confessed, implicated Mark Sievers and accepted a plea agreement. CBS News reported that Mark Sievers was arrested on February 26, 2016; the court record shows he was indicted in May 2016 for first-degree murder and conspiracy to commit murder.

Wright testified that Sievers asked him during a May 2015 wedding weekend in Missouri to arrange the killing, in exchange for a share of life insurance proceeds, and that he recruited Rodgers. Prosecutors cited marital problems, custody concerns and life insurance policies as the motive, according to the Associated Press.

Rodgers was tried first. A jury found him guilty of second-degree murder on October 23, 2019, rather than the first-degree murder prosecutors had sought, NBC 6 reported, and he was later sentenced to life in prison. Mark Sievers was convicted in December 2019 of first-degree murder and conspiracy and was sentenced to death, with a consecutive 30-year term on the conspiracy count. Wright, who had pleaded guilty to second-degree murder in 2016, was sentenced to 25 years on February 10, 2020.

The Florida Supreme Court affirmed Mark Sievers' convictions and death sentence on November 17, 2022. He has continued to challenge them in post-conviction proceedings. According to the Fort Myers News-Press, Lee Circuit Judge Bruce Kyle denied his motion to vacate the conviction and sentence on February 24, 2026, and his attorneys filed a motion for rehearing on March 6, 2026, arguing that his trial lawyers had been ineffective. The same report said Rodgers was also appealing his conviction.

name: Tamla Horsford
summary: Tamla Horsford, a Black mother of five, was found dead at a sleepover party at a white friend's home in Cumming, Georgia. Her death was ruled accidental but her family disputes this.

narrative: On November 4, 2018, forty-year-old Tamla Horsford, a Black mother of five, was found dead in the backyard of a home in Cumming, Georgia, following an adult sleepover party attended by approximately a dozen women—Tamla was the only Black attendee.
The Forsyth County Sheriff's Office quickly ruled her death accidental, concluding she had fallen from a second-floor balcony while intoxicated. Her blood alcohol level was elevated.

Tamla's family disputed the finding, citing injuries inconsistent with a simple fall and noting the speed with which the case was closed. They alleged that Tamla's injuries more closely resembled those from a physical assault.

After public pressure, the Georgia Bureau of Investigation reopened the case in June 2020; in July 2021 it concluded that no criminal charges would be pursued. The case became a symbol of how deaths of Black individuals in predominantly white communities can receive insufficient scrutiny.

summary: Sixteen-year-old Emma Walker was fatally shot in her bed at her family's Knoxville, Tennessee, home on November 21, 2016, by shots fired through her bedroom wall from outside. Her former boyfriend, William Riley Gaul, then 18, was convicted of first-degree murder in May 2018 and sentenced to life in prison, with parole eligibility after 51 years.

narrative: Emma Walker was a 16-year-old high school cheerleader in Knoxville, Tennessee. She had been in an on-and-off relationship for about two years with William Riley Gaul, who by the autumn of 2016 was an 18-year-old freshman and football player at Maryville College, according to ESPN and CBS News. The relationship had recently ended.

ABC News reported that unusual incidents preceded her death. On the Friday night before, Walker received anonymous messages claiming Gaul had been kidnapped, and she found him lying in a ditch. The next morning, a person dressed entirely in black tried to get into her family's home.

In the early hours of Monday, November 21, 2016, two shots were fired from outside the house through the wall of Walker's bedroom while she slept. One bullet struck her behind the left ear and the other lodged in her pillow, ABC News reported. Her mother found her unresponsive that morning.

Investigators learned that a 9mm handgun belonging to Gaul's grandfather had been reported missing. According to ABC News, two of Gaul's friends contacted authorities and agreed to wear hidden recording equipment. The following night they accompanied Gaul as he moved to get rid of the gun, and officers recovered the weapon and arrested him. Yahoo's summary of the case says black clothing and gloves were also recovered. Maryville College dismissed Gaul from its football team after his arrest.

Gaul was tried in Knox County Criminal Court in spring 2018. Prosecutors argued that he acted out of anger over the breakup and knew the layout of the home well enough to aim at where Walker slept. His defence attorney argued that Gaul never intended to hurt her and fired the shots in a plan to frighten her and then appear as her protector, and asked the jury to consider a lesser charge of reckless homicide, CBS News and ESPN reported.

On May 8, 2018, after about four hours of deliberation, the jury found Gaul guilty of first-degree murder, felony murder, stalking, tampering with evidence, theft and possession of a firearm during a dangerous felony. He had pleaded guilty to reckless endangerment, according to CBS News. He received the mandatory sentence of life in prison, under which he must serve 51 years before becoming eligible for parole. According to Wikipedia, a motion for a new trial was denied in 2021 and the Tennessee Court of Criminal Appeals upheld the murder conviction in February 2023.

name: Katelyn Markham
summary: Katelyn Markham, 21, disappeared from her home in Fairfield, Ohio, in August 2011; her skeletal remains were found in April 2013 in Cedar Grove, Indiana, and her death was ruled a homicide. Her fiancé, John Carter, was indicted for murder in March 2023, pleaded guilty to involuntary manslaughter in June 2024 and received the maximum three-year sentence. A judge denied him early release in January 2026.
lastSeen: August 13, 2011, her home in Fairfield, Butler County, Ohio

narrative: Katelyn Markham was 21 and a few weeks from completing a graphic arts degree at the Art Institute of Ohio in Cincinnati when she disappeared from her home in Fairfield, Ohio, in August 2011, according to CBS News. She had been engaged for about a year to John Carter, and the couple planned to move to Colorado, NBC News reported. WCPO noted that she was days away from her 22nd birthday.

She was last seen on August 13, 2011. According to NBC News, Carter called 911 on the night of August 14 to report her missing. He told Fairfield police he had been with her that evening, left for a friend's gathering, and later went to his mother's home. In the years that followed he took part in searches and gave media interviews asking for her return.

On April 7, 2013, skeletal remains identified as Markham's were found in a wooded dump site in Cedar Grove, Indiana, roughly 20 to 30 miles from her home. Authorities ruled the death a homicide but could not determine the cause, CBS News and NBC News reported.

The case was re-examined by investigators working for Butler County Prosecutor Michael Gmoser. A grand jury indicted Carter on two counts of murder in March 2023, and he pleaded not guilty. NBC News reported that the evidence was circumstantial, including witness accounts and writings found in a search of his home, and that Gmoser acknowledged there was no forensic or eyewitness evidence directly linking Carter to the death.

Shortly before trial, Carter pleaded guilty on June 7, 2024, to involuntary manslaughter under a plea agreement, and the murder charges were dropped. On July 18, 2024, Judge Daniel Haughey imposed three years in prison, the maximum for the offense. Gmoser told NBC that the statute of limitations had expired on other possible charges. Prosecutors said Carter had not explained how or why Markham died.

Carter sought early release in October 2025. Judge Haughey denied the motion on January 9, 2026, according to WVXU and WCPO. WCPO reported that after the hearing his attorney said Carter, despite the plea, maintains he did not cause her death; Gmoser described the court case as over. In June 2026 the Ohio House passed 'Katelyn's Law', a bill that would remove the statute of limitations for crimes connected to a murder, FOX19 reported; it then went to the Ohio Senate.

name: Tammy Daybell
summary: Tammy Daybell died at her home in Salem, Idaho on October 19, 2019. A coroner ruled the death natural without an autopsy, but her body was exhumed that December and an autopsy found she died of asphyxiation. Her husband, Chad Daybell, was convicted of her murder on May 30, 2024 and sentenced to death; his appeal is pending. Lori Vallow Daybell was convicted of conspiring to kill her.

narrative: Tammy Daybell lived with her husband, Chad Daybell, in Salem, a rural community in Fremont County, Idaho. On October 9, 2019, according to a timeline compiled by East Idaho News, she called 911 to report that a masked man had shot at her in her driveway with what she took to be a paintball gun. She was not hurt. Court documents later alleged that this had been an attempt on her life by Alex Cox, the brother of Lori Vallow.

Ten days later, on October 19, 2019, Chad Daybell called 911 and said his wife had died in her sleep. The county coroner accepted his account of a cough and earlier health problems, ruled the death natural and did not order an autopsy; East Idaho News has reported that the coroner later testified she would have ordered one had she known better. Tammy Daybell was buried in Springville, Utah, on October 22. NBC News reported that Chad Daybell married Lori Vallow about two weeks after the death.

The death was re-examined after Lori Vallow's children, Tylee Ryan and Joshua 'JJ' Vallow, were reported missing. The Fremont County Sheriff's Office described Tammy Daybell's death as suspicious, and her body was exhumed on December 11, 2019 for an autopsy in Utah. Alex Cox died the following day; he was never charged. The sheriff's office announced in February 2021 that the autopsy was complete. Its finding, that she died of asphyxiation caused by another person, was made public during Lori Vallow Daybell's trial in April 2023, according to the Deseret News.

A grand jury indicted Chad and Lori Daybell in May 2021. In relation to Tammy Daybell, Chad was charged with first-degree murder, both were charged with conspiracy to commit first-degree murder, and Chad was charged with insurance fraud over two life insurance policies. Lori Vallow Daybell was tried first. She was convicted in May 2023, and on July 31, 2023 she was sentenced to consecutive life terms without parole for the conspiracy against Tammy Daybell and for the murders of her two children, according to NBC News.

Chad Daybell's trial began in April 2024. On May 30, 2024, the jury found him guilty on every count, including the murder of Tammy Daybell, the murders of Tylee Ryan and JJ Vallow, and two counts of insurance fraud. On June 1, 2024, the jury decided he should be sentenced to death. His lawyer filed a notice of appeal to the Idaho Supreme Court within days, and East Idaho News reported in July 2025 that the case remained under appeal. Idaho's Supreme Court also reviews every death sentence automatically. Tammy Daybell's family has set up a foundation in her name to promote children's literacy.

Alex Murdaugh, her husband, was convicted of the murders in March 2023, but the South Carolina Supreme Court overturned the convictions on May 13, 2026, citing jury interference by the court clerk. He denies the killings; a retrial is set for April 2027.

narrative: Margaret "Maggie" Murdaugh, 52, and her son Paul Murdaugh, 22, were shot and killed on the evening of June 7, 2021, near the dog kennels on the family's hunting property in Islandton, in rural Colleton County, South Carolina. According to Wikipedia's account of the case, Maggie's husband, attorney Alex Murdaugh, called 911 at 10:06 p.m. and reported finding the two bodies. Trial evidence indicated that Maggie Murdaugh had been shot with a rifle and Paul Murdaugh with a shotgun.

Alex Murdaugh was indicted on two counts of murder in July 2022. His trial began on January 25, 2023, at the Colleton County Courthouse in Walterboro before Judge Clifton Newman. A central piece of evidence was a video recorded on Paul Murdaugh's phone at the kennels at 8:44 p.m., on which witnesses identified Alex Murdaugh's voice. He had told investigators he was not at the kennels that evening. Testifying in his own defense on February 23, 2023, he admitted he had lied about that and said he was the person heard on the recording, but denied killing his wife and son.

Prosecutors argued, NBC News reported, that Murdaugh committed the killings to win sympathy and draw attention away from financial wrongdoing that was about to be exposed. On March 2, 2023, after less than three hours of deliberation, the jury found him guilty of two counts of murder and two weapons counts. He was sentenced the next day to two consecutive life terms.

Murdaugh's lawyers later alleged that the Colleton County clerk of court, Becky Hill, had made improper comments to jurors during the trial. A motion for a new trial was denied on January 29, 2024. NBC News reported that Hill pleaded guilty in 2025 to criminal charges that included showing sealed exhibits to a photographer and lying about it in court, and that she received probation.

On May 13, 2026, the South Carolina Supreme Court unanimously overturned both murder convictions and ordered a new trial. According to NBC News, the court found that Hill had improperly influenced jurors, including by suggesting that they could not trust Murdaugh's testimony. The state attorney general said his office would seek to retry the case as soon as possible.

ABC News reported that Judge Debra McCaslin set the retrial for April 5, 2027, and, in an order dated September 8, 2026, moved it to Sumter County, about 80 miles from Walterboro, after concluding that Murdaugh could not receive a fair trial in Colleton County. Murdaugh continues to deny the killings and is presumed innocent of them pending retrial. He remains in prison on separate matters: he pleaded guilty to financial crimes involving theft from clients and is serving a 27-year state sentence and a concurrent 40-year federal sentence.

narrative: Harmony Montgomery was born in June 2014 and spent parts of her early childhood in foster care in Massachusetts. According to NHPR, she moved several times between her mother's home and foster parents before a Massachusetts judge awarded custody to her father, Adam Montgomery, in February 2019. He took her to Manchester, New Hampshire, where he lived with his wife, Kayla Montgomery, and their two young sons.

Her mother, Crystal Sorey, said she last saw Harmony in a video call around Easter 2019. After months of trying to find her, Sorey contacted Manchester police in November 2021, and police announced a public search on December 31, 2021. The attorney general's office said in January 2022 that the family had been evicted on November 27, 2019, and that investigators believed Harmony disappeared between November 28 and December 10, 2019.

Adam Montgomery was first charged with offences relating to Harmony's welfare, and in October 2022 he was arrested on a charge of second-degree murder, along with falsifying physical evidence, abuse of a corpse and witness tampering. Kayla Montgomery pleaded guilty to perjury, agreed to cooperate with prosecutors, and served an 18-month sentence.

At the trial in February 2024, Kayla Montgomery testified that on December 7, 2019, while the family was living in a car, her husband repeatedly struck Harmony during a drive, and that they later found the child had died. She described the body being hidden in several places over the following months. The defence acknowledged his guilt on the abuse of a corpse and falsifying evidence charges but denied that he killed his daughter, and suggested that Kayla Montgomery was the last person to see her alive. Adam Montgomery did not attend the trial.

On February 22, 2024, the jury found him guilty of second-degree murder, second-degree assault and witness tampering. On May 9, 2024, he was sentenced to a minimum of 56 years on all charges, to follow a sentence of at least 32 years for unrelated firearms convictions. In May 2026 a judge entered a default judgment of about $15.5 million against him in a wrongful death suit brought by Sorey.

On June 11, 2026, the New Hampshire Supreme Court reversed the murder conviction, ruling that trying the murder and assault charges together had jeopardised his right to a fair trial. NHPR reported that the convictions for second-degree assault, falsifying physical evidence, witness tampering and abuse of a corpse were upheld. The attorney general's office said it would retry him, and in September 2026 both sides agreed to an October 2027 start date. Adam Montgomery has maintained that he did not kill his daughter. Prosecutors said searches for Harmony's remains are continuing.

name: Doerman Children
summary: Brothers Clayton, 7, Hunter, 4, and Chase Doerman, 3, were shot dead at their home in Monroe Township, Clermont County, Ohio, on June 15, 2023. Their father, Chad Doerman, pleaded guilty on August 2, 2024 to three counts of aggravated murder and two counts of felonious assault and was sentenced to three consecutive life terms without parole.

narrative: Clayton Doerman, 7, Hunter Doerman, 4, and Chase Doerman, 3, were shot and killed at their family home in Monroe Township, Clermont County, Ohio, on the afternoon of June 15, 2023. Their father, Chad Doerman, then 32, was arrested at the scene. WCPO reported that the shootings happened at about 4:15 p.m., and CBS News reported that deputies found him sitting on a stoop at the house.

According to the account prosecutors gave in court, as reported by NBC News, Doerman had come home early from work and rested with the boys before taking a rifle from a gun safe and loading it. He shot Hunter first. Clayton ran out through the back of the house and was pursued and shot. The boys' 14-year-old half-sister, Doerman's stepdaughter, saw the shootings and tried to get away with Chase; prosecutors said Doerman threatened her with the gun. The children's mother, Laura Doerman, was shot through the thumb while struggling for the rifle, and Chase was then shot.

A grand jury indicted Doerman on nine counts of aggravated murder, eight counts of kidnapping and four counts of felonious assault, WCPO reported, and Clermont County Prosecutor Mark Tekulve initially said he would seek the death penalty. Doerman later entered a plea of not guilty by reason of insanity. In March 2024, Judge Richard Ferenc of the Clermont County Common Pleas Court suppressed Doerman's statements to investigators, finding that his Miranda rights had been violated, including after he said he would wait for a lawyer, according to WCPO.

On August 2, 2024, Doerman pleaded guilty to three counts of aggravated murder and two counts of felonious assault. Under the plea agreement prosecutors dropped the specifications that made him eligible for the death penalty. Judge Ferenc sentenced him the same day to three consecutive terms of life imprisonment without the possibility of parole; CBS News reported a further 16 years on the two felonious assault counts, which related to the boys' mother and the stepdaughter. Tekulve said the decision took into account the trauma of the surviving family members, and the judge noted that the victims' family approved of the agreement. Defense attorneys said Doerman was seriously mentally ill at the time.
Laura Doerman addressed the court at sentencing. According to NBC News, she said she would never forgive him but would not hate him.

In August 2026, news outlets reported that the Clermont County Sheriff's Office had released video of detectives' interviews with Doerman, in which he gave a religious explanation for the killings. The release did not change the legal outcome of the case. Doerman is serving his sentence in the Ohio prison system.

name: Ruby Franke Children
summary: Parenting YouTuber Ruby Franke and her business partner, counselor Jodi Hildebrandt, each pleaded guilty in December 2023 to four counts of aggravated child abuse of two of Franke's children. The case began on August 30, 2023, when Franke's 12-year-old son escaped from Hildebrandt's home in Ivins, Utah. Both women were sentenced on February 20, 2024 to four to 30 years in prison.

narrative: On August 30, 2023, a 12-year-old boy climbed out of a window of a house in Ivins, in Washington County, Utah, and went to a neighbor for help. According to the Washington County Attorney's Office, the neighbor saw duct tape on the boy's ankles and wrists, serious wounds and signs of malnourishment, and called the authorities. Officers who went to the house, which belonged to Jodi Hildebrandt, found the boy's 9-year-old sister hidden in a closet, the office said. Some news reports have given slightly different ages for the younger child.

The children's mother was Ruby Franke, who had run a YouTube channel about her family called 8 Passengers, launched in 2015. Hildebrandt was a mental health counselor and the founder of a counseling and life-coaching business, ConneXions, with which Franke had become involved. Both women were arrested that day. According to the Deseret News, each was originally charged with six counts of aggravated child abuse, a second-degree felony.

Franke pleaded guilty to four counts on December 18, 2023, and Hildebrandt pleaded guilty to four counts on December 27, 2023, according to the county attorney's office. The remaining two counts against each were removed under the plea agreements, and the Deseret News reported that Franke agreed to testify against Hildebrandt. In her plea, Franke admitted to withholding food and water, holding her son's head under water, keeping the two children isolated and making her daughter walk barefoot in the heat, the newspaper reported.

Prosecutors described the abuse as including deprivation of food and water, forced physical labor outdoors in extreme heat, beatings, binding and isolation. The county attorney's office said investigators concluded that the two women were motivated by extreme religious beliefs and held that the treatment would make the children repent.

On February 20, 2024, Judge John J. Walton of Utah's Fifth District Court sentenced each woman to four consecutive prison terms of one to 15 years. Utah law limits consecutive sentences of this kind to 30 years, so the effective sentence for each is four to 30 years, which the county attorney's office described as the maximum for the offense. At sentencing Franke told the court that the charges against her were just, the Deseret News reported. The length of time each woman actually serves will be decided by the Utah Board of Pardons and Parole.

KUTV reported in July 2024 that the board had postponed the women's first hearings from September 2024 to December 2026, ordered mental health reviews due by November 1, 2026, and required both to take part in a cognitive behavioral therapy program beforehand. Today.com reported in December 2025 that both were being held at the Utah State Correctional Facility in Salt Lake City. Wikipedia's article on Franke states that her husband, Kevin Franke, filed for divorce in November 2023 and that the divorce was finalized in March 2025.

narrative: On September 2, 2022, Eliza Fletcher, a 34-year-old junior kindergarten teacher and granddaughter of a Memphis billionaire, was abducted while jogging near the University of Memphis campus around 4:30 a.m. Surveillance footage showed a man approaching her and forcing her into a dark SUV.

summary: Orsolya Gaal, 51, was stabbed more than 50 times in her Forest Hills, Queens home on April 16, 2022, and her body was left in a hockey duffel bag near Forest Park. David Bonola, a handyman who had worked at the house, pleaded guilty to first-degree manslaughter on November 2, 2022 and was sentenced on November 16, 2022 to 25 years in prison.

narrative: Orsolya Gaal was a 51-year-old mother of two who lived in the Forest Hills neighborhood of Queens, New York, with her husband and sons. According to the Queens District Attorney's Office, she returned to her home at about 12:30 a.m. on April 16, 2022. Shortly afterwards David Bonola, a handyman who had done work at the house, entered the residence. Prosecutors said the two argued and that the argument turned violent in the basement, where Bonola cut her throat and stabbed her more than 50 times with a knife.

Security video recorded a man wheeling a duffel bag along the sidewalk at about 4:15 a.m., the District Attorney's Office said. At about 8 a.m. the bag, a hockey bag that NBC New York reported belonged to one of Gaal's sons, was found on Metropolitan Avenue near Union Turnpike, close to Forest Park, with her body inside. A trail of blood led investigators from the bag back to her home. Prosecutors said a knife was later recovered hidden in the house and that a jacket belonging to the defendant was found in Forest Park.

WABC-TV reported that Gaal's younger son was upstairs in the house during the attack and was unaware of it, and that her husband, who was away, received a threatening text message sent from her phone after the killing. Police announced Bonola's arrest on April 21, 2022. NYPD Chief of Detectives James Essig said at the time that she had been stabbed in excess of 55 times, and Lt. Timothy Thompson of Queens North Homicide said investigators believed Bonola and Gaal had been in an intimate relationship. Police described it as an on-and-off affair lasting about two years. According to WABC-TV, Bonola had approached officers voluntarily the night before his arrest and made incriminating statements.

Bonola, then 44 and a resident of South Richmond Hill, Queens, was initially charged with second-degree murder, criminal tampering and criminal possession of a weapon. On May 10, 2022 he was arraigned before Queens Supreme Court Justice Michael Aloise on a 13-count indictment that, according to the District Attorney's Office, included second-degree murder, first-degree burglary, concealment of a human corpse, tampering with physical evidence and fourth-degree criminal possession of a weapon. He faced a possible sentence of 25 years to life if convicted at trial.

The case did not go to trial. On November 2, 2022 Bonola pleaded guilty to manslaughter in the first degree. On November 16, 2022 Justice Aloise sentenced him to 25 years in prison, to be followed by five years of post-release supervision. In announcing the sentence, the District Attorney's Office noted that the killing had left two boys without their mother.

narrative: On the morning of December 14, 2012, a gunman entered Sandy Hook Elementary School in Newtown, Connecticut, and killed 20 first-grade students and six adult members of staff. Two other adults were wounded. According to the report of the State's Attorney for the Judicial District of Danbury, the shooter was Adam Lanza, 20, who had shot and killed his mother, Nancy Lanza, at their Newtown home before driving to the school.

The Connecticut Mirror, summarizing the report, said the first 911 call was received at 9:35:39 a.m. and that Lanza shot himself at 9:40:03 a.m., less than five minutes later. Inside the school he fired 154 rounds from a Bushmaster XM15-E2S semiautomatic rifle. He was also carrying two handguns. His mother had been shot with a .22-caliber Savage Mark II rifle.

State's Attorney Stephen J. Sedensky III released his report on November 25, 2013. It concluded that Lanza acted alone and that there would be no arrests or prosecutions, and the investigation was closed. The report found that the attack had been planned but said the evidence gave no clear indication of why he carried it out or why he chose the school. It described him as increasingly isolated in the period before the shooting and noted that he had been diagnosed with Asperger's disorder in 2005.
The killings led to years of litigation. According to Wikipedia's account, families of nine victims reached a $73 million settlement with the rifle's manufacturer, Remington, in February 2022.

Relatives of the victims also sued Infowars host Alex Jones, who had repeatedly and falsely said the shooting was staged. CBS News reported that a Connecticut jury awarded $965 million in 2022 for defamation and emotional distress and that a judge later added $474 million in punitive damages. In a separate Texas case, the parents of one child were awarded about $50 million. PBS NewsHour reported that Jones acknowledged at trial that the shooting was real.

Jones and his company filed for bankruptcy. The US Supreme Court declined to hear his appeal of the Connecticut judgment on October 14, 2025, CBS News reported. In August 2026, a Texas appeals court upheld $4.1 million in compensatory damages in the Texas case but cut the punitive award from about $45 million to $1.5 million, citing a state cap, according to PBS NewsHour. That ruling did not affect the Connecticut judgment, which PBS put at $1.25 billion, and Jones said he would continue to appeal.

name: Mary Lou Morris
summary: Mary Lou Henderson Morris, 48, was found dead in her burned car near her Baytown, Texas, home on October 12, 2000. Days later, an unrelated Houston-area woman, Mary McGinnis Morris, 39, was found shot in her car. Relatives have raised the possibility of mistaken identity, but the Harris County Sheriff's Office has said it found no link. No one has been charged in either killing.
lastSeen: October 12, 2000, leaving her home in Baytown, Texas, before 6 a.m.

narrative: Mary Lou Henderson Morris was a 48-year-old bank loan analyst who lived in Baytown, east of Houston. According to KPRC (Click2Houston), she worked at a bank off the Katy Freeway in west Houston, had earlier been one of the area's first female wrecker drivers, and was fond of horses and demolition derbies. The Houston Chronicle reported that she left home before 6 a.m. on October 12, 2000, and that her husband, who believed she was on her way to work, contacted authorities after learning she had not arrived.

That evening, Harris County sheriff's deputies were called to a burned-out car in a remote area about three miles from her home. KPRC gives the location as West Cedar Bayou Lynchburg Road, north of Baytown. The vehicle was her Chevrolet Lumina. According to the Chronicle, the remains inside were so badly burned that identification took several days and relied on dental fragments. FOX 26 Houston has reported that the cause of her death was unclear.

Within days, a second woman with the same name was killed in Harris County. Mary McGinnis Morris, 39, a nurse practitioner, was beaten and shot once in the head on October 15, 2000, according to the Chronicle, and her body was found the next morning in her company car on West Little York in northwest Houston. The newspaper reported that shortly before her death she had told a friend by phone that someone was making her uneasy, and that she then called 911. Investigators have not made the contents of that call public. The two women were not related.

The coincidence led to a widely discussed theory that a hired killer had attacked the wrong Mary Morris first. Relatives of Mary McGinnis Morris have said they believe the cases may be connected. Investigators have not endorsed that view: at a December 2004 news conference, a Harris County sheriff's sergeant said the office had found no link or connection between the two cases and did not think one existed. The same report noted that detectives had looked at people close to the second victim, that those individuals denied involvement, and that no one had been charged. A victims' reward fund doubled the reward in the second case to $10,000 at that time.

Both homicides remain unsolved. In June 2023, FOX 26 reported that the cases had inspired a feature film and that Mary Lou Morris's daughter was still seeking answers about what happened and why. KPRC revisited the killings in November 2024 in its cold-case series, again describing both as unsolved investigations of the Harris County Sheriff's Office. Anyone with information has been asked to contact the sheriff's homicide division or Crime Stoppers of Houston.

narrative: On March 26, 1998, thirteen-year-old Tristan Brübach was found murdered in a pedestrian underpass beneath a railway line in the Liederbach area of Frankfurt am Main, Germany. He had been brutally beaten and mutilated.

Tristan was last seen alive at about 3:20 p.m. sitting on a bench in a small park near Frankfurt-Höchst station; his body was found shortly after 5 p.m. in the nearby Liederbach tunnel. Despite people in the area, the perpetrator was never identified.

The investigation was one of the largest in Hessen police history. DNA evidence was collected from the scene, and thousands of individuals were tested over the years. Several suspects were investigated but cleared.
The case remains unsolved and is regularly featured in German true crime media. Frankfurt police continue to pursue leads and have periodically made public appeals for information.

narrative: On July 16, 2011, seventeen-year-old Tyler Hadley bludgeoned both of his parents, Blake and Mary Jo Hadley, to death with a claw hammer in their Port St. Lucie, Florida home. He then spent three hours cleaning up the scene and barricading the master bedroom where he placed their bodies.

That same evening, Tyler hosted a large house party at the home with dozens of teenage guests. He posted about the party on social media and appeared to be in a normal mood, drinking and socializing while his parents' bodies lay in the next room.
A friend whom Tyler had confessed to during the party called police the following morning. Officers found the parents' bodies under towels and debris in the master bedroom.

Tyler Hadley pleaded no contest to two counts of first-degree murder and in 2014 was sentenced to two life sentences without parole. After an appeal based on Miller v. Alabama he was resentenced in December 2018 to life with a review after 25 years.

name: Trudy Appleby
summary: Eleven-year-old Trudy Appleby vanished from Moline, Illinois on August 21, 1996; her body has never been found. In August 2025 a Henry County grand jury indicted Jamison Fisher, a long-named person of interest, on first-degree murder and concealment of a homicidal death. He is presumed innocent and the case is pending.
lastSeen: August 21, 1996, near her home in Moline, Illinois

sources.title: KWQC - Man indicted in Appleby disappearance
Wikipedia - Disappearance of Trudy Appleby

narrative: On August 21, 1996, eleven-year-old Trudy Appleby was last seen in the morning outside her home in Moline, Illinois, getting into a vehicle driven by a man. She had reportedly wanted to go swimming that day.
Trudy never came home. Despite extensive searches of the river and surrounding areas, no trace of her was found.

In 2017, Moline police publicly identified William "Ed" Smith, who had died in 2014, as a suspect. In 2020 they named two more persons of interest, David Whipple (who died in 2022) and Jamison Fisher. In August 2025 Fisher was indicted on first-degree murder charges; he has not been convicted.
Trudy's remains have never been found. Prosecutors allege she was strangled in Henry County; the murder case against Jamison Fisher is pending.

name: Bianca Devins
summary: Seventeen-year-old Bianca Devins of Utica, New York, was killed on July 14, 2019 by Brandon Clark, 21, who had driven her home from a concert in New York City. Clark posted photographs of her body online, and the images spread widely. He pleaded guilty to second-degree murder in February 2020 and was sentenced on March 16, 2021 to 25 years to life in prison.
lastSeen: July 13, 2019, leaving Utica, New York, for a concert in New York City

sources.title: BBC News - Bianca Devins: The teenager whose murder was exploited for clicks
CBS News (48 Hours) - Violent images sent to victim's family a form of "psychological terrorism," expert says
CNY Central - Bridgeport man sentenced to 25 years to life for murder of 17-year-old Bianca Devins
Wikipedia - Murder of Bianca Devins

narrative: Bianca Michelle Devins was 17 and lived in Utica, New York. According to BBC News, she had recently graduated from high school and planned to begin a psychology course at a community college. Her mother, Kim Devins, told CBS News that social media was a large part of her daughter's life and that Bianca had received mental health treatment from a young age.

Police told the BBC they believed Devins met Brandon Andrew Clark, then 21, through Instagram about two months before her death and that the two had since spent time together in person. On Saturday, July 13, 2019, Clark drove her from Utica to New York City to see the singer Nicole Dollanganger perform. Kim Devins told CBS News that her daughter texted after the show to say she was heading home.

According to police statements reported by the BBC, the two argued on the way back, possibly about Devins having kissed another person, and Clark attacked her with a knife. She died in the early hours of July 14. Clark posted photographs of her body on Discord and Instagram. The BBC reported that by about 7:20 a.m. Utica police had received numerous calls about the posts, some from other states, and that Clark also called 911 himself. Officers found him at the end of a dead-end road near a wooded area, where he stabbed himself in the neck. He was arrested, treated in hospital and charged with murder the following day.

The photographs circulated across several platforms for days, and CBS News reported that strangers sent them directly to members of the Devins family. Users told the BBC that their early reports to Instagram were rejected, and the company's handling of the images drew criticism.

According to Wikipedia's summary of court coverage, Clark pleaded not guilty on July 29, 2019, then changed his plea to guilty of second-degree murder on February 10, 2020. Sentencing was delayed by the COVID-19 pandemic, and a later request to withdraw the plea was denied. On March 16, 2021, he was sentenced to 25 years to life in prison; CNY Central reported that Devins's mother, sister and grandfather addressed the court and that Clark apologized to the family.

The case led to legislation. According to Wikipedia, a New York state measure known as Bianca's Law, creating penalties for spreading images of a crime victim with intent to glorify or harass, was signed by Governor Kathy Hochul in late December 2022. The same source says the family sued the Oneida County District Attorney's Office in July 2021 over the release of case material to documentary producers, and that the suit was dismissed in 2022.

name: Rachel & Lillian Entwistle
summary: Rachel Entwistle, 27, and her nine-month-old daughter Lillian Rose were shot dead in their rented home in Hopkinton, Massachusetts, on January 20, 2006; police found them two days later. Rachel's British husband, Neil Entwistle, flew to England and was arrested in London on February 9, 2006. A Massachusetts jury convicted him of two counts of first-degree murder on June 25, 2008.
lastSeen: January 20, 2006, at their rented home in Hopkinton, Massachusetts; bodies found there January 22, 2006

sources.title: BBC News - Briton guilty of family murders
BBC News - Accused 'had plan to sell story'
BBC News - US police 'failed to spot bodies'
BBC News - Fairness of US murder trial questioned
Wikipedia - Neil Entwistle

narrative: Rachel Entwistle, 27, and her daughter Lillian Rose, aged nine months, had moved with Rachel's husband, Neil Entwistle, into a rented house in Hopkinton, Massachusetts, only days before they died. BBC News reported that the couple, who had been living with Rachel's mother and stepfather in Carver, presented themselves as a happy family, and that Neil Entwistle, a British IT worker from Worksop, Nottinghamshire, was looking for work.

According to trial testimony reported by the BBC, Rachel's mother and a friend contacted police when they could not reach the family. An officer looked into the master bedroom on the evening of January 21, 2006, and saw only a pile of bedding. When police returned the next evening, they found mother and daughter together under the covers. The jury heard that Rachel had been shot in the forehead at close range and that the bullet that killed Lillian passed through the baby's body and lodged in her mother's chest.

By then Neil Entwistle had left the country. The BBC reported that he drove to Boston's Logan Airport, bought a one-way ticket and flew to London early the next morning without luggage, going to his parents' home in Worksop. He spoke to Massachusetts police by telephone from there and was initially described as a person of interest. He was arrested at Royal Oak Underground station in west London on February 9, 2006, and returned to the United States; Wikipedia gives the date of his return as February 15, 2006.

At the trial, held in June 2008 at Middlesex County Superior Court in Woburn, prosecutors said the weapon was a .22 calibre Colt revolver belonging to Rachel's stepfather, Joseph Matterazzo, kept at the house in Carver. They told the jury that Entwistle was heavily in debt, had been using websites to seek sexual partners and had searched online for methods of killing and suicide. Entwistle had told police he came home to find his wife and daughter dead and covered them. His defence argued at trial that Rachel had shot the baby and then herself, and that he had concealed this.

The jury rejected that account. After about 13 hours of deliberation, it found Entwistle guilty on June 25, 2008, of two counts of first-degree murder and of illegal possession of a firearm and ammunition, the BBC reported. First-degree murder carries a mandatory sentence of life imprisonment without the possibility of parole in Massachusetts, and Wikipedia records that this sentence was imposed the following day.

According to Wikipedia, the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court rejected his appeal in August 2012 and the US Supreme Court declined to hear the case in January 2013. Entwistle's parents have continued to say they believe he is innocent; the convictions stand.

name: Savannah Spurlock
summary: Savannah Spurlock, a Madison County, Kentucky, mother of four, disappeared after leaving a Lexington bar with three men on the night of January 4, 2019. Her remains were found on July 10, 2019, buried at a Garrard County property belonging to the family of David Sparks. Sparks pleaded guilty to murder in December 2020 and was sentenced to 50 years in prison.
lastSeen: January 4-5, 2019, after leaving a bar in Lexington, Kentucky; according to Kentucky State Police she was at a residence in Garrard County in the morning hours of January 5

narrative: Savannah Spurlock, a mother of four from Madison County, Kentucky, went out in Lexington on the night of January 4, 2019. According to Kentucky State Police, she left a Lexington bar with three people and was at a residence in Garrard County during the morning hours of January 5. She did not return home, and a search that lasted more than six months followed. ABC News and other outlets reported that her youngest children were infant twins.

According to a Kentucky State Police news release, human remains were located shortly before 5 p.m. on July 10, 2019, on Fall Lick Road in Garrard County. An autopsy on July 11 identified them as Spurlock. LEX 18 reported that the discovery followed a report of a foul odour outside the home of David Sparks' parents, and that the grave was in the backyard of that property.

State police arrested David Sparks, then 23, of Lancaster, and charged him with tampering with physical evidence and abuse of a corpse. Sparks was one of the men who had left the bar with Spurlock. ABC News reported that a grand jury indicted him on a murder charge in late August 2019, along with the two earlier charges, and that investigators had described the body as wrapped in plastic bags with the feet bound and buried in a shallow grave. WKYT reported that Sparks was the only person charged in the case.

Sparks pleaded guilty in Garrard County Circuit Court in early December 2020 to murder, tampering with physical evidence and abuse of a corpse. According to LEX 18, he admitted acting alone. The Commonwealth's Attorney told reporters that the prosecution wanted him to admit in open court that he had intentionally caused her death. Authorities did not publicly disclose how she died.

On December 17, 2020, in a hearing held by video link because of the COVID-19 pandemic, Sparks was sentenced to 50 years in prison for murder, with shorter terms on the other two counts running concurrently. LEX 18 reported that he will be eligible for parole after serving 20 years. Members of Spurlock's family told reporters after the hearing that much about what happened that night remains unknown to them.

name: Evelyn Boswell
summary: Fifteen-month-old Evelyn Mae Boswell of Sullivan County, Tennessee, was reported missing on February 18, 2020, about two months after she was last seen. Her remains were found on a relative's property in Blountville on March 6, 2020. Her mother, Megan Boswell, was convicted of first-degree murder and 18 other counts on February 13, 2025, and is serving life plus 33 years.
lastSeen: December 2019, Sullivan County, Tennessee

narrative: Evelyn Mae Boswell was a 15-month-old girl from Sullivan County in northeast Tennessee. According to the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation (TBI), she was reported missing on February 18, 2020, and an AMBER Alert was issued the following evening. A timeline published by WVLT says the investigation began after Evelyn's grandfather, Tommy Boswell Sr., contacted the Department of Children's Services. The TBI said the child had reportedly last been seen on December 26, 2019, while noting that investigators had been given conflicting dates.

Evelyn's mother, Megan Boswell, gave differing accounts of where her daughter was. NewsChannel 9 reported that court records showed she had claimed Evelyn was with the child's father, who was on active military duty, and that she told reporters she had not gone to police because she feared the person who had Evelyn would disappear. WVLT reported that she also pointed investigators to a campground in Virginia. On February 25, 2020, she was arrested and charged with false reporting.

On March 6, 2020, TBI agents and Sullivan County detectives searched a property on Muddy Creek Road in Blountville that belonged to a member of Megan Boswell's family and found human remains. The TBI later confirmed they were Evelyn's. At a hearing on September 23, 2022, a TBI agent testified that the remains were inside a trash bag in a trash can in a playhouse on the property, WCYB reported. At the same hearing, forensic pathologist Dr. Darinka Mileusnic-Polchan testified that the cause of death was asphyxia.

WVLT reported that Megan Boswell was charged with felony murder on August 19, 2020. Her trial was delayed several times and began in February 2025. After eight days, on February 13, 2025, the jury found her guilty on all 19 counts: first-degree murder, two counts of felony murder, aggravated child abuse, aggravated child neglect, tampering with evidence, 11 counts of false reporting, abuse of a corpse, and failure to report a death under suspicious circumstances, according to WCYB.

The jury set her punishment for the murder convictions at life in prison, which WCYB reported would make her eligible for parole after 51 years. At a sentencing hearing for the remaining counts in early September 2025, Judge Jim Goodwin added 33 years, for a total sentence of life plus 33 years. WCYB reported that a motion for a new trial had been filed and that her attorney planned an appeal; no outcome of that appeal was found in the sources reviewed.
Gray Television stations reported that the case led Tennessee to pass a law in 2021 requiring parents to report a missing child within 24 hours of determining that the child is missing.
